## Emergency call triage for plumbers: handling out-of-hours calls and messages
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/emergency-call-out-triage-plumbers/

Emergency call triage for plumbers is a short, fixed set of questions asked of every out-of-hours caller to decide whether the job needs someone tonight, first thing tomorrow, or a normal booking. Safety comes first: a gas smell goes to the gas emergency line (0800 111 999 in Great Britain, 911 in the US), not to you. Every customer hears the call-out fee and agrees to it before anyone is sent.

Emergency call triage for plumbers decides what happens to the 11 pm call about water through the ceiling, and to the WhatsApp message about a dripping tap sent at the same time. Without a set of questions, the on-call engineer gets both, drives out for one that could have waited, and argues about the call-out fee on the doorstep. This page gives you the questions, a set of example urgency categories, auto-replies, a routing plan and fee wording you can adapt. It's written for UK and US plumbers and heating engineers; the safety lines differ by country, so both are given.

### Safety calls are not your calls
Some calls shouldn't be booked at all: the caller needs the emergency service first. Put these lines at the top of your script and your auto-replies, word for word.
- Great Britain: if the customer smells gas or thinks there's carbon monoxide, tell them to call the National Gas Emergency Service on 0800 111 999, from outside if they can.
- Northern Ireland: the Gas Emergency Service is 0800 002 001, according to nidirect.
- US: federal pipeline safety guidance (PHMSA) says to leave, move to a safe place and call 911, then the gas company.
- Anyone feeling unwell, a fire, or water pouring onto live electrics: 999 in the UK, 911 in the US.
- Once the emergency service has made it safe, you can book the repair as normal.

### The triage questions
Ask them in this order, by phone or by text. The first two decide most calls; the rest tell the engineer what to bring and what it will cost.
1. Can you smell gas, or has a carbon monoxide alarm gone off? (If yes: the safety lines above, then stop.)
2. Is water coming through a ceiling, near electrics, or flooding a room?
3. Can you turn the water off at the stopcock (US: the main shut-off valve)? Has it stopped?
4. Do you have any heating or hot water? Is anyone at home elderly, very young or unwell?
5. Is there only one toilet in the home, and is it blocked or overflowing?
6. What's the full address and postcode (US: ZIP code), and is there parking or access we should know about?
7. Can you send a photo or a short video of the problem?
8. Are you the owner, a tenant or a letting agent? (Tenants may need the landlord or agent to approve the work.)
9. Do you agree to the call-out fee of [amount], which covers [the first hour / attendance only]?

### Example urgency categories
These are example categories to adapt, not rules. You decide what counts as an emergency for your business, and the on-call engineer can always overrule the list. Jobs that can wait get a normal quote; in the UK, our [WhatsApp quote follow-up](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/whatsapp-quote-follow-up-tradespeople/) covers what happens next.
| Category (example) | Typical situations | What happens |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Emergency service first | Gas smell, carbon monoxide alarm, fire, water on live electrics | Safety line sent at once; no booking until it's made safe |
| Tonight | Uncontrollable leak, water through a ceiling, stopcock won't turn off, only toilet overflowing | On-call engineer phoned now; fee confirmed before dispatch |
| First thing tomorrow | No heating or hot water with a vulnerable person at home, leak now contained | Booked for the first slot; advice text sent tonight |
| Normal booking | Dripping tap, slow drain, no hot water with an immersion or kettle available | Booking link sent; no call to the engineer |

### Auto-replies for calls and messages you can't answer
Two messages (you approve the wording before anything goes live):
```
1. Out-of-hours auto-reply (text, WhatsApp or email):
Thanks for contacting [Business]. If you smell gas, leave the property and call [0800 111 999 / 911] now. For a water emergency, turn off your stopcock if you can, then reply with: your address, what's happening, and a photo. Our on-call engineer will reply within [30 minutes]. Call-outs after [6 pm] cost [amount], which covers [the first hour].

2. Reply when it can wait until morning:
Thanks, [name]. From what you've described, this can safely wait until tomorrow. We've pencilled you in for [time]. If anything changes (water you can't stop, or a gas smell), reply URGENT or call [on-call number] and we'll look again.
```

### On-call routing
- One rota decides who's on call each night, and the out-of-hours number forwards to that person automatically.
- Messages and missed calls arrive in one list with the triage answers already filled in, so the engineer reads before calling back. An [AI receptionist](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/ai-receptionist-small-business-pros-and-cons/) can ask the same questions on the phone, but gas and safety calls should still reach a person.
- "Tonight" jobs ring or text the on-call engineer at once; if they don't reply within [15 minutes], the backup gets the alert.
- "Normal booking" messages never wake anyone. They wait for the office, with a booking link already sent.
- Every job keeps a note of the fee the customer agreed to, and when.

### Call-out fee wording
Disputes start when the fee is mentioned for the first time at the door. Say it before dispatch, in writing, and ask for a clear yes. If you take a deposit, the same rules apply as for [deposits on quotes](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/how-to-ask-for-a-deposit-on-a-quote/).
Fee confirmation, sent before anyone is dispatched:
```
Hi [name], our engineer [first name] can be with you by about [time]. Our out-of-hours call-out fee is [amount]. It covers [attendance and the first hour of labour]; parts and any further time are extra, and [first name] will tell you the price before doing more. Please reply YES to confirm and we'll send them now.
```

### How Mike Automations builds it
A [free 15-minute call](https://mikeautomations.github.io/call/) about how out-of-hours calls reach you now and what goes wrong. Within 48 hours you get a written plan with a fixed price. It's built on what you already use (your phone line, WhatsApp Business, calendar and job software, where they allow a connection) and goes live in 2-3 days. It costs [$2,000 one-off](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/pricing/), and you pay once it's running and you're happy with it. The triage, the fee and every reply that isn't a fixed template stay with you: a person approves anything AI drafts. If you also miss daytime calls, the [missed call text back](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/missed-call-text-back-contractors/) workflow covers those. Whether the free WhatsApp Business app is enough for out-of-hours messages is covered in [WhatsApp Business app vs API](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/whatsapp-business-app-vs-api/).

### Should AI decide which calls are emergencies?
No. The questions and categories are fixed and written by you. Automation can ask them, sort the answers and alert the right person, but the on-call engineer makes the call, and a person approves any reply that isn't a fixed template.

### What if the customer smells gas but wants us to come anyway?
Send the gas emergency line first and don't book until it has been made safe. In Great Britain that's 0800 111 999, in Northern Ireland 0800 002 001, and in the US the advice is to leave and call 911, then the gas company.

### Can this work with my existing phone number?
Usually. On the call we check what your phone provider and messaging apps allow. If something would need a new number or a paid add-on, you'll see it in the written plan before anything is bought.

### Will tenants get stuck waiting for the landlord?
The triage asks whether the caller is the owner, a tenant or an agent. For tenants, the alert can go to the agent or landlord at the same time, so approval and the engineer's call happen together.

## A job completion sign-off form for contractors, with photos
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/job-sign-off-and-completion-photos/

A job completion sign-off form for contractors records that the work is finished and that the customer has seen it: dated photos of the finished job, any snags still open, and the customer's name and signature. Once it's signed, the final invoice goes out the same day with the photos attached, which removes most of the reasons a customer has to delay paying.

A job completion sign-off form for contractors closes the gap between "we're done" and "we've been paid". Without it, the crew packs up, the office finds out a few days later, the invoice goes out late, and the customer queries something nobody photographed. A sign-off takes five minutes on site and is the same steps on every job, so it can run as a workflow on the crew's phones while you keep the judgement calls. This page is for trades and home service businesses in the UK and the US; the words differ (snag list or punch list) but the process is the same.

### Why jobs stall at the finish line
- The crew finishes but nobody tells the office, so the final invoice waits for days
- There are no photos of the finished work, so a later complaint is your word against theirs
- Small snags are agreed verbally and then forgotten, and they turn into a reason not to pay
- The customer wasn't home at the end, so nobody actually confirmed the job was done
- Extra work agreed during the job never makes it onto the final bill

### A completion checklist for the crew
The crew lead works through this on their phone before leaving site. Keep it short: every extra field is one more reason it gets skipped.
| Item | What to capture | Why it matters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Job details | Job number or address, date, crew lead's name | Ties the sign-off to the right job and invoice |
| Before photos | Taken at the start of the job, already saved against the job | Shows the condition you started from |
| Completion photos | Every area worked on, wide shot and close-ups, plus any meter readings, labels or certificates on site | Shows what was finished and when |
| Snag list (punch list in the US) | Anything still open, who will fix it and by when | Agrees the remaining work in writing instead of verbally |
| Changes | Any extra work agreed on the job, with its approved price | Makes sure it reaches the final invoice |
| Site left clean | A tick and a photo of the area | Answers the most common small complaint |
| Customer sign-off | Name, signature, date, and a box for their own comments | Confirms they've seen the work and lets them raise anything now |

### What the sign-off workflow does
1. The crew lead opens a link on their phone, ticks through the checklist and takes the completion photos. The photos are saved to the job folder with the date. On longer jobs they sit alongside the [site diary photos from each day](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/construction-daily-site-reports/).
2. The customer signs on the crew lead's phone. If they aren't home, the workflow sends them a link with the photos so they can review and sign remotely.
3. If the customer adds a comment or a snag, the office is told straight away and the snag goes on a list with a date to come back.
4. Once the job is signed off, the office gets a draft final invoice: the original price, any approved changes and the photos attached. A person checks it and sends it. More on that step in [the job-done-to-invoice workflow](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/how-to-automate-invoicing-small-business/).
5. If a remote sign-off isn't back within the time you set, for example two working days, the customer gets one reminder and the office is told.
6. The day after sign-off, every customer gets a short message asking how it went and, if they're happy, for a review.
7. Unpaid invoices then move into your normal payment reminders. A courier attaches [proof of delivery to the invoice](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/courier-proof-of-delivery-and-failed-delivery-messages/) in the same way.

### A sign-off message you can copy
Text or email when the customer wasn't on site at the end:
```
Hi [customer name], this is [your name] from [company]. We finished the work at [address] today. Here are the photos of the finished job: [link]

Please take a look and confirm you're happy here: [sign-off link]. If anything isn't right, add it in the comments box and we'll arrange a time to sort it.

Once it's signed off we'll send the final invoice for [amount], which includes [change order number or "no extra work"].

Thanks for having us,
[your name]
```

### Linking sign-off to the final invoice
The point of the sign-off is a clean final invoice, so the two should be joined. The invoice draft is built from the job's quote, plus any extra work that was approved in writing during the job (see [change order approvals](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/change-order-approval-workflow/)), and the sign-off photos go with it (installers send a fuller version as a [solar handover pack](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/solar-installer-paperwork-and-handover/)). A customer who has signed and has the photos in front of them has far fewer questions to raise. If they still don't pay, [automated invoice payment reminders](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/invoice-payment-reminders/) take over on the schedule you set. Open snags are your call: some businesses hold back a small amount until they're fixed, others invoice in full and fix them under the job. Decide your rule once and the workflow follows it.

### The review request: ask everyone
Sending a review request the day after sign-off is a good habit, but ask every customer, not just the ones who seemed pleased. Google's Maps content policy says businesses must not "selectively solicit positive reviews from customers", must not discourage negative reviews, and must not offer incentives such as discounts for reviews. So the message goes to everyone, says the same thing, and offers nothing in return. A customer who replies with a problem gets a call from you, and can still leave a review if they want to. Our guide on [how to ask for Google reviews](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/ask-for-google-reviews-automatically/) has the wording.

### What stays with you
You decide what the checklist includes, what counts as finished, and what happens when a customer won't sign or raises a snag. A person checks every final invoice before it goes out. Photos of a customer's home are personal information, so keep them in your own job records, only for as long as you need them, and say so in your privacy notice. If AI writes up the snag list or drafts a message, a person always approves it first.

### How Mike Automations would build it
A [free 15-minute call](https://mikeautomations.github.io/call/) about how jobs finish and get invoiced in your business today. Within 48 hours you get a written plan with a fixed price and a clear definition of "working". It's built on the tools you already use (phones, your email, a shared drive, and your job management or accounting software where it allows a connection), so your crew doesn't learn a new system. Live in 2-3 days. [Workflow automation is a fixed $2,000](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/pricing/), and you pay once it's running and you're happy with it.

### Does a sign-off stop customers disputing the work later?
It doesn't remove their rights. Customers still have their legal rights if the work turns out to be faulty. What it does is record what was finished, what was still open and when, which makes most disagreements quick to settle.

### What if the customer refuses to sign?
The workflow records that, with their reason, and tells the office. You decide the next step, usually a call. The photos still show the work as it was left.

### Is a signature on a phone screen good enough?
For a sign-off it's a record of what the customer confirmed. In the UK, section 7 of the Electronic Communications Act 2000 says an electronic signature is admissible in evidence. In the US, the federal ESIGN Act says a signature can't be denied legal effect just because it's electronic. If your contract says something specific about completion, follow your contract.

## A deposit protection 30-day reminder for letting agents
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/tenancy-deposit-protection-30-day-reminder/

In England and Wales, a landlord or letting agent who takes a tenancy deposit must protect it in a government-approved scheme and give the tenant the prescribed information within 30 days of receiving it. A deposit protection 30-day reminder starts a clock the day the money arrives and chases both tasks until a person has confirmed each one is done. Missing either deadline can lead to a court order to pay the tenant up to three times the deposit.

A deposit protection 30-day reminder is one of the simplest things a letting agent can automate and one of the most expensive to get wrong. Two things must happen within 30 days of the deposit arriving: the deposit goes into an approved scheme, and the tenant gets the prescribed information. Both are routine, which is exactly why they slip during a busy move-in week. This page covers private lettings in England and Wales only. Scotland and Northern Ireland have their own deposit schemes and rules.

### The two 30-day rules
Gov.uk says a landlord or letting agent must put the tenant's deposit in a scheme "within 30 days of getting it". In England and Wales there are three approved schemes: Deposit Protection Service, MyDeposits and Tenancy Deposit Scheme. Each offers a custodial option (the scheme holds the money) or an insured option (you hold it and pay for insurance). In England the duty sits in section 213 of the Housing Act 2004. As amended by the Renters' Rights Act 2025 from 1 May 2026, it applies to deposits taken under assured tenancies, which replaced assured shorthold tenancies for most private lets that day. The same section requires the prescribed information to be given to the tenant, and to anyone who paid the deposit for them, within the same 30 days. Gov.uk lists what the tenant must be told:
- The address of the rented property and the amount of the deposit
- How the deposit is protected, and the name and contact details of the scheme and its dispute service
- Your name and contact details as landlord or agent, and those of any third party who paid the deposit
- The reasons you might keep some or all of the deposit, and how the tenant can ask for it back
- What to do if they can't reach you at the end of the tenancy, and what happens if you disagree about the deposit

### Wales: same deadline, different law
In Wales, private lets have been occupation contracts under the Renting Homes (Wales) Act 2016 since 1 December 2022. Section 45 of that Act says that within 30 days of the deposit being paid, the landlord must meet the scheme's initial requirements and give the contract-holder, and anyone who paid on their behalf, the required information. The approved schemes are the same three. The Welsh rules on what happens after a breach are different from England's, so check the Welsh Government's guidance for properties in Wales.

### What happens if you miss the 30 days (England)
These are the consequences in the Housing Act 2004 as it stood on legislation.gov.uk in November 2026. They apply where the deposit wasn't protected in time or the prescribed information wasn't given in time. Protecting late does not remove the risk of a penalty claim.
- The tenant, or a former tenant, can apply to the county court (section 214). Gov.uk says this is done on form N208.
- If the court agrees, it must order the deposit to be repaid or paid into a custodial scheme within 14 days, and it must order the landlord to pay the tenant at least the amount of the deposit and up to three times it.
- Under section 215, as replaced from 1 May 2026, the court can only make a possession order on an assured tenancy if the deposit is in a scheme and the prescribed information has been given. There are exceptions, for example certain antisocial behaviour grounds, or once the deposit has been returned or a claim about it has been settled.
- In Wales, section 46 of the 2016 Act stops a landlord giving certain notices to end the contract while the deposit rules haven't been met.

### A 30-day reminder timeline
Day 1 is the day the deposit is received, because the Housing Act counts the 30 days from that date. The lead times below are suggestions: the aim is to finish in the first week and keep the rest as a safety margin.
| Day | What happens | Who |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Day 1 | Deposit received. The workflow logs the amount, the date, who paid it and the property, and starts the 30-day clock | Workflow, from your accounts or a team member's note |
| Day 2 | Reminder to register the deposit with your scheme, with the tenancy details pre-filled in the message | Named member of staff |
| Day 3 | Reminder to send the prescribed information, with the scheme's own form and your tenancy details attached | Named member of staff |
| Day 5 | Check that the scheme certificate is filed and the tenant (and any third-party payer) has been sent the information. If not, a second reminder | Workflow, then staff |
| Day 14 | Anything still missing goes to the branch or lettings manager | Workflow, then manager |
| Day 21 | Daily reminders to the manager until both items are confirmed | Workflow, then manager |
| Day 30 | Deadline. If either item is still open, the director is told the same morning | Workflow, then director |

### The move-in checklist
The workflow keeps this checklist for every new tenancy and only closes it when a person has ticked each item and attached the evidence. Later dates in the tenancy, such as rent reviews, are covered in [tenancy renewal reminders](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/tenancy-renewal-reminders-letting-agents/).
1. Deposit amount checked against the tenancy agreement. In England, the Tenant Fees Act 2019 caps it at five weeks' rent, or six weeks' if the annual rent is £50,000 or more.
2. Deposit registered with the scheme, and the scheme's certificate or reference saved to the tenancy file.
3. Prescribed information completed on the scheme's form and checked by a second person.
4. Prescribed information sent to every tenant, and to anyone who paid the deposit for them, with the date and method recorded.
5. Proof of sending saved: an email receipt, a signed copy, or a note of how it was handed over.
6. Clock closed, with the dates both 30-day items were completed recorded against the tenancy.

### A message you can copy
Email to the tenant with the prescribed information:
```
Subject: Your deposit for [property address] is protected

Hi [tenant name],

We received your deposit of £[amount] on [date received]. It is now protected with [scheme name], reference [scheme reference].

Attached is the prescribed information about your deposit: how it is protected, how to contact the scheme and its dispute service, and how to get your deposit back at the end of your tenancy. Please read it and keep it somewhere safe.

If someone else paid the deposit for you, we've sent them a copy too.

Please reply to confirm you've received this email and the attachment.

Thanks,
[your name]
[agency name]
```

### What stays with you
The legal duties stay with the landlord and with you as their agent, and the workflow doesn't change that. It doesn't fill in or send the prescribed information on its own: a person checks every form and sends it. You choose the lead times and who is told when. If a tenancy has an unusual feature, such as a deposit paid in instalments or by a council scheme, a person decides how it is handled. This page is a summary of the rules as they stood in November 2026, not legal advice; read the gov.uk guidance on [deposit protection for landlords](https://www.gov.uk/deposit-protection-schemes-and-landlords) and ask an adviser if you're unsure.

### When does the 30-day clock start?
In England, section 213 of the Housing Act 2004 counts the 30 days from the day the landlord or agent receives the deposit, not the day the tenancy starts. In Wales it runs from the day the deposit is paid. The workflow starts the clock from the date the money is received.

### Do we need to protect a holding deposit?
Gov.uk says a holding deposit paid before the agreement is signed doesn't need protecting. Once the person becomes a tenant it counts as a deposit and must be protected, so the clock starts then.

## Tenancy renewal reminders for letting agents, after the 2026 changes
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/tenancy-renewal-reminders-letting-agents/

Tenancy renewal reminders for letting agents work differently in England now: since 1 May 2026 most private tenancies are assured periodic tenancies with no end date, so there is no fixed term to renew. What still needs a reminder is the yearly rent review, done on Form 4A with at least 2 months' notice, plus lease end dates for US rentals. A workflow can track each date, ask the landlord for a decision and prepare the notice, while a person approves it.

Tenancy renewal reminders used to mean one thing for a letting agent: a fixed term is ending, so ask the landlord and the tenant what happens next. In England that job has changed. Most private tenancies no longer end on a date, so the dates that matter are rent reviews, notices from tenants and the yearly checks you run alongside them, like [gas safety and EICR renewals](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/letting-agent-compliance-certificate-reminders/). In the US, leases still have end dates, and renewal reminders work much as they always have. This page covers both, with a date table, a workflow and two templates.

### What changed in England on 1 May 2026
Gov.uk's overview of the Renters' Rights Act for landlords (published 1 May 2026) says the changes came into effect on 1 May 2026, that all existing assured shorthold tenancies change to assured periodic tenancies, and that you cannot have an end date on the tenancy agreement. The commencement regulations (S.I. 2026/421 on legislation.gov.uk) apply this to assured tenancies that are not social housing. Rent can go up no more than once a year: the landlord fills out Form 4A and gives it to the tenant with at least 2 months' notice, and the tenant can ask the tribunal to decide the rent if they think it is above the open market rent. The government's implementation roadmap (November 2025) says tenants can end their tenancy by giving two months' notice. If a rent went up under the old rules shortly before 1 May 2026, read the transitional provisions in S.I. 2026/421 before you serve a new notice. This applies to England only: Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland have their own tenancy laws, so check those separately.

### The dates that still need a reminder
The legal minimums come from the sources above. You can time a [routine inspection](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/property-inspection-scheduling/) near each rent review. The lead times in the last column are suggestions you can change, not rules.
| Date | Applies to | Who acts | When to start (suggested) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Yearly rent review | Assured periodic tenancies in England | Landlord decides, your team prepares Form 4A | 4 months before the earliest date a new rent could start |
| Form 4A served | Same | Your team, once the landlord has approved the figure | At least 2 months before the new rent starts (gov.uk); aim for 10 weeks to allow for delivery |
| Tenant gives notice | Assured periodic tenancies in England | Your team | Same day: confirm the end date, tell the landlord, book the check-out |
| Lease end date | US leases with a fixed term | Property manager and owner | 90, 60 and 30 days before, or earlier if the lease or state law needs longer notice |
| Rent increase notice | US month-to-month tenancies (California as an example) | Property manager | At least 30 days for a rise of 10% or less, 90 days above 10% (California Attorney General) |

### Where renewal and rent review dates slip
- The rent review date lives in one person's calendar, so it's missed when they're on leave
- The landlord is asked about a new rent too late, and the 2 months' notice pushes the increase back
- Nobody can quickly see when each tenancy's rent last changed, so the once-a-year rule is checked by hand
- A tenant's notice arrives by email and nobody starts the check-out, deposit and re-let steps until days later
- US lease renewal offers go out late, so the tenant has already decided to leave

### What an automated reminder workflow does
1. Keeps one list of every tenancy with its start date, current rent, the date the rent last changed and the earliest date a new rent can start, in the spreadsheet or software you already use.
2. Four months before a review is possible, emails the landlord the current rent and asks: keep it the same, propose a new figure, or talk first.
3. Chases the landlord twice if there's no answer, then tells a named person on your team.
4. Once the landlord confirms a figure, drafts Form 4A with the tenancy details filled in and puts it in front of a person to check and serve.
5. Logs the date served and how it was sent, and works out the earliest date the new rent can start.
6. When a tenant's notice arrives, records the end date, alerts the landlord and starts your check-out and re-let tasks.
7. For US leases, sends the owner a renewal decision request at 90 days and the tenant a renewal offer once the owner agrees.

### Rent review email to a landlord (England)
Email asking a landlord for a rent review decision:
```
Subject: Rent review for [property address]: your decision by [date]

Hi [landlord name],

The rent at [property address] is [current rent] a month and last changed on [date of last change]. The earliest date a new rent could start is [earliest date].

Under the rules in England, a new rent needs a Form 4A notice with at least 2 months' notice to the tenant, and rent can only go up once a year. The tenant can ask the tribunal to decide the rent if they think it's above the market rate.

Please reply with one of these:
1. Keep the rent as it is
2. Propose a new rent of [amount]
3. I'd like to talk it through first

If we hear back by [date], the notice can go out in time for [earliest date].

Thanks,
[your name]
[agency name]
```

### Lease renewals in the US
In the US, notice periods for renewals, non-renewals and rent increases are set by state law, sometimes by city law, and by the lease itself, so the workflow follows the rules you give it for each property. California is one example: the state Attorney General says a rent increase of 10% or less needs 30 days' notice and a larger one needs 90 days, and that a phone call, text or email announcing the increase is not enough. Check the rules for every state and city you manage in before you set your reminder dates. New US tenancies start earlier, with [rental application document collection](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/rental-application-document-collection/): ID, pay stubs and references gathered in one place.
Lease renewal offer to a US tenant:
```
Subject: Your lease at [property address] ends on [lease end date]

Hi [tenant name],

Your lease at [property address] ends on [lease end date]. The owner would like to offer you a renewal:

New term: [term]
Rent: [amount] a month, starting [date]

Please reply by [reply-by date] to say whether you'd like to renew, or if you have questions. If we don't hear from you, we'll follow up on [follow-up date].

Thanks,
[your name]
[company name]
```

### What stays with you
The landlord decides whether the rent changes and by how much, and your team checks every notice before it's served. New tenancies still start with the [30-day deposit protection deadline](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/tenancy-deposit-protection-30-day-reminder/). The workflow does not decide what the market rent is or give legal advice, and it doesn't serve anything on its own. If AI drafts a landlord email or fills in a form, a person always approves it first. Disputes, tribunal referrals and anything unusual about a tenancy go straight to a named person, the same way you'd handle [repairs above a landlord's approval limit](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/landlord-repair-approval-limits/). Missed rent follows the same principle, with a person approving every step; see [rent arrears letters](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/rent-arrears-reminders-letting-agents/).

### Do tenancies in England still need renewing?
For most private tenancies, no. Gov.uk says existing assured shorthold tenancies became assured periodic tenancies on 1 May 2026, with no end date. ## Property inspection scheduling for letting agents and property managers
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/property-inspection-scheduling/

Property inspection scheduling is the routine of booking each managed property's inspection, giving the tenant proper notice, reminding everyone the day before and sending the report to the landlord. In England, section 11(6) of the Landlord and Tenant Act 1985 lets the landlord, or someone they authorise in writing, enter at reasonable times of the day to view the property's condition, on 24 hours' notice in writing to the occupier. A workflow can run the calendar, notices and report sharing, while a person does the inspection and decides what happens next.

Property inspection scheduling is simple for one property and messy for a hundred. Each one has its own due date, a tenant who needs written notice and a convenient time, an inspector's diary, and a landlord waiting for the report. Most agencies run it from a calendar and memory, so inspections drift and reports sit in someone's inbox. The steps are the same every time, so they can run as a workflow while your team does the visits. This page covers the notice rules in England and the US, a schedule you can adapt and the messages to send.

### The notice rules
In England, section 11(6) of the Landlord and Tenant Act 1985 (on legislation.gov.uk) says that where the landlord's repairing duty is implied, which covers most tenancies of under seven years, the landlord or anyone they authorise in writing may enter at reasonable times of the day, on 24 hours' notice in writing to the occupier, to view the property's condition and state of repair. Treat 24 hours as the minimum, not the plan: giving a week's notice and offering another time makes the visit easier for everyone. Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland have their own tenancy laws, so check those for properties there. In the US, landlord entry is set by state law and the lease. California is one example: the state Department of Real Estate guide says entry is allowed only for specific reasons, that 24 hours' written notice is generally treated as reasonable (6 days if the notice is mailed), and that the landlord does not have the right to enter just for a general inspection. Check the rules in each state you manage in. None of these laws sets how often you should inspect: that's agreed with each landlord in your management terms.

### An inspection schedule you can adapt
For illustration: a pattern many agencies could start from. Change the timings to match what you've agreed with each landlord. You can time one visit near the yearly [rent review](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/tenancy-renewal-reminders-letting-agents/).
| Step | When (for illustration) | What goes to whom |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Check-in inventory | Move-in day | Report and photos to the landlord and the tenant |
| First routine inspection | About 3 months after move-in | Report to the landlord; repairs logged as jobs |
| Routine inspections | Every 6 months, or as agreed with the landlord | Report to the landlord; tenant thanked and told of any next steps |
| Propose a date | 14 days before the inspection is due | Message to the tenant with two or three times to choose from |
| Written notice | At least 7 days before (the legal minimum in England is 24 hours) | Written notice to the tenant with the date, time window and reason |
| Reminder | 1 day before | Short reminder to the tenant and the inspector |
| Report shared | Within 2 working days of the visit | Report to the landlord after a person has reviewed it |

### Where inspection scheduling breaks down
- Due dates live in one calendar, so inspections drift by months when that person is busy
- Notice goes out by phone, so there's no written record of the date and time you gave
- The tenant can't do the time offered, and the rebooking falls through the gaps
- The report is written but sits in a folder, and the landlord never sees it
- Repairs spotted during the visit never become jobs in [your maintenance process](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/letting-agent-maintenance-requests/)

### What an automated scheduling workflow does
1. Keeps one list of every property with its last inspection date, how often the landlord wants inspections and the next due date.
2. Two weeks before a due date, messages the tenant with a few times to choose from, based on your inspector's free slots.
3. When the tenant picks a time, books it in the inspector's calendar and sends the tenant written notice with the date, time window and reason for the visit.
4. If the tenant doesn't reply, sends one follow-up and then tells a named person on your team to call.
5. The day before, reminds the tenant and the inspector.
6. After the visit, collects the report and photos, puts them in front of a person to review, then sends the report to the landlord and logs the date.
7. Turns each repair the inspector noted into a job, so it goes through your usual approval steps, and sets the next inspection date.

### Inspection notice to a tenant
Written notice of a routine inspection:
```
Subject: Routine inspection at [property address] on [date]

Hi [tenant name],

This is written notice that [inspector name] from [agency name] will visit [property address] on [date] between [time window] for a routine inspection. We're checking the condition of the property and whether anything needs repairing, on behalf of your landlord.

You don't need to be home. If you'd like to be there, or the time doesn't suit you, reply to this email or call [phone number] and we'll find another time.

If you've noticed anything that needs fixing, let us know before the visit so we can look at it while we're there.

Thanks,
[your name]
[agency name]
```

### Sending the report to the landlord
Email to the landlord with the inspection report:
```
Subject: Inspection report for [property address], [inspection date]

Hi [landlord name],

We inspected [property address] on [inspection date]. The full report and photos are attached.

Summary:
- Overall condition: [condition]
- Repairs needed: [list, or "none"]
- Anything for you to decide: [list, or "nothing"]

Where a repair is within your agreed limit, we'll arrange it and let you know. Anything above that, we'll send you a quote to approve first.

The next inspection is due around [next date].

Thanks,
[your name]
[agency name]
```

### What stays with you
A person does every inspection and reviews every report before the landlord sees it. Your team decides what counts as a repair, what's urgent and what to raise with the tenant. Repair costs go through the landlord's [approval limit for repairs](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/landlord-repair-approval-limits/). If AI drafts a summary of the report or a message to a tenant, a person always approves it first. Photos stay in the property file you already use and are shared only with the landlord and the tenant. In the US, that file usually starts earlier, with the pay stubs, ID and references gathered for [a rental application](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/rental-application-document-collection/).

A [free 15-minute call](https://mikeautomations.github.io/call/) about how you book inspections today and where they slip. It's built on the tools your agency already uses (your email, calendars, a shared spreadsheet or drive, and your property management software where it allows a connection), so nobody learns a new system. ### How much notice do I have to give a tenant for an inspection?
In England, section 11(6) of the Landlord and Tenant Act 1985 sets 24 hours' notice in writing, at reasonable times of the day. Many agents give more, and offer another time if it doesn't suit. In the US it depends on the state and the lease: California, for example, generally treats 24 hours' written notice as reasonable but doesn't allow entry just for a general inspection.

### How often should we inspect?
The law doesn't set a frequency. It's agreed with each landlord in your management terms. The workflow follows whatever pattern you set for each property.

## Will writing client questionnaire: get it back before the meeting
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/will-writing-client-questionnaire/

A will writing client questionnaire collects the facts a solicitor or will writer needs before the first meeting: personal details, family, assets, executors, guardians and gifts. It works best sent automatically when a client gets in touch, with short reminders until it is complete, and the meeting booked once it is back. The questionnaire gathers facts only: advice, capacity and the client's wishes are for the adviser to explore in the meeting.

A will writing client questionnaire should stop the first meeting from becoming a fact-finding session. In practice, the form goes out once, comes back half done the night before, or never comes back at all, and the meeting is spent listing children's dates of birth and guessing what the house is worth. Sending it, chasing it and spotting when it is complete are the same steps for every client, so they can run as a workflow. Everything that needs judgement stays with you. This page is for solicitors and will writers in England and Wales, and it sits alongside the wider [client intake workflow for small law firms](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/law-firm-client-intake/).

### Why the questionnaire stalls
- It is a long form about difficult things, so clients put it off
- It goes out as an attachment once, and nobody checks whether it came back
- Couples making mirror wills each have half the answers
- Clients don't know figures such as pension values, and stop at the first question they can't answer
- The meeting is booked first, so it goes ahead with gaps or gets moved

### Client questionnaire field list
This is a starting point to adapt, not a template that tells anyone what their will should say. Ask for estimates where exact figures are hard to find, and let clients mark a field "don't know" rather than stop.
| Section | Fields | Why you ask before the meeting |
| --- | --- | --- |
| About you | Full name and any former names, date of birth, address, phone, email, occupation | Identifies the client and how to reach them |
| Relationships | Marital or civil partnership status, any plans to marry, previous marriages, partner's name | gov.uk notes that getting married cancels any will made before |
| Children and dependants | Names, dates of birth, children from earlier relationships, anyone else who depends on you | Shapes the guardian and gift questions |
| Existing will | Do you have a will? Its date, who holds it, any codicils | So the adviser can compare old and new |
| Property | Homes and land, how each is owned (alone or jointly), rough value, mortgage | How a property is owned affects how it passes |
| Other assets | Bank and savings accounts, investments, pensions, life policies, business interests, assets abroad | Rough values are fine at this stage |
| Debts | Mortgages, loans, credit cards | Completes the picture of the estate |
| Executors | Who you would like, their contact details, any back-up choices | Gives the adviser names to discuss |
| Guardians | Who you would like to look after children under 18 | Only if there are young children |
| Gifts and wishes | Specific gifts, charities, funeral wishes, anyone you plan to leave out | Prompts the conversation, does not settle it |

### How the chasing works
1. A client asks about a will by phone, email or web form, as now.
2. The same day they get a short message with a secure link to the questionnaire. A couple making mirror wills each get their own link, so one doesn't answer for the other.
3. The client can stop and come back later. Each section saves as they go.
4. If nothing has come back after 3 days, a short, friendly reminder goes out. A second follows after 7 days.
5. After a third quiet week, the matter goes on a list for a person to phone. No more automatic messages.
6. When the required fields are complete, the client gets a link to book the meeting. Not before.
7. Your fee earner gets a one-page summary of the answers, and the full questionnaire is saved to the matter file.

### Reminder you can copy
Email reminder, 3 days after the questionnaire was sent:
```
Hi [first name], it's [your name] at [firm name]. Just a reminder about your will questionnaire: [secure link]. It saves as you go, so you can do it in a few sittings. If you don't know an exact figure, a rough estimate is fine. Once it's done, you'll get a link to book your appointment. Any questions, reply to this email or call [phone].
```

### What must stay with the adviser
The form gathers facts. It does not take instructions. gov.uk says a will is only valid if the person making it is 18 or over, makes it voluntarily and is of sound mind, and those are questions for a person, not a form. Paragraph 3.1 of the SRA Code of Conduct for Solicitors says you act on instructions from the client or someone properly authorised, and if you have reason to suspect instructions don't represent the client's wishes, you don't act until you are satisfied they do. The SRA's 2022 guidance on vulnerable clients and third parties says to get the client's signed authority before taking instructions through someone else, and to check those instructions with the client. So the workflow sends links only to the client's own contact details, never to the relative who made the enquiry, and the adviser still goes through every answer in the meeting. Will writing itself is not regulated the same way for everyone: the Legal Services Board recommended regulating all will writing in February 2013 and the Lord Chancellor declined in May 2013, so unregulated will writers work to their own code or membership body.

### Keeping the answers safe
The questionnaire holds personal data about the client and about other people: children, executors, guardians and beneficiaries. Ask only what you need, keep it in tools your firm already controls, send links rather than attachments, and limit who can see it. Our [GDPR checklist for automating client data](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/gdpr-checklist-automating-client-data/) covers the general points, and the same chasing pattern used for [source of funds evidence in conveyancing](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/conveyancing-source-of-funds-document-chasing/) applies here. When the will is eventually needed, the executors face a longer list; see [probate document collection](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/probate-document-collection/).

A [free 15-minute call](https://mikeautomations.github.io/call/) about how will enquiries come in today and where the questionnaire gets stuck. Within 48 hours you get a written plan with a fixed price and a clear definition of "working". It's built on the tools you already use (your case management system, email and forms, where they allow a connection), so your team doesn't learn a new system. Live in 2-3 days. [Workflow automation is a fixed $2,000](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/pricing/), and you pay once it's running and you're happy with it.

### Can the questionnaire take the client's instructions?
No. It collects facts so the meeting can focus on advice. The adviser takes instructions, checks they reflect the client's own wishes, and decides with the client what the will says.

### What if a relative fills it in for the client?
The links go only to the client's own email or phone. If a relative is involved, the SRA's guidance on third parties applies, and that is for the adviser to handle in person.

### Do couples share one questionnaire?
They can share the household sections, but each person gets their own link for their own wishes, so neither answers for the other.

### Does it replace our case management system?
No. It works with what you use. Where your system already sends forms, we only automate the gaps, such as reminders, the call list and the booking link.

## Physio rebooking reminders for patients who don't book their next session
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/physio-rebooking-reminders/

Physio rebooking reminders are short, automatic messages to patients who finish a session in the middle of a treatment plan without booking the next one. A daily list shows reception who is unbooked, one or two gentle messages offer a booking link, and anyone still unbooked goes to a person to call. The clinician decides whether more sessions are needed; the messages only make it easy to book.

Physio rebooking reminders deal with a quiet leak in most clinics. A patient finishes session two of six, says "I'll check my diary and ring you", and never does. Nobody notices for weeks, because nothing is missing from the diary: there is just an empty slot that was never booked. Finding those patients and sending a polite nudge is the same check after every session, so it can run on its own while your clinicians keep every clinical decision. It follows on from [patient intake before the first appointment](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/physio-clinic-patient-intake-forms/), and it suits physio, sports therapy, osteopathy and similar clinics in the UK and the US.

### Why patients drop out between sessions
- They meant to book from home, then life got in the way
- They felt better and weren't sure whether to come back
- The time they wanted wasn't free, and nobody offered another
- Reception was busy at checkout, so the next session was never raised
- No one has a list of patients who are part-way through a plan with nothing booked

### What the workflow does
1. At the end of each session, the clinician records the plan as they do today: how many more sessions, or discharged.
2. Each evening, the workflow checks your booking software for patients whose plan has sessions left and no future appointment.
3. Reception gets that list the next morning, so they can call anyone they know well before any message goes out.
4. Patients not called get a short message with a booking link two days after their last session. If your clinic software has no booking page, [a Google Calendar or Calendly booking link](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/google-calendar-appointment-schedules-vs-calendly/) can supply one.
5. If they still haven't booked a week later, one more message goes out, with the option to reply "no more sessions".
6. After that, no more automatic messages. The patient goes on a list for the clinician to decide: a call, a letter, or close the episode. An [audiology recall workflow](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/hearing-care-recall-reminders/) ends the same way, with a person deciding what happens next.
7. Anyone who books, replies "stop" or is discharged drops out of the sequence straight away.

### Rebooking reminder sequence
| When | Who | What happens |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Session ends, plan has sessions left, nothing booked | Workflow | Patient is added to the next morning's unbooked list |
| Next morning | Reception | Reviews the list, calls patients who need a personal touch, marks them done |
| Day 2 after the last session | Workflow | First message: a booking link and the clinic phone number |
| Day 9 | Workflow | Second and last message, with an easy way to say no |
| Day 16 | Clinician | Reviews who is still unbooked and decides what happens next |
| Any time | Workflow | Booking, discharge or a "stop" reply ends the sequence |

### Messages you can copy
Keep the wording neutral. Don't mention the condition, the treatment or how the last session went: the message may be read by someone else, on a shared phone or a lock screen. Dental practices face the same gap with [recall reminders](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/dental-recall-follow-up/), and opticians with [eye test recalls](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/optician-eye-test-recall/). Yoga and pilates studios use the same idea for [class packs that are about to expire](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/fitness-studio-intro-offer-follow-up/).
First message, 2 days after the last session (text or email):
```
Hi [first name], it's [clinic name]. You don't have your next appointment booked yet. If you'd like to book, you can choose a time here: [booking link], or call us on [clinic phone]. If you've decided not to book, just reply NO and we won't message you about it again.
```

### A gentle check-in for the second message
Second and last message, a week later:
```
Hi [first name], it's [clinic name] checking in. If you'd like another appointment, you can book here: [booking link]. If you have questions about whether you need one, reply and we'll ask [clinician name] to give you a call. We won't send any more reminders about this.
```

### Health data: UK and US
In the UK, the regulator's guidance at ico.org.uk lists data concerning health as special category data under UK GDPR, and from 30 September 2026 that regulator is the Information Commission, which took over from the Information Commissioner under the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025. The fact that someone is a patient part-way through treatment is health data, so the unbooked list and the messages need the same care as the clinical record (see our [GDPR checklist for automating client data](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/gdpr-checklist-automating-client-data/)). ICO direct marketing guidance treats appointment reminders sent purely for administration as service messages, but adds that a message with promotional content counts as marketing, so leave offers and discounts out. In the US, HHS guidance under HIPAA says providers may leave appointment reminder messages but should limit the information they give, and treats appointment reminders as part of treatment rather than marketing. Patients can also ask to be contacted a different way, for example by email instead of text, and the workflow should honour that. Your clinic decides its own lawful basis, policies and texting consent, ideally with your data protection or compliance adviser.

### What stays with your clinicians
Whether a patient needs more sessions is a clinical decision, made by the clinician and the patient. The workflow only reads the plan the clinician recorded (the same record that holds the intake form answers) and makes booking easy. It never tells a patient they need treatment, never pushes after a "no", and never decides to close an episode. If AI drafts a reply to a patient's question, a person reads and approves it before it is sent.

A [free 15-minute call](https://mikeautomations.github.io/call/) about how sessions are booked and how plans are recorded today. Within 48 hours you get a written plan with a fixed price and a clear definition of "working". It's built on the tools you already use (your practice management or booking software, email and text, where they allow a connection), so your team doesn't learn a new system. Live in 2-3 days. [Workflow automation is a fixed $2,000](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/pricing/), and you pay once it's running and you're happy with it.

### Will it message patients who have been discharged?
No. It only looks at patients whose clinician recorded sessions left in the plan, and anyone discharged, booked or who replied "stop" drops out straight away.

### Doesn't our booking software already send reminders?
Most send reminders for appointments that are already booked. This covers the gap: patients with nothing booked. On the call we check what your software does on its own and only automate what's missing.

### Is it pushy?
Two short messages at most, both with an easy way to say no, then a person decides. The aim is to make booking easy for patients who meant to, not to pressure anyone.

### Is it safe to text patients about appointments?
Keep messages neutral, with no clinical details. In the UK health data is special category data under UK GDPR; in the US, HHS says reminders should limit what they disclose. Your clinic keeps its own lawful basis, consent and policies.
