## Power Automate consultant for small business: what to hire for and what to check
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/power-automate-consultant-small-business/

A Power Automate consultant for small business builds automated workflows (flows) inside the Microsoft 365 account a firm already pays for, connecting Outlook, Excel, SharePoint, Forms and Teams. Microsoft's licensing documentation says most Microsoft 365 plans already let users run cloud flows with standard connectors, so many small-firm jobs need no new subscription; premium connectors such as Salesforce or Stripe need Power Automate Premium, listed at $15 per user a month paid yearly in November 2026. The work worth paying for is getting the licences, ownership and failure alerts right, not only the clicks.

A Power Automate consultant for small business is who you look for when the firm runs on Microsoft 365 and someone has said "Power Automate can do that" but nobody has time to work out how. If you're searching for a Power Automate expert, this page sets out what small firms typically hire help for, what the tool costs according to Microsoft's own pages (checked 11 November 2026), the limits in Microsoft's documentation that catch people out, and the questions to ask anyone before they build in your account. It applies wherever you are: the licences and limits are the same in the UK, the US, Ireland, Canada, Australia and New Zealand.

### What small businesses usually hire Power Automate help for
- New enquiries: a Microsoft Forms or website form saved to an Excel table or SharePoint list, an acknowledgement sent from the shared mailbox, and a message to the person on duty in Teams.
- Attachments filed for you: invoices, ID documents or signed letters saved from Outlook to the right client folder in SharePoint or OneDrive. [Outlook automation for accountants](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/outlook-automation-for-accountants/) shows where Outlook rules stop and a flow takes over.
- Approvals: supplier invoices, quotes or holiday requests sent to a manager with Approve and Reject buttons in Outlook or Teams, and the answer recorded. See [supplier invoice approval](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/supplier-invoice-approval-workflow/) for the full workflow.
- Reminders on a schedule: chasing documents, renewals or [unpaid invoices](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/invoice-payment-reminders/) from one Excel tracker, stopping when the client replies.
- A weekly summary: open jobs, overdue items or new enquiries pulled from a list and emailed every Monday.
- Rescuing flows someone else built: a flow that stopped, sits in a former employee's account, or nobody understands.
- Moving flows into a solution and adding co-owners, so they survive a staff change.
- Connecting an outside app (a CRM, payments or accounting tool), which usually means a licence decision first.
- Desktop flows for an old Windows program with no online connection, clicking through the screen as a person would.

### What Power Automate costs (Microsoft's prices, checked 11 November 2026)
Microsoft says its listed prices are for marketing purposes and the final price is shown at checkout. Standard connectors include Office 365 Outlook, Excel Online (Business), SharePoint, OneDrive for Business, Microsoft Forms, Microsoft Teams and Standard approvals. Microsoft's premium list includes Salesforce, Stripe and Word Online (Business), and the Xero connector listed there is a third-party one. [Power Automate vs Zapier](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/power-automate-vs-zapier-small-business/) compares the cost with Zapier's for the same job.
| Licence | Price on Microsoft's pricing page | What it covers |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Included in most Microsoft 365 business plans | No extra cost | Cloud flows with standard connectors only, 6,000 actions a day per user (Microsoft Learn) |
| Power Automate Premium | $15 per user a month, paid yearly (£11.50 ex VAT on Microsoft's UK page) | Premium and custom connectors, desktop flows run attended on your own PC, 40,000 actions a day per user |
| Power Automate Process | $150 per bot a month, paid yearly (£115.30 ex VAT) | Licenses one flow or one machine on its own, whoever runs it: 250,000 actions a day. The flow must sit in a solution |
| Power Automate Hosted Process | $215 per bot a month, paid yearly (£165.30 ex VAT) | Everything in Process, plus a Microsoft-hosted machine for desktop flows |

### Limits in Microsoft's documentation that catch small firms out
- A run can last 30 days at most, and Microsoft keeps run history for 30 days. An approval nobody answers within 30 days times out.
- A flow whose trigger or actions fail continuously for 14 days is turned off.
- A flow that isn't triggered for 90 days might be turned off. Microsoft says flows owned by users with premium or Process licences aren't subject to this, and owners are emailed 30 days before.
- If a flow passes to a new owner with no premium licence and it uses premium features, Microsoft says it runs for 30 days and then turns off until a licence is bought.
- A flow that isn't in a solution can't have its owner changed in place. Building in a solution from day one avoids rebuilding later.
- With the free Power Automate licence you can't share flows, so a flow built that way belongs to one person.
- Generating a Word document from a template uses Word Online (Business), which is a premium connector. Many people find this out after building the rest.

### DIY, or hire someone?
| Your situation | Usually | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| One simple flow, every app a standard connector, someone in-house enjoys this | Do it yourself | Microsoft's templates cover common jobs, and it costs nothing extra |
| Several people depend on it, or it touches client data | Hire, or get it reviewed | Ownership, co-owners, failure alerts and permissions need setting up properly |
| Needs a premium connector or an outside app | Get advice first | The licence choice (Premium or Process) changes the cost every year |
| Existing flows broke and the builder has gone | Hire | Someone has to read the flow, fix the connections and move it to a safe owner |
| The process isn't agreed yet | Neither, yet | Map the steps on paper first; a flow can't fix an unclear process |

### Questions to ask any Power Automate consultant before they start
Our [questions to ask before hiring an automation expert](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/questions-to-ask-before-hiring-an-automation-expert/) go further, and [consultant vs freelancer vs DIY](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/automation-consultant-vs-freelancer-vs-diy/) compares the options.
1. Will the flows be built in our Microsoft 365 tenant, inside a solution, with one of our staff as co-owner?
2. Which connectors will each flow use, which are premium, and which licence does each flow need? Put it in writing.
3. Whose account will the connections run under, and what happens when that person leaves?
4. Who gets the email when a run fails, and what should they do?
5. What access do you need? A named account we create and can switch off is better than our admin password.
6. What does "working" mean, written down, and do we pay before or after it meets that?
7. What do we get at handover: a list of flows, what each does, and how to turn each one off?

```
We run on Microsoft 365 ([plan name, if known]). We'd like a Power Automate flow that does this: when [what starts it], it should [steps in order], and [who] should be told when [event]. Apps involved: [Outlook / Excel / SharePoint / Forms / Teams / others]. Roughly [number] times a week. It must not [anything it must never do, for example email a client without a person checking]. Please tell us: which connectors it needs and whether any are premium, which licences we'd need, who will own the flow, how we'll know if it fails, your fixed price, and when we pay.
```

## n8n consultant for small business: what to hire for and what to check
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/n8n-consultant/

An n8n consultant for small business plans, builds and looks after automated workflows in n8n, a workflow tool that runs either on n8n's own cloud or on a server you control. Most small firms hire one to connect their email, forms, spreadsheets and accounting software, to choose between n8n Cloud and self-hosting, and to make sure failed runs are noticed and fixed. A good one builds in your own n8n account, so you own every workflow and login.

An n8n consultant for small business is who you call when you've picked n8n, or are close to it, and want the workflows built properly without learning the tool yourself. If you're searching for an n8n expert, you probably already know n8n can do the job: it connects hundreds of apps and can run code steps and AI steps. The hard parts are elsewhere: where it runs, who keeps it updated, what happens when a run fails, and who owns it when the builder moves on. This page covers the jobs small firms usually hire help for, the questions to ask anyone before you hire them, n8n's own prices and limits as published on 11 November 2026, and how Mike Automations would do it. Still choosing a tool? Read [Zapier vs Make vs n8n](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/zapier-vs-make-vs-n8n/) first.

### What small businesses hire n8n help for
- New enquiries: a website form or email lands in a spreadsheet or CRM, the enquirer gets a reply straight away and you get an alert. See [replying to new enquiries fast](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/reply-to-new-enquiries-fast/).
- Document chasing: reminders go to each client until their files arrive, and every file is saved to the right folder in Google Drive, OneDrive or Dropbox.
- Invoice reminders: unpaid invoices in Xero or QuickBooks trigger polite reminders on a schedule you set, as in [automated payment reminders](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/invoice-payment-reminders/).
- Inbox sorting: emails with attachments are read, labelled and filed, and the details go into a sheet for someone to check.
- AI drafting with a person in charge: an AI step drafts a reply or a summary, and nothing is sent until a person approves it. More in [AI agents for small business](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/ai-agent-for-small-business/).
- Moving from Zapier or Make: rebuilding existing automations in n8n, usually because of the cost per run, then switching the old ones off.
- Rescuing a half-built project: a DIY workflow, or one left by a freelancer, that works on some days and not others.
- Hosting and upkeep: choosing between n8n Cloud and self-hosted, setting up failure alerts and keeping the instance updated.
- Weekly reports: numbers from several tools collected into one email or sheet every Monday morning.

### What n8n itself costs (n8n's pricing page, 11 November 2026)
n8n prices its cloud plans by workflow executions: one execution is one full run of a workflow, however many steps it has. Prices are in euros, as n8n shows them, and the figures below are for yearly billing. Monthly billing costs more. Check n8n.io/pricing before you buy, because n8n changes its plans often.
| Plan | Price (billed yearly) | Executions a month | Where it runs |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Starter | €20 a month | 2,500 | n8n Cloud |
| Pro | From €50 a month | 10,000 | n8n Cloud |
| Business | €667 a month | 40,000 | Self-hosted only |
| Community edition | No licence fee (you pay for a server) | Set by your server | Self-hosted |
| Enterprise | Priced by n8n's sales team | Custom | Cloud or self-hosted |

### Limits and gotchas from n8n's own documentation
- Run time: n8n's pricing page lists a maximum execution time of 5 minutes on Starter and 40 minutes on Pro, with 5 runs at the same time on Starter and 20 on Pro. A free trial allows 1,000 executions with a 180-second timeout, so a trial isn't a fair test of a heavy workflow.
- Data location: n8n says data on its hosted plans is stored in the EU, on servers in Frankfurt, Germany. Self-hosted, it's wherever you put it. If you handle client data, check this against a [GDPR checklist](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/gdpr-checklist-automating-client-data/).
- Updates: n8n's docs say it upgrades every Cloud instance at least every two weeks, so security fixes reach everyone. On a self-hosted server that job is yours, and n8n's advice is to update at least once a month.
- Failed runs: n8n's error-handling docs describe an error workflow, starting with an Error Trigger node, that you choose in each workflow's settings. It runs when an execution fails, for example to send you an email. If nobody sets one up, a failure can go unnoticed.
- Sharing files: n8n's docs warn that exported workflow files include credential names and IDs, and that steps imported from cURL can contain login headers. Clean them before a file is emailed anywhere.
- The licence: self-hosted n8n is under n8n's Sustainable Use License, which allows use for your own internal business purposes. n8n says people are free to charge for consulting and support. What isn't allowed is letting your customers connect their own accounts and build workflows on your n8n.

### DIY or hire: a quick decision table
For the wider comparison, read [consultant vs freelancer vs DIY](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/automation-consultant-vs-freelancer-vs-diy/). If the Cloud or self-hosted question is the sticking point, [n8n Cloud vs self-hosted](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/n8n-cloud-vs-self-hosted-small-business/) sets out the costs and the upkeep.
| Your situation | Do it yourself | Hire help |
| --- | --- | --- |
| One simple workflow, such as form to sheet to email | Yes, n8n's templates are a good start | Only if you have no time |
| Workflows that touch client money or client files | Risky without careful testing | Yes |
| You want to self-host to save on fees | Only if someone will update and back it up every month | Yes, and agree in writing who looks after the server |
| An AI step that writes to customers | Not without an approval step | Yes, with a person approving every message |
| A DIY workflow that keeps failing | Worth one more evening | Yes, if it's still failing after that |


## Make.com consultant for small business: what to hire for and what to check
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/make-com-consultant/

A Make.com consultant for a small business plans, builds and fixes scenarios in Make, the visual automation tool, so your forms, email, spreadsheets, accounting and booking apps pass work to each other without anyone retyping it. Hire one when a workflow has branches, reshapes data or has to run reliably every day; do it yourself when it's two apps in a straight line. Whoever you hire, the scenarios should live in your own Make organization, with you as the owner.

Looking for a Make.com consultant or a Make expert for your small business? Usually a scenario turned out harder than the videos suggested, one someone else built has stopped, or you know the workflow you want but lack the hours. This page covers the jobs worth paying for, what Make costs, the limits in Make's own documentation, and what to ask anyone before you hire them, including us.

### What small businesses usually hire a Make consultant for
- New enquiries: a form or email goes into a sheet or CRM, the enquirer gets a reply and you get an alert.
- Client onboarding: a signed proposal creates the client folder, sends the welcome email and adds the first tasks.
- Document chasing: reminders that stop when the file arrives.
- [Invoice payment reminders](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/invoice-payment-reminders/) from Xero or QuickBooks, with a person checking anything unusual.
- Reading emails and PDFs: an AI step pulls out the details of an order or supplier invoice, and a person approves them.
- Bookings: new appointments copied to a calendar and a sheet, with a confirmation and a reminder.
- A weekly summary of jobs won, invoices outstanding and documents missing.
- Fixing a scenario that has switched itself off or fails on some runs.
- Cutting credit use: instant triggers instead of checking every minute, and filters earlier.

### DIY or hire: a quick decision table
| Your situation | Do it yourself | Hire help |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Two apps, one action, no branches (form to sheet) | Yes, Make's templates cover this | Not worth paying for |
| Several steps with if/then paths | If you enjoy it and have a spare week | Usually worth it |
| Data must be reshaped (dates, names, line items) | Possible, with patience | Usually worth it |
| Client or money data, has to work every day | Only if you'll watch the run history | Yes, with error alerts and a handover |
| A scenario keeps switching itself off | Check the run history first | If you can't see why in an hour |
| You're not sure Make is the right tool | Read the comparisons below | Ask for a plan before any build |

### What Make itself costs, and where the credits go
Make bills in credits. Its pricing FAQ, checked on 11 November 2026, says most actions use 1 credit and some features using Make's own AI provider use more. The Free plan includes 1,000 credits a month; paid plans are priced by the credits you buy. Credits expire at the end of the term. If you run out, scenarios stop until credits are added, and incoming webhooks are queued. Extra credits come in bundles of 1,000 or 10,000. Prices change, so check make.com/en/pricing when you buy; our post [is Make.com worth it?](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/is-make-com-worth-it-small-business/) has a credit worksheet. Make's help centre adds:
- A trigger uses 1 credit per run even when it finds nothing, so checking a sheet every minute spends credits all day.
- Routers, filters, error handlers and Make Functions are free, so filtering early costs nothing.
- The Make Code app uses 2 credits per second of running time.
- AI Toolkit steps on Make's own AI provider use 1 credit plus credits based on token usage; with your own AI provider on a paid plan, a fixed 1 credit.

### Limits and gotchas from Make's own documentation
- Scenarios switch themselves off. Make's scenario settings page says a scenario is deactivated after a set number of errors in a row, and one that starts with an instant trigger after the first error, with some exceptions. A good build has error handlers and an alert to a person.
- Failed runs aren't kept unless you ask. Make says incomplete executions are disabled by default; with "Store incomplete executions" on, an unfinished run is saved for retry.
- Sensitive data in logs. "Keep data confidential" stops Make keeping the data a run handled. Worth turning on for client documents and payment details.
- Who owns what. Make's help centre says all scenarios, users and data belong to an organization, each organization has its own plan and billing and one owner, and only the owner can transfer ownership. If a consultant builds in their own organization, you don't own the work.

### What to check before you hire anyone
The same questions apply to a freelancer, an agency or a one-person specialist. The longer list is in [questions to ask before hiring an automation expert](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/questions-to-ask-before-hiring-an-automation-expert/), and [consultant vs freelancer vs DIY](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/automation-consultant-vs-freelancer-vs-diy/) compares the options. Copy this checklist into your first email:
Checklist to send any Make.com consultant:
```
1. Will you build in our own Make organization, with us as the owner and you invited as an admin or member?
2. Will the app connections (Gmail, Xero, Sheets...) be made with our accounts, not yours?
3. Is the price fixed, and what exactly counts as "working"?
4. Will the scenarios use instant triggers where the apps allow, and roughly how many credits a month do you expect them to use?
5. What happens when a run fails: error handlers, stored incomplete executions, an alert to whom?
6. Will you turn on "Keep data confidential" for scenarios that handle client or payment data?
7. Where will AI be used, and does a person approve its output before anything is sent?
8. What do we get at handover: a written description of each scenario, the logins list, and how to pause it?
9. Who fixes it if an app changes in three months, and what does that cost?
10. When do we pay: before, during, or once it's running?
```

### When Make isn't the right tool
A good consultant will say so. Two or three popular apps in a straight line are often quicker in Zapier; long, high-volume workflows or data that must stay on your own server may suit n8n; and if everything lives in Microsoft 365, Power Automate may already be in your licence. [Zapier vs Make vs n8n](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/zapier-vs-make-vs-n8n/) and [n8n cloud vs self-hosted](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/n8n-cloud-vs-self-hosted-small-business/) set out the trade-offs. If the job is mostly judgement rather than moving data, read about [AI agents for small business](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/ai-agent-for-small-business/) first.

## Zapier expert for small business: what to hire for, and what to check first
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/zapier-expert-for-small-business/

A Zapier expert for a small business is someone you pay to plan, build and fix Zaps, Zapier's automated workflows, so that your forms, inbox, spreadsheet, CRM and accounts software pass information to each other without retyping. It's worth hiring help when a workflow has several steps, touches money or client data, or keeps breaking; simple two-app Zaps are usually fine to build yourself. Whoever builds it, the Zaps should live in your own Zapier account, with a written list of what each one does.

Searching for a Zapier expert or a Zapier consultant for your small business usually means one of three things: you know what you want automated but not how, you've built a few Zaps and they keep failing, or your task bill has crept up and you're not sure why. Below: the jobs worth paying for, what to ask before hiring, what Zapier costs and the limits in its own help docs. It also says plainly what Mike Automations is: one person who builds automations on the tools you already use, not a certified Zapier partner.

### What small businesses usually hire Zapier help for
- New enquiries: a website form or Facebook lead goes into a spreadsheet or CRM, the owner gets a message and the enquirer gets a reply within minutes. See [replying to new enquiries fast](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/reply-to-new-enquiries-fast/).
- Chasing documents or information from clients, with reminders that stop as soon as the client sends what's missing.
- [Invoice payment reminders](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/invoice-payment-reminders/) that read due dates from Xero, QuickBooks or a spreadsheet.
- Bookings: a booking app creates a calendar event, a confirmation and a reminder the day before.
- Filing and summaries: attachments saved to the right client folder, and a weekly list of new leads and unpaid invoices.
- AI steps that draft a reply or pull details out of an email, with a person approving before anything is sent. More on that in [AI agents for small business](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/ai-agent-for-small-business/).
- Fixing Zaps that error, run twice or stopped running, and tidying an account nobody fully understands any more.
- Cutting task use: rebuilding Zaps so filters run early and fewer steps run on records that don't need them.

### What Zapier itself costs (checked 11 November 2026)
This is Zapier's bill, which you pay to Zapier directly, whoever builds your Zaps. Figures are from zapier.com/pricing with yearly billing; the page says paying yearly saves up to 33% compared with monthly.
| Plan | Price on the pricing page | What you get |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Free | $0 | 100 tasks a month, two-step Zaps only, new data checked every 15 minutes, one user |
| Professional | From $19.99 a month (750 tasks) | Multi-step Zaps, premium apps, webhooks, checks every 2 minutes, one user |
| Team | From $69 a month | Up to 25 users, shared workspace and shared app connections, checks every minute |
| Enterprise | Contact sales | Unlimited users and admin controls |

### Limits and gotchas from Zapier's own help docs
- A task is a successful action. Zapier's help centre says triggers, filters and Formatter steps don't count, but each successful action step does, so a five-step Zap uses far more tasks than a two-step one. The [Zapier vs Make vs n8n comparison](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/zapier-vs-make-vs-n8n/) works through an example.
- When you reach your task limit, Zaps pause until the next usage period, unless you turn on pay-per-task billing, which Zapier charges at a higher rate per task.
- Zapier says it will turn a Zap off automatically if 95% of its runs error and it has run more than 20 times in the past 7 days. If nobody watches the alerts, a Zap that has stopped can go unnoticed for days.
- Free and Professional are one-user plans. If several people need to see or edit the Zaps, that means Team.
- On the free plan Zapier checks for new data every 15 minutes, so "instant" replies to enquiries usually need a paid plan or an instant trigger.

### DIY or hire: a quick decision table
| Your situation | Usually | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Two apps, one action, nothing sensitive | Do it yourself | Zapier's templates and editor are built for this |
| Several steps, branches or a CRM in the middle | Get help, or at least a review | Errors and duplicates hide in the edge cases |
| Money, invoices or client documents involved | Get help | A wrong step can email the wrong client or chase a paid invoice |
| Zaps erroring, running twice or switched off | Get help | Someone needs to read the Zap history and fix the cause |
| Task bill growing every month | Get a review | Filters, the order of steps or a different tool may cost less |
| Many branches, high volumes, data on your own server | Compare tools first | Another tool may suit better |

## Carpet cleaning repeat booking reminders that fill the diary from past customers
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/carpet-cleaning-repeat-booking-reminders/

Carpet cleaning repeat booking reminders are messages sent to past customers when their next clean is likely due, worked out from the date and rooms of their last job, inviting them to book again. A repeat booking workflow sends those reminders on your schedule, follows up open quotes, confirms bookings with an on-the-way text on the day, sends aftercare advice after the clean, and asks once for a review. It runs from one list of every customer and job, so the quiet months are filled from people who already know you. The cleaner still quotes, cleans and decides what each job needs.

Carpet cleaning repeat booking reminders are the cheapest work a cleaning business can win, and most firms never send them. A customer has their lounge and stairs cleaned, is delighted, and then forgets you exist until they search again two years later and book whoever ranks first. Meanwhile quotes go unchased and the van sits idle in February. This page sets out a workflow that reminds past customers on a schedule, follows up quotes, keeps the booking day smooth, and asks for reviews, with the UK and US rules on texting and emailing customers built in.

### What the workflow does
1. Keeps one list of every customer with their address, the rooms and items cleaned, the date, the price and how they prefer to be contacted, from your job software, invoices or a spreadsheet.
2. Replies to new enquiries with your service area, starting prices and a link to book a quote or a clean, as [replying to enquiries fast](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/reply-to-new-enquiries-fast/) describes.
3. Follows up each quote on your schedule until the customer books, declines or asks to be contacted later.
4. Confirms each booking with the date, arrival window, what the customer should do before you arrive (clear small items, note stains, keep pets away) and how to pay.
5. On the day, sends an on-the-way text when you leave the previous job.
6. After the clean, sends aftercare advice (drying time, when to put furniture back, how to treat a spill) and the invoice if unpaid.
7. A few days later, sends one review request with your review link.
8. On the interval you choose for each customer, for example a year after the last clean, sends a reminder with what was cleaned last time and a link to rebook, with one follow-up if there's no reply.

### A reminder schedule you can copy
| When | Channel | What it says |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Quote sent | Email and text | Price, what's included, how to book, how long the price holds |
| Quote day 3 and day 10 | Text | Short follow-ups; stop when they answer |
| Booking made | Email and text | Date, arrival window, how to prepare, how to pay |
| Day before | Text | Reminder and arrival window |

| After the clean | Email | Aftercare advice, invoice if unpaid |
| 3 days after | Text or email | One review request |
| Your interval, e.g. 12 months | Text or email | Time for another clean? Last time: [rooms]. Book here |
| Interval plus 3 weeks, no reply | Text | One follow-up, then nothing until next interval |

### A repeat booking reminder you can copy
Sent on your interval after the last clean (edit the words in brackets):
```
Hi [first name], it's [your name] from [business name]. It's about [interval] since we cleaned your [rooms or items] at [street], so it may be due another clean. You can book here: [link], or reply with a day that suits you and I'll confirm. If you'd rather not get these reminders, reply STOP. Thanks, [your name]
```

### The rules for texting and emailing past customers
A reminder that invites a past customer to book again is direct marketing, so the rules apply. In the UK, the Privacy and Electronic Communications Regulations generally require consent to send marketing by text or email, with an exception the ICO describes as the soft opt-in: you can email or text an existing customer about your own similar services if you collected their details in the course of a sale, gave them a clear chance to opt out at the time, and give them a simple way to opt out in every message. The ICO also says to keep a suppression list of people who have objected. In the US, marketing text messages sent with automated systems need the recipient's prior express written consent under the Telephone Consumer Protection Act rules enforced by the FCC, and the sender has to be able to prove it. The workflow records how and when each customer agreed, includes the opt-out in every message, and stops the moment someone replies STOP. Service messages about a booked job (confirmations, on-the-way texts) are not marketing. Check ico.org.uk and fcc.gov for the current rules.

## Bike shop service bookings and repair updates that keep the workshop quiet
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/bike-shop-service-bookings-and-repair-updates/

A bike shop service workflow confirms each booking, sends a drop-off receipt with the bike's details, texts the mechanic's quote for approval before any chargeable work, tells the customer about parts delays without them asking, sends a ready-to-collect message with the total, and reminds each customer when their next service is due. Every bike has one record from booking to collection, so the mechanic fixes bikes instead of answering the phone. The shop still diagnoses, prices and repairs.

Bike shop service bookings and repair updates are the same handful of messages, sent by whoever is nearest the phone, usually late. The customer drops a bike off, hears nothing, and rings on day two. The mechanic finds a worn chain and cassette, fits them, and the customer disputes the bill because nobody asked. Spring arrives and every bike in the city needs a service in the same fortnight. This page sets out a workflow that confirms bookings, records approvals before chargeable work, keeps customers informed through the job, and brings them back on a service schedule, including the extra checks for e-bikes.

### The messages, in order
1. Booking: the customer books online or in the shop and gets a confirmation with the date, what to bring (keys, charger for an e-bike) and your drop-off window. A reminder goes the day before.
2. Drop-off receipt: the bike (make, model, frame number if you record it), the fault or service booked, the ticket number and your terms.
3. Quote: after the mechanic's check, the customer gets what was found, the price for parts and labour, and the expected ready date. They reply YES or NO, or tap a link. The reply is saved on the job.
4. Parts delay: if a part is on order, the customer gets the new expected date without asking, and again if it slips.
5. Extra work found: a second approval request in the same format before any additional chargeable work.
6. Ready: a text with the total, how to pay and your opening hours. Uncollected bikes get a reminder after a week and then on your terms.
7. After collection: one review request a few days later, sent once.
8. Service reminder: on the schedule you set from the last service date, a message inviting the customer to book, with your booking link.

### A status-to-message table you can copy
| Status | Message | Channel |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Booked | Confirmation: date, drop-off window, what to bring | Email and text |
| Day before | Reminder | Text |
| Dropped off | Receipt with ticket number and terms | Text and email |
| Checked | Findings, price, ready date. Reply YES to approve | Text |
| Waiting for part | Part ordered, new expected date | Text |
| Ready | Ready to collect. Total [amount]. Open until [time] | Text |
| Ready 7 days, uncollected | Reminder with storage terms | Text |
| Collected | One review request | Text or email |
| Service due | Time for a service, book here | Text or email |

### A quote text you can copy

```
Hi [first name], [shop name] here about ticket [number] ([bike]). We've checked it over. Along with the [service booked], it needs [parts or work], because [plain reason]. The total would be [price] including parts, ready by [day]. Reply YES to go ahead with everything, or SERVICE ONLY for just the service, and we'll have it ready as agreed. Questions? Call [phone].
```

### E-bikes: what to record at drop-off
E-bikes need a few extra lines on the drop-off receipt: battery and charger received or not, the motor system, and whether the customer has reported any fault with the electrics. In Great Britain, gov.uk's rules for electrically assisted pedal cycles say an EAPC's motor must have a continuous rated power output of no more than 250 watts and must not propel the bike when it is travelling at more than 15.5 mph; a bike outside those limits is treated as a motor vehicle and must be registered and taxed. If a customer asks you to alter a bike beyond those limits, your workshop policy decides, and the record should show what was asked and what you did. The workflow can add the e-bike lines to the receipt automatically when the bike type is set. Check gov.uk for the current rules; a government consultation has proposed changes.

### What UK consumer law expects of a repair
The Consumer Rights Act 2015 treats every contract to supply a service as including a term that the trader must perform it with reasonable care and skill (section 49), and, where no time is fixed, within a reasonable time (section 52). Prices and times you state to the customer can become part of the contract, which is a good reason to put them in a message the customer approves rather than agree them at the counter. The workflow records what was said and what the customer replied. Check legislation.gov.uk for the current text. US shops should check their state's consumer protection rules.

- Reviews are never asked for, as [this guide](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/ask-for-google-reviews-automatically/) explains

It never approves work for the customer or changes a price. If AI drafts a reply to a customer question, a person approves it first.

## Sign and print shop artwork approvals that get a recorded yes before anything prints
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/sign-and-print-shop-artwork-approvals/

An artwork approval workflow for sign and print shops collects the customer's files against your specification, sends each proof with a clear approve or request-changes choice, chases until the customer answers, and records the approved proof version with the date and the name of the person who approved it before the job is released to production. It then sends the deposit request, production updates and the ready or install message, so a reprint argument is settled by the record rather than by memory. The shop still designs, checks files and prints.

Sign and print shop artwork approvals are where a job's margin disappears. The customer sends a logo as a screenshot, the proof goes out by email, the customer replies "looks good" to a different proof, and the finished sign has last year's phone number. Reprinting costs the shop the job's profit and the customer's trust. This page sets out a workflow that collects files against your spec, sends proofs with a recorded approval, holds production until that approval exists, and keeps the customer informed through production to collection or installation. It also covers who owns the artwork, which matters more than most shops realise.

### What the workflow does, enquiry to installed sign
1. Enquiries get a reply with what you need to quote: size, material, quantity, single or double sided, where it's going, and your artwork specification.
2. The quote goes out with the deposit amount, your terms and the lead time from approval, not from order.
3. When the customer accepts, a file intake link collects the artwork with your spec shown: file types, resolution, bleed, fonts outlined, colour mode. Files that miss the spec get an automatic note asking for the right version.
4. Your designer prepares the proof and uploads it. The customer gets it with two buttons: approve, or request changes with a comment box.
5. If there's no answer, the customer is reminded on your schedule. Each new proof version is numbered; approvals are tied to a version.
6. When a proof is approved, the record saves the version, the date, the time and the approver's name, and the job is released to production. Nothing prints before this.
7. The customer gets production updates at the stages you choose, then a ready-to-collect or install-booked message, and the invoice.
8. After collection or installation, one review request goes out with a photo of the finished job if you took one.

### An artwork specification table you can copy
Show this on your file intake page and in the quote. Adjust to your equipment:
| Item | What you need | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| File type | PDF, AI or EPS for vector; TIFF or high-resolution JPEG for photos | Vector scales cleanly; screenshots don't |
| Colour | CMYK for print; note any brand colour references | Screen colours (RGB) print differently |
| Fonts | Outlined or converted to curves, or the font files supplied | Missing fonts substitute silently |
| Bleed and safe area | Your figure, stated in millimetres or inches | Trimming is never perfect |
| Size | Final size at 100% or a stated scale | Avoids guessing |
| Approval | One named person approves each proof version | Settles who said yes to what |

### A proof message you can copy
Sent with each proof version (edit the words in brackets):
```
Hi [first name], proof [version number] for your [job description] is ready: [link]. Please check every word, number and colour, and the size shown. If it's right, tap Approve. If anything needs changing, tap Request changes and tell us what. We print only from an approved proof, so the lead time of [lead time] starts when you approve. Thanks, [your name], [shop name]
```

### Who owns the artwork
If your designer creates artwork for a customer, the default position under the UK's Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988 is that the author is the first owner of copyright, and paying for a commission does not by itself transfer it. Gov.uk's guidance on ownership of copyright works says a contract is the way to settle who owns what. Decide your policy (keep it, assign it on full payment, or license it) and put it in your terms, so the customer who wants the file for a van wrap next year knows where they stand. The reverse matters too: when a customer supplies a logo or photos, your terms should say they confirm they have the right to use them. The workflow shows the terms at quote and at file intake and records that they were seen. US copyright law has a similar default for independent contractors; take advice on your own terms.

- The lead time is counted from the order date while the customer sits on the proof for a week
- Deposits aren't taken and the approved sign is never collected
- Install dates are agreed by phone and nobody books the access or the fitter
- Changes after approval are done for free because nobody can show when approval happened; the [change order workflow](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/change-order-approval-workflow/) covers the same problem on sites
- Agencies face the same approval chaos, as [this guide to client approvals](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/agency-client-approvals/) explains

## Music school lesson scheduling and term fees that run from one timetable

A music school scheduling and fees workflow keeps one timetable of every student, teacher, room and lesson time, sends weekly lesson reminders and the term's invoice from it, offers make-up slots when a lesson is missed or a teacher is away, chases unpaid fees on your schedule, and collects exam entry details and fees before your board's closing date. Parents and adult students see one consistent message from the school rather than texts from individual teachers. The teachers still teach and decide who is ready for an exam.

Music school lesson scheduling and term fees are a weekly tangle of texts between parents, teachers and whoever runs the office. ### What the workflow does, each week and each term

## Martial arts school memberships and gradings that run from one list
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/martial-arts-school-memberships-and-gradings/

A martial arts membership and grading workflow follows up every trial class until the student joins or says no, sends membership paperwork and payment requests, chases failed payments, tracks attendance against your grading requirements, and invites eligible students to the next grading with the date, fee and what to bring. Results and the next belt's requirements go out after the grading. Everything sits in one list of students, so the instructor teaches instead of chasing. The instructor still decides who is ready to grade.

Martial arts school memberships and gradings are run, in most clubs, by the instructor on their phone between classes. A trial student comes once and nobody follows up. A direct debit fails and the student trains for two months unpaid. Grading day arrives and half the class didn't know they were eligible, while the other half turn up without the fee. This page sets out a workflow that handles trials, sign-ups, payments, attendance and gradings from one list, with the instructor approving every grading invitation. ### Membership contracts and the UK rules
Membership terms are a consumer contract. In the UK, the Consumer Rights Act 2015 says unfair terms don't bind the consumer, and the Competition and Markets Authority's guidance on unfair contract terms (CMA37) explains how it judges them. Long minimum periods with no fair way to cancel are exactly the kind of term to check with that guidance or a solicitor. Keep your terms plain: the minimum period, how to cancel, what happens when a payment fails, and how fees change. The workflow puts the terms in front of the member before they sign and records that they saw them. In the US, automatic renewal and cancellation rules vary by state; check yours. ## Swim school term bookings and a waiting list that fills places itself
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/swim-school-term-bookings-and-waiting-list/

A swim school term booking workflow asks every current family to re-enrol before the term ends, sends term fee requests and reminders, offers each freed place to the right families on the waiting list by age and stage, and confirms the new class with the time, pool and what to bring. It keeps one list of every swimmer with their stage, class, payment status and waiting list position, so places are filled in hours rather than sitting empty for a term. The teachers still decide when a swimmer moves up.

Swim school term bookings and the waiting list are a seasonal admin crunch. Four times a year, every family needs to re-enrol, pay and confirm their slot, while a hundred names on a waiting list want to know when a place will come up. The spreadsheet is updated at the poolside between classes and the email inbox fills with "has my payment gone through?". This page sets out a workflow that runs re-enrolment on a timeline, chases fees, fills cancelled places from the waiting list automatically, and confirms stage moves to parents, so the office spends the term teaching rather than emailing.

### What the workflow does, each term
1. Four weeks before the term ends, every current family gets a re-enrolment message with their swimmer's class, day and time for next term, the fee and a confirm or release link.
2. Families who confirm get the fee request; payment is recorded as it arrives and a receipt goes out.
3. Families who don't reply get reminders on your schedule, then a final notice that the place will be released on a date.
4. Released places are matched to the waiting list by age, stage and preferred day, and offered to the first matching family with a time limit to accept.
5. If they don't accept in time, the place goes to the next family. Accepted places get a confirmation with the pool, time, what to bring and your policies.
6. Term fee reminders go to anyone unpaid by the due date, then on your schedule until paid or the place is released.
7. When a teacher records a stage pass, the parent gets a message with the new stage, what it means and whether the class changes.
8. A week before term, every family gets a start-of-term message; mid-term, anyone who has missed several classes gets a check-in.

### A term timeline you can copy
| When | Who gets it | What it says |
| --- | --- | --- |

| 2 weeks before | Not yet confirmed | Reminder, place held until [date] |
| 1 week before | Still not confirmed | Final notice, place released on [date] |
| Release date | Waiting list, best match first | A place has come up: day, time, stage, accept within [hours] |
| Fee due date | Confirmed, unpaid | Fee reminder with payment link |
| 1 week before new term | All enrolled | Start date, pool, what to bring, policies |
| Stage pass recorded | The swimmer's family | New stage, what changes |

```
Hi [first name], good news from [swim school]. A place has come up for [child's name] in our [stage] class on [day] at [time] at [pool], starting [date]. The term fee is [fee]. ```
```

## Hearing care recall reminders that bring patients back on time
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/hearing-care-recall-reminders/

Hearing care recall reminders are messages that tell each patient when their next hearing check, hearing aid service or follow-up is due and invite them to book, sent from one list of every patient with their last appointment, their devices and their warranty dates. A recall workflow sends the reminders on your schedule, confirms bookings, reminds patients the day before, and flags anyone who hasn't rebooked, so the practice's diary fills from its own patient list rather than from new enquiries. The audiologist still decides what care each patient needs.

Hearing care recall reminders are the steadiest work in an independent audiology practice, and the easiest to let slip. Every patient with hearing aids needs regular checks, cleaning and adjustments, and every device has a warranty that runs out on a date you already hold. Yet most recalls still start from a report someone remembers to run in a quiet week. This page sets out a recall schedule you can copy, the messages to send, how to handle patients who prefer a phone call, and the regulatory points for the UK and the US. It does not touch clinical content: what a patient needs is always the audiologist's decision.

### What the workflow does
1. Keeps one list of every patient with their last appointment, their devices and purchase dates, warranty end dates and preferred contact method, from your practice software or a spreadsheet.
2. You set the recall intervals (for example an annual hearing check and a six-monthly service) and approve the message wording.
3. Sends each patient their recall by their preferred channel: text, email, or a call list for those who want to be phoned.
4. Confirms the booking, sends a reminder the day before, and asks the patient to bring their devices and any questions.
5. After a fitting, sends the follow-up check-in on your schedule, with how to reach you if something isn't right.
6. Before a warranty ends, tells the patient the date and invites them in for a check while it's covered.
7. Reminds patients who buy consumables (batteries, wax guards, domes) when a reorder is likely due, if you offer that.
8. Each week, lists everyone who passed their recall date without booking, for a personal call.

### A recall schedule you can copy
Set the intervals to match your clinical protocol. This is an example of the messages, not clinical advice:
| Trigger | When | Message |
| --- | --- | --- |
| New fitting | 1 to 2 weeks after | How are you getting on? Here's how to reach us, and your follow-up date |
| Service due | 3 weeks before | Your hearing aids are due a clean and check. Book here or reply |
| Service due | 1 week before, not booked | Short reminder |
| Annual check | 4 weeks before | Your yearly hearing check is due. Book here |
| Warranty ending | 2 months before | Your warranty ends on [date]. Book a check while it's covered |
| Booked | Day before | See you tomorrow at [time]. Please bring your devices |
| Missed recall | Weekly list | A person calls |

### A recall text you can copy
Service recall, 3 weeks before (edit the words in brackets):
```
Hi [first name], it's [practice name]. Your hearing aids are due their [service type] around [month]. It takes about [duration] and keeps them working at their best. Book here: [link], reply with a day that suits you, or call [phone] and we'll find a time. [audiologist name]
```

### The regulatory points, UK and US
- UK: hearing aid dispensers are regulated by the Health and Care Professions Council. The HCPC states that only a registered hearing aid dispenser may assess or test a person's hearing or prescribe a hearing aid in the private sector. Recall messages invite patients to book; they don't assess anything.
- UK: if your messages promote products or services beyond the recall, the ICO's direct marketing rules apply. A recall for care the patient already receives is a service message; a battery offer is marketing. Keep the two apart and keep a record of each patient's permission.
- US: the FDA's over-the-counter hearing aid rule, published in the Federal Register in August 2022, allows adults 18 and over with perceived mild to moderate hearing loss to buy certain hearing aids without a prescription. Practices that see OTC users for checks can recall them the same way.
- US: marketing text messages sent with automated systems need the recipient's prior express written consent under the Telephone Consumer Protection Act rules enforced by the FCC. Appointment reminders are treated differently from marketing; take advice and record consent for anything promotional.
- Everywhere: patient records are health data. Keep the recall list to the minimum (name, contact, dates, devices) and keep clinical notes in your practice system.

### Where recalls usually break
- Recall reports are run when the diary is quiet, so busy months produce no recalls at all
- Older patients who prefer a phone call get a text they never open; the workflow puts them on a call list instead
- Warranty dates sit in a drawer with the receipts
- Fitting follow-ups depend on the audiologist remembering, which [physio rebooking reminders](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/physio-rebooking-reminders/) and [dental recall follow-up](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/dental-recall-follow-up/) solve the same way
- Patients cancel late or forget, which [reducing no-shows](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/reduce-appointment-no-shows/) covers
- Nobody asks happy patients for a review, so new patients find the chain down the road first

### What stays with you
Every clinical decision, every recall interval and every conversation about a patient's hearing. The workflow sends your words on your schedule, records bookings and replies, and gives you the list of people to call. It never assesses, advises or prescribes. If AI drafts a reply to a patient question, a person approves it first.

## Phone repair shop job updates that stop the "is it ready yet?" calls
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/phone-repair-shop-job-updates/

A phone repair job update workflow gives every device a record from check-in: the customer gets a receipt with the fault and the passcode arrangement, then the diagnosis and price to approve by text, a message if a part is delayed, a ready-for-collection text with the total, and one review request after collection. Each status change in your till or repair software, or on a simple board, triggers the right message, so the technician fixes phones instead of answering the phone. The shop still diagnoses, prices and repairs.

Phone repair shop job updates are the same five messages, sent hundreds of times a month, usually late. The customer drops a phone off, hears nothing, and rings twice before lunch. The technician stops work to answer, then forgets to ask approval for the extra part, then the customer comes in before it's ready. This page sets out a workflow that sends each message when the job status changes, records the customer's approval before any chargeable work, and gives you a daily list of jobs that have been waiting too long. It also covers what UK consumer law expects of a repair service.

### The messages, in order
1. Check-in receipt: the device, the fault as described, the ticket number, how you handle passcodes and data, your terms, and when to expect a diagnosis.
2. Diagnosis and quote: what's wrong, what you'll do, the price, how long it takes and the warranty you give. The customer replies yes or no, or taps a link. The reply is saved on the job.
3. Parts delay: if a part isn't in stock, the customer is told the new date without having to ask, and again if it slips.
4. Extra work found: a second approval request, in the same format, before any additional chargeable work.
5. Ready for collection: the total, how to pay, your opening hours and what to bring (the ticket, ID if you ask for it).
6. Not collected: a reminder after a week, then on the schedule in your terms, until the device is collected.
7. After collection: one message a few days later asking how it went, with a link to your review page. Sent once.

### A status-to-message table you can copy
| Status in your system | Message | Channel |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Checked in | Receipt with ticket number, fault, passcode and data note, terms | Text and email |
| Diagnosed | Fault, fix, price, time, warranty. Reply YES to approve | Text |
| Approved | Thanks, we've started. Expected ready: [date] | Text |
| Waiting for part | Part ordered, new expected date | Text |
| Ready | Ready to collect. Total [amount]. Open until [time] | Text |
| Ready 7 days, not collected | Reminder, plus your storage terms | Text |
| Collected | One review request after a few days | Text or email |

### A diagnosis and quote text you can copy
Sent when the technician records the diagnosis (edit the words in brackets):
```
Hi [first name], [shop name] here about ticket [number] ([device]). The fault is [fault in plain words]. We can fix it by [repair], for [price] including the part, ready by [day]. Our repairs come with a [warranty period] warranty on the part and the work. Reply YES to go ahead or NO and we'll have it ready to collect as it is. Questions? Call [phone].
```

### What UK consumer law expects of a repair
The Consumer Rights Act 2015 treats every contract to supply a service as including a term that the trader must perform it with reasonable care and skill (section 49), and, where no time is fixed, within a reasonable time (section 52). Information you give the customer about the service, such as the price and the time, can become part of the contract. That is a good reason to put the price, the time and the warranty in a message the customer approves, rather than agreeing them at the counter. The workflow records what was said, when, and what the customer replied. Check the current text on legislation.gov.uk before you rely on it. US shops should check their state's consumer protection rules.

### Passcodes, data and privacy
Customers hand you a device full of personal data. Your check-in message should say how you handle passcodes, whether you need one, and what you do and don't look at. In the UK, the ICO is the regulator for personal data; keep passcodes only as long as the repair needs them and delete them from your records afterwards. The workflow can store the passcode arrangement as a yes or no flag rather than the code itself, and remind the technician to clear it when the job closes. For wider privacy points when you automate customer data, see the [GDPR checklist](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/gdpr-checklist-automating-client-data/).

### Where repair shops lose time
- Customers ring for updates because nobody told them the diagnosis, so the technician is answering the phone instead of repairing
- Extra work is done without a recorded approval and the customer disputes the bill
- Parts delays are discovered by the customer at the counter
- Repaired devices sit on the shelf for weeks, with no reminders and no storage terms applied
- Walk-in quotes are given verbally and the customer comes back quoting a different price; [quote follow-up](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/whatsapp-quote-follow-up-tradespeople/) covers the same problem for trades
- Calls go unanswered when the shop is busy, which a [missed-call text-back](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/missed-call-text-back-contractors/) fixes

### What stays with you
Diagnosis, pricing, the repair itself and every decision about data and passcodes. The workflow sends the right message when you change a status, records approvals and reminds you of jobs that are stuck. It never approves work on the customer's behalf or changes a price. If AI drafts a reply to a customer question, a person approves it first.

## Custom cake orders and deposits that don't live in your DMs
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/custom-cake-orders-and-deposits/

A custom cake order workflow replies to each enquiry with your lead time and starting prices, collects the design details, date, servings and allergen requirements on one form, sends the deposit request and the balance reminder on your schedule, and confirms the collection or delivery slot the day before. Every order sits in one record with the confirmed design and the allergen answers, so the weekend's bakes are built from a list rather than from scrolling messages. The baker still designs, prices and bakes.

Custom cake orders and deposits usually run through a phone: an enquiry on Instagram, a photo of a design, a deposit by bank transfer with no reference, and a collection time agreed three weeks ago in a thread you can't find. The cake is wonderful and the admin is a mess. This page sets out a workflow that answers enquiries while your hands are covered in buttercream, collects every detail once, takes the deposit and the balance on time, and sends the collection message the day before. It also covers the allergen information the UK's Food Standards Agency says a food business must provide.

### What the workflow does, enquiry to collection
1. Every enquiry from your website form, email or social inbox gets a reply within minutes: whether the date is free, your lead time, your starting prices by size, and a link to the order form.
2. The order form collects the date, servings, flavours, design notes and photos, delivery or collection, and the allergen question in your words.
3. You price the order and approve the quote. The customer gets it with the deposit request, your terms and the date the slot is held until.
4. When the deposit is paid, the order is confirmed, the date is blocked and the customer gets a confirmation that repeats the design, flavours and the allergen answers.
5. On your schedule, the balance reminder goes out, with a reminder a few days later if unpaid.
6. The day before, the customer gets the collection or delivery time, your address or theirs, and how to carry and store the cake.
7. Each week you get the bake list: every order for the coming days with design, flavours, servings, allergen notes and payment status.
8. A few days after the event, one message asks how it went and links to your review page.

### Allergen information: what the UK rules say
The Food Standards Agency says that if you provide non-prepacked food, you must supply allergen information for every item that contains any of the 14 allergens, and that written information supported by a conversation works best. A bespoke cake is non-prepacked food. The workflow asks the allergen question on the order form in your words, records the customer's answer, repeats it in the confirmation, and prints it on your bake list and the collection label. It does not decide what is safe to bake: you do. If you also sell packaged cakes from a counter, the prepacked for direct sale rules are different and are not covered here. Check food.gov.uk for the current guidance, and your local authority for registration. US bakers should check their state's rules on home and cottage food production.

### A deposit and balance schedule you can copy
| When | Channel | What it says |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Enquiry day | Email or message | Date free or not, lead time, starting prices, order form link |
| Quote sent | Email and text | Price, design summary, deposit amount, your terms, slot held until [date] |
| Deposit paid | Email | Confirmed: design, flavours, servings, allergen answers, collection date |
| 2 weeks before | Text | Balance due by [date], payment link |
| 1 week before, unpaid | Text | Reminder: balance still due |

To get you a price, fill in this short form with the design, flavours and any allergies: [form link]. I'll come back with a quote and a deposit link within [time]. [your name], [business name]

### Cancellations and the consumer rules
Your terms set the deposit, when the balance is due and what happens if the customer cancels. In the UK, the Consumer Contracts (Information, Cancellation and Additional Charges) Regulations 2013 give consumers a 14-day right to cancel many contracts made online or by phone, but regulation 28 excludes goods made to the consumer's specification or clearly personalised, and goods liable to deteriorate or expire rapidly. A custom cake is both. You still have to give the required pre-contract information, so put your terms in the quote and make sure the customer sees them before they pay. The workflow does that and records it. US rules differ by state. Check the current rules on legislation.gov.uk before you rely on them.

### Where cake orders usually go wrong
- The deposit arrives by bank transfer with no reference and nobody knows whose it is
- The design was agreed from a photo in a thread and the customer remembers a different photo
- Allergies were mentioned in a voice note and never written down
- Two orders are taken for the same Saturday because the diary is in your head

## Florist wedding and event orders, from the first enquiry to delivery day
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/florist-wedding-and-event-orders/

A wedding and event order workflow for florists replies to every enquiry with your availability and starting prices, books the consultation, sends the proposal and deposit request, and then collects the final details (counts, colours, venue access, delivery times) on a timeline you set before the event. Everything for one event sits in one record, so the week-before checklist is built from what the couple actually confirmed. The florist still designs, prices and makes the flowers.

Florist wedding and event orders are the most profitable work in the shop and the easiest to lose track of. An enquiry arrives on Instagram, a consultation is booked by text, the proposal goes out by email, and the final count changes twice on WhatsApp. By the week of the wedding, the details live in four places and you are rereading messages at midnight. This page sets out a workflow that keeps every event in one record, replies to enquiries while you are at the bench, and collects the final details on a schedule, so Friday's weddings are built from a checklist rather than a memory.

### What the workflow does, enquiry to delivery
1. Every enquiry from your website form, email or social inbox gets a reply within minutes: the date is free or not, your starting prices, and a link to book a consultation.
2. The consultation booking confirms the time and asks the couple to send inspiration photos, the venue and their rough budget beforehand.
3. After the consultation, you write the proposal in your template and the workflow sends it with the deposit request and the date the quote holds until.
4. If there is no reply, the couple gets a gentle follow-up on your schedule.
5. When they pay the deposit, the event is booked, the date is blocked in your calendar and a timeline of what you'll ask for and when goes to the couple.
6. On the timeline, the workflow asks for the final count of tables and bouquets, colour changes, venue contact and access times, delivery and collection windows, and chases until each item is answered.
7. The week before, you get a checklist built from the confirmed record: items, quantities, delivery stops and times, venue contact, and anything still missing.
8. The day after, the couple gets a thank-you and one request for a review, sent once.

### A timeline you can copy
Set the timing to suit how you order flowers. This assumes a wedding booked months ahead:
| When | What the couple gets | What you get |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Enquiry day | Availability, starting prices, consultation link | A new record with the date and venue |
| After consultation | Proposal, deposit request, quote expiry date | Reminder if unpaid after a week |
| Deposit paid | Confirmation and the timeline of what you'll ask for | Date blocked in the calendar |
| 8 weeks before | Request for colour or style changes and venue contact | Replies saved on the record |
| 4 weeks before | Final counts: tables, bouquets, buttonholes, installations | Chased until answered |
| 2 weeks before | Delivery and collection windows, access, balance due date | Order sheet draft |
| Week of | Confirmation of times and stops | Checklist built from the record |
| Day after | Thank-you and one review request | Record closed |

The pre-contract information you must give still applies, so state your terms clearly before the deposit is taken. US rules differ by state. ## Painter and decorator quotes, colour sign-off and start-date messages that run themselves

A quote and colour sign-off workflow for painters and decorators sends each quote the same day as the visit, follows it up on a schedule until the customer answers, and then collects a written sign-off of every colour, finish and room before the first coat goes on. Painter and decorator quotes and colour sign-off are the two places a decorating job goes wrong before it has started. ### What the workflow does

4. When they accept, a colour and finish sign-off form goes out: one line per room and surface, with the paint brand, colour name, code and finish to fill in or confirm.

## Real estate lead follow-up automation for agents: fast replies, showings and long-term nurture
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/real-estate-agent-lead-follow-up/

Real estate lead follow-up automation is a workflow that catches every buyer or seller inquiry from portals, your website and missed calls, sends a personal first reply within minutes, offers showing times, and keeps in touch with people who aren't ready to move yet. The agent still has every real conversation; the workflow makes sure no lead waits and no lead is forgotten. In the US, texts and calls must follow the FCC's TCPA rules, and in Australia, emails and texts must follow the Spam Act 2003.

Real estate lead follow-up automation fixes the part of the job that slips first when you're busy: answering new inquiries. Leads arrive from property portals, your website, open house sign-in sheets, social ads and missed calls, often while you're in a showing or at a closing. By the evening, a lead that came in at 11 AM has heard nothing, and they've already asked another agent the same question. This page sets out a follow-up schedule you can copy, a first-reply message, how showing bookings can run on their own, and the US and Australian messaging rules to check before any of it goes live.

### Where agents lose leads
- Portal and website inquiries land in an inbox nobody checks during showings
- Every lead gets one reply, then nothing, because the next step lives in the agent's head
- Buyers who are 6 to 12 months out get dropped, and they buy with whoever kept in touch
- Showing times go back and forth over five texts before anything is booked
- Leads sit in email, a CRM, a spreadsheet and a phone, so nobody can see who's waiting
- Missed calls from unknown numbers are never returned: a [missed-call text-back](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/missed-call-text-back-contractors/) closes that gap

### A lead follow-up schedule you can copy
Adjust the timing to your market. The rule that matters: every lead has a next step and a date, and the automated messages stop as soon as the person replies, so a human takes over.
| When | Channel | What happens |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Within 5 minutes | Text and email | Personal first reply: you got their inquiry, one question about what they need, a link to pick a showing or call time |
| Same day, no reply | Agent task | Call reminder for the agent, with the lead's details and the listing they asked about |
| Day 2 | Email | Two or three similar listings, plus the booking link |
| Day 5 | Text | Short check-in: still looking, or should I hold off for now? |
| Day 14 | Email | Offer of a price guide or market update for their area |
| Monthly after that | Email | New listings that match what they said they want, until they reply or unsubscribe |
| Any reply | Agent task | Automated messages stop and the lead goes on the agent's call list |

### A first reply you can copy
First text to a new portal or website lead (edit the words in brackets):
```
Hi [first name], this is [agent name] with [brokerage]. Thanks for asking about [address]. Are you hoping to see it this week, or still getting a feel for the area? You can pick a time to view it here: [booking link]. Or just reply and I'll call you. Reply STOP to opt out.
```

### How showing bookings can run on their own
1. The lead picks a time from your booking link, which only shows the slots you've opened for that listing.
2. The workflow checks the showing rules you've set for the property (seller notice, lockbox or accompanied only) and sends you or the listing agent a request when approval is needed.
3. Once confirmed, the buyer gets the address, time, your phone number and parking notes, plus a reminder the day before and two hours before. The [no-show reminder schedule](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/reduce-appointment-no-shows/) has wording you can reuse.
4. After the showing, the buyer gets one message asking what they thought, and their answer is saved on the lead.
5. If they liked it, you get a task to call. If not, they move to the monthly listing emails with their new notes.

### US rules to check before you text or call leads
This is a summary of the FCC's rules in 47 CFR 64.1200 as published on ecfr.gov in November 2026, not legal advice. Check with your broker and your state's rules too.
- Marketing calls or texts sent with an autodialer or a prerecorded voice to a cell phone need the person's "prior express written consent": a signed agreement that names the phone number. Put a clear consent line on your website and open house forms, and keep the record.
- Telephone solicitations to a home must not be made before 8 a.m. or after 9 p.m. in the lead's local time. A good workflow holds messages overnight anyway.
- Numbers on the National Do Not Call Registry can't get telephone solicitations, with exceptions such as an established business relationship. The rule counts someone who inquired about your services in the last three months, or did business with you in the last 18 months.
- Under the current rule text, a reply of "stop", "quit", "end", "revoke", "opt out", "cancel" or "unsubscribe" revokes consent, and opt-outs must be honored within 10 business days at most. The workflow should stop every message at once.

### Australian rules for emails and texts
Under the Spam Act 2003 (legislation.gov.au), commercial emails and texts with an Australian link need the person's consent, must accurately identify who sent them and must include a working unsubscribe. The Act says an unsubscribe takes effect within 5 business days, and the ACMA enforces it. Your workflow should record where each lead's consent came from and stop messages as soon as someone unsubscribes.

### A consent and data checklist
- Every form that collects a phone number has a consent line, saved with the date and the form it came from
- Every text says who it's from and how to opt out
- An opt-out or unsubscribe stops all automated messages, on every channel, at once
- No automated message goes out overnight in the lead's own time zone
- One list holds every lead, its source, its next step and its date: a [spreadsheet or a CRM](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/spreadsheet-vs-crm-small-service-business/) both work

### What stays with you
Every real conversation, pricing advice, offers and negotiation. The workflow sends the first reply, books the showing and reminds you who to call. If AI drafts a reply to a lead's question, you approve it before it goes. For more first-reply wording, see [how to reply to new inquiries fast](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/reply-to-new-enquiries-fast/).

### How Mike Automations would build this
