## Personal trainer client check-ins, bookings and package renewals
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/personal-trainer-client-check-ins/

Personal trainer client check-ins are short, regular questions a trainer sends each client between sessions, usually weekly, about training, sleep, food, energy and anything that hurt, sometimes with progress photos. An automated check-in workflow sends the form on the same day each week, chases anyone who hasn't replied, puts the answers in one place for the trainer to read, and reminds clients before their session package runs out. The trainer still reads every answer and gives every piece of advice.

Personal trainer client check-ins are what keep a client going between sessions, and they're the first thing to slip when you're busy. You mean to message everyone on Sunday, you get through half, and the rest hear nothing until they turn up. Package renewals go the same way: the client uses their last session, nobody mentions it, and a month later they've drifted off. Below: a check-in form to copy, a session and renewal timeline, and the consent you need for progress photos and health details in the UK and the US.

### What a check-in workflow covers
- Session bookings: a confirmation when a session is booked, a reminder the day before with the place and what to bring, and a note if it's moved.
- The weekly check-in: one short form, sent on the same day each week, with a reminder to anyone who hasn't filled it in.
- Progress photos and measurements: collected through the form at the interval you set, only from clients who agreed to it.
- Package renewals: a message when a client has two sessions left, with their options, so nobody runs out without noticing.
- Your summary: one list of who checked in, who didn't, and any answer that mentions pain, illness or a missed week, so you know who to message first. Martial arts schools keep a similar list of attendance against [the requirements for each grading](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/martial-arts-school-memberships-and-gradings/).

### A weekly check-in form you can copy
Keep it short. A client will answer six questions every week. They won't answer twenty. Put it in Google Forms, Microsoft Forms or your coaching app, and send the link by text, WhatsApp or email.
Weekly check-in questions (edit to suit your clients):
```
1. How many of your planned workouts did you do this week? [0 to 7]
2. How was your energy this week? [1 to 5]
3. How did you sleep, on average? [Poorly / OK / Well]
4. How closely did you stick to your food plan? [1 to 5]
5. Anything sore, painful or worrying? If yes, tell me what and where. [Free text]
6. What's one thing you want to work on next week? [Free text]
Optional, only if you agreed to it: upload this week's progress photos (front, side, back).
```

### A session and renewal timeline
This assumes clients buy sessions in packages and do a weekly check-in. Adjust the days to your own week:
| When | Channel | What happens |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Session booked | Text or email | Confirmation with date, time, place and your cancellation policy |
| Day before each session | Text | Reminder with the time and place, and how to move it |
| Sunday, 6 PM | Text, WhatsApp or email | Weekly check-in link |
| Monday, 10 AM, no reply | Text | One reminder: "Two minutes, and it helps me plan your week" |
| Monday, noon | Your inbox | Summary of answers, with anything about pain or illness at the top |
| 2 sessions left in the package | Email | Sessions used, the renewal options and how to pay |
| Package used up, not renewed | Your list | You decide whether to call, ask in person or let it rest |

### Progress photos and health details: get consent first
A check-in collects personal information, and some of it is sensitive. Get this right before you automate anything.
- UK: the ICO says "data concerning health" is special category data, and that it covers information revealing something about a person's physical or mental health. Injuries, medical conditions and answers to a health questionnaire usually count. To use special category data you need one of the Article 9 conditions, and the ICO lists explicit consent as the first of them. For a trainer, that means a clear tick-box saying what you collect and why.
- Progress photos are personal data, and the ICO says digital photos of people don't automatically count as biometric data. They become biometric only after specific technical processing used to identify someone. Store them in one place only you can open, never in a shared group chat.
- Ask for photos as a separate, optional consent. A client can say yes to check-ins and no to photos, and can change their mind at any time. The form should still work without them.
- US: HHS's summary of the HIPAA Privacy Rule says it covers health plans, healthcare clearinghouses and healthcare providers who send health information electronically for standard transactions such as insurance claims. Most independent trainers who don't bill insurance are none of those, but check your state's privacy rules and treat health answers with the same care.
- Health screening: many trainers use the PAR-Q+ before a client starts. The form itself says its clearance is valid for a maximum of 12 months from the date it's completed and becomes invalid if the person's condition changes, so the workflow can remind you when a client's screening is a year old.

### Consent rules for the messages themselves
- Session reminders and check-in links are service messages for something the client has paid for. A message selling a new package or a nutrition add-on is marketing.
- UK: the ICO's PECR guidance allows emails and texts to your own customers about similar services under the "soft opt-in", if you got their details while selling to them, offered a simple opt-out at the time, and include an opt-out in every message.
- US: the FCC requires the person's consent before automated marketing texts to a mobile. Collect a clear tick-box when a client signs up and honour STOP replies straight away.

### Where check-ins usually break
- Check-ins live in a dozen WhatsApp chats, so nobody can see who replied
- A client mentions a sore knee in a long message and it gets missed
- Progress photos end up in your phone's camera roll next to your own pictures
- Clients use their last session and nobody mentions renewing
- Late cancellations eat your diary: [salon cancellation policy and deposits](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/salon-cancellation-policy-and-deposits/) sets out a policy that works the same way for sessions
- Missed sessions creep up: [reducing appointment no-shows](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/reduce-appointment-no-shows/) has a reminder pattern to copy

### What stays with you
Every piece of training, nutrition or injury advice. The workflow sends forms, chases replies, files photos, counts sessions and flags answers that mention pain. It never replies to a check-in with advice, changes a programme or tells anyone they're fine to train. If a client reports pain or a health change, you read it and you decide, and that may mean sending them to a GP or a physio. If AI drafts a summary or a reply, a person always approves it before it's sent. Monthly direct debit failures are a separate job, covered in [gym failed payment follow-up](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/gym-failed-payment-follow-up/), and if you also run group classes, see [fitness studio intro offer follow-up](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/fitness-studio-intro-offer-follow-up/). For storing client data safely, the [GDPR checklist for automating client data](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/gdpr-checklist-automating-client-data/) goes further.

To see the steps for your business first, [build your plan here](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/plan/?g=personal-trainer-client-check-ins).

Yes. Either works. The workflow sends the link, notices who hasn't answered and collects the answers into one sheet or summary for you.

### Do I need consent to collect progress photos?

## Service charge reminders for block management: demands, chasers and leaseholder queries
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/block-management-service-charge-reminders/

Service charge reminders for block management are the demands and follow-up messages a managing agent sends leaseholders so service charges are paid on time, from one list of every flat, its share and its due dates. In England, section 21B of the Landlord and Tenant Act 1985 says each service charge demand must come with the prescribed summary of tenants' rights and obligations, or the leaseholder may withhold payment. A workflow can attach the summary every time, send the reminders on schedule and log every query, while a person decides on arrears action.

Service charge reminders take up a lot of a block manager's week. Demands go out to dozens of leaseholders, some need three reminders, and a question about the reserve fund sits in someone's inbox for a fortnight. Get the paperwork wrong and the money may not be legally due yet. This page sets out what a demand in England must include, a reminder schedule and template you can copy, and how queries fit in.

### What every service charge demand must include (England)
Checked on legislation.gov.uk in November 2026, for residential long leases in England. Wales has its own summary regulations. This is a checklist for your process, not legal advice.
- The summary of rights and obligations. Section 21B of the Landlord and Tenant Act 1985 says a service charge demand must be accompanied by this summary. If it isn't, the leaseholder may withhold payment, and the lease's late-payment terms don't apply meanwhile.
- Its prescribed form. The Service Charges (Summary of Rights and Obligations, and Transitional Provision) (England) Regulations 2007 set the title "Service Charges - Summary of tenants' rights and obligations", the wording, and print of at least 10 point. Copy it from the current version on legislation.gov.uk, not an old letter.
- The landlord's name and address. Section 47 of the Landlord and Tenant Act 1987 says a written demand must give them, plus an address in England and Wales for notices if the landlord is outside it. Otherwise the service charge is treated as not due until the information is given.
- An address for notices. Under section 48 of the same Act, service charges are treated as not due until the landlord has given the leaseholder an address in England and Wales for notices.
- A separate summary for administration charges, such as a late-payment fee, under Schedule 11 to the Commonhold and Leasehold Reform Act 2002.

### Two deadlines your system should watch
Gov.uk said on 15 July 2026 that, under the Leasehold and Freehold Reform Act 2024, a new service charge demand form and an annual report to leaseholders will come into force "as soon as possible from 2027". Until then the current rules apply. Build your demand template so the wording can be swapped in one place when that happens.
- The 18-month rule. Section 20B of the Landlord and Tenant Act 1985 says leaseholders don't have to pay costs incurred more than 18 months before the demand, unless within those 18 months they were told in writing about the costs and that they would have to contribute. A workflow can flag costs nearing 18 months that haven't been demanded.
- Section 20 consultation. The Service Charges (Consultation Requirements) (England) Regulations 2003 apply to works costing any one leaseholder more than £250, or a long-term agreement costing any one leaseholder more than £100 in an accounting period. A workflow can warn you when a quote crosses those amounts. The consultation stays with you.

### A service charge reminder schedule you can copy
Set the timing to match your leases. This assumes half-yearly charges due in advance:
| When | What goes out | Who checks it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 4 weeks before the due date | Demand with the summary of rights, landlord's name and address, the flat's share and how to pay | Property manager approves the batch |
| Due date | Short email: payment due today, with the payment reference | Automatic |
| 7 days after | Friendly reminder with the balance and the original demand attached again | Automatic |
| 21 days after | Firmer reminder, offer to discuss a payment plan, contact name and phone | Automatic, stops if a query is open |
| 35 days after | Flat goes on the property manager's list with the full history | Property manager decides next steps |

### A reminder email you can copy
7-day reminder (edit the words in brackets):
```
Subject: Service charge for [flat number, block name], [period]

Dear [leaseholder name],

Our records show the service charge of £[amount] for [period], due on [due date], hasn't been received yet. The original demand, with the summary of your rights and obligations, is attached again for your reference.

You can pay by bank transfer to [account details] using the reference [reference]. If you've already paid, please reply with the date and we'll match it.

If you have a question about the charge or would like to talk about paying in instalments, reply to this email or call [name] on [phone].

Kind regards,
[name]
[managing agent], managing agent for [landlord or RMC name], [landlord's address]
```

### Handling leaseholder queries in the same process
1. Every reply is logged against the flat, with the date it arrived.
2. Reminders for that flat pause while the query is open.
3. The query goes to the right person: accounts for payments, the property manager for budgets and works, the [repair request list](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/letting-agent-maintenance-requests/) if it's a repair.
4. Requests for a cost summary or receipts get their own deadline. Gov.uk says leaseholders can ask for a summary of how the charge is worked out and see receipts, and that it's a criminal offence for the landlord not to provide it.
5. AI can draft a first reply from your budget and past answers. A person approves it before it's sent.
6. When the query is closed, reminders restart.

### What stays with you
Budgets, apportionments, section 20 consultations, every arrears decision and anything involving forfeiture, a tribunal or court. The workflow keeps the list, attaches the right documents, sends on time and records what happened. For a step-by-step chasing sequence in lettings, the [rent arrears reminder guide](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/rent-arrears-reminders-letting-agents/) uses a similar structure. Leaseholder details are personal data, so read the [GDPR checklist for automating client data](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/gdpr-checklist-automating-client-data/) before anything is connected.

To see the steps for your blocks first, [build your plan here](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/plan/?g=block-management-service-charge-reminders). ## Insurance broker claims updates: documents, status messages and insurer chasers
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/insurance-broker-claims-updates/

Insurance broker claims updates are the messages a broker sends a client while a claim is open: what documents are still needed, what the insurer or loss adjuster is doing, and what happens next. Automating them means each claim sits in one log with its stage and the date of the last contact, so the client gets a request or an update at set points and the insurer gets a polite chaser when a reply is overdue. A broker still writes or approves anything that gives a view on cover, liability or a settlement.

Insurance broker claims updates are the part of broking clients remember most. A client who has just had a flood, a theft or a van written off wants to know two things: what you need from them, and where the claim has got to. In a small brokerage, the answer usually sits in one account handler's inbox, and the client finds out by ringing. This page sets out what the FCA rules say about claims for insurers and intermediaries, a status message plan you can copy, the documents to ask for, and the parts of claims work that can run on their own. Renewals follow the same pattern, covered in [insurance broker renewal reminders](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/insurance-broker-renewal-reminders/).

### Where claims updates go wrong in a small brokerage
- The claim is notified to the insurer, then nobody tells the client what happens next
- Document requests go out one at a time, so the client sends photos this week and the repair estimate next month
- Chasing the insurer or the loss adjuster depends on someone remembering to check
- The client rings for an update and the handler who knows the claim is out
- Nobody can see at a glance which claims are waiting on the client, which on the insurer, and which have gone quiet

### What the rules say about claims (UK and US)
We checked these on 11 November 2026. In the UK, ICOBS 8.1 in the FCA Handbook says an insurer must handle claims promptly and fairly, give reasonable guidance to help a policyholder make a claim and appropriate information on its progress, not unreasonably reject a claim, and settle promptly once terms are agreed. For brokers, ICOBS 8.3 says that a firm without authority to deal with a claim should forward the claim notification to the insurer promptly, or tell the policyholder immediately that it can't deal with it. It also notes that a broker arranging a policy is likely to be the customer's agent, and that a broker who also acts for the insurer on claims must manage that conflict and tell the customer. For retail customers, the Consumer Duty (PRIN 2A.6) says firms must not put unreasonable barriers in the way when a customer wants to submit a claim, and names unreasonable delays in asking for or processing information and evidence as something to avoid. In the US, claims handling is set by each state. Many states base their rules on the NAIC's Unfair Claims Settlement Practices model act, which treats an insurer failing to acknowledge claim communications "with reasonable promptness" as an unfair practice; exact deadlines differ by state. This is a summary, not compliance advice: check the current position with your compliance support or your state insurance department.

### A claims update plan you can adapt
The stages and timings below are an example, not a rule. Set them per claim type: a windscreen claim and a commercial fire claim don't move at the same pace.
| Stage | Message to the client | Who does it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Claim reported | Thank you, here's your claim reference, here's what happens next and who your contact is | Automatic, from the broker's notes |
| Same day | Claim notified to the insurer, with the insurer's reference once you have it | Broker notifies, workflow confirms |
| Documents needed | One list of everything still needed, with an upload link | Automatic, broker picks the list |
| Every few days until complete | Reminder listing only what is still missing | Automatic |
| Waiting on the insurer | Status update: what the insurer or loss adjuster is doing and when you'll next check | Automatic, at the interval you set |
| Insurer reply overdue | Polite chaser to the claims handler with your reference | Drafted automatically, broker sends |
| Decision or offer | Outcome explained in plain words, with next steps | Broker writes or approves |
| Settled or closed | Confirmation, and how to complain if they're unhappy | Broker approves, workflow sends |

### Documents to ask for, by claim type
Ask once, with everything on one list, and the reminders only mention what's still missing. Check the list against what each insurer asks for. A checklist to start from:
- Every claim: policy number, date and time of the incident, what happened in the client's words, best phone number
- Property damage: photos of the damage, repair estimates or invoices, receipts or proof of ownership for damaged items
- Theft: the police crime reference number, a list of stolen items with values, proof of ownership
- Motor: the other driver's details, photos of both vehicles, witness details, the repairer's estimate
- Business interruption: the period affected and the figures the insurer asks for, often from the client's accountant
- Liability claims: any letter or claim form received from the third party, sent on unanswered

### A claims update message you can copy
Status update while waiting on the insurer (edit the words in brackets):
```
Subject: Your claim [claim reference]: update

Hi [first name],

A quick update on your [policy type] claim for [short description] on [incident date].

Where it is: [the insurer has appointed a loss adjuster / the insurer is reviewing the documents / we are waiting for the repairer's report].

What we need from you: [nothing at the moment / the items listed here: link].

What happens next: we will check with the insurer again on [date] and update you then, even if there's no news.

If anything changes on your side, reply to this email or call us on [phone].

[your name]
[brokerage name]
```

### A chaser to the insurer you can copy
Sent when an insurer reply is overdue (broker approves):
```
Subject: [insurer claim reference] / [client name]: update requested

Hello,

We're following up on the claim above, notified on [date]. Our last contact was on [date], when [what was agreed or requested].

Could you let us know the current position and the next step? Our client is asking for an update.

Thank you,
[your name]
[brokerage name], [phone]
```

### What an automated claims workflow does
1. Keeps one claims log, in your broker system or a spreadsheet, with the stage, the insurer's reference and the date of the last contact for each claim.
2. Sends the client an acknowledgement with your reference and named contact when a claim is logged.
3. Sends the document list for that claim type, with an upload link, and files what comes back next to the claim.
4. Reminds the client about only the documents still missing, and stops when the list is complete.
5. Sends a status update at the interval you set, so the client hears from you before they need to ring.
6. Drafts a chaser to the insurer when a reply is overdue, for a broker to approve and send.
7. Gives the team one view of every open claim and who it's waiting on.

### What stays with your team
Notifying the claim, every view on cover or liability, and any conversation about an offer or a rejection. The workflow never tells a client whether they're covered and never accepts a settlement. Bad news goes out from a person, not a template. If AI summarises a client's account of the incident or drafts an update, a broker reads and approves it before it goes out. Claims files hold personal and sometimes health data, so check the [data protection points for automating client data](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/gdpr-checklist-automating-client-data/).

A [free 15-minute call](https://mikeautomations.github.io/call/) about how claims run in your brokerage today and where clients wait. Within 48 hours you get a written plan with a fixed price and a clear definition of "working", for example: every open claim has a stage and a next update date, and no client goes longer than the interval you set without hearing from you. It's built on the tools you already use (your broker system or spreadsheet, email, forms and texts, where they allow a connection), so nobody learns a new system. Live in 2-3 days. [Workflow automation is a fixed $2,000](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/pricing/), and you pay once it's running and you're happy with it, as set out in the [pay-when-happy agreement](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/agreement/). To see the steps first, [build your plan here](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/plan/?g=insurance-broker-claims-updates).

### Does this replace our broker software or claims system?
No. It reads the claims log you already keep and does the requesting, reminding and updating around it. If your software can't be connected, a spreadsheet or a daily export can be the claims log.

### Can the workflow tell a client whether a claim is covered?
No. Cover, liability and settlement are broker decisions. The workflow sends requests and progress updates, and a broker writes or approves anything that gives a view on the outcome.

### What do the FCA rules say about brokers and claims?
ICOBS 8.3 says a broker without authority to handle a claim should forward the notification to the insurer promptly, or tell the policyholder immediately that it can't deal with it. ICOBS 8.1 puts the duty to handle claims promptly and fairly on insurers.

Yes, if that's how your clients prefer to reply. The files are saved to the claim the same way. See [text or WhatsApp for documents](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/text-or-whatsapp-clients-for-documents/) for the trade-offs.

## Courier proof of delivery, failed delivery rebooking and invoices with the POD attached
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/courier-proof-of-delivery-and-failed-delivery-messages/

Courier proof of delivery (POD) is the record that a parcel reached the right place: the time, the name of the person who took it or where it was left, a photo and, if needed, a signature. A small courier can send that record to the customer automatically the moment the driver marks the drop as done, send a rebooking message when a delivery fails, and attach the POD to the invoice so nobody has to dig it out when a customer asks.

Courier proof of delivery is the part of the job that customers only care about when something goes wrong. A business customer says the parcel never arrived, a shop asks for the signature before it pays your invoice, or a failed delivery sits in the van for three days because nobody told the recipient how to rebook. In a small courier firm the proof often exists, on a driver's phone or in an app, but it doesn't reach the people who need it unless someone in the office sends it. This page sets out what a good POD contains, the messages to send after each drop and each failed attempt, a failed delivery message you can copy, and how to get the POD onto the invoice.

### What a proof of delivery should contain
Agree the list with your business customers before you build anything, because some of them will ask for more than others. A useful POD record has:
- The job or consignment reference that also appears on your invoice
- Date and time the driver marked the drop as done
- Where it was left: handed over, reception, a neighbour (with house number) or an agreed safe place
- The name of the person who took it, and a signature if the customer asked for one
- A photo of the parcel at the drop point, taken so it shows the door or the label, not people
- The driver's name or ID, and any note (damaged packaging, refused, wrong address)

### Why your customers want it
If you deliver for shops or online sellers in the UK, they usually carry the risk until the parcel arrives. Section 29 of the Consumer Rights Act 2015, on legislation.gov.uk, says goods sold to a consumer stay at the trader's risk until they come into the physical possession of the consumer or a person the consumer named to take them (with an exception when the consumer commissions their own carrier). So a retailer facing a "never arrived" claim needs your POD quickly. In the US, who carries the loss depends on the sale terms and state law, so ask each retail customer what proof they want from you and put it in writing. Either way, a POD that arrives on its own, within minutes, saves you the phone call.

### The messages after every drop and every failed attempt
| Moment | Who gets it | What it says |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Out for delivery | Recipient | Today's delivery window, the reference and how to leave instructions or pick a safe place |
| Delivered | Sender (your customer), and the recipient if they want it | Delivered at [time], left [where], received by [name], with the photo and a link to the full POD |
| Failed attempt | Recipient, copied to the sender | Why it failed, where the parcel is now, and a link or reply to choose a new day or a safe place |
| No reply after 24 hours | Recipient | One reminder with the same options |
| Still no reply after your agreed limit | Your office and the sender | Return or hold decision, made by a person |
| End of the day or week | Your office | Invoice draft for each customer with every POD for those jobs attached |

### A failed delivery message you can copy
Sent when the driver marks an attempt as failed (edit the words in brackets):
```
Hi [first name], we tried to deliver your parcel from [sender] today at [time] but [reason: nobody was in / we couldn't get access]. It's back at our depot. Reply 1 to rebook for [next working day], 2 to pick another day, or 3 to tell us a safe place to leave it. Reference: [reference]. [courier name], [phone]
```

### How the workflow runs
1. Jobs come in from your booking form, email or the spreadsheet your customers fill in, and each one gets a reference.
2. The driver uses the app or form they already have to mark each drop: delivered (with photo, name and signature if needed) or failed (with a reason).
3. Delivered: the POD is saved to a folder by customer and date, and the sender gets the delivered message with the photo straight away.
4. Failed: the recipient gets the rebooking message by text or WhatsApp, and their reply updates the job for the next route.
5. Anything the workflow can't match, such as an unclear reply or a damaged-parcel note, goes to the office list for a person to handle.
6. At the end of each day or week, invoice drafts are made in your accounts software with the PODs attached. A person checks and sends them.

### Getting the POD onto the invoice
Most "we never got it" payment disputes end when the customer sees the photo. Xero's developer documentation says an attachment can be set to show with an accounts receivable invoice when the customer views it online, so the POD photos sit next to the invoice they're paying. QuickBooks Online also lets you add attachments to an invoice, but whether they go out with the invoice email depends on your settings, so test it with one invoice first. If a customer still hasn't paid, the [invoice payment reminder workflow](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/invoice-payment-reminders/) carries on from there, with the POD link in each reminder.

### Where courier paperwork usually breaks
- Photos stay on the driver's phone, and the office has to ask for them when a customer complains
- The POD reference doesn't match the invoice line, so nobody can prove which drop it was
- Failed deliveries are rebooked by phone, and a recipient who doesn't answer waits days
- Customers ring to ask "has it arrived?" because nobody sent the delivered message, and calls missed while driving can be covered by a [missed-call text-back](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/missed-call-text-back-contractors/)
- Invoices go out once a month with no proof, and payment waits until the office finds it

### What stays with you
Routes, prices, damage and lost-parcel claims, and every decision to return or hold a parcel. The workflow sends the messages, files the proof and drafts the invoices. Photos and signatures are personal data, so keep them only as long as your customers need them and say so in your privacy notice: the [GDPR checklist for automating client data](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/gdpr-checklist-automating-client-data/) covers the UK side. If AI drafts a reply to a recipient, a person always approves it before it's sent.

No. If your drivers already use an app that records drops, it starts from that. If they don't, a simple form on their phone that takes a photo, a name and a signature is enough.

## Grant reporting deadlines: one calendar, reminders and report drafts for small charities
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/grant-reporting-deadline-reminders/

Grant reporting deadlines are the dates in each grant agreement by which a charity or nonprofit must send its funder progress, financial and final reports. A small charity can automate them by keeping every grant and its report dates in one calendar, reminding the right staff weeks ahead, collecting the figures and stories each report needs, and drafting the report for a person to check and send. For US federal awards, the Uniform Guidance (2 CFR 200.344) says a recipient must submit all final reports no later than 120 calendar days after the period of performance ends.

Grant reporting deadlines catch small charities out for a simple reason: each funder sets its own dates, forms and questions, and they live in a dozen grant agreements in a shared drive. The person who wrote the bid has often moved on by the time the report is due, and someone ends up chasing staff for numbers and photos the week of the deadline. A missed report can hold up the next payment or count against you in the next bid. This page gives you a grants calendar you can copy, a reminder timeline, a message to collect what each report needs, and the parts that are worth automating.

### Where the deadlines come from
Most of your dates are set by the funder, in the grant agreement or offer letter, not by law. Read each agreement for the report type, the due date, the format (an online portal, a form or a letter) and what happens if it's late. A few dates are fixed by rules, checked on 11 November 2026:
| Rule | Who it applies to | What the source says |
| --- | --- | --- |
| US Uniform Guidance, 2 CFR 200.328 and 200.329 | Recipients of US federal awards | Annual financial and performance reports are due no later than 90 calendar days after the reporting period; quarterly or semiannual reports no later than 30 calendar days after it |
| US Uniform Guidance, 2 CFR 200.344 | Recipients and subrecipients of US federal awards | All final reports are due no later than 120 calendar days after the period of performance ends. Subrecipients report to the pass-through entity within 90 calendar days, or an earlier agreed date |
| IRS annual return | US tax-exempt organisations | The IRS says Form 990, 990-EZ or 990-PF is due by the 15th day of the 5th month after the end of your accounting period: 15 May for a calendar year |
| Charity Commission annual return | Charities in England and Wales that must file one | Gov.uk says you must submit it within 10 months of the end of your financial year: 31 October for a 31 December year end |

### A grants calendar you can copy
One row per report, not per grant. A three-year grant with six-monthly reports has six rows plus a final report. Keep it in a spreadsheet your team already uses; the [Airtable or Google Sheets question](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/airtable-vs-google-sheets-small-business/) can wait.
| Column | Example (for illustration) |
| --- | --- |
| Funder and grant name | Community trust, youth mentoring grant |
| Report type | Six-month progress report |
| Period covered | 1 April to 30 September |
| Due date | 31 October |
| Where it's submitted | Funder's online portal |
| Owner | Project lead |
| Who supplies what | Project lead: numbers and a case story. Finance: spend against budget |
| Status | Not started, collecting, drafting, approved, sent |
| Date sent and confirmation | Saved receipt or portal screenshot |

### A reminder timeline that works
1. When a grant is awarded: someone enters every report date from the agreement into the calendar, and the agreement is saved with it. This is the one manual step, and it's the one that matters most.
2. Six weeks before a due date: the owner gets an email listing what the report needs, with the funder's questions copied from the agreement or last year's form.
3. Four weeks before: each person who supplies figures, photos or a case story gets a request with a simple form and a date two weeks before the deadline.
4. Two weeks before: anyone who hasn't replied gets one reminder, and the owner sees who is still missing.
5. Ten days before: the answers are pulled into a draft report in the funder's order, for the owner to edit.
6. Five days before: the draft goes to whoever signs it off (your chief officer, treasurer or a trustee).
7. After sending: the date and the confirmation are logged, and the next report date for that grant moves to the top of the list.

### A data request you can copy
Request to project staff, four weeks before the report (edit the words in brackets):
```
Hi [first name], our [report type] for [funder] is due on [due date]. It covers [period start] to [period end]. Could you fill in this short form by [date two weeks before]: [form link]. It asks for: [number of people supported], [sessions or activities run], [one short story of the difference it made, with the person's permission], [up to three photos, with consent to share], and [anything that didn't go to plan]. If a figure isn't available yet, say so in the form and give your best estimate. Thanks, [your name]
```

### What's worth automating, and what isn't
- Worth automating: the reminders, the requests to staff, the follow-ups, pulling answers into a draft in the funder's order, and logging what was sent and when.
- Worth automating: a spend-against-budget table from your accounts export, so finance isn't retyping figures. Someone checks it before it goes out.
- Keep with a person: what the report says. An AI tool can draft text from your staff's answers, but a person reads every word, checks every figure and approves it before it goes to a funder.
- Keep with a person: anything about a change to the project, an underspend or a missed target. Talk to the funder first, then report.
- Keep with a person: consent for stories and photos. The workflow can ask for it and record it, but someone decides what's shared. Our [GDPR checklist for automating client data](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/gdpr-checklist-automating-client-data/) covers the basics for UK organisations.

### It fits with the rest of your admin
The same calendar and reminder pattern runs other repeat charity work. Gift Aid claims and donor records are covered in [Gift Aid declarations](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/charity-gift-aid-declarations/), and chasing figures from staff works much like [timesheet chasing for recruiters](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/recruitment-timesheet-chasing/). If you're not sure where to start, a [process map](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/process-map-template-small-business/) of how one report gets written today will show where the time goes.

A [free 15-minute call](https://mikeautomations.github.io/call/) about how you track grants and write reports today. Within 48 hours you get a written plan with a fixed price and a clear definition of "working". It's built on the tools you already use (a shared drive, a spreadsheet, email and online forms), so your team doesn't learn a new system. Live in 2-3 days. To see the steps first, [build your plan here](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/plan/?g=grant-reporting-deadline-reminders).

### When are grant reports usually due?
Whenever the grant agreement says. Many funders ask for progress reports during the grant and a final report after it ends. For US federal awards, 2 CFR 200.344 says final reports are due no later than 120 calendar days after the period of performance ends.

### Can AI write our grant reports?
It can draft from your staff's answers and your figures, which saves starting from a blank page. A person always checks every figure and approves the text before it's sent. Nothing goes to a funder automatically.

## RFI and submittal tracking for small general contractors
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/construction-rfi-and-submittal-tracking/

RFI and submittal tracking means keeping one log of every request for information and every submittal on a job, with who has it, when it was sent and the date a response is due under your contract. An automated workflow numbers each item, sends it to the architect, engineer or sub, reminds them before the due date, files the answer in the job folder and gives you a weekly list of what is late. Your project manager still writes the questions and decides what to build.

RFI and submittal tracking is where small general contractors lose days without noticing. A question about a detail goes to the architect by email, the answer comes back three weeks later in a reply to a different thread, and the crew has already built it the old way. Shop drawings sit with a sub because nobody asked twice. A small GC usually runs this from inboxes and memory. This page sets out what a log needs, a log layout you can copy, an RFI template, and the parts that can run on their own while you keep the decisions.

### RFIs and submittals: what each one is
- An RFI (request for information) is a written question to the design team when the drawings or specs are unclear, conflict or leave something out. The answer can change the work, so it may lead to a [change order](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/change-order-approval-workflow/).
- A submittal is something you or your subs send for review before the work is built or the material is ordered: shop drawings, product data, samples, test reports and closeout documents.
- On federal jobs, the unified submittal list used with UFGS Section 01 33 00 (Submittal Procedures, published on WBDG) sorts submittals into 11 types, from SD-01 Preconstruction Submittals and SD-02 Shop Drawings to SD-11 Closeout Submittals. Private specs often have a similar Division 01 section.
- The federal clause FAR 52.236-21 says the contractor must coordinate shop drawings and review them for accuracy, completeness and compliance with the contract before submitting, and that the contracting officer's approval does not relieve the contractor of responsibility for errors or omissions in them. Private contracts often say much the same.

### Where tracking breaks on a small job
- RFIs go out as loose emails with no number, so nobody can say how many are open
- The response time in the contract or spec is never written into the log, so nobody knows when an answer is late
- A sub's shop drawings are due to you but nobody chases them until the material is needed
- A submittal returned for revisions is filed as done, and the resubmittal never happens

### What an RFI and submittal log should hold
Keep one row per item, not one row per email. For illustration, a log on a small commercial fit-out might look like this on May 12:
| No. | Type | Subject | With | Sent | Due back | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| RFI-007 | RFI | Ceiling height conflict at corridor B | Architect | May 1 | May 8 | Late, second reminder sent |
| RFI-008 | RFI | Door hardware set for room 104 | Architect | May 6 | May 13 | Open |
| SUB-03-01 | Shop drawings | Storefront framing | Glazing sub to GC | Requested Apr 28 | May 9 | Late from sub, call today |
| SUB-05-02 | Product data | Flooring, second submission | Architect | May 2 | May 16 | Under review |
| SUB-02-01 | Samples | Paint colors | Owner | Apr 20 | Apr 30 | Approved, filed |

### Setting the response dates
The due date in your log should come from the contract, not from habit. Look in the general conditions and the Division 01 spec sections for how RFIs and submittals must be sent and how long the reviewer has. Some contracts give a number of days, some ask for a submittal schedule agreed at the start, and some only say the review must be reasonably prompt. Write whatever yours says into the log when the job starts, and every item gets its due date automatically. If it is silent, agree a turnaround with the architect in writing. This page isn't legal advice: if a late answer turns into a claim for time or money, take your log to your attorney.

### An RFI you can copy
RFI email to the architect (edit the words in brackets):
```
Subject: RFI-[number], [project name]: [short subject]

Hi [name],

RFI number: [number]
Drawing or spec reference: [sheet, detail or section]
Question: [one clear question]
Our suggested answer: [what you propose, or "none"]
Possible effect on cost or schedule: [none known / describe]
Answer needed by: [date from the contract or agreed turnaround]

Photos or marked-up drawings are attached. Please reply to this email so the answer is filed with the RFI.

Thanks,
[your name], [company], [phone]
```

### What the automated workflow does
1. Your project manager fills in a short form for each RFI or submittal, on a phone or laptop, with the job, the question or item, the reference and any photos. A question raised in a [daily site report](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/construction-daily-site-reports/) can start the same form.
2. The workflow gives it the next number, works out the due date from the turnaround you set for that job and adds a row to the log.
3. It emails the item to the right reviewer from your own address, using the template, with the attachments in one place.
4. It reminds the reviewer a few days before the due date and again on the day, and tells you when an item is late. For submittals a sub owes you, it chases the sub on the dates you set, the same way a [COI tracker](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/subcontractor-coi-tracking/) chases certificates.
5. When the reply arrives, it files the answer and any marked-up drawings in the job folder, updates the status and tells the site lead. A submittal returned for revisions goes back on the list as a resubmittal, not as done.
6. If an answer may change cost or time, it creates a task for you to decide whether a change order is needed.
7. Every Monday it sends you one list per job: open items, items due this week and late items, with how many days each is late.

### What stays with you
Writing the questions, reviewing a sub's drawings before they go out, deciding what to build and whether to ask for a change order. The workflow keeps the log, sends and chases on time and files the answers. If AI drafts a reminder or summarizes an answer, a person checks it before it's sent or used.

A [free 15-minute call](https://mikeautomations.github.io/call/) about how you handle RFIs and submittals today and where items get lost. Within 48 hours you get a [written plan with a fixed price](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/how-it-works/) and a clear definition of "working". It's built on the tools you already use (email, a spreadsheet, your job folders), so your team doesn't learn a new system. Live in 2-3 days. [Workflow automation is a fixed $2,000](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/pricing/), and you pay once it's running and you're happy with it, under a [pay-when-happy agreement](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/agreement/). To see the steps for your jobs first, [build your plan here](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/plan/?g=construction-rfi-and-submittal-tracking) or [try the demo](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/try/).

### What's the difference between an RFI and a submittal?
An RFI asks the design team a question about the drawings or specs. A submittal sends something for review before it's built or ordered, such as shop drawings, product data or samples.

### How long does an architect have to answer an RFI?
Whatever your contract says. Some contracts set a number of days, some tie reviews to an agreed submittal schedule, and some only say reasonably prompt. Put your contract's terms into the log so every item has a due date.

### Do I need dedicated construction project software?
Not for a few jobs at a time. A log in a spreadsheet with automatic numbering, reminders and filing covers most small GCs. If you run many large projects with big design teams, dedicated software may fit better.

### Can subs send their submittals through the same workflow?
Yes. Each sub gets a request with an upload link and a due date, gets reminded until it arrives, and you review it before it goes to the architect.

## Pool service visit reports, sent from the route without the evening paperwork
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/pool-service-visit-reports/

Automated pool service visit reports are short reports that go to the pool owner after every route stop, built from what the technician enters on their phone: the water readings, the chemicals added, the work done and before-and-after photos. The same workflow can send repair quotes for the owner to approve in writing and remind them about the monthly service bill, while the technician still decides what the pool needs.

Pool service visit reports are what owners judge you on. Most owners never see the technician, so a report with readings and a photo of a clean pool is the only proof the visit happened. Many small pool companies still send these by hand at the end of the day, or not at all, and the first the owner hears about a cracked pump lid is a bill. This page is for small pool service companies in the US and Australia. It covers what a visit report should hold, the flow from route stop to paid invoice, a report message you can copy, and what stays with the technician.

### Where pool route admin goes wrong
- Reports are typed up at night from notes and memory, so readings get mixed up between pools.
- The owner gets no report at all, then asks why the water is green after a storm.
- A technician spots a worn pump seal or a leaking valve, mentions it to nobody, and it fails a month later.
- Repair quotes are agreed in a phone call, and nobody can show what the owner said yes to.
- Gate codes, dogs and locked equipment pads are written on scraps of paper, so a new technician loses time at every stop.
- Recurring service bills go out late or get missed when the office is busy in peak season.

### What a pool visit report should include
Keep every report in the same layout so owners learn where to look. As a reference point for readings, the CDC's home pool guidance (checked November 2026) recommends a pH of 7.0 to 7.8 and free chlorine of at least 1 ppm in pools, or at least 2 ppm if you use cyanuric acid (stabilizer), and at least 3 ppm in hot tubs. The CDC also tells owners to test chlorine and pH at least twice a day, which a weekly visit can't do, so the report is a good place to remind them. Your own targets and any local health rules come first; in Australia, check your state's guidance.
1. Owner, pool address, date and time of the visit, and the technician's name.
2. Water readings taken on site: free chlorine, pH and whatever else you test (alkalinity, stabilizer, salt).
3. Chemicals added and how much.
4. Work done: skimming, brushing, vacuuming, baskets emptied, filter cleaned or backwashed.
5. Before and after photos of the water, plus a photo of anything that needs attention.
6. Equipment notes: pump, filter, heater, chlorinator, with any issue found.
7. Anything the owner should do before the next visit, and the next visit date.

### From route stop to paid invoice
For illustration: a weekly service customer on a monthly bill. Your visit frequency and billing terms are your own.
| When | What happens | Automatic or a person? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Morning of the route | Technician gets each stop's gate code, access notes, last readings and any open repairs | Automatic |
| At the pool | Technician fills in a short form on their phone: readings, chemicals, work done, photos | Technician |
| After the stop | Report built from the form and sent to the owner by email or text, then saved to the pool's record | Automatic, office spot-checks |
| Reading out of range | Flagged to the office and noted for the next visit | Automatic, a person decides what to do |
| Repair found | Photo, description and price sent to the owner with approve and decline links; the reply is saved | Draft automatic, a person sets the price |
| Repair approved | Job added to the schedule and the owner told the date | Automatic |
| Start of the month | Service invoice raised in your accounting tool, with a reminder if it isn't paid by the due date | Automatic |

### A visit report message you can copy
Sent after each visit (edit the words in brackets):
```
Hi [first name], your pool at [address] was serviced today at [time] by [technician].

Readings: free chlorine [x] ppm, pH [x], [other readings].
Added: [chemicals and amounts].
Done: [skimmed, brushed, vacuumed, baskets emptied, filter cleaned].
Photos: [link]

[Note: we noticed [issue]. We'll send you a quote to approve before doing any work.]

Next visit: [day, date]. Questions? Reply to this message or call [phone].
[company name]
```

### Repair approvals in writing
Extra work is where pool companies lose money and goodwill. When the technician finds a problem, the owner should get a photo, a plain description and a price, and the work waits until they say yes. That reply is saved against the pool, so there is no argument when the bill arrives. It works the same way as a [change order approval](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/change-order-approval-workflow/) for builders. If the owner doesn't reply, one reminder goes out after a couple of days, then the office calls. Quotes that go quiet can follow the pattern in our [estimate follow-up email templates](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/estimate-follow-up-email-templates-contractors/).

### Recurring billing reminders
Most pool service is billed monthly or per visit on a standing arrangement. The workflow can raise each invoice from the visits recorded in the month, list the visit dates, send it from QuickBooks or Xero, and remind the owner if it's unpaid by the due date, as set out in our [invoice payment reminders](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/invoice-payment-reminders/) guide. If you take card or bank payments on a schedule, it can also tell you when a payment fails so someone calls the owner before the next visit.

### What stays with the technician and the office
The workflow sends, files and reminds. It doesn't test water, choose chemicals or diagnose equipment. The technician decides what the pool needs, the office sets repair prices, and any message written by AI is approved by a person before it's sent. Complaints, green-pool call-outs and safety concerns go straight to a person. Seasonal services work the same way: see [lawn care seasonal renewals](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/lawn-care-seasonal-renewals/) and [pest control contract visits](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/pest-control-contract-visits-and-reports/).

Within 48 hours you get a written plan with a fixed price and a clear definition of "working". It's built on the tools you already use (your pool or field service app, a phone form, email or text, QuickBooks or Xero), so your technicians don't learn a new system. Live in 2-3 days. [Workflow automation is a fixed $2,000](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/pricing/), and you pay once it's running and you're happy with it, as set out in the [pay-when-happy agreement](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/agreement/). To see the steps for your pool company first, [build your plan here](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/plan/?g=pool-service-visit-reports).

### What should a pool service visit report include?
The visit date and technician, water readings, chemicals added, work done, before and after photos, any equipment issue and the next visit date. Keep the same layout every time.

### What chlorine and pH levels does the CDC recommend for a home pool?
The CDC's home pool guidance recommends pH 7.0 to 7.8 and free chlorine of at least 1 ppm, or at least 2 ppm if you use cyanuric acid. Hot tubs need at least 3 ppm. Local health rules can differ.

## SIA licence expiry tracking and shift confirmations for security companies
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/security-company-licence-and-shift-confirmations/

SIA licence expiry tracking means keeping one list of every officer's SIA licence number, type and expiry date, and reminding each officer to renew in time. Gov.uk says SIA licences last 3 years, do not renew automatically, and can be renewed from 4 months before expiry without losing the time left. A security company can use the same list to confirm every shift by text and to check each officer's licence is valid on the shift date before they are deployed.

SIA licence expiry tracking is the job nobody in a small security company owns until a licence runs out the week before a big event. Expiry dates sit on officers' cards or in a spreadsheet nobody checks against the SIA register. Shift confirmations are no better: a WhatsApp group and a scheduler who finds out at 6 AM that a site is uncovered. Below are the licence rules as gov.uk states them, a reminder schedule and messages you can copy, and a shift confirmation routine that runs from the same list.

### The SIA licence rules your tracking should follow
From the SIA's pages on gov.uk, checked in November 2026. The SIA updates its criteria (the current ones are in its May 2026 Get Licensed booklet), so check before you rely on them.
- All licences last 3 years, except a vehicle immobiliser licence (Northern Ireland only), which lasts 1 year.
- A licence does not renew automatically. If it has already expired, the officer cannot renew: they must apply for a new licence.
- Officers can apply to renew 4 months before expiry. Any time left on the current licence is added to the new one.
- The fee is £204 for a new licence or a renewal, since 1 April 2026. An employer can pay it once the officer links their SIA online account with the employer's.
- Door supervisors and security guards renewing need the Level 2 refresher award for their role, and to take it they need an Emergency First Aid at Work qualification (or equivalent) valid for at least another 12 months. So track first aid expiry too.
- Front line officers must wear their licence where it can be seen while working, unless the work is covert.
- Gov.uk says you must check someone has the correct licence before hiring them, on the SIA register. The SIA's free Licence Status Checker lets a business keep watchlists of its officers, for example by site.

### Why a record of each check matters
Section 5 of the Private Security Industry Act 2001 makes it an offence to provide security services through someone doing licensable work without the licence for it, with up to five years in prison on indictment. The same section gives a defence if you can show you took all reasonable steps to stop that happening. A dated log of every licence check, reminder and reply is the kind of evidence that defence relies on. It is not a guarantee, and this is not legal advice.

### A licence reminder schedule you can copy
This assumes you hold each officer's licence number, licence type, expiry date and first aid expiry date. Gov.uk says the SIA cannot tell you exactly how long an application will take, so start early.
| When | Who gets it | What happens |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 5 months before expiry | Officer | Check the first aid certificate will still be valid for 12 months; if not, book first aid and the refresher course |
| 4 months before (renewal opens) | Officer, copy to the office | Renewal is open: the steps, whether you pay the fee, and a request to reply with the application reference |
| Every 2 weeks until a reference arrives | Officer | Short reminder with the expiry date and the link to the SIA online account |
| 8 weeks before, no reference | Manager | Name goes on a call list |
| 4 weeks before, still not renewed | Scheduler | Officer is flagged: no shifts booked past the expiry date for that role |
| Every week | Office | Every active officer is checked on the SIA register or watchlist and the date of the check is saved |

### A licence renewal message you can copy
Sent 4 months before expiry (edit the words in brackets):
```
Hi [first name], your SIA [licence type] licence ends on [expiry date]. You can renew from today, and you won't lose the time left on it. You'll need the Level 2 refresher award and a first aid certificate valid for at least 12 more months. [We pay the £204 fee: please accept the link request from us in your SIA online account. / You pay the fee yourself.] Please reply with your application reference once you've applied. We can't book you on shifts after [expiry date] until the new licence shows on the SIA register. [your name], [company], [phone]
```

### How shift confirmations work from the same list
1. When the rota is published, each officer gets one message per shift: site, address, times, role, uniform and site contact.
2. Before it goes, the workflow checks the officer's licence type matches the role and is valid on the shift date. If not, the shift goes back to the scheduler.
3. The officer replies YES or NO by your deadline, for example 48 hours before. The reply is saved against the shift.
4. No reply by the deadline: one more message, then the shift goes on the scheduler's list to phone.
5. A NO sends a cover request to free officers with the right licence. The scheduler picks who gets it.
6. The day before, a reminder. Shifts starting less than 11 hours after the officer's last finish are flagged: gov.uk gives workers 11 hours' daily rest, but lists security and surveillance among the exceptions to some working time limits, so a person decides.
7. Optional: the officer replies ON when they arrive, and no reply 15 minutes after the start alerts the duty manager. This doesn't replace your lone worker system.

### A shift confirmation text you can copy
Sent when the rota is published:
```
Hi [first name], new shift for you: [day, date], [start] to [finish], [site name], [address]. Role: [security officer / door supervisor]. Uniform: [uniform]. Site contact: [name, phone]. Please reply YES to confirm or NO if you can't make it, by [deadline]. [company]
```

### Where licence tracking and confirmations usually break
- Expiry dates are typed from the card once and never checked against the SIA register, so a suspended or revoked licence goes unnoticed
- Nobody tracks first aid expiry, so an officer finds out at renewal time that they can't book the refresher yet
- Confirmations are a thumbs-up in a group chat, so there is no record of who agreed to which shift

### What stays with you
Checking documents and the register, and deciding who works where, stay with a person. The workflow keeps the list, sends messages on time and records replies. Licence and conviction details are sensitive personal data: keep only what you need and see our [GDPR checklist for automating client data](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/gdpr-checklist-automating-client-data/). If AI drafts a message or a reply, a person always approves it before it's sent. Care and recruitment businesses run a similar routine for [carer compliance documents](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/home-care-agency-carer-compliance/) and [candidate compliance](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/candidate-compliance-document-chasing/).

### How early can an officer renew an SIA licence?
Gov.uk says 4 months before the current licence expires. Time left on the old licence is added to the new one, so renewing early loses nothing.

### What happens if a licence expires before it is renewed?
Gov.uk says an expired licence can't be renewed, so the officer must apply for a new one. They can't do licensable work for you until the new licence is granted.

### Can we pay for or submit renewals for our officers?
Gov.uk says an employer can pay the fee once the officer links their SIA online account with yours. Submitting applications on an officer's behalf is through the SIA's Licence Assist and Licence Management services, which are for SIA approved contractors only.

## Tattoo consent forms and deposits, plus age checks, aftercare and touch-ups
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/tattoo-studio-consent-and-deposits/

Tattoo consent forms and deposits can run as one automated booking workflow: the client pays a deposit to hold the slot, gets the consent and health form to fill in before the day, and receives aftercare instructions and a touch-up reminder afterwards. In Great Britain the Tattooing of Minors Act 1969 makes it an offence to tattoo anyone under 18, so the workflow should ask for photo ID before the session and the artist should check it in person. A person still reviews every health answer and makes every decision about whether to tattoo.

Tattoo consent forms and deposits are where most studio admin goes wrong: a deposit agreed in a DM and never written down, a paper consent form filled in at the counter while the client is nervous, a health answer nobody followed up, and aftercare that depends on the client keeping a leaflet. This page gives you the UK rules as the official sources state them, a deposit policy and a pre-appointment message you can copy, and the run of messages a studio can send without anyone typing them. It's written for UK studios first, with notes for US studios.

### The rules your booking process has to follow
Checked on the official sources on 11 November 2026. This is a summary, not legal advice.
- Age, Great Britain: the Tattooing of Minors Act 1969 (on legislation.gov.uk) makes it an offence to tattoo a person under 18, except for medical reasons by a qualified doctor or someone working under their direction. The defence is that you had reasonable cause to believe the person was 18 or over, and did believe it. Parental consent is not an exception. The Act doesn't extend to Northern Ireland.
- What counts: the Act defines a tattoo as putting into the skin any colouring material designed to leave a permanent mark.
- Licence, England and Wales: gov.uk says you must register both yourself and your premises with the local council. In Greater London (except the City of London) you need a Special Treatments Licence instead, which you renew on a timetable your council sets, sometimes every 18 months. You must display your certificate and any byelaws on the premises. Scotland and Northern Ireland have their own schemes: ask your council.
- Deposits, UK: the CMA's unfair contract terms guidance (CMA37, updated 22 July 2026) says a genuine deposit can be kept in full if it works as a binding reservation, you tell the client at the earliest opportunity that it's needed, and the circumstances for keeping it are clear and narrow. It adds that such a deposit "will not normally be more than a small percentage of the price".
- Health answers, UK: the ICO says data concerning health is special category data, which needs extra care. Your consent form asks about skin conditions, medication and pregnancy, so store it securely, limit who can see it and decide how long you keep it.
- US studios: tattooing is regulated mainly at state and local level, so the minimum age, any parental consent rule, ID rules and licensing come from your state, county or city health department. Check yours and put the exact rule into your forms.

### A deposit policy you can copy
Edit the brackets. Show it before the client pays, in the confirmation and in every reminder. There's more on wording in [how to ask for a deposit](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/how-to-ask-for-a-deposit-on-a-quote/).
Tattoo deposit and rescheduling policy:
```
Deposits
We take a deposit of [£/$ amount] to book your appointment. It holds your slot and covers design time, and it comes off the price of your tattoo on the day.

Moving your appointment
You can move your appointment [once] for free with at least [72] hours' notice, using the link in your confirmation. Your deposit moves with you.

Late cancellations and no-shows
If you cancel with less than [72] hours' notice, or don't come, we keep the deposit.

Age and ID
We only tattoo people aged 18 or over. Bring photo ID showing your date of birth. If you can't show it, we can't tattoo you, and [the deposit moves to a new date / the deposit is kept].

If we cancel
If we need to cancel or move your appointment, you get your deposit back in full, or keep it towards a new date if you prefer.
```

### The message sequence, from enquiry to touch-up
Most studio admin breaks in the gaps: deposits agreed in DMs, paper forms in a drawer, clients without ID, aftercare on a leaflet. One sequence closes them. Fast, consistent [replies to new enquiries](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/reply-to-new-enquiries-fast/) are the first step.
| When | What's sent | Who acts |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Enquiry received | Thanks, what we need (idea, placement, size, reference images, budget) and our age rule | Artist reviews the idea and quotes |
| Quote accepted | Deposit link with the policy and available dates | Client pays and picks a date |
| Deposit paid | Confirmation: date, time, artist, deposit paid, free-to-move deadline | Automatic |
| 5-7 days before | Consent and health form link, ID reminder, prep tips you've written | Client fills in the form |
| Form returned | Answers that need a look (medication, skin, pregnancy, allergies) go to the artist | Artist reads and decides, and may call the client |
| Form not returned, 2 days before | Reminder with the link | Automatic, then a call list |
| Day before | Reminder with address, time and "bring your ID" | Automatic |
| On the day | Artist checks ID in person and the client signs the final consent | Artist |
| Same evening | Your written aftercare instructions | Automatic |
| A few weeks after | Healed photo request and touch-up booking link, if your policy includes one | Client replies, artist decides |

### A pre-appointment message you can copy
Sent 5-7 days before the session (edit the brackets):
```
Hi [first name], your tattoo with [artist] is on [day, date] at [time]. Before then, please fill in our consent and health form: [link]. It takes about 5 minutes and [artist] reads it before your session. On the day, bring photo ID showing your date of birth: we only tattoo people aged 18 or over. Need to move? It's free until [day, time]: [link]. See you soon, [studio name]
```

### What stays with the artist
- Whether to tattoo: any yes on a health question goes to the artist, never to an automatic rule. The workflow flags, a person decides.
- The ID check: the form can ask for a date of birth, but the artist looks at the photo ID in person on the day.
- Aftercare advice: the messages send the instructions you wrote, word for word. They don't answer health questions. A client who replies with a worry about healing goes straight to the artist.
- Keeping a deposit: the workflow lists late cancellations and no-shows, and you decide each one. Someone who was ill isn't treated like someone who forgot. More on this in [reducing no-shows](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/reduce-appointment-no-shows/).
- Anything AI drafts, such as a reply to an enquiry, is approved by a person before it's sent.

### Can someone under 18 get a tattoo in the UK with a parent's consent?
Not in Great Britain. The Tattooing of Minors Act 1969 makes it an offence to tattoo anyone under 18, except for medical reasons by a qualified doctor or someone under their direction. Parental consent isn't an exception. The Act doesn't extend to Northern Ireland.

### How much deposit can a tattoo studio keep?
UK law sets no figure. The CMA's guidance says a deposit you keep should work as a genuine reservation with clear, narrow conditions, told to the client at the earliest opportunity, and will not normally be more than a small percentage of the price.

### Can the consent form be digital?
Yes, as long as it asks what your licence conditions, local byelaws and insurer require. Many studios still have the client sign or confirm it on the day. Store it securely, because it holds health information.

## Med spa consent forms, pre-treatment checks and aftercare messages
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/med-spa-consent-forms-and-aftercare/

Med spa consent forms can be sent automatically as soon as a client books, so the medical history, age check and treatment consent come back before the appointment and the practitioner reviews them before anything is done. After the treatment, the same workflow sends the clinic's own written aftercare for that treatment, a check-in message and a review or top-up booking reminder. The practitioner still takes consent in person and makes every clinical decision; the automation only moves the forms and messages.

Med spa consent forms are where an aesthetics clinic's admin piles up. Every booking for anti-wrinkle injections, filler, peels or laser needs a medical history, a consent form, sometimes photos, and a written aftercare sheet. In a small clinic that often means a clipboard in reception, a form emailed once and never chased, and an aftercare leaflet the client loses. This page sets out the rules to build into the booking flow, a schedule you can copy, and what should never be automated. It is not medical or legal advice.

### Rules to build into the booking flow
These were checked on official sources in November 2026. They decide which questions the form asks and when a booking should stop.
- England: under the Botulinum Toxin and Cosmetic Fillers (Children) Act 2021 (legislation.gov.uk, in force since 1 October 2021), it is an offence to give botulinum toxin, or a filler injection for a cosmetic purpose, to anyone under 18 in England. A business also commits an offence if it makes arrangements for this, unless the person giving it is a doctor or a regulated health professional acting on a doctor's directions. The Act gives a business a defence if it took all reasonable precautions, so an age question at booking and an ID check on the day are worth having.
- England, coming next: on 21 October 2026 gov.uk published draft rules limiting higher-risk procedures (such as deep chemical peels and some laser treatments) to qualified health professionals, out for consultation until 13 January 2027. A separate licensing scheme for Botox and lip filler clinics is still planned, with no date given.
- UK data: the ICO lists data concerning health as special category data under UK GDPR. You need a lawful basis and a separate Article 9 condition to process it, so medical history forms need more care than a booking form.
- US data: under 45 CFR 160.103, HIPAA covers health care providers who transmit health information electronically in connection with a covered transaction, such as billing a health plan. Whether that includes your med spa depends on how you bill, so ask your adviser. Either way, treat the forms as confidential health information.
- US practice rules: who may inject, and who must assess a client first, is set by each state's medical and nursing boards. Build the form around what your medical director signs off.

### A message schedule you can copy
Change the timing to suit your treatments. Every message uses wording your practitioner has approved:
| When | What goes out | Who acts on it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| On booking | Confirmation, date of birth question, medical history and consent form for that treatment, pre-treatment instructions | Booking stops if the client says they're under 18 |
| 3 days before, form not back | Reminder with the form link | Automatic |
| 1 day before | Appointment reminder, plus a second form reminder if it's still missing | Reception gets a list of anyone still missing a form |
| Form returned | Answers filed to the client record, flagged answers sent to the practitioner | Practitioner reviews before the appointment |
| On the day | Nothing automatic | Practitioner goes through consent in person and checks ID if age is in doubt |
| Same day, after treatment | The clinic's written aftercare sheet for that treatment, and who to contact with a concern | Automatic, from the treatment recorded |
| 2-3 days after | Short check-in: any questions? Replies go to the clinic inbox, not a bot | A person reads and answers every reply |
| Your review interval | Review or top-up booking invitation, with a booking link | Automatic |

### A pre-treatment message you can copy
Sent on booking (edit the words in brackets; your practitioner approves the instructions):
```
Hi [first name], you're booked for [treatment] with [practitioner] on [date] at [time]. Before your appointment, please fill in your medical history and consent form here: [secure link]. It takes about [x] minutes and goes straight to your practitioner. Please also read the pre-treatment notes: [link to clinic's own notes]. If anything in your health or medication changes before the day, reply to this message or call us on [phone]. [clinic name]
```

### What the intake form should cover
Your practitioner decides the questions. Most clinics include:
- Date of birth, asked at booking, not only on the day
- Medical history, current medication and allergies, in the form your prescriber or medical director has written
- Previous treatments, with dates, and any problems after them
- Treatment-specific consent, one form per treatment type, with the version number saved on the client record
- Separate consent for photos: clinical records is one question, using photos on your website or social media is another
- Marketing permission as its own tick box, never bundled into treatment consent

### What stays with your practitioner
The consultation, the consent conversation, the decision to treat and every answer to a clinical question. The workflow moves forms, flags answers and sends aftercare the practitioner wrote. It never gives medical advice, never answers a worry about swelling or a reaction, and never decides who is suitable. Every reply goes to a person. If AI drafts any message, a person approves it before it's sent.

### Where it usually goes wrong
- Consent forms are filled in on paper and scanned weeks later, or not at all
- One generic form is used for every treatment, so the specific risks aren't covered
- Aftercare is a leaflet the client loses, and they message on Instagram at 10 PM instead
- Review requests only go to clients who seemed happy. Google's review policy bans selectively asking for positive reviews, so [ask every client the same way](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/ask-for-google-reviews-automatically/)
- Top-up reminders depend on someone remembering to check the diary, and clients drift to another clinic
- No-shows and late cancellations with no deposit, covered in [salon deposits and cancellation policies](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/salon-cancellation-policy-and-deposits/)
