## Rent arrears reminder letters for letting agents, from the first missed day to the landlord's decision
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/rent-arrears-reminders-letting-agents/

Rent arrears reminder letters for letting agents are a set sequence of messages that go to a tenant from the day after rent is missed, each one firmer than the last, with an offer to talk and agree a repayment plan. Since 1 May 2026 in England, gov.uk says a landlord can only use the mandatory rent arrears ground (Ground 8) once the tenant owes at least 3 months' rent, and must give 4 weeks' notice on Form 3A before going to court. A workflow can send the reminders and keep the record, while a person decides every legal step.

Rent arrears reminder letters are where a lot of agencies lose time and goodwill at once. Someone has to spot the missed payment in the bank feed, write to the tenant, remember to follow up, update the landlord and keep notes good enough to rely on months later. When the team is busy, the first reminder goes out on day 12 instead of day 2, and the arrears are already harder to clear. This page covers the rules in England as gov.uk states them today, a chasing schedule, two templates you can copy and what a workflow can do without ever taking a legal step on its own.

### The rent arrears rules in England after 1 May 2026
These come from gov.uk's grounds for possession guidance for landlords and letting agents (updated 1 May 2026) and its page on giving notice to evict tenants, checked in November 2026. They apply to England only. Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland have their own rules.
- Ground 8 (mandatory): the tenant must owe at least 3 months' rent, or 13 weeks' rent if rent is paid weekly or fortnightly, both on the day notice is given and at the date of the hearing. If they pay it down below that before court, this ground can't be used.
- Gov.uk says that if the arrears are only there because the tenant has not yet received their Universal Credit, you will not be able to evict them under Ground 8.
- Ground 10 (some rent owed) and Ground 11 (rent repeatedly paid late) are discretionary: the court only makes an order if it thinks it is reasonable.
- All three need 4 weeks' notice before you can apply to court. The notice is a section 8 notice on Form 3A, and gov.uk says to keep proof of service, for example on form N215.
- The court will not make an order unless the tenant's deposit has been dealt with properly: returned, or still protected in an approved scheme with the prescribed information given. This is why the [30-day deposit protection deadline](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/tenancy-deposit-protection-30-day-reminder/) matters long after move-in.
- Gov.uk says that after 31 July 2026 you will not usually be able to use a section 21 notice to start an eviction.

### If the tenant gets Universal Credit
Gov.uk's private renting page says that if a tenant on Universal Credit is at least 2 months late on rent, the tenant or the landlord can ask for the rent to be paid straight to the landlord (an Alternative Payment Arrangement). The DWP's Universal Credit guide for landlords (updated 10 June 2026) says a private landlord asks through the Apply for a Direct Rent Payment service, that the tenant has up to 14 days to object, and that deductions for arrears can be up to 15% of the tenant's standard allowance. Your workflow can flag a tenancy when it reaches 2 months behind and the tenant is known to claim, so a person decides whether to apply.

### A chasing schedule you can copy
The legal points come from gov.uk above. The timings below are suggestions to agree with each landlord, not rules. Each step stops the moment the rent is paid or a repayment plan is agreed.
| When | Who | What happens |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Day 1 after the due date | Workflow | Friendly text or email: rent not received, the amount, how to pay, and a reply option if something has gone wrong |
| Day 5 | Workflow | Second reminder by email, with an offer to agree a payment date or plan |
| Day 10 | Your team | Phone call. The outcome is logged against the tenancy |
| Day 14 | Workflow, approved by a person | Formal arrears letter: amount owed, a statement, a date to pay or call by, and where to get free advice |
| One month behind | Workflow | Landlord gets an update with the statement, the contact log and the options. The landlord decides the next step |
| Two months behind | Your team | Check whether a Universal Credit direct payment request applies. Landlord update again |
| Any legal step | Landlord and a person on your team, with advice | Whether to serve Form 3A, which ground, and when. Never sent by the workflow |

### First reminder text (day 1)
Friendly first reminder (edit the words in brackets):
```
Hi [first name], this is [agency name]. We haven't received the rent of [amount] for [property address], due on [due date]. If you've already paid, please ignore this. If something has gone wrong, reply here or call [phone] and we can talk it through. Pay to: [payment details]. Thanks, [your name]
```

### Formal arrears letter (day 14)
Firm, fair arrears letter for a person to approve before sending:
```
Subject: Rent arrears at [property address]: please pay or contact us by [date]

Dear [tenant name],

Our records show rent arrears of [total owed] at [property address]. A statement is attached showing each payment due and received since [date].

We wrote to you on [date of first reminder] and [date of second reminder], and tried to call on [date of call].

Please do one of these by [date, at least 7 days away]:
1. Pay the full amount to [payment details]
2. Contact us on [phone] or [email] to agree a repayment plan you can afford

If you are having trouble paying, Citizens Advice and your local council can give free, confidential advice. If you claim Universal Credit and your housing payment is late or has changed, please tell us so we can take that into account.

If we don't hear from you by [date], we will update your landlord, who will decide what happens next.

Yours sincerely,
[your name]
[agency name]
```

### What an automated arrears workflow does
1. Checks rent received against rent due each day, from your bank feed, accounting software or property management software, and lists every tenancy with a shortfall. Block managers run a similar check on [service charge demands and reminders](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/block-management-service-charge-reminders/) to leaseholders.
2. Sends the day 1 and day 5 reminders by text, WhatsApp or email, in your wording, and stops as soon as a payment lands.
3. Puts the day 10 call on a named person's list, with the amount, the history and a box to log the outcome.
4. Drafts the formal letter with the statement attached, and waits for a person to approve it before it goes.
5. Records every message, call and reply against the tenancy, with dates, so the file is ready if the landlord needs it later.
6. Tracks repayment plans: reminds the tenant before each instalment and alerts your team the day one is missed.
7. Sends the landlord a short update at one and two months behind, with the statement and the options, and logs their decision.

### What stays with you
Every decision about a tenant stays with a person: whether to agree a plan, when to call, and above all whether to serve a notice or go to court. That decision belongs to the landlord, with legal advice where needed. The workflow never serves a notice, never threatens eviction and never sends a formal letter without a person approving it. If AI drafts a message, a person always approves it before it goes. Arrears data is personal data, so keep it to what you need and follow the points in our [GDPR checklist for automating client data](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/gdpr-checklist-automating-client-data/). For chasing other unpaid invoices the same way, see [invoice payment reminders](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/invoice-payment-reminders/), and for the other dates your team tracks, [tenancy renewal and rent review reminders](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/tenancy-renewal-reminders-letting-agents/).

A [free 15-minute call](https://mikeautomations.github.io/call/) about how your agency spots and chases missed rent today. Within 48 hours you get a written plan with a fixed price and a clear definition of "working". To see the steps for your agency first, [build your plan here](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/plan/?g=rent-arrears-reminders-letting-agents).

### How much rent must a tenant owe before a landlord can use Ground 8?
In England, since 1 May 2026, gov.uk says at least 3 months' rent (or 13 weeks if rent is weekly or fortnightly), both when notice is given and at the hearing. The notice period is 4 weeks. Arrears caused only by a Universal Credit payment that hasn't arrived don't count.

### Can the workflow serve a section 8 notice?
No. It drafts letters, sends reminders and keeps the record. Whether to serve Form 3A, and on which ground, is the landlord's decision, made with a person on your team and legal advice where needed.

### Does it handle partial payments and repayment plans?
Yes. It works out the running balance from what was due and what came in, and tracks each instalment of an agreed plan, alerting your team the day one is missed.

The rules on this page are for England. Wales and Scotland have their own tenancy laws, so the legal steps differ. The reminder and record-keeping steps work the same way, with the legal wording set for each country.

## Fitness studio intro offer follow-up, from first class to membership
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/fitness-studio-intro-offer-follow-up/

Fitness studio intro offer follow-up is the set of messages a yoga, pilates or boutique fitness studio sends to someone on a trial or intro pack: a welcome before the first class, a check-in after it, a nudge if they stop booking, and a clear choice of membership or class pack before the offer ends. The same workflow can remind class-pack holders before their credits expire. A person at the studio still handles the replies and any conversation about price.

Fitness studio intro offer follow-up is where most new members are won or lost. Someone buys a two-week intro or a three-class pass, comes once, enjoys it, then life gets busy. Nobody notices until the offer has run out, and by then the moment has passed. Instructors are teaching, the front desk is checking people in, and the follow-up sits on a list nobody gets to. This page gives you a timeline to copy, a message you can paste into your own system, the same idea for class packs that are about to expire, and the consent rules for email and texts in the UK and the US.

### What a good intro offer follow-up does
It doesn't push. It helps the person come back a second and third time, because that's when the habit forms, and it makes the next step obvious before the offer ends. Every message should come from a named person at the studio, be short, and have one link: book a class, or choose a plan. It also stops the moment they buy a membership or a pack, so nobody gets a "don't miss out" message the day after they signed up. Martial arts schools follow up a trial class the same way, [until the student joins or says no](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/martial-arts-school-memberships-and-gradings/).

### An intro offer timeline you can copy
This assumes a two-week intro offer. Stretch or shorten the gaps for a 30-day offer or a three-class pass:
| When | Channel | What it says |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Straight after purchase | Email | Welcome, what to bring, where to park, how to book and cancel, and the date the offer ends |
| Evening before first class | Text or email | Class time, instructor's name, arrive 10 minutes early, how to cancel |
| Day after first class | Text or email | How was it? Two or three classes that suit a beginner this week, with the booking link |
| No class booked for 5 days | Text | A short, friendly nudge from a named person, with one suggested class |
| 4 days before the offer ends | Email | What they've used so far, the membership and pack options side by side, and the end date |
| Day the offer ends, not bought | Office list | A person decides whether to call, have a word after class, or let it go |
| 2 weeks later, not bought | Email | One last message: the door is open, here's the timetable. Then the messages stop |

### A check-in text you can copy
Day after the first class (edit the words in brackets):
```
Hi [first name], it's [your name] from [studio name]. Thanks for coming to [class name] yesterday, I hope you enjoyed it. If you'd like a next step, [class name] on [day] at [time] is a good one for this week. Book here: [link]. Your intro offer runs until [end date]. Reply STOP to opt out.
```

### Class-pack expiry reminders
Class packs with an expiry date cause a different problem: people forget they have credits, the pack lapses, and they feel they lost money. A reminder before expiry is good service, and it brings people back into classes. The same list that drives the intro follow-up can do this:
1. Keep each pack's purchase date, expiry date and credits left, from your booking app's export or a spreadsheet.
2. Three weeks before expiry, if credits are left: "You have [n] classes left on your pack, valid until [date]. Here's this week's timetable."
3. One week before: a shorter reminder with the booking link.
4. If your policy allows extensions (illness, injury, travel), say so in the reminder and explain how to ask. A person approves each extension.
5. When the last credit is used or the pack expires, send one message with the options to continue: a new pack or a membership. [Personal trainers](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/personal-trainer-client-check-ins/) do the same when a session package runs low.

### Consent rules for these messages
- UK: the ICO's PECR guidance (checked November 2026) says you can email or text your own customers about similar products or services under the "soft opt-in", if you got their details during a sale or while they were discussing buying, gave them a simple way to opt out when you collected the details, and include an opt-out in every message. Someone who bought an intro offer usually fits. A name from a bought list doesn't.
- Booking confirmations and class reminders with no sales content are service messages. The follow-up that suggests a membership is marketing, so it needs the opt-out.
- US: the FCC's consumer guidance says texts sent to a mobile phone with an autodialer need the owner's consent first, and that commercial texts need written consent while informational texts can rely on oral consent. Collect a clear tick-box for marketing texts at checkout, and honour STOP replies straight away.
- Never mention injuries, health conditions or anything a client told an instructor in private in an automated message.

### Where intro offer follow-up usually breaks
- The booking app sends one generic email and nothing else, so the personal follow-up depends on who's on shift
- People who already bought a membership keep getting "your offer ends soon" messages
- Nobody can see who came once and never booked again until the offer has expired
- Pack expiry is only noticed when the client tries to book and can't
- New enquiries from Instagram or the website wait hours for a reply: [replying to new enquiries fast](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/reply-to-new-enquiries-fast/) covers that part

### What stays with you
Your classes, your prices and every conversation about which plan suits someone. The workflow keeps the list, sends messages on time, stops them when someone buys, and tells you who needs a personal word. It doesn't offer discounts on its own. If AI drafts a message or a reply, a person always approves it before it's sent. Failed membership payments are a separate job, set out in [gym failed payment follow-up](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/gym-failed-payment-follow-up/). No-shows and late cancellations are covered in [salon cancellation policy and deposits](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/salon-cancellation-policy-and-deposits/), which works the same way for classes.

Within 48 hours you get a written plan with a fixed price and a clear definition of "working". It's built on the tools you already use (your booking or studio software's exports, a spreadsheet, email, texts or WhatsApp), so your team doesn't learn a new system. Live in 2-3 days. To see the steps for your studio first, [build your plan here](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/plan/?g=fitness-studio-intro-offer-follow-up).

### Doesn't my booking software already do this?
Many booking apps send a welcome email and booking confirmations. Fewer check who hasn't booked again, stop messages the moment someone buys, or hand you a list of people to speak to. The workflow can start from your app's data and add only what's missing.

### Can I send these by text in the UK?
The ICO says the soft opt-in covers emails and texts to your own customers about similar services, if you gave them a way to opt out when you took their details and include one in every message.

### What about US studios?

## Therapy practice client intake, consent and session reminders
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/therapy-practice-client-intake-and-session-reminders/

Therapy practice client intake can run on its own without touching anything clinical: when a new client books, they get the intake form, the consent and privacy notice and your cancellation policy, then reminders until it's done, and a reminder before every session. The messages carry only logistics (day, time, room or video link), never the reason someone is in therapy. The therapist still reads every form, holds every clinical conversation and decides on any late-cancellation fee.

Therapy practice client intake is mostly admin, and that's where small counselling and psychotherapy practices lose hours. Forms get emailed and never checked, consent sits in another folder, and the cancellation policy is first explained when a fee is due. None of that needs a clinician's judgement, so it can run as a workflow. This page covers what to automate, what to keep out of messages, the UK and US privacy rules, and a reminder you can copy. Physiotherapists face the same job, covered in [physio patient intake forms](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/physio-clinic-patient-intake-forms/).

### What to automate and what never to automate
| Job | Automate? | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sending intake, consent and policy forms after booking | Yes | Same steps for every new client |
| Reminding clients whose forms aren't back | Yes | Short, polite, stops when the form arrives |
| Session reminders by email or text | Yes | Logistics only: day, time, place or video link |
| Filing completed forms to the client's record | Yes, where your software allows | Keeps everything in one place |
| Reading intake answers and risk questions | No | Clinical judgement stays with the therapist |
| Replying to a client in distress | No | Always a person, with your own crisis wording |
| Charging a late-cancellation fee | No, a person decides | The system flags it, the therapist chooses |

### The intake workflow, step by step
1. A new client books an assessment or first session, online or after a call, as they do today.
2. Within minutes they get one email with links to the intake form, the consent and contracting form and your cancellation policy.
3. If the forms aren't back three days before the first session, a short reminder goes out, then another the day before.
4. Completed forms are saved to the client's record in your practice software, or to a restricted folder only the practice can open.
5. The therapist gets a note that the forms are in and reads them before the first session. Nothing in the answers triggers an automatic message to the client.
6. Each booked session gets a reminder. A missed session puts a task on the therapist's list instead of sending anything.

### Keep the messages discreet
A reminder can be read on a lock screen or a shared laptop, so write every message as if someone else might see it.
- Use a neutral sender name if the client asks for one, and record each client's chosen channel and any request not to be texted
- Say the day, time and place or video link. Never the reason for therapy, the therapist's specialism or anything from the intake form
- Send links to forms rather than attachments, and keep forms in tools your practice controls
- Stop all messages when a client ends therapy or asks you to

### Privacy rules in the UK and the US
UK: the ICO lists data concerning health as special category data under UK GDPR, and its guidance says you need both a lawful basis under Article 6 and a separate condition under Article 9. The ICO also says you must carry out a data protection impact assessment if you plan to process special category data on a large scale. See our [GDPR checklist for automating client data](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/gdpr-checklist-automating-client-data/).

US: for practices covered by HIPAA, the HHS FAQ on email (checked November 2026) says the Privacy Rule lets providers email patients if they apply reasonable safeguards, such as checking the address and limiting what an unencrypted email says. A patient can ask to be contacted another way, and you should accommodate that if it's reasonable. HHS also says a vendor that creates, receives, maintains or transmits protected health information for you, such as a cloud service, needs a business associate agreement. Check every tool will sign one before client data goes in.

US self-pay clients: CMS says people who aren't using health insurance to pay must get a good faith estimate of expected charges. If the session is booked 3 to 9 business days ahead, it's due within 1 business day; 10 or more business days ahead, within 3 business days. The intake email is a natural place to send it.

### A session reminder you can copy
Text or email, sent the day before a session (edit the words in brackets):
```
Hi [first name], a reminder of your appointment with [therapist first name] on [day] at [time], [at address / by video: link]. If you need to change it, please let us know by [cancellation deadline] by replying here or calling [practice phone]. [Practice name]
```

### A late-cancellation policy that's easy to follow
Put the policy in the intake email, ask the client to confirm it on the consent form, and repeat the deadline in every reminder. When a session is cancelled late or missed, the workflow adds it to the therapist's list with the date and the policy wording. The therapist decides whether to charge, waive it or call the client first. If you bill an insurer in the US, check your contract before charging a client for a missed session. See also [how to reduce no-shows](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/reduce-appointment-no-shows/) and [cancellation policies and deposits](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/salon-cancellation-policy-and-deposits/).

### What stays with you
Every clinical decision: what the forms ask, reading the answers, every conversation, fees, discharge and anything to do with risk. If AI ever drafts a message, a person approves it before it's sent, and no session content goes into an AI tool.

## Catering quote follow-up, then final guest numbers and dietary requirements on time
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/catering-quotes-and-final-numbers/

Catering quote follow-up is the run of polite messages a caterer sends after a quote goes out, until the client books, asks for changes or says no. Once an event is booked, the same workflow asks the client for final guest numbers and dietary requirements by a cut-off date you set, chases anyone who misses it, and puts the answers into one sheet the kitchen works from. The caterer still sets every price, menu and allergen answer; the workflow only sends, chases and records.

Catering quote follow-up is where many caterers lose work without noticing. A quote goes out for a 120-guest wedding or an office lunch, the client says it looks great, and then nothing. A week later they've booked someone who rang them back. Once an event is booked, the second chase starts: final numbers, dietary requirements and allergies, the timings, the venue contact, the balance. These arrive in pieces by email, text and phone calls, often the day before your cut-off or after it. This page is for event and contract caterers in the UK and the US. It sets out a follow-up schedule, a final numbers request you can copy, what the food safety regulators say about allergen information, and how the whole chase can run on its own.

### Where catering bookings slip
- A quote goes out and nobody follows it up, because the kitchen is busy with this week's events
- The client asks for a revised menu, you send version 2, and the follow-up stops there
- Final numbers come in late, so you order and staff for a guess
- Dietary requirements arrive as "a few veggies and one nut allergy" with no names or table numbers
- The balance date passes because it was written in the contract, not in anyone's calendar
- The event lead, the kitchen and the front-of-house team each work from a different version of the details

### A quote follow-up schedule you can copy
Timings are a starting point. A wedding quote can wait a few days between messages; a quote for an office lunch next week can't. Every message stops as soon as the client replies, books or says no. If you're still slow to answer the first enquiry, start there: [replying to new enquiries fast](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/reply-to-new-enquiries-fast/) matters more than any follow-up.
| When | Message | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Same day as the enquiry | Quote with menu options, price per head, what's included and how long the price holds | Gives the client one clear thing to say yes to |
| 2 days after the quote | Short check-in: any questions, or anything to change on the menu? | Catches clients who meant to reply |
| 5 days after | Date reminder: you're holding the date for them until [date], then it goes back on sale | A real reason to decide |
| 10 days after | Last message: happy to help if plans change, no further chasing | Closes the quote politely |
| Client says yes | Booking confirmation, contract or terms, and the deposit request | Turns a yes into a booking |

### After the booking: the final numbers timeline
Every date here is counted back from the event, so a new booking gets its whole schedule the moment you enter the event date. Set the actual cut-offs in your own terms; the ones below are an example.
1. On booking: confirmation of date, venue, menu, price per head and the deposit paid. If you take a deposit, the post on [how to ask for a deposit on a quote](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/how-to-ask-for-a-deposit-on-a-quote/) has wording you can use.
2. 4 weeks before: menu choices locked in, and a link to a short form for final details (numbers, dietary requirements, timings, venue contact, access and parking).
3. 2 weeks before: final numbers and dietary requirements due. Anyone who hasn't filled in the form gets a reminder that day, and another 2 days later. If a separate baker makes the cake, [the custom cake order needs its own allergen answers](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/custom-cake-orders-and-deposits/), collected on the baker's form.
4. 10 days before: the balance invoice goes out, with reminders if it isn't paid. The [invoice payment reminder workflow](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/invoice-payment-reminders/) covers this part.
5. 1 week before: the event sheet goes to your kitchen and event lead, built from the client's own answers, with each dietary requirement and allergy listed by guest or table.
6. After the event: a thank-you message and one review request. Sent once, never chased.

### A final numbers request you can copy
Final details request, 4 weeks before the event (edit the words in brackets):
```
Hi [first name], we're looking forward to [event] on [date] at [venue]. To get everything right on the day, please fill in this short form by [cut-off date]: [link]

It asks for:
1. Final guest numbers (adults and children)
2. Any dietary requirements or allergies, with the guest's name or table number
3. Serving times and the running order
4. The contact on the day at the venue, plus access and parking details

After [cut-off date] we can add guests but can't reduce numbers on the invoice. If anything changes, just reply to this email. Thanks, [your name], [business name], [phone]
```

### Allergen information: what the regulators say
The workflow collects what the client tells you about their guests. It doesn't answer allergen questions; that comes from your recipes and your kitchen. What the regulators say, checked in November 2026:
- UK: the Food Standards Agency's allergen guidance for food businesses lists 14 allergens and says you must supply allergen information for every item that contains any of them when you sell food that isn't prepacked.
- The FSA says this information can be given verbally only if a written notice in a clearly visible position tells customers how to get it, and that for buffets you give it for each item, not for the buffet as a whole.
- The FSA also says that when food is sold at a distance, such as by phone or online, allergen information must be available before the purchase is completed and when the food is delivered.
- US: the FDA lists nine major food allergens: milk, eggs, fish, crustacean shellfish, tree nuts, peanuts, wheat, soybeans and sesame. Sesame was added by the FASTER Act, which took effect on 1 January 2023.
- The FDA's labelling rules cover packaged food and generally exclude food sold by food-service businesses that isn't pre-packaged with a label. State and local food codes can add their own rules, so check with your local health department.

### What stays with you
Your menus, prices, minimum numbers and cancellation terms. Every allergen answer and every decision about what the kitchen can safely make. Late changes and unhappy clients are a phone call, not an automated message. If AI drafts a reply to a client, a person always approves it before it's sent. Guests' allergy and health details are sensitive: the workflow keeps them in one place your team can see, and nowhere else.

## Private dining enquiries and group bookings: reply fast, take the deposit, get final numbers
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/restaurant-group-booking-and-private-dining-enquiries/

Private dining enquiries and large group bookings follow the same steps every time: a fast reply with menus and prices, a provisional hold, a deposit, final numbers and dietary requirements by a set date, then a reminder before the event. A restaurant can run those steps from one enquiry list, so every organiser gets a reply within minutes and every chase goes out on time, while the manager still sets prices, approves menus and decides on every exception.

Private dining enquiries and large group bookings are some of the most valuable covers a restaurant takes, and the easiest to lose. The enquiry arrives by email, the website form, Instagram or a phone call during service. Whoever picks it up sends the menus when they get a minute, while the organiser is asking two other places and often books the one that replied first. After that come the deposit, the menu choices, the final numbers and the allergies, usually chased by hand. This page sets out the workflow, a reply you can copy, a timeline for every group booking, and the UK and US rules to know before you write your terms.

### The workflow, step by step
1. Every enquiry, from your website form, email, booking app, social messages or a phone note, lands in one list with the date, party size, occasion and contact details.
2. Within minutes, the organiser gets the right pack for their size and date: set menus, room, any minimum spend, deposit terms and a link to hold the date. If the date is full, the reply offers the nearest free dates.
3. A manager checks anything outside the normal rules, such as a buyout or a special menu, before a reply goes out.
4. A chosen date is held provisionally until a set day, and the hold shows in your diary or booking system.
5. The deposit request goes out with the terms. If it isn't paid by the hold date, the organiser gets one reminder, then the manager decides whether to release the date.
6. Once the deposit is paid, the organiser gets a confirmation with everything agreed and the date final numbers are due.
7. A form collects each guest's name, menu choice and allergies, with reminders until it's complete.
8. The kitchen and front of house get one sheet for the night: numbers, choices, allergies, timings and the balance to take.

### A first reply you can copy
Reply to a private dining or group enquiry (edit the words in brackets):
```
Hi [first name],

Thanks for getting in touch about [occasion] for [party size] on [date]. That date is [available / filling up / full, and the nearest free dates are ...].

For a group your size we offer [room or area], with these set menus: [link to menus, prices and allergen information]. [There's a minimum spend of [amount] for the room.]

To hold the date we take a deposit of [amount per person / total], which comes off the final bill. You can hold it provisionally until [day] here: [link]. Final numbers and any dietary requirements are due [number] days before.

If you'd rather talk it through, reply with a good time to call, or ring us on [phone] outside service hours ([times]).

[Your name], [restaurant name]
```

### A timeline for every group booking
Change the timings to suit your restaurant. This assumes the event is booked a few weeks ahead:
| When | What happens | Who |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Within minutes of the enquiry | Reply with the right menus, deposit terms and a link to hold the date | Automatic, unless it needs a manager |
| Hold date (for example 5 days) | Deposit request, then one reminder before the hold ends | Automatic, manager decides on release |
| Deposit paid | Confirmation with the agreed details and the final numbers deadline | Automatic |
| 14 days before | Pre-order and dietary form sent to the organiser | Automatic |
| 7 and 3 days before | Reminders until the form is complete | Automatic |
| Final numbers deadline | Numbers locked, kitchen sheet sent to the team | Automatic, chef checks |
| Day before | Reminder with the time, address and room | Automatic |
| After the event | Thank you, balance if any, one review request | Automatic |

### Rules to check before you write your terms
Checked on official sources in November 2026. This isn't legal advice: have your own terms checked.
- UK deposits: the CMA's unfair contract terms guidance (CMA37, updated 22 July 2026) says a genuine deposit can be kept in full if it works as a binding reservation, you say at the earliest opportunity that it's needed, and the conditions for keeping it are clear and narrow. Such a deposit "will not normally be more than a small percentage of the price". More in [how to ask for a deposit](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/how-to-ask-for-a-deposit-on-a-quote/).
- UK allergens: the Food Standards Agency says you must supply allergen information for every item containing any of the 14 allergens. You can give it verbally with a clearly visible written notice, but the FSA advises written information supported by a conversation. Link it in your first reply.
- UK service charges: since 1 October 2024, the Employment (Allocation of Tips) Act 2023 and its statutory code of practice require employers in Great Britain to pass on all tips, gratuities and service charges they control to workers, with no deductions other than tax and National Insurance.
- US automatic gratuities: the IRS says a payment is a tip only if the customer voluntarily decides to pay it and decides the amount. It gives "a mandatory 18% charge for large parties" as an example of a service charge, which is treated as wages when paid to staff. Ask your CPA before changing how you charge large parties.
- US deposit and cancellation terms depend on state law, so have yours checked locally.

### What stays with you
Your prices, menus, minimum spends and deposit terms. Whether to release a date, waive a deposit or take a party bigger than the room. Every allergy conversation: the workflow puts what guests write on the kitchen sheet, the chef checks it, and a person talks to the guest if anything is unclear. If AI drafts a reply, a person approves it before it's sent.

## Short-term rental guest messaging automation, from booking to review
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/short-term-rental-guest-messages/

Short-term rental guest messaging automation sends each guest the right message at the right point in their stay (booking confirmation, check-in instructions, a first-evening check, a checkout reminder and one review request) and tells your cleaner when to turn the property round, all from one list of bookings. Airbnb's own scheduled messages cover messages inside Airbnb; a wider workflow is worth it when you take bookings on more than one channel, manage several properties or need the cleaning schedule to follow every booking change.

Short-term rental guest messaging automation is about the same handful of messages you send for every stay: thanks for booking, here's how to get in, is everything working, checkout is tomorrow, would you leave a review. With several properties, direct bookings and a cleaner who needs to hear about every change, they slip. A guest arrives without the key safe code, or the cleaner turns up at a property whose booking was cancelled two days ago. This page, for holiday let hosts and small property managers, covers what Airbnb's built-in tools do, a message timeline to copy and the cleaner side most hosts forget.

### What Airbnb's scheduled messages already do
Start with what's already inside the platform. Airbnb's help centre (checked November 2026) describes scheduled messages as quick replies sent before or after reservation events such as a new booking, check-in or checkout, in the listing's time zone. They can fill in "details" such as the guest's first name, check-in date and time, address, directions and Wi-Fi name and password, but only if those details are filled in on your listing; otherwise they show as unavailable. Airbnb says some messages are skipped by default for last-minute bookings and short stays, unless you turn on the setting to send them, and you get a notification when a message is skipped or sent at a different time. If all your bookings come through Airbnb and you have one or two listings, set these up first. You may not need anything else.

### When a wider workflow is worth it
- You take bookings from more than one place (Airbnb, another platform, your own website, repeat guests by email) and want the same messages for all of them
- You manage several properties, each with its own access code, parking notes and house rules
- Your cleaner works from texts or a WhatsApp group, and cancellations or date changes don't always reach them
- You want one place that shows which guest has had which message, rather than checking each platform

### A guest message timeline you can copy
Adjust the timings to your own check-in and checkout times. For Airbnb bookings, keep guest messages inside Airbnb's own messaging.
| When | To | What it says |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Straight after booking | Guest | Thanks, the dates, what happens next and how to ask a question |
| Straight after booking | Cleaner | New turnover added: property, when the previous guest leaves, when this guest arrives |
| 3 days before arrival | Guest | Expected arrival time, parking, anything worth bringing |
| Morning of arrival | Guest | Full check-in instructions: address, key safe or access code, Wi-Fi, house rules link |
| Evening of day one | Guest | Short check: is everything working? Reply here if not |
| Day before checkout | Guest | Checkout time, what to do with keys, bins and dishes |
| Day before checkout | Cleaner | Turnover reminder: property, time it's free, next check-in time |
| Day after checkout | Guest | Thanks, and one review request |
| Any cancellation or date change | Cleaner and you | The turnover is moved or removed, and the cleaner confirms they've seen it |

### A check-in message template
Morning of arrival (edit the words in brackets):
```
Hi [first name], we're looking forward to having you at [property name] today. Check-in is from [time].

Address: [full address]. [Parking note].
Getting in: the key safe is [location], code [code]. The code works from [time] today.
Wi-Fi: [network], password [password].
House rules: [link]. The most important ones are [quiet hours] and [parties / smoking rule].

If anything isn't right when you arrive, reply here and we'll sort it. Enjoy your stay.
[your name]
```

### Keeping the cleaner in step
The turnover is where things usually go wrong, because the cleaning schedule lives somewhere other than the bookings. The workflow keeps one list of every stay across your properties and builds the cleaning rota from it.
1. Every new booking, from any channel, adds a turnover to the rota: the property, when the previous guest leaves and when the next one arrives.
2. The cleaner gets the week's turnovers each Monday, then a reminder the day before each one.
3. A cancellation or date change moves or removes the turnover and texts the cleaner. If they haven't confirmed by the evening, you get an alert.
4. After each clean, the cleaner replies "done" with any notes (something broken, supplies low, items left behind). Photos go to a shared folder for that property.
5. Anything the cleaner reports goes on your list. Nothing is promised to a guest or an owner without you.

### Review requests: ask once, ask fairly
Airbnb's help centre says guests and hosts have 14 days from the day of checkout to write a review for a stay, and reviews are published once both have written theirs or when that window closes. So the review request should go the day after checkout, not a week later. Airbnb's reviews policy says hosts must not incentivise or pressure anyone to influence a review, and a review must not be given or withheld in exchange for something of value, such as a discount or a refund. For direct bookings, the same message can link to your Google review page; the [guide to asking for Google reviews automatically](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/ask-for-google-reviews-automatically/) covers that side.
Review request, the day after checkout:
```
Hi [first name], thanks for staying at [property name]. We hope the trip went well. If you have a minute, a review would help other guests know what to expect. And if anything wasn't right, please tell us here so we can fix it. [your name]
```

### Where guest messaging usually breaks
- Access codes are wrong because one property's details were copied into another's message
- A booking made the night before arrival gets the pre-arrival message after the check-in one
- The cleaner never hears about a cancellation and cleans an empty property, or misses a new same-day booking
- An AI tool answers a guest's complaint on its own and promises a refund nobody agreed

### What stays with you
Pricing, refunds, damage claims, complaints and every decision about a guest. The workflow keeps the booking list, sends the agreed messages on time and keeps the cleaner informed. Guest names, phone numbers and access codes are personal and security details, so they stay in your own accounts, and the [GDPR checklist for automating client data](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/gdpr-checklist-automating-client-data/) applies if you or your guests are in the UK or EU. If AI drafts a reply to a guest, a person always approves it before it's sent.

## Financial adviser annual review paperwork: booking, fact-find, ID and sign-off
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/financial-adviser-client-review-paperwork/

Financial adviser annual review paperwork is everything around an ongoing client's review: booking the meeting, getting the fact-find and attitude to risk updated, refreshing ID where needed, and getting the suitability report signed. A workflow can invite each client when their review falls due, chase the updated details, log every attempt to engage, and show the adviser whose report is waiting for a signature. The adviser still gives all the advice and writes or approves every report.

Financial adviser annual review paperwork is the part of ongoing advice that slips. The meeting itself is the easy bit. Before it, someone has to find a date, send the fact-find, chase the client who hasn't returned it and check whether their ID is still current. After it, the suitability report goes out and waits for a signature. This page is for small UK advice firms and planners. Mortgage advisers have a similar job before each case: see [mortgage broker document collection](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/mortgage-broker-document-collection/). Insurance brokers have theirs at each [policy renewal](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/insurance-broker-renewal-reminders/).

### Why the paper trail matters
In February 2025 the FCA published its review of ongoing financial advice services at 22 large firms. It found suitability reviews were delivered in most cases, but where a firm made no attempt at a review, the FCA said redress is likely to be due. It asked every advice firm to check it can evidence that it delivered the services its contracts and the rules require, and named inadequate record keeping as poor practice. The review notes that under COBS 9A reviews must be at least annual, and that since July 2023 firms should consider their Consumer Duty fair value obligations when setting charges. Its good practice includes reasonable attempts to engage clients, and a policy for stopping fees when a client hasn't engaged for a period. All of that depends on a dated record of each invitation, reminder and reply. Read the review on fca.org.uk for the detail that applies to your firm.

### Keeping ID and client details current
If your firm is in scope of the Money Laundering Regulations 2017, regulation 27(8) says customer due diligence applies to existing customers at other appropriate times on a risk-based approach, and when you become aware that a customer's circumstances relevant to your risk assessment have changed. The annual review is a natural point to ask whether anything has changed: address, name, job, source of wealth. Your own AML policy sets when ID must be refreshed; the workflow simply reads that date and adds the ID request to the review pack when it is due. For more on the checks themselves, see [AML client ID checks for small UK firms](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/aml-client-id-checks-workflow/).

### The review cycle, step by step
1. Each morning the workflow reads review due dates from your back office system or spreadsheet.
2. A set period before the due date, the client gets an invitation with your booking link and a request for any changes since last year.
3. The fact-find update and attitude to risk questions go out as a short form, pre-filled with what you already hold so the client only corrects it.
4. If your AML policy says the client's ID is due for refresh, the request is added to the same message with a secure upload link.
5. Clients who don't reply get two reminders on your schedule. Every invitation, reminder and reply is logged against the client with a date.
6. After the last reminder, the client appears on the adviser's list for a phone call. You decide what happens next.
7. Once the adviser approves the suitability report, it goes out for e-signature, with one reminder if it isn't signed.
8. The signed report and the updated fact-find are filed to the client's record, and next year's review date is set.

### An invitation you can copy
Annual review invitation:
```
Subject: Your annual review with [firm name]

Hi [client name],

It's time for your annual review, which is part of the ongoing service you have with us. Please pick a time that suits you here: [booking link].

Before we meet, please check the details we hold and update anything that has changed: [fact-find link].

[If ID is due: We also need an up-to-date copy of your photo ID and a recent proof of address. You can upload them securely here: [upload link].]

If you'd rather not have a review this year, just reply and let me know, and we'll talk about what suits you.

Thanks,
[adviser name]
[firm name]
```

### What the review log should show
| Item | What is recorded | Who acts |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Review due | Due date from your back office, invitation date | Workflow |
| Engagement attempts | Each invitation and reminder, with date and channel | Workflow |
| Client response | Booked, declined, no reply, or asked to stop the service | Client, logged by the workflow |
| Fact-find and risk profile | Date updated, changes flagged for the adviser | Client fills in, adviser reviews |
| ID refresh | Due or not under your policy, documents received | Workflow requests, your team verifies |
| Suitability report | Date approved, date sent, date signed | Adviser approves, client signs |

### What stays with you
All advice and every regulatory judgement. You decide what the review covers, whether a recommendation is suitable, what goes in the report, whether ID is acceptable and what to do about a client who doesn't engage. The workflow invites, reminds, logs and files. It never changes a client's investments, never writes a recommendation on its own and never decides to stop a fee. If AI drafts a report summary or a message, a person approves it before it goes out.

## Architect fee proposal follow-up, stage approvals and a drawing sign-off log
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/architect-fee-proposals-and-approvals/

Architect fee proposal follow-up is chasing a prospective client after you send a fee proposal, until they accept, decline or ask for changes, and then getting the agreed terms confirmed in writing. A workflow can send polite reminders on a schedule, turn an accepted proposal into terms for signature, ask the client to approve each design stage in writing, and keep a log of which drawing revisions they signed off and when. The architect still sets the fee, does the design and decides when work moves on.

Architect fee proposal follow-up usually happens when someone remembers. You spend an afternoon on a fee proposal for a house extension, send it, and hear nothing. Weeks later the client rings to say they'd like to start next Monday. Then the design moves on faster than the paperwork: the client says "looks great" on a call, nobody writes it down, and at technical design they want the kitchen moved. This page is for small architecture and design practices in the UK and the US. Surveyors have a similar booking-to-report routine: see [surveyor booking and report delivery](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/surveyor-booking-and-report-delivery/).

### Why written terms and stage sign-off matter
In the UK, the Architects Registration Board's Code of Conduct and Practice says architects meet Standard 4 when they provide clear, understandable, written terms of engagement before starting work, and keep accurate records of their work and decisions. ARB's guidance on terms of engagement adds that you should get the client's confirmation that they understand and agree the terms, that a new commission needs new terms, and that any changes should be recorded in writing with a copy to the client. The RIBA Plan of Work 2020 Overview lists signing off the Stage Report at the end of each stage among the client's tasks, and says stage outcomes must be completed and signed off before moving to the next stage. In the US, the AIA's B101-2017 owner-architect agreement sets out basic services in five phases: schematic design, design development, construction documents, procurement and construction. Whatever your contract calls the stages, the point is the same: a dated, written yes before you move on.

### The fee proposal follow-up
1. You send the fee proposal from your usual email or proposal tool. The workflow logs the date, the fee and the stages it covers.
2. After 3 working days, a short check-in asks whether the client has any questions about the scope.
3. After 7 working days, a second message offers a short call and restates when the proposal is valid until.
4. After 14 working days, a last note says you'll close the file unless they'd like to go ahead. Then it stops.
5. If the client replies at any point, the reminders stop and the reply goes to you.
6. When they accept, your terms of engagement go out for e-signature, and the project only opens once they're signed.

### A follow-up you can copy
Fee proposal check-in:
```
Subject: Your fee proposal for [project name]

Hi [client name],

I wanted to check the fee proposal I sent on [date] arrived safely, and whether you have any questions about what's included. In short, it covers [stages] for a fee of [fee or basis].

If it would help, I'm happy to talk it through on a short call: [booking link].

The proposal is valid until [date]. If your plans have changed, just let me know and I'll close the file.

Thanks,
[architect name]
[practice name]
```

### Stage approvals and the drawing sign-off log
At the end of each stage, the workflow sends the client the stage report or drawing set with a single question: do you approve this stage so we can move on? The reply, or the e-signature, is saved with the date and the drawing revision numbers it covers. If the client asks for changes instead, the request is logged against the stage and nothing moves on until you've answered. Later changes to an approved design are logged as variations, so a fee discussion starts from the record, not from memory. It works the same way as [client approvals at an agency](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/agency-client-approvals/), and the proposal follow-up above matches how a [translation agency chases quotes](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/translation-agency-quotes-and-file-intake/). Interior designers need the same written yes for each item they order; see [client approvals and purchase orders for interior designers](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/interior-designer-client-approvals-and-orders/).
| Project | Stage | Drawings and revision | Sent | Client decision | Date |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [project name] | Stage 2 Concept Design | [drawing numbers, rev] | [date] | Approved / Changes requested | [date] |
| [project name] | Stage 3 Spatial Coordination | [drawing numbers, rev] | [date] | Waiting, reminder sent [date] |  |
| [project name] | Variation: [short description] | [drawing numbers, rev] | [date] | Approved, fee agreed | [date] |

### What stays with you
The fee, the scope, the terms and every design decision. You decide what goes in a proposal, when a stage is ready to send, whether a change is a variation and what it costs. The workflow sends, reminds, logs and files. It never sends a proposal or a drawing you haven't released, and it never tells a client a stage is approved on your behalf. If AI drafts a cover note, a person approves it before it goes out.

## MSP client onboarding checklist, with renewal and review reminders
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/msp-client-onboarding-and-renewals/

An MSP client onboarding checklist is the list of everything an IT support company needs from a new client before it can support them properly: admin access granted the right way, an asset list, key contacts, and every renewal date. A workflow can send the checklist, track what comes back, chase what is missing, and then remind you about contract, licence, domain and certificate renewals and book each quarterly review. Your engineers still check every access grant and every renewal before anything is bought or changed.

An MSP client onboarding checklist stops the first month of a new contract turning into a scavenger hunt. The contract is signed, but nobody knows who holds the domain login, which laptops exist, or when the firewall licence runs out. Then, a year later, a certificate expires on a Saturday and the client finds out before you do. Collecting the same information from every client, and watching the same dates, is repeat work, so it can run as a workflow while your team does the technical work. This page is for small IT support companies and managed service providers in the UK and the US. Marketing agencies have a similar job when a client signs: see [client onboarding for agencies](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/agency-client-onboarding-automation/). Insurance brokers run a similar date-driven routine for [policy renewals](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/insurance-broker-renewal-reminders/).

### The onboarding checklist
Send it as one form the day the contract is signed. Keep it to what you need in the first two weeks; the rest comes from your own discovery tools once you have access.
| Item | What to ask for | Why it matters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Contacts | Main contact, who approves spending, who to call out of hours, who can request new users and leavers | You know whose request to act on |
| Admin access | Access granted to your team through the vendor's partner or delegated admin route, never a shared password by email | Access is traceable and can be removed later |
| Domains and DNS | Registrar, who holds the login, expiry dates | A lapsed domain takes email and the website down |
| Assets | Laptops, desktops, phones, printers, network kit, and who uses each one | The starting point for your asset register |
| Software and licences | Each subscription, number of seats, renewal date, who pays | Feeds the renewal calendar |
| Backups | What is backed up, where, and when a restore was last tested | You find the gaps before you need a restore |
| Suppliers | Internet provider, phone system, line of business software and their support contacts | You know who to call when it isn't your fault |

### Access: do it the vendor's way
Ask clients to grant access rather than hand over credentials. For Microsoft 365, Microsoft's Partner Center documentation (2026) describes granular delegated admin privileges (GDAP) as least-privileged, time-bound access that customers must explicitly grant to their partner. Because the access is time-bound, its end date belongs on the same renewal calendar as everything else.

### The onboarding sequence
1. When the contract is signed, the client gets a welcome email with the onboarding form and the access instructions for the services they bought.
2. Each answer fills the client's record: contacts, assets, licences and renewal dates.
3. After 2 working days, a reminder lists only what is still missing.
4. After 5 working days, the account manager gets a task to call the client.
5. When the checklist is complete, an engineer reviews it and confirms access works before the client is marked live.
6. The first quarterly review is booked for three months after go-live.

### The renewal calendar
Every date from onboarding goes into one calendar, not [a spreadsheet nobody owns](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/spreadsheet-vs-crm-small-service-business/), and the workflow warns you in good time. Two kinds of date deserve extra care. ICANN's Expired Registration Recovery Policy says registrars must send at least two reminders before a domain expires, roughly a month and a week before, but those go to whoever registered the domain, which is often not you. And the CA/Browser Forum voted in April 2025 to cut the maximum life of public TLS certificates from 398 days to 47 days, in steps from March 2026 to March 2029. Automatic renewal is the answer for certificates; the calendar catches the ones that aren't set up for it. The reminder times below are a starting point you can change.
| What renews | First reminder | Who acts |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Your support contract | 90 days before, to the account manager | You, with a review of the contract |
| Software subscriptions and licences | 60 days before, with seat count and current users | You check seats, the client approves the spend |
| Domains | 60 days before, and again at 14 days | Whoever holds the registrar login |
| TLS certificates not on automatic renewal | 30 days before | An engineer |
| Warranties and hardware support | 60 days before | You recommend, the client decides |
| Partner or delegated admin access | 30 days before it ends | An engineer and the client |

### A renewal message you can copy
Licence renewal notice to the client:
```
Subject: [software] renews on [date]

Hi [contact name],

Your [software] subscription renews on [date]. You currently pay for [number] licences and [number] people are using them.

Our suggestion: [renew as is / reduce to N licences / move to a different plan], because [one-line reason].

Please reply by [date] to approve, or let us know if anything has changed (new starters, leavers, a different plan). If we don't hear from you, it will renew as it is.

Thanks,
[your name]
[company]
```

### Quarterly reviews, booked automatically
A week before each quarter ends, the client's main contact gets a booking link for a review. The workflow drafts the agenda from what you already hold: renewals in the next 90 days, devices out of warranty, tickets raised and actions still open from last time. A person edits it before the meeting, and if nobody books within a week, the account manager is reminded to call.

### What stays with you
Every technical judgement. You decide what access to request, check that it works, and recommend what to renew, cut or replace. The client approves every purchase. The workflow collects, tracks and reminds; it never buys a licence or changes a client's systems on its own. If AI drafts a review agenda or a renewal note, a person approves it before it goes out.

It's built on the tools you already use (your ticketing system, email, calendar and shared drive, where they allow a connection), so your team doesn't learn a new system. Live in 2-3 days. ## A photography booking workflow, from enquiry to gallery delivery
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/photographer-booking-contracts-and-deposits/

A photography booking workflow is the fixed sequence every booking goes through: reply to the enquiry, send the contract and deposit invoice, collect a pre-shoot questionnaire, remind the client about the balance, deliver the gallery and ask for a review. Because the steps and their timing are the same for every shoot, they can run on their own from your calendar, while you decide prices, availability and anything unusual. It suits wedding, portrait, family and commercial photographers and videographers.

A photography booking workflow saves you from running every booking out of your inbox. An enquiry comes in on a Saturday while you are shooting a wedding, you reply on Tuesday, and the couple has already booked someone who answered first. Then there is the contract that went out without the deposit invoice, the questionnaire you forgot to send, and the balance you chase awkwardly a week before the day. None of this is creative work: it is the same messages at the same points for every client, so it can run as a workflow. This page is for photographers and videographers in the UK and the US.

### The booking timeline
A typical sequence for a dated shoot such as a wedding or event. The timings are examples; you set your own in your terms.
| When | What happens | Who |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Within minutes of an enquiry | A reply with your availability for that date, your packages and a link to book a call | Automatic, from your calendar |
| When the client says yes | Contract for e-signature and the deposit invoice, sent together | Automatic, after you confirm the package and price |
| When the contract is signed and the deposit paid | The date is blocked in your calendar and the client gets a confirmation | Automatic |
| Six weeks before the shoot | Pre-shoot questionnaire: timings, locations, key people, shot list, anything to avoid | Automatic, with a reminder if it isn't back |
| Four weeks before | Balance reminder with the amount, due date and payment link | Automatic; you get a list of anyone unpaid |
| A week before | Final details confirmed: timings, addresses, contact on the day | You check the answers |
| Delivery | Gallery link, how long it stays online, how to order prints | You choose the date; the message is automatic |
| A few days after delivery | A short thank you and a review request, sent to every client | Automatic |

### Reply fast, and say whether the date is free
Most enquiries are really one question: are you free on this date, and what does it cost? An automatic reply that checks your calendar and sends the right package guide answers both while the client is still looking. If the date is taken, it says so politely. Wedding and event venues face the same first question, and the [venue enquiry follow-up workflow](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/event-venue-enquiry-follow-up/) answers it the same way. Florists get the same question about a wedding date, and [an automatic reply with availability and starting prices](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/florist-wedding-and-event-orders/) works for them too.

### Contract and deposit together
Send the contract and the deposit invoice in the same message, and only block the date when both are done. Your contract should say what the deposit is for (holding the date and turning other work away), when it is not refundable, when the balance is due and what happens if either side cancels. Our guide on [how to ask for a deposit on a quote](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/how-to-ask-for-a-deposit-on-a-quote/) covers the wording, and a [wedding planner's payment schedule](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/wedding-planner-supplier-and-payment-schedules/) shows how deposits and balances fit around one date. A [tattoo studio's design deposit](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/tattoo-studio-consent-and-deposits/) works on the same principle, with a consent form added. Bakers taking [custom cake orders](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/custom-cake-orders-and-deposits/) can send the confirmed design and the deposit request together in the same way.

### Cancellation rights: check before you rely on the deposit
Consumer law can give clients a right to cancel shortly after booking. In the UK, the Consumer Contracts Regulations 2013 give consumers 14 days to cancel a service contract made at a distance (online, by email or by phone) or away from your business premises, starting the day the contract is made, and regulation 36 says you must not start the service in that period unless the client expressly asks you to. There are exceptions, so take advice. In the US, the FTC's Cooling-Off Rule gives buyers until midnight of the third business day to cancel some sales made at their home or at a temporary location such as a convention centre or a fair, for sales of $130 or more at temporary locations; sales made entirely online, by mail or by phone are not covered. That matters if you take bookings at wedding fairs, and state laws vary too. The workflow can send the right cancellation wording with every contract, but the wording itself should come from you and your adviser.

```
Thanks,
[your name]
```

### Gallery delivery and the review request
When you mark a gallery as ready, the client gets the link, how long it will stay online and how to download or order prints. A few days later, a short message thanks them and asks for a review. Google's Maps content policy says businesses must not offer incentives such as discounts for reviews, must not discourage negative reviews and must not "selectively solicit positive reviews", so the request goes to every client and offers nothing in return. Our guide on [asking for Google reviews](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/ask-for-google-reviews-automatically/) has the wording.

## A wedding planner payment schedule, with supplier reminders that run on their own
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/wedding-planner-supplier-and-payment-schedules/

A wedding planner payment schedule lists every instalment the couple owes and every supplier deposit, balance and confirmation date, counted back from the wedding day. A workflow can send each reminder on its date, ask suppliers to confirm their final details, send the couple a final details questionnaire and share the finished timeline with everyone. The planner still agrees every amount, approves every message and handles anything that goes wrong.

A wedding planner payment schedule is the spine of every booking: the couple's instalments, a dozen suppliers with their own deposits and balance dates, and a run of confirmations in the last few weeks. On one wedding it lives in your head. On fifteen weddings across a season it lives in a spreadsheet you check late at night, hoping nothing slipped. Every date on it is counted back from the wedding day, and the reminders are the same on every booking, so this part can run on its own while you spend your time with couples and suppliers. This page is for wedding and event planners in the UK and the US; the same schedule works for parties and corporate events.

### Where the dates slip
- A couple's instalment is due, nobody reminds them, and you only notice when the venue asks for its balance
- A supplier's balance date passes because it was in their contract, not in your calendar
- Suppliers aren't asked to confirm arrival times, numbers and contacts until the final week
- The couple's final details (guest numbers, dietary needs, table plan, key contacts) arrive in pieces over WhatsApp
- The timeline goes out as version 6, and the photographer is still working from version 4

### A schedule counted back from the wedding day
A starting template. The months and amounts are yours to set in your own contract and your suppliers' contracts; what matters is that every date is calculated from the wedding date, so a new booking gets its whole schedule the moment you enter it. Venues run a similar countdown from first enquiry to signed contract; see [venue hire enquiry follow-up](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/event-venue-enquiry-follow-up/).
| When | Couple | Suppliers | Your check |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| On booking | Signed contract and booking payment | Hold dates with the venue and key suppliers | Contract and payment received |
| Your mid-point date | Next instalment reminder | Supplier deposits due under their contracts | Each deposit recorded against the supplier |
| About 8 weeks before | Final details questionnaire sent | Request for final details: arrival, set-up time, contact on the day | Answers chased until complete |
| About 6 weeks before | Final balance reminder, on the date your contract sets | Supplier balances due under their contracts | Every balance paid or flagged |
| About 3 weeks before | Draft timeline to review | Draft timeline to review | Changes collected in one place |
| About 1 week before | Final timeline and contact sheet | Final timeline, confirmation requested | Every supplier has confirmed |

### What the workflow does
1. You add a booking: wedding date, the couple, the package price and each supplier with their contract amounts and due dates. The full schedule is built from the wedding date.
2. A few days before each of the couple's instalments, they get a friendly reminder with the amount and how to pay. Once the payment shows in your accounts, the reminder stops.
3. Before each supplier deposit or balance is due, you get a reminder to pay it, or the couple does if they pay that supplier directly.
4. At your chosen point before the day, the couple gets the final details questionnaire as a form. Missing answers are chased by name, not with another "please complete the form".
5. Each supplier gets a short request to confirm arrival time, set-up needs and their contact on the day. Replies are logged against the booking. The florist can run the same check on their side with [a wedding and event order workflow for florists](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/florist-wedding-and-event-orders/).
6. The timeline is built from the questionnaire and the supplier replies. You check and edit it, then it goes to the couple and every supplier as one link, so everyone always sees the latest version.
7. Each morning you get a list: payments due this week, suppliers who haven't confirmed, couples with unanswered questions.

### A balance reminder you can copy
Email or message to the couple, a few days before the balance date:
```
Hi [names],

Not long now! A quick reminder that the final balance of [amount] for your wedding on [date] is due on [due date], as set out in your contract.

You can pay by [payment method or link]. If you've already sent it, thank you, and please ignore this.

If anything about the payment is a problem, just reply and we'll talk it through.

Next up: your final details questionnaire will arrive on [date], so we can build your day's timeline.

Best wishes,
[your name]
[business name]
```

### A note on bookings made remotely (UK)
If a couple books without meeting you at your business premises, for example over a video call with an e-signature, the Consumer Contracts Regulations 2013 usually give them a cancellation period that ends 14 days after the day the contract is entered into. Regulation 36 says you must not start providing the service in that period unless they expressly ask you to, and if they then cancel they pay a proportionate amount for what you have done. So the booking step should send your cancellation information with the contract and record whether the couple asked you to start straight away. Check your own wording with an adviser; this is not legal advice. For wording the booking payment itself, see [how to ask for a deposit](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/how-to-ask-for-a-deposit-on-a-quote/).

### What stays with you
You agree every price, payment date and supplier, and you approve the wording of every message before the first booking uses it. When a couple misses a payment, asks for more time or changes the plan, you decide what happens: the workflow tells you and pauses reminders until you say so. You check every timeline before it goes out. Couples' details and guests' dietary or access needs are personal information, so keep them in your own records and only for as long as you need them. If AI drafts the timeline or a message, a person approves it first. Photographers run the same contract-and-deposit steps on their side: see the [photography booking workflow](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/photographer-booking-contracts-and-deposits/). Caterers chasing [final guest numbers and dietary requirements](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/catering-quotes-and-final-numbers/) are working to the same date.
