### When is Form 1099-NEC due for the 2026 tax year?
Monday, February 1, 2027, for both the IRS copy and the contractor's copy. The usual date is January 31, but in 2027 that is a Sunday, and the IRS moves weekend due dates to the next business day.

### Does the $2,000 threshold apply to 2025 payments?
No. The IRS says the higher threshold applies to tax years beginning after 2025, so it covers payments made from January 1, 2026. Forms for 2025 payments used the $600 threshold.

### Do payments made through PayPal or by card need a 1099-NEC?
No. The IRS instructions say card payments and third-party network payments are reported by the payment company on Form 1099-K, not by the payer on Form 1099-NEC.

### Can clients collect W-9s themselves?
They can, but they usually forget until January. A workflow can do it on their behalf, from your address or theirs, with wording you approve.

## What to automate first in a small service business
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/what-to-automate-first-small-business/ (2026-11-10)

What to automate first in a small business: the job that happens every week, follows the same steps each time, and costs you money or a client when someone forgets it. Usually that is chasing something: documents, quotes, unpaid invoices or replies to new enquiries. Start with one process, define what "working" means in one sentence, and only then pick the tool.

What to automate first in a small business is a question about your week, not about software. Most small firms don't need "AI transformation". They need one annoying, repetitive job to stop depending on someone remembering it. For the bigger picture of what can run on its own, see our [small business automation guide](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/small-business-automation/).
Picking the right first process matters more than picking the right tool. A good first automation [pays for itself quickly](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/automation-roi-worksheet/), is easy to check, and teaches you what to automate next. A bad one takes weeks, breaks often and puts you off the whole idea. Below is a simple test you can run on your own business in half an hour, a scorecard to fill in, and the jobs that usually win. Before you build, it's worth reading the [mistakes that sink small business automations](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/small-business-automation-mistakes/).

### Step 1: list the jobs that repeat
Take a sheet of paper or a blank spreadsheet and write down every job you or your team did in the last two weeks that felt like admin. Don't judge them yet. Typical entries: sending the same email to a new client, asking for missing documents, typing enquiry details into a spreadsheet, chasing a customer who hasn't replied to a quote, sending appointment reminders, reminding people to pay.
Look through your sent emails and your phone's message history if you can't remember. The jobs you do without thinking are often the ones that take the most time in total.

### Step 2: score each job on five questions
Give each job 0, 1 or 2 points on each question. The highest total is your first automation. A tie goes to the job that is easiest to describe step by step.
| Question | 0 points | 1 point | 2 points |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| How often does it happen? | A few times a year | Monthly | Every week or every day |
| Are the steps the same each time? | Every case is different | Mostly, with a few exceptions | Yes, I could write them down now |
| What happens when it's forgotten? | Nothing much | A delay or an awkward call | A lost job, a late filing or a client who leaves |
| Does it need your judgement? | Yes, every time | Only at one step | No, it's sending, logging or reminding |
| Is the information already digital? | Paper only | Partly | Yes: email, forms, a spreadsheet, your job or accounting software |

### Step 3: check the winner against the usual first automations
In most small service businesses, the top score lands on one of the jobs below. They repeat, they follow a pattern, and the cost of forgetting them is real. If your winner is on this list, you're on safe ground.
- [Collecting documents from clients](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/bookkeeper-document-collection/), with reminders until everything is in (accountants, bookkeepers, mortgage brokers, solicitors).
- Following up on estimates and quotes that went quiet (trades, cleaners, agencies).
- Appointment confirmations and reminders, with an easy way to reschedule (clinics, salons, home services).
- Logging every new enquiry in one list and sending a quick, honest first reply.
- Asking every customer for a review after the job, the same way each time.
- Sending invoices and polite reminders about unpaid ones (our guide to [automating invoicing for a small business](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/how-to-automate-invoicing-small-business/) covers both ends).
- Onboarding a new client: engagement letter, ID checks, welcome email and first document request.

### What not to automate first
- Anything that happens a few times a year. The build won't pay back soon, and you'll forget how it works between runs.
- A process nobody can describe step by step yet. [Fix the process on paper first](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/process-map-template-small-business/), or you'll automate the confusion.
- Decisions that need your judgement: pricing, advice, hiring, complaints. Automate the steps around them instead, such as gathering the information and putting it in front of you.
- Anything where one wrong message would do real damage, unless a person approves each message. If AI drafts something, a person should approve it before it goes out.
- Your whole business at once. One process, live and trusted, beats five half-built ones.

### Step 4: define "working" in one sentence
Before anything is built, write one sentence that says what the automation must do and how you'll know it's doing it. It keeps the build focused and gives you a clear test. Some examples:
- "Every estimate gets two follow-ups, and every Monday I get a list of the ones still open."
- "Every new client gets the document checklist on day one, a reminder every 5 days, and I can see who is still missing what."
- "Every enquiry gets a reply within 5 minutes and lands in one sheet with the date, source and job."

### Step 5: pick the tool last
Only now does the tool matter. Most first automations run on what you already have: your email, a form, a shared spreadsheet or drive, your accounting or job software, plus an automation platform such as Zapier, Make or n8n to connect them. If you already use a CRM, check what it can do on its own first, as in [HubSpot's free CRM automation limits](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/hubspot-free-crm-automation-limits/). Our comparison of Zapier, Make and n8n explains how each one charges and who each suits. If you're weighing up building it yourself against hiring someone, [consultant vs freelancer vs DIY](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/automation-consultant-vs-freelancer-vs-diy/) compares the options, and the guide to business automation cost breaks down the build, the software and the support.

### For illustration: three jobs, scored
For illustration only, here is how a small plumbing business might score three jobs. Chasing quiet estimates: weekly (2), same steps (2), lost jobs when forgotten (2), no judgement (2), estimates already sent by email (2): total 10. Ordering parts: weekly (2), varies by job (1), delays when forgotten (1), needs judgement (0), partly digital (1): total 5. Yearly service reminders to past customers: monthly batches (1), same steps (2), lost repeat work (2), no judgement (2), customer list in a spreadsheet (2): total 9. The estimate follow-up goes first and the service reminders second. Parts ordering stays manual.

### How we would build your first one
If you'd rather not build it yourself, book a [free 15-minute call](https://mikeautomations.github.io/call/) and tell me which job scored highest. Within 48 hours you get a written plan with a fixed price and a clear definition of "working". It's built on the tools you already use, so nobody learns a new system. Live in 2-3 days. [Workflow automation is $2,000 one-off](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/pricing/) ($1,500 for the first 3 clients), and you pay once it's running and you're happy with it.

### How do I know if a process is worth automating?
If it happens weekly, follows the same steps, and forgetting it costs you a job, a client or a penalty, it's worth automating. If it happens a few times a year or needs your judgement at every step, leave it manual for now.

### Should my first automation use AI?
Only if a step genuinely needs reading or writing text, such as sorting enquiries or drafting a reply. Most first automations are plain sending, logging and reminding. Where AI drafts something, a person should approve it before it's sent.

### How long does a first automation take to build?
A single process with clear steps usually takes days, not weeks. Ours go live in 2-3 days after the written plan is agreed.

## Zapier vs Make vs n8n: which one suits a small business?
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/zapier-vs-make-vs-n8n/ (2026-11-10)

Zapier vs Make vs n8n, in short: Zapier is the easiest to start with and connects the most apps, but it charges per task, so busy multi-step workflows cost more. Make handles branching workflows on a visual canvas and charges per credit, roughly one per step. n8n charges per workflow run on its cloud plans and can be self-hosted, which suits firms that want data on their own server and have someone technical to look after it.

Zapier vs Make vs n8n is the question most small businesses hit as soon as they decide to automate something. All three connect your apps and move information between them: a form is filled in, a row is added, an email goes out. The differences are how much they ask of you, how they handle complicated workflows, where they run, and above all how they charge.
This comparison is written for [small service businesses](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/service-businesses/) with no developer on staff: accountants, trades, clinics, agencies. Prices below were checked on each vendor's own pricing page on 10 November 2026. Prices change often, so check them again before you buy.

### The comparison table (checked 10 November 2026)
Sources: zapier.com/pricing, make.com/en/pricing and n8n.io/pricing, all read on 10 November 2026. Zapier's pricing page notes that some actions use more than one task, depending on the step type and AI model.
|  | Zapier | Make | n8n |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| What you pay for | Tasks: each action that completes successfully. Triggers, Filters, Paths and Formatter steps don't count. | Credits: most module actions use 1 credit. Routers and error handlers are free; some AI features use more. | Executions: one run of the whole workflow, however many steps it has (cloud plans). |
| Free option | Free plan: 100 tasks a month, two-step Zaps only, 15-minute checks | Free plan: 1,000 credits a month, 2 active scenarios, 15-minute minimum interval | Community Edition: free to self-host, on your own server |
| Entry paid plan | Professional from $19.99 a month billed yearly ($29.99 monthly) for 750 tasks | Core $12 a month for 10,000 credits, as shown on monthly billing; yearly payment is cheaper | Starter €20 a month billed yearly for 2,500 executions, hosted by n8n |
| Apps | 9,000+ apps (zapier.com/pricing, 10 Nov 2026) | 3,500+ apps on the pricing page | 2,000+ integrations, plus an HTTP Request node for other apps with an API |
| Hosting | Zapier's cloud only | Make's cloud only (AWS, EU or North America) | n8n's cloud, or self-hosted on your own server |
| Learning curve | Gentlest | Moderate: visual canvas, more settings | Steepest, especially self-hosted |
| Best fit | Straight-line workflows between popular apps | Workflows with many branches, loops and data shaping | High-volume or data-sensitive workflows, with technical help available |

### Zapier: easiest to start, priced per task
- The easiest of the three to learn, and the largest library of ready-made app connections.
- Strongest for straight-line steps between popular apps. It can branch (Paths), filter, loop and run code, but long workflows with many paths get expensive and harder to follow.
- Every action that completes counts as a task, so a five-step Zap that runs 300 times a month uses far more tasks than a two-step one.
- The free plan only allows two-step Zaps, so most real business workflows need a paid plan.

### Make: visual workflows, priced per credit
- A visual canvas that shows the whole workflow, which makes branching, loops and reshaping data easier to see.
- Good for workflows with several paths and conditions, for example "if the client is VAT registered, ask for these documents, otherwise ask for those".
- Make now bills in credits (it used to count "operations"). Most actions use one credit, so the cost tracks the number of steps that run.
- A steeper learning curve than Zapier. Expect to spend time understanding how data moves between modules. Whether that effort pays off is the question in [is Make.com worth it for a small business](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/is-make-com-worth-it-small-business/).

### n8n: priced per run, can live on your own server
- On n8n's cloud plans you pay per execution: one run of the whole workflow, however many steps it has. Long workflows that run often can come out much cheaper than per-step pricing.
- The Community Edition can be [self-hosted](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/n8n-cloud-vs-self-hosted-small-business/) at no licence fee. n8n's Sustainable Use License allows use for your own internal business purposes, not for reselling n8n as a service.
- Self-hosting means someone has to install it, keep it updated, back it up and keep it secure. If nobody in the business can do that, use n8n's cloud or another tool.
- Comfortable with custom code when a step needs it.

### A worked cost example (for illustration)
For illustration only: an accounting firm wants a workflow that runs each time a client uploads a document. It has one trigger and four actions: save the file to the client folder, update the tracking sheet, check what's still missing, and email the client a thank-you that lists what's left. Say it runs 300 times a month.
|  | How usage is counted | Usage per month | Plan that covers it (list price, 10 November 2026) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Zapier | 4 actions x 300 runs | About 1,200 tasks | Professional, 1,500-task tier: $39 a month billed yearly |
| Make | 5 modules (trigger included) x 300 runs | About 1,500 credits | Core, 10,000 credits: $12 a month |
| n8n Cloud | 1 execution per run | 300 executions | Starter, 2,500 executions: €20 a month billed yearly |

### How to read the example
The numbers are a rough guide, not a quote. Real usage depends on how each step is built: polling triggers, searches inside a step and AI actions can all change the count. Use each vendor's own pricing page with your real volumes before deciding.
At this size, all three cost less than an hour of someone's time each month. The subscription is rarely the deciding factor for a small business. What decides it is [who builds the workflow](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/automation-consultant-vs-freelancer-vs-diy/), who fixes it when an app changes, and whether your data may leave your own systems.

### How to choose: four questions
1. [Write the process down first](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/process-map-template-small-business/): what starts it, every step, every app involved and what should happen when something is missing.
2. Is it a straight line between two or three popular apps? Zapier is usually enough and the quickest to set up. If you want it built for you, see what a [Zapier expert for small business](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/zapier-expert-for-small-business/) does.
3. Does it have many conditions, loops or data to reshape? Make or n8n will be cleaner and usually cheaper per run. If you'd rather hire help, see what to check in a [Make.com consultant](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/make-com-consultant/) or an [n8n consultant](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/n8n-consultant/).
4. Must the data stay on servers you control, or will it run thousands of times a month? n8n, self-hosted or on its cloud, is the usual answer, as long as someone can maintain it.

### What matters more than the tool
The tool is rarely what makes an automation reliable. What matters is handling the cases that go wrong: a missing field, a duplicate, an email that bounces, an app that changes its login. Whichever you choose, make sure someone is told when a run fails, and that the workflow lives in your own account, not someone else's, so you're never locked in.

### Or skip choosing
If you'd rather not learn any of them, book a [free 15-minute call](https://mikeautomations.github.io/call/). Within 48 hours you get a written plan with a fixed price and a clear definition of "working". The workflow is built on whichever tool fits the process, in your own accounts, and documented. Live in 2-3 days. [Workflow automation is $2,000 one-off](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/pricing/) ($1,500 for the first 3 clients), and you pay once it's running and you're happy with it.

### Is n8n free?
The self-hosted Community Edition has no licence fee for your own internal business use, but you pay for the server and someone's time to run it. n8n's hosted cloud plans start at €20 a month billed yearly (checked 10 November 2026).

### Which is cheapest for a small business?
For a few simple two-app workflows, any of them can cost little or nothing. For long workflows that run often, per-run pricing (n8n) or per-credit pricing (Make) usually works out cheaper than per-task pricing (Zapier). Check each vendor's pricing page with your real volumes.

### Can I switch tools later?
Yes, but workflows don't transfer between them automatically; each one has to be rebuilt. Writing the process down step by step makes a rebuild much quicker.

## WhatsApp Business app vs API: which one does a small business need?
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/whatsapp-business-app-vs-api/ (2026-11-11)

The WhatsApp Business app vs API choice comes down to who sends the messages. The WhatsApp Business app is a phone app for a business that answers customers by hand, with quick replies, labels, a catalogue and greeting and away messages. The WhatsApp Business Platform (the API) lets software send and receive messages, such as reminders and confirmations, but Meta charges per delivered message, business-started messages must use templates Meta has approved, and the customer must have opted in.

The WhatsApp Business app vs API question comes up as soon as a small business wants WhatsApp to do more than one person typing on one phone. Maybe you want booking reminders to go out on their own, or new enquiries logged in your CRM, or two people answering the same number.
This guide compares the two side by side, using Meta's own pages as checked on 11 November 2026: what each one does, how the API is charged, the limits and rules that catch people out, and a short checklist to decide. If you are still choosing between WhatsApp, SMS and email for client messages, start with [texting clients for documents](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/text-or-whatsapp-clients-for-documents/), which covers the consent rules in the UK and US.

### The two products in one sentence each
Meta's WhatsApp Business site describes the app as "for small businesses who personally manage conversations with customers" and the Platform as "for medium to large businesses communicating with customers at scale through programmatic access". In plain words: the app is for a person, the Platform is for software.
"Medium to large" is Meta's framing, not a rule. A five-person clinic or a trades firm can use the Platform too, usually through a provider that connects it to the tools they already run. The real question is whether you need messages to be sent or read by a system rather than by someone holding the phone.

### Side-by-side comparison
The app features in the first column are listed on Meta's WhatsApp Business app features page. Meta also offers Meta Verified for the app, which the same page says includes linking up to 10 devices and agents to one account.
|  | WhatsApp Business app | WhatsApp Business Platform (API) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Who sends messages | A person, from a phone or linked device | Your software, a booking system or a CRM, plus people using a shared inbox tool |
| Built-in tools | Quick replies, labels, catalogue, greeting and away messages | None of its own: you get an interface for your systems, or a provider's inbox |
| Starting a conversation | Type a message to a contact | Only with a message template Meta has approved |
| Replying to a customer | Any time | Free-form replies only within 24 hours of the customer's last message |
| Cost | Meta's per-message pricing is for the Platform | Charged per delivered message you send, by type |
| Volume limits | Not designed for bulk sending | Starts at 250 unique people per 24 hours for business-started messages, rising in tiers |
| Connects to other systems | No | Yes: CRM, calendar, forms, invoicing, AI tools |

### How Meta charges for the API in 2026
Meta's developer pricing page says the Platform has charged per message since 1 July 2025, replacing the old per-conversation pricing. You pay only for messages your business sends, and only when they are delivered. Messages customers send to you are not charged.
- Template messages can be sent at any time and come in three types: marketing, utility (for example an appointment confirmation) and authentication (one-time codes). Each type has its own rate.
- Free-form replies ("service" messages) can only be sent while the 24-hour customer service window is open. That window starts when the customer messages or calls you, and resets each time they write again.
- Changes from 1 October 2026: Meta's pricing page says service messages are charged again after a monthly free allowance of 1,000 per business phone number (it doesn't roll over), and utility templates sent inside the customer service window are now chargeable too.
- Meta says businesses with no payment method on file by 30 September 2026 may find their service messages stop being delivered. If you set this up now, add a payment method in WhatsApp Manager before you go live.
- Rates change, so check the current rate card on Meta's pricing page for the countries your customers are in before you budget.

### Limits and rules that catch small businesses out
- Templates first. Meta's template documentation says templates must have an approved status before they can be sent, that review is automatic on creation or editing, and that it "can take up to 24 hours". Write your reminder and confirmation templates early.
- Messaging limits. Meta's messaging limits page says new business portfolios can reach 250 unique people per moving 24 hours with messages sent outside a customer service window. The next tier is 2,000, reached by verifying your business or by sending 2,000 delivered messages outside the window to unique people within 30 days using high-quality templates. After that, limits rise to 10,000, 100,000 and unlimited automatically if your quality stays high and you've used at least half your limit in the last 7 days.
- Opt-in. The WhatsApp Business Messaging Policy says you may only message people who have given you opt-in permission to receive messages from you, and that you must respect any request to stop, on or off WhatsApp.
- A route to a person. The same policy allows automation, but says businesses must have "prompt, clear, and direct escalation paths" to a human, such as a handover in the chat, phone or email.
- AI chatbots. The Meta Terms for WhatsApp Business Platform (section 4.7) bar providers whose main product is AI, such as a general-purpose chatbot, from using the Platform. An AI feature that is incidental to your own business, like drafting a reply to a booking question, is outside that ban, but Meta decides what counts as primary. Keep AI to drafts a person approves; see [ChatGPT for small business admin](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/chatgpt-for-small-business-admin/).
- Data. Customer names, numbers and chat history are personal data under UK GDPR and similar laws. Our [GDPR checklist for automating client data](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/gdpr-checklist-automating-client-data/) covers what to record before you connect anything.

### Can you keep the app and use the API on the same number?
Yes, in most cases. Meta calls it onboarding WhatsApp Business app users, and providers often call it coexistence. You keep using the app on your phone, and the same number is connected to the Platform through a provider. Meta's developer guide says the last 6 months of individual chats and your contacts with a WhatsApp number can be synchronised, as long as you do it within 24 hours of connecting.
There are trade-offs, all from the same Meta guide:
- Broadcast lists are disabled: you can't create new ones and existing lists become read-only.
- Disappearing messages, view once and live location are turned off for one-to-one chats.
- Group chats are not synchronised, because the Platform doesn't support group chats.
- Numbers used both ways have a fixed throughput of 20 messages per second, which is far more than a small business needs.
- Meta lists inactivity of the primary phone for about 14 days as a reason the connection can drop, so the phone with the app needs to be used.

### Which one do you need? A five-question check
Answer these honestly. If every answer is "no", stay on the app and use its quick replies and away messages well. Two or more "yes" answers usually mean the Platform is worth setting up.
Checklist: WhatsApp Business app or API?:
```
1. Do you send the same message (reminder, confirmation, "we're on our way") more than 20 times a week?   yes / no
2. Do two or more people need to answer the same WhatsApp number at once, with a record of who said what?   yes / no
3. Should WhatsApp messages be triggered by another system (bookings, quotes, invoices, a web form)?   yes / no
4. Do you need replies, photos or documents saved to a CRM, job sheet or client folder automatically?   yes / no
5. Do you lose enquiries because nobody sees the message until evening?   yes / no

Before you switch, write down:
- Which templates you need (wording for each, and whether it is marketing or utility)
- How customers opt in (booking form, quote acceptance, first message)
- Who handles a reply when the customer wants a person
- Whether you need to keep using the app on the same number
```

### Typical small-business uses for the Platform
For illustration, these are the jobs where the Platform earns its cost for a service business. Each starts from a system you already have, not from WhatsApp:
1. A customer books online, and a utility template confirms the time and sends a reminder the day before. See [reducing appointment no-shows](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/reduce-appointment-no-shows/).
2. A new enquiry arrives on WhatsApp, the details are logged in your CRM or spreadsheet, and the right person is told straight away. See [replying to new enquiries fast](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/reply-to-new-enquiries-fast/).
3. A quote is sent and, if there's no reply in a few days, a polite follow-up goes out. See [WhatsApp quote follow-up for tradespeople](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/whatsapp-quote-follow-up-tradespeople/).
4. The customer replies with a photo or document, and it is saved to the right job or client folder instead of staying in someone's phone.
5. Anything sensitive or unusual is handed to a person, who replies from a shared inbox.

### Is the WhatsApp Business API free?
No. Meta's pricing page says it charges per delivered message the business sends, by type (marketing, utility, authentication, service). Since 1 October 2026 each business phone number gets 1,000 free service messages a month, and messages customers send you are not charged.

### Can I use the WhatsApp Business app and the API on the same number?
Usually, yes. Meta lets businesses onboard an existing WhatsApp Business app number to the Platform and keep using the app. Broadcast lists, disappearing messages, view once and live location are turned off in one-to-one chats, and group chats are not synchronised.

## How to automate data entry from emails and PDFs, with a person checking
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/automate-data-entry-from-emails-and-pdfs/ (2026-11-11)

To automate data entry from emails and PDFs, send every document to one inbox, pull out the fields you need with a parser (for fixed formats), OCR (for scans and photos) or AI extraction (for varied layouts), and write them into your spreadsheet, CRM or accounting software as drafts. A person then checks each draft against the original before it's approved, because extraction tools can misread a number or fill in a value that isn't there.

You can automate data entry from emails and PDFs without buying a new system. Most small businesses already have the pieces: an inbox, a spreadsheet or CRM, and accounting software that can read a bill. What's missing is the route between them, and a clear rule for who checks what.
This guide covers the three ways to get data out of a document, what the tools you may already pay for can do today, and a review step that keeps mistakes out of your records.

### What data entry from emails and PDFs looks like in a small business
It's usually the same few documents, every day: a supplier invoice as a PDF attachment, an enquiry from a website form, a booking confirmation, a purchase order from a customer, a timesheet, a scanned delivery note. Someone opens each one, finds six or seven values, and types them into another screen.
The values are the same every time, even when the layout isn't, so it suits automation. But one wrong digit in an amount or a bank detail costs more than the typing ever did. The goal is a person who checks, instead of a person who types.

### Three ways to get data out of a document
Each method suits a different kind of document. Many workflows use two of them: a parser for the emails that always look the same, and AI extraction for the PDFs that don't.
| Method | What it does | Best for | Weak spot |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Rule-based parsing | Finds text by position or by the words around it, such as the number after "Total" | Emails sent by a system: web forms, booking notifications, order confirmations | Breaks when the sender changes the layout |
| OCR (optical character recognition) | Turns a scan or photo into text a computer can read | Scanned letters, photographed receipts, delivery notes | Gives you text, not fields; poor photos give poor text |
| AI extraction | Reads the document and returns the fields you ask for, whatever the layout | Supplier invoices and PDFs from many different senders | Can misread or make up a value, so every result needs checking |

### Rule-based parsing: for emails that always look the same
If the email comes from a system, such as your website form, a booking tool or a marketplace, the layout barely changes. A parser can lift the fields out reliably and cheaply.
One example is Email Parser by Zapier. Zapier's help centre says you create a mailbox and get an @robot.zapier.com address, then highlight the words in a sample email that you want as data and label each one. It also warns that "parsing emails can be tricky": each item should sit on its own line, values should look the same every time, and forwarded emails cause problems because of extra threads and signatures. That's true of every rule-based parser, not just this one. Our [Zapier vs Make vs n8n comparison](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/zapier-vs-make-vs-n8n/) covers where the parsed data can go next. And if your form can post its answers straight into a spreadsheet, skip the email step entirely.

### OCR: for scans and photos
OCR turns a picture of text into text. It doesn't know which number is the invoice number, so you still need a step after it. You may have it already: Google Drive is a free example. Google's Drive help says you can convert PDFs and photo files (.jpeg, .png and .gif) to text by right-clicking the file and choosing Open with, then Google Docs. The same page sets limits worth knowing: the file should be 2 MB or smaller, text should be at least 10 pixels high, and "lists, tables, columns, footnotes, and endnotes are not likely to be detected". That last point matters for invoices, which are mostly tables. Use OCR to make a scan searchable, and use extraction to pull the fields.

### AI extraction: for documents from many different senders
Supplier invoices are the classic case: twenty suppliers means twenty layouts. An AI model can read each one and return the same fields: supplier, date, invoice number, net, tax, total, due date.
The catch is accuracy. Anthropic's own guidance on reducing hallucinations says that even the most advanced language models "can sometimes generate text that is factually incorrect or inconsistent with the given context", and that its techniques reduce this but don't eliminate it. Two of those techniques help here: tell the model it may leave a field blank when it can't find the value, and ask it to quote the exact text it took each value from, so the person checking can see where it came from. More on where AI fits, and where plain rules are better, in [AI vs automation: what's the difference](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/ai-vs-automation-difference/).

### Check what your accounting software already does
Before you build anything for bills and receipts, use the extraction your accounting software already includes. Both of these were checked on the vendors' help pages on 11 November 2026.
- Xero: each organisation has a unique bills email address. Xero's help says that when you email a bill to it, Xero uses smart document capture to create a draft bill with the document attached, and if it can read the document it fills in the Contact, Date, Total, Due date, Reference and Description. You can email up to 10 bills in one email, up to 25MB in total, and the bill must be an attachment, not in the body of the email. If the supplier isn't a contact yet, the draft says "No contact" and you fix it before approving.
- QuickBooks Online: an admin sets up a forwarding address ending in @assist.intuit.com. Intuit's help says QuickBooks pulls the date, amount, vendor and last four digits of the card from each receipt, which you then review in the Receipts tab. Each file should hold only one receipt, files must be PDF, JPEG, JPG, GIF or PNG between 46KB and 20MB, and users must send from the email address they sign in with.

### Where a custom workflow earns its place
The built-in tools stop at the edge of the accounting software. A workflow covers data that isn't a bill, and the steps around the bill:
- Order emails or purchase orders that should become a job in your CRM or job sheet.
- Timesheets, delivery notes or signed forms whose details go into a spreadsheet for invoicing or payroll.
- Bills that need an approver before they're entered. Our [supplier invoice approval workflow](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/supplier-invoice-approval-workflow/) shows that route.
- Clients who send documents to a person's inbox instead of the capture address. For bookkeepers, [collecting receipts from clients](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/collect-receipts-from-bookkeeping-clients/) covers the chasing side.

### How to set it up: six steps
1. Pick one document type. Not "all our paperwork": one, such as supplier invoices or website order emails. Note roughly how many arrive a week and who types them in today.
2. Give it one front door: a shared inbox or a dedicated address that every sender uses. In Gmail or Outlook, a rule can forward matching emails there automatically; [Gmail automation for accountants](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/gmail-automation-for-accountants/) explains how filters work.
3. List the fields, and nothing more. Write down exactly which values you need and where each one goes. Fields you don't use are just more to check.
4. Choose the method per sender type: a parser for system emails, your accounting software's capture for bills and receipts, AI extraction for everything with a varied layout.
5. Write the result as a draft, never as a final record: a draft bill, a row marked "to check", a CRM lead with status "new". Keep a link to the original document on every record.
6. Have a person check and approve. They compare the draft against the original, fix anything wrong, and approve. Only then does anything get paid, invoiced or sent.

### The human check: a checklist to copy
The check is quick when the draft and the original sit side by side. Give whoever approves this list, and add your own rules to it.
Review checklist for extracted data (copy and adapt):
```
Before approving an extracted record:

[ ] Open the original document from the link on the record.
[ ] Supplier or customer name matches an existing contact (not a new near-duplicate).
[ ] Document number matches, and it isn't already in the system (duplicate check).
[ ] Date and due date are right, and read the right way round (day/month vs month/day).
[ ] Net, tax and total match the document, and net + tax = total.
[ ] Currency is right.
[ ] Any blank field: find the value or mark it "not on document". Never guess.
[ ] Bank details: if they differ from the details on file, STOP. Confirm by phone using a number you already hold, not one from the email.
[ ] Category or account code makes sense for this supplier.
[ ] Approve, or send back with a note saying what was wrong.
```

### Personal data and accuracy
If the documents contain personal data, such as names, addresses or customer details, the rules on accuracy apply to whatever your workflow writes. The UK ICO's guidance on the accuracy principle, Article 5(1)(d) of the UK GDPR, says you should take all reasonable steps to make sure the personal data you hold is not incorrect or misleading, and correct or erase it as soon as possible if it is. A person checking each extracted record is one of those reasonable steps.
Also decide where documents go and who can see them before you switch anything on, especially if an AI service reads them. Our [GDPR checklist for automating client data](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/gdpr-checklist-automating-client-data/) walks through those questions.

### Mistakes to avoid
- Letting extracted data post straight to final records. Every record starts as a draft until a person approves it.
- Using AI where a parser would do. If an email is sent by a system and never changes, rules are cheaper and more predictable.
- No error route. Decide where documents go when extraction fails (a "couldn't read" folder that someone checks daily), so nothing disappears.

### How Mike Automations would set this up
We'd start with the one document type that takes the most typing. Documents arrive at one address, the fields are pulled out with the simplest method that works (your accounting software's own capture first), and each record lands as a draft with a link to the original and anything uncertain flagged. A person checks and approves. Nothing is paid, invoiced or sent without that approval. You can see the idea in the [demo](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/try/), or sketch your own workflow in the [plan builder](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/plan/).
It begins with a [free 15-minute call](https://mikeautomations.github.io/call/) about which documents you retype today. Within 48 hours you get a written plan with a fixed price. It's built on the tools you already use, it's live in 2-3 days, and it costs [$2,000 one-off](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/pricing/), paid once it's running and you're happy with it (see the [pay-when-happy agreement](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/agreement/)).

### Can I automate data entry from PDF invoices?
Yes. Start with your accounting software: Xero's help says emailing a bill to your organisation's bills address creates a draft bill and fills in fields like Contact, Date, Total and Due date when it can read the document, and QuickBooks Online pulls the date, amount and vendor from forwarded receipts for review. For other PDFs, AI extraction can return the fields you need, with a person checking each one.

### Is AI data extraction accurate enough to trust?
Not without a check. Anthropic's own guidance says even the most advanced language models can sometimes generate text that is factually incorrect, and its techniques reduce this without eliminating it. Write extracted data as drafts and have a person compare each one against the original before approving.

### Do I need special software to parse emails?
Often not. For emails sent by a system, a parser such as Email Parser by Zapier can pick out labelled fields. For bills and receipts, your accounting software's own capture may already do the job.

## How long does business automation take? Realistic timelines and what slows them down
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/how-long-does-business-automation-take/ (2026-11-11)

How long business automation takes depends on the size of the job. One workflow, such as document chasing or invoice reminders on tools you already use, can go from first call to live in under a week: a written plan within 48 hours and a build of 2-3 days. A custom system with its own logins and data takes weeks (at Mike Automations, a first version in 3-4 weeks), and most delays come from waiting for access, decisions and approvals, not from the build itself.

How long does business automation take? Less than most owners expect for one workflow, and longer than they hope for a whole new system. The build is rarely the slow part. The slow parts are deciding exactly what should happen, getting access to the right accounts, and agreeing the wording of anything that goes to a client.
This guide gives realistic timelines by type of project, the steps every project goes through, the things that add days or weeks, and a short checklist you can use to keep your own project moving. If you haven't picked a process yet, the [small business automation overview](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/small-business-automation/) shows the common ones.

### Typical timelines by type of project
These are planning ranges, not promises. Where a time is Mike Automations' own, it says so. Where it depends on something outside anyone's control, such as a vendor review, the table names the source.
| Type of project | Example | Typical time to live | What decides it |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| One workflow on tools you already use | Chasing missing documents, invoice reminders, replies to new enquiries | Mike Automations: plan within 48 hours of the call, build usually 2-3 days, usually under a week from call to live | How clear the steps are, and how fast access is given |
| A workflow that sends WhatsApp templates | Appointment reminders through the WhatsApp Business Platform | As above, plus template review: Meta says a decision can take up to 24 hours | Template wording, and whether a template is rejected and appealed |
| A workflow in a Microsoft 365 business | Outlook or SharePoint automations | As above if the connection is allowed; otherwise it waits for your admin | Your consent settings in Microsoft Entra ID |
| An AI step inside a workflow | Drafting replies or reading invoice details for a person to approve | A similar build to a workflow; allow extra time on live work while a person checks every draft | How varied your real emails and documents are |
| A custom system | Clients, jobs, documents and tasks in one place, with a login per person | Mike Automations: first version live in 3-4 weeks, plus 60 days of fixes | Scope: number of users, tools connected, data moved over |
| Doing it yourself | Building a workflow in Zapier, Make or Power Automate | Depends on your spare hours, often spread over several evenings | Learning time and testing time |

### The steps every automation project goes through
Whoever builds it, a well-run project follows roughly the same steps. Knowing them shows you where the time actually goes.
1. A short call about the problem: what eats your week, how it's done today, which tools you use and what "done" looks like. At Mike Automations this is a free 15-minute call.
2. A written plan with a fixed price: what gets automated and what stays manual, which tools it connects to, how you'll know it works, and when it goes live. Ours arrives within 48 hours of the call.
3. Access: the builder gets only the access the workflow needs, in your own accounts (email, drive, accounting or booking software). This is the most common cause of delay.
4. Wording approval: you approve the text of every message that will go to a client before anything is switched on.
5. The build and testing: usually 2-3 days for one workflow, tested on dummy records first and then on a few real ones.
6. A walkthrough: a short session in plain English on what it does, where to look and how to pause it.
7. Live on real work: it runs on your actual clients while someone watches it closely and fixes anything that doesn't behave as the plan said.

### What slows an automation project down
In most small businesses the work waits on people, not on software. These are the usual causes, and almost all of them are in your hands.
- Nobody has written down how the process works today. If three people do it three different ways, someone has to choose one first. A [process map](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/process-map-template-small-business/) done before the call saves days.
- Access takes a week to arrive. Nothing can be built until the builder can log in, so have the account owner ready on the day the plan is accepted.
- Your Microsoft 365 settings block new apps. Microsoft's documentation on user and admin consent (Microsoft Entra ID) explains that an administrator can stop users from consenting to apps, and then only someone with the right admin role can approve the connection. If an outside IT firm runs your Microsoft 365, tell them early.
- Message templates need approval. On the WhatsApp Business Platform, Meta's template review page says an approval decision can take up to 24 hours, and an appeal against a rejection is also decided within 24 hours.
- The wording goes round and round. Client-facing messages are where owners rightly slow down. Agree who signs off the wording, and by when.
- The scope grows mid-build. "While you're in there, could it also..." is how a three-day job becomes three weeks. Write new ideas down and treat them as the next workflow.
- Messy data. Duplicate clients, missing email addresses or a spreadsheet with ten tabs need tidying before an automation can rely on them.
- Too big a first project. Start with one repetitive, rule-based job. Our [5-point test for what to automate first](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/what-to-automate-first-small-business/) helps you choose.

### A checklist to keep your project fast
Copy this into a note before your first call. If you can tick most of it, a single workflow really can be live within a week.
Automation project readiness checklist:
```
Before the call
[ ] I can describe the process in 5-10 steps, from what starts it to what "finished" means
[ ] I know which tools are involved (email, drive, accounting, booking, forms)
[ ] I have one recent real example of the process, start to finish
[ ] I know what "working" looks like (e.g. every client with missing items gets a reminder every 7 days)

When the plan is accepted
[ ] The account owner can give access the same day
[ ] If we use Microsoft 365: our admin knows an app connection may need their approval
[ ] If we send WhatsApp templates: our WhatsApp Business account is already set up
[ ] One person signs off client-facing wording, by [date]

During the build
[ ] New ideas go on a "next workflow" list, not into this one
[ ] Test records are ready (a dummy client, a test invoice)
[ ] Someone checks the first real messages that go out
```

### Is fast too fast?
A short build only works if the plan is clear and the testing is honest. Three habits stop speed turning into mistakes.
- A person approves anything an AI step prepares, at least until it has proved itself on your real work. AI that drafts is quick; AI that sends unchecked is a risk.
- Every automation has a pause switch, and you know where it is.
- The handover is written down: what it does, where it runs and who to call. Our [automation handover checklist](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/automation-handover-checklist/) lists what you should get.

### What happens after it goes live
Going live isn't the end. The first weeks on real work show the cases nobody thought of: a client who replies from a different address, a document with an odd file name. Expect small fixes. At Mike Automations small fixes are included for 60 days after go-live, and after that support is optional at $150 a month.
Automations also need occasional attention when one of your tools changes. Our guide on [whether automations need maintenance](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/do-automations-need-maintenance/) explains what to expect.

### How Mike Automations keeps it to days, not months

You start with a [free 15-minute call](https://mikeautomations.github.io/call/). Within 48 hours you get a written plan with a fixed price. The build is usually 2-3 days, and then it runs on your real work. No deposit and no hourly billing.
Not sure what to automate yet? The free [plan builder](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/plan/) suggests workflows for your type of business, and the [demo](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/try/) shows one running. If you're comparing quotes, our guide to [business automation cost](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/business-automation-cost/) explains what you should be paying for, and [how to brief an automation project](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/how-to-brief-an-automation-project/) gives you a template that cuts planning time.

### How long does it take to automate one business process?
For one process on tools you already use, such as document chasing or invoice reminders, the build is usually 2-3 days. With Mike Automations the written plan arrives within 48 hours of a free 15-minute call, so it's usually live in under a week.

### How long does a custom business system take to build?
Weeks rather than days, because it has its own logins, screens and data. At Mike Automations a first version is live in 3-4 weeks, with 60 days of fixes, and the scope and price are agreed in writing before work starts.

### What is the most common cause of automation delays?
Waiting on people: access to accounts, decisions about how the process should work, and sign-off of client-facing wording. Outside reviews can add time too; for example, Meta says WhatsApp template review can take up to 24 hours.

## AI receptionist for small business: pros, cons and what to keep human
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/ai-receptionist-small-business-pros-and-cons/ (2026-11-11)

An AI receptionist for a small business is software that answers calls or chats in a natural voice, answers common questions, takes messages and books appointments when nobody is free to pick up. It works well for routine, predictable calls such as opening hours, booking slots and taking a name and number, and badly for emergencies, complaints, price promises and anything it has to guess. Before you switch one on, tell callers they are talking to an AI and whether the call is recorded, check the recording consent rules where you and your callers are, and keep a quick route to a real person.

An AI receptionist for small business promises what a good receptionist does: every call answered, every enquiry written down, nobody kept waiting. For a one or two person business where the phone rings while you're on a job, with a client or driving, that's a real problem worth solving. Missed calls are often missed work.
But a voice that sounds human is not a person who understands your business. Below: what it does well, where it goes wrong, the recording and consent rules to check, what to keep human, and a greeting script to copy.

### What an AI receptionist actually is
Most products sold as an AI receptionist answer the phone (or a website chat) with a generated voice, reply from information you give them, and then take a message, book a slot, send a text or pass the call to you. The "AI" is a language model that decides what to say. Our [AI vs automation](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/ai-vs-automation-difference/) post explains where AI helps and where plain rules are better.
Here's how it compares with the other ways to handle calls you can't answer (general descriptions, not specific products).
| Option | What the caller gets | Good for | Watch out for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Voicemail | A recorded greeting and a beep | Very low call volume | Many callers hang up and ring the next business |
| Missed-call text back | A text soon after with a link to book or reply | Trades and services where callers want a quick answer | Only works for mobiles; the text needs one clear next step |
| Human answering service | A person who takes a message | Callers who need reassurance | A monthly cost; they only know what you tell them |
| AI receptionist | A natural voice that answers questions and books | Routine, repeated questions and bookings | Wrong answers said confidently; consent and recording rules |
| Your own staff | Someone who knows the business | Anything sensitive, urgent or unusual | Cost, and cover for breaks and holidays |

### The pros: what it handles well
- Answering out of hours and when you're busy, so the caller gets a response instead of a ring-out.
- The same handful of questions you answer every day: opening hours, where you are, which areas you cover, whether you do a certain service, how to book.
- Taking a clean message (name, number, what they need, how urgent) and sending it to you by text or email.
- Booking into fixed slots in a calendar you already use, and sending a confirmation. Pair it with reminders to [reduce no-shows](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/reduce-appointment-no-shows/).
- A written summary of each call, so nothing depends on memory.

### The cons: where it goes wrong
- It can make things up. Language models sometimes give a confident answer that isn't in the information you gave them: a price, an opening time, a promise to come out today. If it says it, the caller heard it from your business.
- Names, numbers and addresses get misheard, especially on a bad line, with background noise or with strong accents. A wrong digit in a phone number means a lost lead.
- Emergencies need judgement. A burst pipe, a gas smell, a distressed patient or a client in trouble should reach a person straight away, not a booking flow. Our [emergency call-out triage guide](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/emergency-call-out-triage-plumbers/) shows how to route urgent calls by simple rules.
- Upset callers get more upset talking to a machine, and some callers won't talk to one at all.
- Call content is personal data. Recordings and transcripts sit with the provider, so you need to know where they are stored, for how long and who can see them. Our [GDPR checklist for automating client data](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/gdpr-checklist-automating-client-data/) covers the questions to ask.
- Someone still has to keep its information up to date. When your prices, hours or services change, it keeps saying the old thing until you change it.

### Rules to check before you switch it on
This is a starting list for a conversation with your adviser, not legal advice. The rules depend on where you are, where your callers are and what your business does.
- UK: the ICO's guidance on monitoring calls says you must tell people that you are recording the call and why, and that a recorded message is good practice. Fuller privacy information, such as how long you keep recordings, can follow by email or a link.
- US, federal law: 18 U.S.C. 2511(2)(d) allows a private person to record a call they are part of, or where one party has given prior consent, as long as it isn't for a criminal or tortious purpose.
- US, states: some states require everyone's consent. California Penal Code section 632 makes it an offence to record a confidential communication without the consent of all parties. If you have callers in other states, check each state's rule, or simply tell every caller at the start.
- US, outbound calls: in February 2024 the FCC confirmed in a Declaratory Ruling (FCC 24-17) that the TCPA's rules on an "artificial or prerecorded voice" cover AI-generated voices. If your AI receptionist also makes calls, for example call-backs or reminders, those calls generally need the called person's prior express consent.
- EU, including Ireland: the AI Act includes transparency rules so that people know when they are interacting with an AI system such as a chatbot. Check the current timetable for when these duties apply to you. The duty to build this in sits mainly with the provider of the AI system, so ask yours how it tells callers they're speaking to an AI.
- Regulated work: clinics, law firms, financial advisers and accountants have extra rules on confidentiality and record-keeping. Check with your regulator or professional body before an AI handles calls about patients, cases or money.

### What to keep human
A simple test: if a wrong answer would cost you money, a customer or trust, a person should give it. The AI can collect the details and hand them over.
| Call type | AI receptionist | Person |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Opening hours, location, areas covered | Yes | No need |
| Booking a standard appointment | Yes, into fixed slots | Only if it's unusual |
| Taking a message for a call-back | Yes | Calls back |
| Quotes and prices | Only fixed, published prices | Anything that depends on the job |
| Emergencies and urgent problems | Recognise them and pass on at once | Yes |
| Complaints and refunds | Take details, say who will call | Yes |
| Health, legal or money questions | No | Yes |
| Anything it isn't sure about | Say so and take a message | Yes |

### How to try an AI receptionist safely
1. List the ten questions callers ask most often, with the answer you give. This becomes the only information it's allowed to use.
2. Write down what it must never do: quote a price that isn't on your list, promise a time, give advice, or argue.
3. Decide what counts as urgent for your business and where those calls go: your mobile, a colleague, or an emergency line.
4. Set the greeting to say it's an automated assistant and, if you record, that the call is recorded and why. Use the script below.
5. Start with out-of-hours calls only, or one line, for two to four weeks. Keep your main number answered the old way.
6. Read every call summary and listen to a sample of recordings each week. Note every wrong answer and fix the information behind it.
7. Ask the provider where recordings and transcripts are stored, how long they're kept and how to delete them. Widen it only after a full week with no wrong answers that matter.

### Greeting and handover script to copy
Change the parts in [brackets]. Keep it short: callers want to get to the point.
AI receptionist greeting, urgent handover and call summary:
```
Greeting:
"Hello, you've reached [business name]. I'm an automated assistant, and this call is recorded so we can follow up on your enquiry. I can answer common questions, book an appointment or take a message for [owner name]. If you'd rather speak to a person, just say 'person' at any time. How can I help?"

If the caller says it's urgent or mentions [urgent words, e.g. leak, no heating, gas smell]:
"That sounds urgent. I'm passing you to [name] now."
If nobody answers: "I couldn't reach [name], so I've sent your details marked urgent. If anyone is in danger, please call [emergency number] now."

If it doesn't know the answer:
"I don't want to give you the wrong answer. I'll take your details and [owner name] will call you back [today before 6 pm / on the next working day]."

Summary sent to you after every call:
Name: [name]
Number (read back and confirmed): [number]
What they need: [one line]
Urgent: [yes/no]
Best time to call back: [time]
Anything promised on the call: [should be "nothing"]
```

### A cheaper first step for many businesses
If the real problem is calls you can't answer, you may not need a voice AI at all. A [missed-call text back](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/missed-call-text-back-contractors/) sends the caller a text with a booking link or a short form, and you reply when you're free. It runs on simple rules: no AI voice, nothing to mishear. The same idea works for web forms and email, and our post on how to [reply to new enquiries fast](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/reply-to-new-enquiries-fast/) has templates.
AI then earns its place behind the scenes, drafting replies and summaries you approve. See our guide to an [AI agent for small business](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/ai-agent-for-small-business/).

Most small businesses get further by fixing what happens around the call first: missed-call texts, an enquiry log, a booking link and a summary of each enquiry sent to you. If an AI receptionist still makes sense after that, I'll say which calls it should take and which stay with you. ### Is an AI receptionist worth it for a small business?
It can be if you get many routine calls you can't answer: questions about hours, areas and bookings. If most calls need judgement, such as quotes, complaints or emergencies, a missed-call text back plus a quick call-back from you is often simpler and safer.

### Do I have to tell callers they're talking to an AI?
It's the honest thing to do, and in the EU the AI Act includes transparency rules so people know when they are talking to an AI system. In the UK, the ICO says you must tell callers if you record the call and why.

### Is it legal to record calls with an AI receptionist in the US?
Federal law (18 U.S.C. 2511(2)(d)) allows recording where one party consents, but some states, such as California under Penal Code section 632, require the consent of all parties to a confidential call. Telling every caller at the start is the simplest way to cover both.

## Google Calendar appointment schedules vs Calendly for a small business
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/google-calendar-appointment-schedules-vs-calendly/ (2026-11-11)

Google Calendar appointment schedules vs Calendly comes down to what you already pay for. If your business is on a Google Workspace plan such as Business Standard, appointment schedules already give you several booking pages, email reminders and Stripe payments at no extra cost. Calendly is worth paying for when you need things Google doesn't offer, such as PayPal payments, bookings shared out across a team, or ready-made links to tools like HubSpot and Zapier.

Google Calendar appointment schedules vs Calendly is a common question for a small business that wants clients to book their own calls, consultations or visits. Both give you a booking page with your free times on it. Both put the booking straight into your calendar. The differences are in what's free, what you pay for, and what happens after someone books.
This post compares the two for a small service business: an accountant booking discovery calls, a clinic booking first appointments, a tradesperson booking quote visits. Features and prices below were checked on Google's help centre and on Calendly's pricing page on 11 November 2026. Both change often, so check again before you buy.

### What Google Calendar appointment schedules give you for free
Google's help page "Compare premium features of appointment schedules" says that with a personal Google Account or the Workspace Business Starter plan, you can create a single booking page. You set your available hours and the meeting length, share the link or embed it on your website, and bookings appear in your calendar. The booking form always asks for first name, last name and email, and you can add your own questions.
The same page lists what needs an eligible subscription: more than one appointment schedule, automatic email reminders, checking availability across several calendars, accepting payments, email verification to stop spam bookings, schedules on secondary calendars, and up to 20 co-hosts.
Eligible plans, per that page, are Google One Premium, Google AI Pro and Google AI Ultra, Workspace Individual, Business Standard and Plus, Enterprise Standard and Plus, Education and Nonprofits. Workspace Frontline, Essentials and older Workspace subscriptions that are no longer sold can't create appointment schedules at all.

### What the paid Google plans add
A few limits worth knowing: Google says you can only create a schedule on a computer, not in the Calendar app on Android or iPhone, and that the default minimum notice is 4 hours, so today may show no free slots right after you set it up.
- Several schedules: for example a 15-minute intro call and a 60-minute consultation, each with its own booking page.
- Email reminders: Google's "Create an appointment schedule" page says you can send up to 5 reminders, but you can't edit their text.
- Payments: you connect a Stripe account to Google Calendar and can then ask for payment when someone books.
- Email verification: people who aren't signed in to a Google Account get a code by email before the booking goes through, which cuts spam bookings.
- Checking other calendars: the schedule can look at more than one of your calendars, so a personal appointment blocks the slot.
- Buffer time between appointments and a maximum number of bookings per day are settings on the schedule itself. Google's help page doesn't say which plan they need, so check in your own account.

### What Calendly's free and paid plans give you
Calendly's pricing page lists four plans: Free, Standard, Teams and Enterprise. Free gives you one event type, one connected calendar, unlimited one-on-one meetings and a booking page you can customise. It does not include automatic meeting reminders, payments, removing Calendly branding, or the HubSpot, Mailchimp and Zapier connections.
Standard costs $12 per seat a month billed monthly, or $10 billed yearly (£10 or £8 on the UK prices). It adds unlimited event types, six connected calendars, automatic reminders, Stripe and PayPal payments at booking, cancellation policies, removal of Calendly branding and the HubSpot, Mailchimp and Zapier connections.
Teams costs $20 per seat a month billed monthly, or $16 billed yearly (£17 or £13). It adds round-robin distribution between staff and routing forms that screen people and send them to the right person. Enterprise starts at $15,000 a year. Calendly needs a seat for each person who hosts meetings; the people booking don't need an account.

### Side by side
This table sums up the vendors' own pages as of 11 November 2026. "Paid Google plan" means one of the eligible subscriptions listed above.
| What you need | Google, free account or Business Starter | Google, paid eligible plan | Calendly Free | Calendly Standard |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Booking pages / event types | 1 | More than one | 1 | Unlimited |
| Automatic email reminders | No | Yes, up to 5, fixed text | No | Yes |
| Take payment at booking | No | Stripe | No | Stripe or PayPal |
| Check more than one calendar | No | Yes | 1 calendar connected | Up to 6 calendars |
| Spam protection by email code | No | Yes | Not listed | Not listed |
| HubSpot / Zapier links | Through Google Calendar itself | Through Google Calendar itself | No | Yes |
| Share bookings out across staff | No | Not listed (co-hosts only) | No | No, needs Teams |

### Which one to pick: a quick decision guide
1. Check your Google plan first. If you're on Business Standard or above, Workspace Individual or Google One Premium, you already have the paid appointment schedule features. Start there before paying for anything.
2. If you only need one booking link and can live without reminders, either free option works. Calendly Free shows Calendly branding; removing it needs Standard.
3. If you need to take a deposit or full payment when someone books, both paid options do it with Stripe. Choose Calendly Standard if your clients expect PayPal.
4. If bookings should go to whichever team member is free, or to the right person based on answers, you need Calendly Teams, which lists round-robin and routing forms. Google's premium list mentions co-hosts, not sharing bookings out between staff.
5. If you want reminder wording in your own voice, or a text message the day before, the built-in reminders may not be enough. Google's reminder text can't be edited. That's where a separate automation helps.
6. Write down what should happen after a booking: welcome email, intake form, CRM record, invoice. If that list is long, the booking tool matters less than the automation behind it.

### What happens after the booking
Neither tool, on its own, runs the rest of your process. A booking is the start of the work: the client needs an intake form, maybe a document list, a reminder they'll actually read, and a follow-up after the appointment. Our guide to [reducing appointment no-shows](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/reduce-appointment-no-shows/) covers the reminder side in detail.
With Google, every booking is a normal Google Calendar event, so anything that can watch your calendar can react to it: [Google Apps Script](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/google-apps-script-for-small-business/), Zapier, Make or n8n (see [Zapier vs Make vs n8n](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/zapier-vs-make-vs-n8n/)). With Calendly, the HubSpot, Mailchimp and Zapier connections are listed on Standard and above, not on Free.
For illustration, a physio clinic might use one booking page for first assessments. Each booking then triggers an intake form, a reminder two days before in the clinic's own wording, and a rebooking message after the session, much like our [physio rebooking reminders](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/physio-rebooking-reminders/) page describes. A salon could add a deposit and a cancellation policy, as in [salon deposits and cancellation policies](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/salon-cancellation-policy-and-deposits/).

### Checklist before you switch on online booking
Copy this list and tick it off, whichever tool you choose.
Online booking set-up checklist:
```
[ ] Which Google plan are we on? (Admin console or Google One settings)
[ ] How many types of appointment do we offer? (names and lengths)
[ ] Which calendars must block a slot? (work, personal, shared team)
[ ] Minimum notice before a booking, and how far ahead people can book
[ ] Buffer time between appointments and maximum bookings per day
[ ] Questions on the booking form (only what you need before the meeting)
[ ] Do we take payment or a deposit at booking? Stripe only, or PayPal too?
[ ] Cancellation and rescheduling policy, written in one or two sentences
[ ] Reminders: when, by email or text, and in what words
[ ] What happens after booking: intake form, CRM record, welcome email, invoice
[ ] Who checks new bookings each day, and who covers when they're away
[ ] Where the booking link goes: website, email signature, Google Business Profile
```
