### Is Google Calendar appointment scheduling free?
Partly. Google says a personal Google Account or Workspace Business Starter can create a single booking page. More than one schedule, automatic email reminders, payments, email verification and checking several calendars need an eligible plan such as Business Standard, Workspace Individual or Google One Premium.

### Can Google Calendar appointment schedules take payments?
Yes, on an eligible plan. You connect a Stripe account to Google Calendar and can then request payment when someone books. Google's help pages mention Stripe only; Calendly's paid plans accept Stripe and PayPal.

### How much does Calendly cost in 2026?
Calendly's pricing page on 11 November 2026 shows Free, Standard at $12 per seat a month ($10 billed yearly), Teams at $20 per seat a month ($16 billed yearly), and Enterprise from $15,000 a year. UK prices are £10 (£8 yearly) for Standard and £17 (£13 yearly) for Teams.

### Does Calendly Free send reminders?
No. Calendly's pricing page lists automatic meeting reminders on Standard and above, not on Free.

## Microsoft Forms vs Google Forms for a small business: which to use for client intake
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/microsoft-forms-vs-google-forms-small-business/ (2026-11-11)

In the Microsoft Forms vs Google Forms choice, a small business should usually pick the one that matches the email and file storage it already uses: Google Forms if you run on Gmail and Google Drive, Microsoft Forms if you run on a Microsoft 365 business plan. Two limits decide most client-intake cases: Microsoft Forms only allows file upload questions when responders are inside your own organisation, and a form made with a free personal Microsoft account stops at 200 responses (Microsoft support, November 2026). Google Forms accepts uploads from outside people, but they must sign in to a Google Account first.

Microsoft Forms vs Google Forms looks like a small choice until a client can't upload their documents, or a form quietly stops taking enquiries. Both tools are good at the basics: questions, required fields, simple branching and a list of responses. The differences that matter for a small service business are who can answer, what they can send you, and what happens to each response once it arrives.
This post compares the two for client intake, booking requests, job requests and onboarding questionnaires. Every limit below comes from Microsoft's and Google's own help pages, checked in November 2026. If you're still deciding where the answers should live, read [Airtable vs Google Sheets](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/airtable-vs-google-sheets-small-business/) too.

### The short answer: follow your email and storage
A form is only the front door. The answers end up in a spreadsheet, the files end up in a folder, and someone gets a notification. If those already live in Google (Gmail, Drive, Sheets), Google Forms drops straight into that. If they live in Microsoft 365 (Outlook, OneDrive, SharePoint, Excel, Teams), Microsoft Forms does the same on that side.
Mixing them works, but it means one more login and one more place where client data sits. For most small firms, the boring answer is the right one: use the form tool that comes with the account you already pay for, then check the two limits in the next sections before you build a client-facing form on it.

### Microsoft Forms vs Google Forms side by side
The table covers what matters for client-facing forms. Sources are Microsoft's "Form, question, response, and character limits in Microsoft Forms" and "Add questions that allow for file uploads" pages, the Microsoft Forms connector reference, and Google's Docs Editors Help pages on file uploads, responses and sections.
|  | Microsoft Forms | Google Forms |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Account you need to build forms | A Microsoft account; business plans get much higher limits | A Google Account |
| Responses per form | 5,000,000 on business and education accounts; 200 on a free personal account; 1,000 on a paid personal account | No cap stated on the Google help pages checked |
| Questions per form | Up to 200 | Not stated on the pages checked |
| File uploads from responders | Only when the form is limited to people in your organisation; up to 10 files per question, 10MB, 100MB or 1GB each | Allowed; responders must sign in to a Google Account; you set file types, number and maximum size |
| Where uploaded files go | Your OneDrive for Business, under Apps > Microsoft Forms | A new folder in your Google Drive |
| Where answers go | The Forms results view, with export | The Summary tab, or a new or existing linked Google Sheet |
| Branching | Branch to a later question or section | "Go to section based on answer" on Multiple choice and Dropdown questions |
| Built-in automation hook | Power Automate trigger "When a new response is submitted"; works with organisational accounts only | Apps Script installable form submit trigger on the form or the linked sheet |

### Limit 1: file uploads from clients
This is the one that catches most small firms out. Microsoft's help page says the file upload question is only available when the form is set to "Only people in my organization can respond" or "Specific people in my organization can respond". Your clients are not in your organisation, so a Microsoft form that asks a new client for their ID, a photo of the job or last year's accounts can't take the files directly. Staff forms (timesheets, site photos, expense receipts) work fine.
Google Forms does accept files from outside people, but Google's help page says responders need to sign in to a Google Account to answer a file upload question. Plenty of clients have one. Some don't, and some will give up at the sign-in screen. Google also says the question type isn't available if the form is stored in a shared drive or your administrator has turned on Data Loss Prevention.
The practical fix on either side is the same: keep the form for questions, and send one secure upload link for documents. We cover the options in [document requests without a portal](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/document-requests-without-a-portal/) and [client portal vs email for document collection](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/client-portal-vs-email-document-collection/).

### Limit 2: response caps on free Microsoft accounts
Microsoft's limits page gives a form made with a free personal Microsoft account a cap of 200 responses, and a paid personal account (such as Microsoft 365 Personal or Family) 1,000. Business and education accounts get up to 5,000,000. A sole trader who built an enquiry form on a personal Outlook.com login can hit 200 in a busy year without noticing. Check which account owns the form before you put it on your website.
Microsoft also caps each user at 400 forms (including those in the recycle bin) and 200 questions per form. Neither is likely to bother a small business, but old test forms do count towards the 400.

### What happens after someone presses Submit
A form saves you typing. The real time savings come from what happens next: the enquiry gets a reply, the job lands in your list, the right person is told. Both tools can start that, in different ways.
- Microsoft Forms: Power Automate has a standard Microsoft Forms connector with a "When a new response is submitted" trigger. Microsoft's connector page says it only works with organisational accounts, so you need a business account, not a personal one. From there a flow can post to Teams, add a row to Excel or a SharePoint list, or draft an Outlook email. Our [Outlook automation guide](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/outlook-automation-for-accountants/) shows the kind of flows that fit.
- Google Forms: responses can go into a linked Google Sheet, and Google Apps Script has an installable form submit trigger on both the form and the sheet. That's enough to send a confirmation, create a folder or post a task. See [Google Apps Script for small business](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/google-apps-script-for-small-business/) for what it can and can't do, and [automating Google Workspace for a small business](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/google-workspace-automation-services/) for when to hire help.
- Either one: Zapier, Make and n8n can pick up new responses too, which helps when the next step is in a tool outside Microsoft or Google, such as a CRM or Xero. [Power Automate vs Zapier](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/power-automate-vs-zapier-small-business/) compares the two most common choices.

### How to choose in five steps
1. Write down where your email, files and spreadsheets live today. If it's all Google, start with Google Forms. If it's all Microsoft 365 business, start with Microsoft Forms.
2. Check who owns the form. A Microsoft form on a free personal account stops at 200 responses; move it to a business account before it goes on your website.
3. List what clients need to send. If the answer includes files, plan a separate secure upload link for Microsoft Forms, and decide whether a Google sign-in is acceptable for your clients on Google Forms.
4. Decide where each answer goes next: a sheet, a CRM, a job list, a reply email. Pick the form tool whose automation hook reaches that place with the least glue.
5. Build one form, send it to yourself and one friendly client, and fix anything confusing before you replace your current intake email.

### A client intake question list you can copy
Most intake forms ask too much. This list works in either tool. Keep anything sensitive (bank details, ID numbers, health information) out of the form and collect it through a secure channel instead. If you're in the UK or EU, our [GDPR checklist for automating client data](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/gdpr-checklist-automating-client-data/) covers what to check first.
Client intake form: questions in order:
```
Section 1: About you
1. Full name (required)
2. Business name, if any
3. Email address (required)
4. Phone number
5. Best way to reach you: Email / Phone / Text (multiple choice)

Section 2: What you need
6. What can we help with? (dropdown: [service 1] / [service 2] / [service 3] / Something else)
   Branch: "Something else" goes to question 7, the rest skip to question 8
7. Tell us briefly what you need (short paragraph)
8. When do you need it by? (date)
9. How did you hear about us? (dropdown)

Section 3: Next step
10. Is there anything we should know before we call you? (paragraph, optional)
11. Confirmation: "I agree to [business name] contacting me about this request and storing these answers as described in our privacy notice: [link]" (required checkbox)

Confirmation message:
"Thanks, [first name]. We've got your request and will reply within [one working day]. If you need to send documents, we'll email you a secure upload link."
```

### Common mistakes with intake forms
- Building the form on a personal account, then losing access when the person who made it leaves.
- Adding a Microsoft file upload question to a client-facing form. It only works for people in your organisation, so clients can't answer it.
- Sending responses to an inbox nobody owns. Name one person who acts on new submissions, or have a workflow assign them.
- No reply after Submit. A confirmation message plus a real reply within a working day does more than a longer form. Our guide to [replying to new enquiries fast](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/reply-to-new-enquiries-fast/) has message templates.
- Asking for the same details twice: once on the form, again on the first call. Read the answers before you ring.

### Is Microsoft Forms or Google Forms better for a small business?
Neither is better across the board. Use the one that matches your email and file storage: Google Forms for Gmail and Google Drive, Microsoft Forms for a Microsoft 365 business plan. Check file uploads and response limits before using either for client intake.

### Can clients upload files to a Microsoft Form?
Not if they're outside your organisation. Microsoft's help page says file upload questions are only available when the form is set to "Only people in my organization can respond" or "Specific people in my organization can respond". Send clients a secure upload link instead.

### Do people need a Google account to fill in a Google Form?
Not for ordinary questions. For a file upload question, Google's help page says responders need to sign in to a Google Account. Uploaded files go to a new folder in the form owner's Google Drive.

### How many responses can a Microsoft Form take?
Microsoft's limits page says up to 5,000,000 per form on business and education accounts, 200 on a free personal Microsoft account and 1,000 on a paid personal account, as of November 2026.

## HubSpot free CRM automation: what it can and can't do
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/hubspot-free-crm-automation-limits/ (2026-11-11)

HubSpot free CRM automation is limited to one simple workflow per form, with one action: an email sent after someone submits the form. Multi-step workflows need a Professional or Enterprise plan, and pipeline stage automations start at Sales Hub or Service Hub Starter. For follow-ups, reminders and chasing on the free plan, most small businesses connect a separate automation tool to HubSpot instead.

HubSpot free CRM automation is narrower than most people expect when they sign up. The free CRM is a good customer list: contacts, deals, forms, a booking page, email templates and quotes. But the part that does things for you on its own, the workflows, sits on the paid plans.
This post sets out what the free plan can automate today, what each upgrade adds, and when it makes more sense to keep HubSpot free and add a separate automation next to it. Every limit below was checked on HubSpot's own pages on 11 November 2026. HubSpot changes its plans often, so check its help articles before you decide.

### What the free HubSpot CRM includes
HubSpot's free CRM page says the free tools come with up to two users and 1,000 contacts, with no expiry date. It lists, among other things:
- Contact, company and deal records, with a deal pipeline and a reporting dashboard.
- A form builder for your website, and live chat.
- Email templates, email scheduling and email tracking from your own inbox.
- Meeting scheduling, sales quotes and payment links.
- Tickets, so customer issues can be logged, assigned and tracked.

### What the free plan can automate
Two things run on their own on the free plan, and both are small.
First, form automations. HubSpot's help article on form automations (last updated 28 September 2026) says that on the free tools you can create one "Send an email after form submission" simple workflow for each form, with a limit of one action per simple workflow. So when someone fills in your enquiry form, HubSpot can send them one email. That's it: no second email three days later, no task for you, no change to a deal.
Second, the booking page. HubSpot's scheduling pages article (30 September 2026) says users of the free tools can create a single one-on-one scheduling page, with HubSpot's default branding. Bookings land in your calendar and on the contact record. Group and round robin pages need a Sales Hub or Service Hub Starter plan or higher.
Everything else on the free plan, such as moving a deal, creating a follow-up task or chasing an unpaid quote, is done by hand.

### What needs a paid HubSpot plan
- Workflows (the full multi-step builder with delays, branches and actions on deals, tickets and companies): HubSpot's "Create workflows" article lists Professional or Enterprise subscriptions of Marketing Hub, Sales Hub, Service Hub, Data Hub, Smart CRM or Revenue Hub. HubSpot's sales pricing page, though, lists a limited number of workflows on Starter too, so check what your own account offers before you pay to upgrade.
- Sequences (a run of one-to-one sales emails that stops when the person replies): the sequences article (17 August 2026) lists Sales Hub or Service Hub Professional or Enterprise, and an assigned Sales or Service seat.
- Pipeline stage automations (create a task, send an internal email notification or edit the record when a deal or ticket enters a stage): the board view automations article (2 September 2026) lists Sales Hub and Service Hub at Starter, Professional and Enterprise. Free accounts aren't listed.
- More actions after a form: the form automations article says Starter, Professional or Enterprise accounts without Marketing Hub get up to three actions in the simple workflow, and Marketing Hub Starter gets up to ten. Still one simple workflow per form.

### Free vs Starter vs Professional: the automation table
A summary of the help articles above, as at 11 November 2026. "Starter" means Sales Hub or Service Hub Starter unless it says Marketing Hub.
| Automation | Free | Starter | Professional |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Email after a form is submitted | Yes, 1 simple workflow per form, 1 action | Up to 3 actions (Marketing Hub Starter: up to 10) | Yes, plus full workflows |
| Task or internal alert when a deal changes stage | Not listed | Yes (Sales or Service Hub) | Yes |
| Multi-step workflow with delays and branches | No | No | Yes |
| Sequences that stop on reply | No | No | Yes (Sales or Service Hub, with a seat) |
| Booking page | 1 one-on-one page, HubSpot branding | Adds group and round robin pages | Yes |

### When to add a separate automation instead of upgrading
Upgrading makes sense when your team lives in HubSpot all day and you want everything in one place. But many small service businesses use HubSpot as a contact list and do the real work elsewhere: quotes in a job app, invoices in Xero or QuickBooks, messages on WhatsApp. For them, the missing automations usually cross tools, and a HubSpot workflow wouldn't see those tools anyway.
The free account can still be connected to other tools. HubSpot's technical limits page lists 250,000 API calls a day and 100 calls every 10 seconds for free accounts, and tools such as Zapier and n8n list HubSpot connections. So an outside automation can read and update your free HubSpot records. If you're choosing between those tools, see [Zapier vs Make vs n8n](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/zapier-vs-make-vs-n8n/).
Work through these steps before you pay for anything:
1. Write down the three follow-ups you most often forget: for example, chasing a quote after five days, a reminder the day before a visit, and a nudge when an invoice is overdue.
2. For each one, note where the trigger lives. If it's in HubSpot (a form, a deal stage), HubSpot can handle it on the right plan. If it's in your invoicing, booking or job tool, a HubSpot workflow can't see it on its own.
3. Check the table above. If everything you need is in the Starter column and lives in HubSpot, compare the Starter price with the time it saves you.
4. If you need multi-step follow-ups but not the rest of Professional, price a separate automation that reads and updates HubSpot instead, or ask a [HubSpot automation consultant](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/hubspot-automation-consultant/) to price both routes.
5. Whichever you pick, have a person approve any message that goes to a customer before it's switched on, and keep the wording in one place you can edit.

### A checklist before you upgrade HubSpot or add another tool
Copy this into a note and fill it in. It makes the decision, and any brief you give a builder, much clearer. If you're not sure which follow-up to start with, read [what to automate first](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/what-to-automate-first-small-business/).
HubSpot automation checklist:
```
HubSpot automation checklist

[ ] Our HubSpot plan today: [Free / Starter / Professional]
[ ] Users who need a login: [number] (free allows up to 2)
[ ] Contacts today: [number] (free allows 1,000)

Follow-up 1: [what should happen]
    Trigger: [form submitted / deal stage / invoice overdue / booking made]
    Trigger lives in: [HubSpot / Xero / QuickBooks / calendar / job app]
    Steps: [1 email / email then reminder / task for me]
    Needs a person to approve? [yes / no]

Follow-up 2: [...]
Follow-up 3: [...]

[ ] Can the free plan do it? (1 email after a form, nothing else)
[ ] Does Starter cover it? (task or alert on deal stage, up to 3 form actions)
[ ] Does it need Professional? (multi-step workflows, sequences)
[ ] Or does the trigger live outside HubSpot? Then price a separate automation.
```

### Common free-plan workarounds that cause trouble
- One form per follow-up: some people build several near-identical forms to get more "one email" automations. It works for a while, then nobody knows which form is live.
- Manual deal moves with no reminder: the free plan won't create a task when a deal sits in "Quote sent". A quote nobody chases is the most common gap. Our [estimate follow-up templates](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/estimate-follow-up-email-templates-contractors/) give you the wording.
- Copying data between HubSpot and your invoicing tool by hand: two lists drift apart within weeks. Decide which one is the master record for each field.
- Slow replies to new enquiries: the single form email is a good start, but a person still needs to reply properly. See [how to reply to new enquiries fast](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/reply-to-new-enquiries-fast/).

You approve the wording, and a person always approves anything AI drafts before it goes out. You can sketch your own first with the [plan builder](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/plan/).

### Does the free HubSpot CRM have workflows?
Not the full workflow builder. HubSpot's help centre lists workflows for Professional and Enterprise plans. The free tools get one simple workflow per form, with one action: an email sent after the form is submitted (checked 11 November 2026).

### Can HubSpot free send automatic follow-up emails?
Only one, straight after a form is submitted. Timed follow-ups and sequences that stop when someone replies need a paid plan: sequences are listed for Sales Hub or Service Hub Professional or Enterprise, with a seat.

## How to automate invoicing for a small business, from job done to invoice sent
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/how-to-automate-invoicing-small-business/ (2026-11-11)

To automate invoicing for a small business, connect the moment a job is marked done to your accounting software, so a draft invoice is created from the quote or job details, checked by a person, and sent with a payment link. Then let reminders run on a schedule until it's paid. Xero and QuickBooks already handle repeating invoices and reminders; a workflow fills the gap between finishing the work and the invoice existing.

If you want to know how to automate invoicing for a small business, start with where invoices actually get stuck. It's rarely the invoicing software. It's the gap between the job being finished and someone in the office knowing it's finished, finding the quote, and typing the invoice. That gap is where days go, and sometimes whole invoices.
Below: the invoicing chain step by step, what Xero and QuickBooks already automate, where the gaps are, a 7-step setup, an invoice checklist and an email template. Getting paid after the invoice is sent is covered in our guide to [automated invoice payment reminders](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/invoice-payment-reminders/).

### The invoicing chain: where the time goes
Every invoice in a service business goes through the same five steps. Automation doesn't replace the steps; it moves the information from one to the next without someone retyping it. The table shows each step, what can happen on its own, and where a person should still look.
| Step | What starts it | What can happen automatically | Where a person checks |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Job done | Staff mark the job complete, or the customer signs off | The office is told straight away, with photos and notes attached | Is the job really finished, or is there a snag to fix first? |
| 2. Invoice drafted | The job is marked complete | A draft invoice is created from the accepted quote or job record, with the right customer and items | Extras, discounts, hours that went over the quote |
| 3. Invoice approved | The draft is ready | The draft lands in one list for review | One person approves; nothing goes out unapproved |
| 4. Invoice sent | Approval | Email with the invoice, a PDF and a payment link; a copy saved to the job folder | Only if the customer replies with a question |
| 5. Paid | Payment arrives | Reminders run on a schedule and stop when it's paid | Overdue invoices after the last reminder get a personal call |

### What Xero and QuickBooks already automate
Before building anything, switch on what you already pay for. These are the invoicing features both tools describe in their own help pages, checked on 11 November 2026. Menu names change between versions, so follow the vendor's article for the exact clicks.
- Xero repeating invoices: Xero Central says a repeating invoice template set to "Approve for Sending" approves each invoice and emails it to the customer on the date it's created, following the schedule you set. It also notes that the first invoice is only sent if its invoice date is in the future. You can choose plain "Approve" instead, and send each one yourself.
- Xero invoice reminders: Xero Central says you can turn on automatic reminders and create up to five, each set to go a number of days before or after the due date. They only go out for invoices marked as sent, and you can choose not to send reminders for amounts under a figure you set.
- Xero quotes to invoices: Xero Central describes a "Create invoice" button on a quote, so an accepted quote can become the invoice without retyping.
- QuickBooks Online recurring invoices: Intuit's help article (updated August 2026) describes three template types. Scheduled templates create the transaction automatically, Reminder templates remind you to create and send it yourself, and Unscheduled templates are saved for you to use by hand each time.
- QuickBooks Online invoice reminders: Intuit says you can set up to three automatic reminders, up to 90 days before or after the due date, and that they're sent only for invoices you've already emailed. QuickBooks Online Advanced users can build reminders with workflows instead. More on this in our post on [QuickBooks Online client reminders](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/quickbooks-client-reminders/).
- QuickBooks Online estimates to invoices: Intuit's help pages describe a "Convert to invoice" action on an estimate, and progress invoicing if you bill a job in stages.

### The gaps the built-in features don't cover
Repeating invoices suit fixed monthly work, like a retainer or a maintenance contract. Most service businesses also have one-off jobs, and that's where the built-in features stop. The common gaps:
- Nobody tells the office the job is done. The work finishes on Tuesday, the paperwork arrives on Friday, and the invoice goes out the week after.
- The job lives in one tool and the invoice in another, so someone copies from the job app, calendar or spreadsheet into Xero or QuickBooks.
- Extras get lost. Parts, additional hours or a change agreed on site never reach the invoice, because they were in a text message.
- Deposits aren't deducted. If you took a [deposit on the quote](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/how-to-ask-for-a-deposit-on-a-quote/), the final invoice has to show it, and that's easy to miss.
- No proof attached. A customer who queries an invoice wants the sign-off, photos or timesheet behind it. If that's on someone's phone, the invoice waits.

### How to automate invoicing in 7 steps
1. Write down your invoicing chain as it works today: who marks a job done, where the details live, who types the invoice, and how long each step takes. A rough [process map](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/process-map-template-small-business/) is enough.
2. Switch on what your accounting software already does: repeating invoices for fixed monthly work, automatic reminders, and quote-to-invoice. Write the reminder emails in your own voice.
3. Pick one trigger for "job done". It could be a status in your job app, a [completion sign-off form](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/job-sign-off-and-completion-photos/) the customer signs, or a timesheet being approved. One trigger, used every time.
4. Connect that trigger to a draft invoice. The workflow finds the customer and the accepted quote, adds the line items, any extras recorded on the job and any deposit already paid, and creates a draft in Xero or QuickBooks. It doesn't send anything yet.
5. Add one approval step, because a wrong invoice costs more goodwill than a late one. The owner or office manager gets a short daily list of drafts to check, with anything that changed from the quote highlighted. Credit notes and write-offs stay manual. Approving sends the invoice with a payment link and saves a copy, with the job photos or sign-off, to the job folder.
6. Let reminders run, and stop them the moment the invoice is paid. After the last reminder, the invoice goes on a list for a personal call instead of another email.
7. Check it weekly for the first month. Look for jobs marked done with no draft, and drafts that sat unapproved. Fix the rule, not the invoice.

### Checklist: what goes on every invoice
An automated invoice is only as good as the details it pulls in. For the UK, the gov.uk page "Invoicing and taking payment from customers" lists what an invoice must include. Use it as the checklist your workflow fills in, and check your own country's rules if you're elsewhere. If you and your customer are both VAT registered, gov.uk says you must use a VAT invoice, which needs more information than this.
Invoice checklist (from gov.uk, UK):
```
[ ] A unique invoice number
[ ] Your business name, address and contact details
[ ] The customer's business name and address
[ ] A clear description of what you're charging for
[ ] The date the work was done (supply date)
[ ] The date of the invoice
[ ] The amount(s) charged
[ ] VAT amount, if applicable
[ ] The total amount owed
[ ] Sole traders: your name and any business name, plus an address for legal documents if you use a business name
[ ] Limited companies: the full company name as on the certificate of incorporation

Also worth adding (not required by gov.uk):
[ ] Payment terms and due date
[ ] Any deposit already paid, deducted
[ ] A payment link
[ ] Your quote or job reference
```

### Template: the email that goes with the invoice
Keep it short. The customer needs the amount, the due date and one way to pay. Put the job reference in the subject so it's easy to find later.
Subject: Invoice [invoice number] for [job or service], [address or project]:
```
Hi [first name],

Thanks for choosing [business name]. Your invoice for [job or service] is attached.

Amount due: [amount]
Due date: [due date]
Deposit already paid: [deposit amount, or delete this line]

You can pay online here: [payment link]

The completion photos and sign-off are here if you'd like to see them: [link to job folder]

If anything on the invoice doesn't look right, just reply to this email and I'll sort it out.

Thanks,
[your name]
[business name]
[phone]
```

### How Mike Automations would set this up
We'd build the chain on the tools you already use: your job app or calendar, Xero or QuickBooks, and your email. When a job is marked done, a draft invoice is created from the quote, with extras and deposits included, and you approve it from one list. Reminders then run until it's paid. You can [sketch your own version with the plan builder](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/plan/) or [watch a one-minute demo](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/try/) first.
It starts with a [free 15-minute call](https://mikeautomations.github.io/call/) about how invoices go out today. Within 48 hours you get a written plan with a fixed price. It's built on the tools you already use, it's live in 2-3 days, and it costs [$2,000 one-off](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/pricing/), paid once it's running and you're happy with it, under our [pay-when-happy agreement](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/agreement/).

### Can Xero send invoices automatically?
For repeating work, yes. Xero Central says a repeating invoice template set to "Approve for Sending" emails each invoice to the customer on the date it's created. For one-off jobs, the invoice has to be created first, which is where a workflow from your job app helps.

### Does QuickBooks Online send automatic invoice reminders?
Yes. Intuit says you can set up to three automatic reminders, up to 90 days before or after the due date, for invoices you've already emailed.

### Should automated invoices go out without anyone checking them?
Fixed recurring invoices can. One-off invoices are better created as drafts and approved by a person, because extras, discounts and changes from the quote are where mistakes happen.

## Airtable vs Google Sheets for a small business: which one to use
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/airtable-vs-google-sheets-small-business/ (2026-11-11)

In the Airtable vs Google Sheets choice, a small business should stay on Google Sheets when the data is one simple list that a few people edit and the main job is sums and sharing, and pick Airtable when the work has linked records (customers, jobs, invoices) and needs proper forms, views per person and built-in automations. Google Sheets is free with a Google account; Airtable's Free plan stops at 1,000 records per base and its Team plan costs $20 per editing seat per month billed annually (Airtable, November 2026).

Airtable vs Google Sheets is a question that usually comes up when a spreadsheet has started doing a database's job. There's a tab for customers, a tab for jobs, a tab for invoices, and a lot of copying between them. Someone suggests Airtable, and someone else asks why you'd pay for something Google gives you free.
This post is for small service businesses (trades, agencies, clinics, practices, cleaning and property firms) choosing between the two. It covers what each is good at, the current plan limits and prices from the vendors' own pages, a decision table, and a checklist to run before you move anything. If you're also weighing up a CRM, read [spreadsheet vs CRM for a small service business](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/spreadsheet-vs-crm-small-service-business/) as well.

### The real difference: a spreadsheet vs a database with a spreadsheet face
Google Sheets is a spreadsheet. Every cell can hold anything, formulas work across the whole grid, and you can add a column or a tab in seconds. That freedom is why everyone starts there.
Airtable looks like a spreadsheet but works like a database. Each column has a fixed type (date, single select, attachment, link to another table), and records in one table can link to records in another. A job can point to its customer, and the customer can show every job without a lookup formula. You can then build views (a calendar, a kanban board, a filtered list for one person), forms and simple apps on top of the same data.
So the question is less "which is better" and more "is my data one list, or several things that relate to each other?"

### Where Google Sheets wins
- Cost: Sheets comes with a free Google account and with every Google Workspace plan. There are no per-seat charges for the spreadsheet itself.
- Numbers: formulas, pivot tables and charts are what spreadsheets are built for. Pricing calculators, budgets and job costing sit more naturally in Sheets.
- Size: Google's Drive help page says a spreadsheet created in or converted to Google Sheets can hold up to 20 million cells or 100MB. A small business rarely gets near that.
- Everyone already knows it. Staff, clients and your accountant can open a shared sheet without learning anything new.
- It connects to everything. Google Forms writes straight into a sheet, and every major automation tool (Zapier, Make, n8n) can read and write Google Sheets. If your team works in Microsoft 365 instead, compare [Google Forms with Microsoft Forms](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/microsoft-forms-vs-google-forms-small-business/) first.

### Where Airtable wins
- Linked records: customers, jobs, quotes and invoices in separate tables that point to each other, so you change a phone number once.
- Field types: a status column that only accepts your stages, a date field that is always a date, an attachment field for photos and PDFs. Fewer typos, cleaner data.
- Views and interfaces: each person sees the filtered list or calendar they need, without hiding columns in a shared sheet and hoping nobody unhides them.
- Built-in automations: "when a record enters this view, send an email" or "when the status changes, notify the office", with no code. The number of runs depends on your plan (see below).
- Forms that feed the right table, including attachments, so enquiries and documents land as proper records.

### Airtable plans and limits in November 2026
Airtable charges per seat. Its pricing page says read-only collaborators, form submissions and share links are free on the Team and Business plans. Its help centre also lists Team plan commenters as billable, so check who counts before you invite your whole team. The figures below come from airtable.com/pricing and Airtable's "plans overview" help article, checked on 11 November 2026. They change, so check them again before you buy.
|  | Airtable Free | Airtable Team | Google Sheets |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Price | $0 | $20 per seat per month billed annually, $24 billed monthly | Free with a Google account |
| Size limit | 1,000 records per base | 50,000 records per base | 20 million cells or 100MB per spreadsheet |
| Attachments | 1GB per base | 20GB per base | Files live in Google Drive, linked from cells |
| Built-in automations | 100 runs per workspace per month | 25,000 runs per workspace per month | None without Apps Script or another tool |
| API calls | 1,000 per workspace per month | 100,000 per workspace per month | Google Sheets API, with Google's own limits |
| Editors | Up to 5 editors or creators | Every editor is a paid seat | Anyone you share with |
| Revision history | 2 weeks | 1 year | Version history built in |

### Three limits that catch small businesses out
Google Sheets has limits too, but they bite when you automate it. Google's Apps Script quotas page lists, for a free Gmail account, 100 email recipients per day from a script and 90 minutes a day of total trigger runtime (Google Workspace accounts get 1,500 recipients and 6 hours). That's fine for reminders, not for a mailing list.
- The Free plan's 1,000 records is per base, not per table. A customer table, a jobs table and an invoices table all count towards the same 1,000. A business doing a few jobs a day can fill that within a year.
- When you hit a record limit, Airtable's pricing page says you keep access and your data isn't removed, but you can't add more records until you upgrade. That's a bad thing to discover on a busy Monday.
- Airtable's help centre says the Business and Enterprise Scale plans need a private email domain, so Gmail or Yahoo addresses can't upgrade to them. The Team plan has no such rule.

### What it costs a small team: an illustration
For illustration only: a cleaning company with an owner, an office manager and two supervisors who all edit the data. On Airtable Team billed annually that is 4 seats at $20, so $80 a month or $960 a year. If the two supervisors only need to see their own schedule, they could use a read-only view instead, and the bill drops to 2 seats, $40 a month. On Google Sheets the same four people pay nothing extra for the sheet.
That gap is real, but compare it with the time spent fixing a broken sheet, copying data between tabs and chasing jobs that fell through. The money question is what each option saves you, not just what it costs. Our post on [what business automation costs](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/business-automation-cost/) walks through that sum.

### Decision table: Airtable or Google Sheets?
| Your situation | Better fit | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| One list (leads, stock, a price list) edited by 1-3 people | Google Sheets | Free, familiar, nothing to link |
| Mostly numbers: budgets, quotes, job costing | Google Sheets | Formulas and pivot tables are its strength |
| Customers, jobs and invoices that relate to each other | Airtable | Linked records replace copy and paste between tabs |
| Field staff need a simple view or form on their phone | Airtable | Interfaces and forms per person |
| Clients or outsiders need to see or edit it | Google Sheets | Share a link; no new tool to learn and no seat to pay for |
| You want reminders and status emails without code | Airtable | Built-in automations, with more runs on paid plans |
| It must work with tools you already pay for | Either | Both connect to Zapier, Make and n8n |
| Over 1,000 records and no budget for seats | Google Sheets | Airtable Free will stop you adding records |

### Checklist before you move from Google Sheets to Airtable
Copy this into a note and tick it off before anyone starts importing. Most failed moves skip the first three steps.
Sheets to Airtable move checklist:
```
[ ] 1. Write down the 3-5 things the sheet is really used for (e.g. book jobs, chase quotes, invoice).
[ ] 2. List the "things" in your data: customers, jobs, quotes, invoices, staff. Each becomes a table.
[ ] 3. Clean the sheet: one customer per row, no merged cells, one date format, no notes in number columns.
[ ] 4. Count rows across all tabs. Over 1,000 in total? Budget for the Team plan.
[ ] 5. Decide who edits and who only views. Only editors need paid seats.
[ ] 6. Import one table, check it, then import the next and link them.
[ ] 7. List every formula and automation the sheet runs today and rebuild each one.
[ ] 8. Reconnect forms and Zapier, Make or n8n steps that pointed at the old sheet.
[ ] 9. Run both side by side for one week. Fix what's missing.
[ ] 10. Make the old sheet read-only and put a link to the new base at the top.
```

### The third option: keep the sheet and automate around it
Often the pain isn't the spreadsheet itself. It's that nothing happens unless someone remembers. A quote sits unanswered, an invoice goes overdue, a new enquiry waits a day for a reply. That can be fixed without moving your data anywhere.
A workflow can watch a Google Sheet, notice a quote that's had no reply for a week, draft the follow-up for you to approve, and update the row when the customer answers. The same goes for [invoice payment reminders](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/invoice-payment-reminders/) and [replying to new enquiries fast](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/reply-to-new-enquiries-fast/). If you later move to Airtable, the workflow moves with you. Our comparison of [Zapier, Make and n8n](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/zapier-vs-make-vs-n8n/) explains the tools that do the connecting.
1. Pick the one job that goes wrong most often. Our guide to [what to automate first](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/what-to-automate-first-small-business/) helps you choose.
2. Write down how it works today, step by step, using a [process map template](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/process-map-template-small-business/).
3. Decide where the data should live: the sheet you have, or a new Airtable base if the data really is several linked things. If it's Airtable and you want help, an [Airtable consultant for a small business](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/airtable-consultant-small-business/) can design the base and move the data across.
4. Automate the chasing and the copying, and keep a person approving anything that goes to a customer.

### Is Airtable better than Google Sheets for a small business?
Only when your data is several linked things, such as customers, jobs and invoices, or when you need forms, per-person views and built-in automations. For one simple list or number-heavy work, Google Sheets is free and does the job.

## Is Make.com worth it for a small business?
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/is-make-com-worth-it-small-business/ (2026-11-11)

Make.com is worth it for a small business when you have workflows with several steps or branches and you build them carefully: the paid Core plan is listed at $12 a month for 10,000 credits, and most actions use one credit. It stops being good value when a scenario checks for new data every minute (each check uses a credit even when nothing is found), when nobody in the business can maintain it, or when the job is simple enough for a tool you already pay for.

Is Make.com worth it for a small business? For most small service businesses the subscription is not the question. Make's entry price is low. What decides whether it's worth it is how its credits are counted, how your scenarios are built, and who looks after them when something breaks.
This post explains Make's pricing model as it stands today, shows where the credits actually go, and gives you a short worksheet to estimate your own usage. Plan details were checked on make.com/en/pricing and Make's help centre on 11 November 2026. Make changes its pricing from time to time, so check the page again before you buy. If you're still choosing between tools, read [Zapier vs Make vs n8n](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/zapier-vs-make-vs-n8n/) first.

### What Make charges for: credits, not users
Make's pricing FAQ says that since August 27, credits are the billing unit. Each action a scenario performs uses credits: most actions use 1 credit, while some AI features that use Make's own AI provider can use more. Adding a row to a Google Sheet, searching for a contact, sending an email or reshaping some data each count.
Make's help page "How features use credits" (updated 11 November 2026) adds three details that matter for your bill:
- Trigger modules use 1 credit per run, whether or not they find anything. A scenario that checks a spreadsheet for new rows uses a credit for every check, even an empty one.
- Each later module runs once per item. Make's operations guide gives the example of a form trigger that returns 10 responses: every module after it runs 10 times.
- Some modules are free: routers, filters, error handlers (Rollback, Break, Resume, Commit, Ignore), the subscenario modules and Make Functions. The Make Code app uses 2 credits per second of running time.

### Make's plans at a glance (checked 11 November 2026)
These are the figures on make.com/en/pricing at the 10,000-credit level. The page also says paying annually in advance is cheaper than paying monthly, so check which billing option a price refers to before you compare it with anything else.
|  | Free | Core | Pro | Teams |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Listed price | $0 | $12 a month | $21 a month | $38 a month |
| Credits | 1,000 a month | 10,000 a month ($1.20 per 1,000) | 10,000 a month ($2.10 per 1,000) | 10,000 a month ($3.80 per 1,000) |
| Active scenarios | 2 | Unlimited | Unlimited | Unlimited |
| Shortest schedule | Every 15 minutes | Every minute | Every minute | Every minute |
| Longest single run | 5 minutes | 40 minutes | 40 minutes | 40 minutes |
| Largest file | 5 MB | 100 MB | 250 MB | 500 MB |
| Run history kept | 7 days | 30 days | 30 days | 30 days |

### Other plan rules worth knowing
- Unused credits don't roll over. The pricing FAQ says credits expire at the end of the term. On yearly billing for Pro and Teams, credits last for the year instead of the month.
- If you run out, scenarios stop until credits are added. Incoming webhooks are queued (up to your queue limit) and processed later. You can buy extra credits in bundles of 1,000 or 10,000, or turn on automatic top-ups on Core, Pro and Teams.
- Make is hosted on AWS in the EU or North America, on every plan. If you handle client data under UK GDPR or GDPR, that's one of the questions to settle before you build. Our [GDPR checklist for automating client data](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/gdpr-checklist-automating-client-data/) covers the rest.
- Unlimited users on every plan, so a colleague can have access at no extra cost.

### The polling trap: where credits really go
This is the part most small businesses miss. A scheduled trigger uses a credit every time it checks, so how often it checks can cost more than the work itself. The arithmetic below uses Make's "1 credit per trigger run" rule. It's for illustration: your numbers will differ.
For illustration: an enquiry workflow with one trigger and four actions (save the enquiry, add the contact, send a reply, alert the owner), handling 200 enquiries a month.
| How the scenario starts | Trigger credits a month | Action credits (4 x 200) | Total a month | Plan that covers it |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Instant trigger (webhook): runs only when an enquiry arrives | About 200 | 800 | About 1,000 | Free, just (and it allows only 2 active scenarios) |
| Checks every 15 minutes | About 2,880 (96 checks a day x 30) | 800 | About 3,680 | Core |
| Checks every minute | About 43,200 (1,440 a day x 30) | 800 | About 44,000 | More than the 10,000 Core credits: extra credits or a bigger tier |

### How to keep the credit count down
- Use an instant trigger (a webhook) where the app offers one, so the scenario runs when something happens instead of checking on a timer.
- If you must poll, check as rarely as the job allows. Most admin work doesn't need a one-minute check: every 15 minutes or once an hour is usually fine.
- Combine items before acting on them. Make's operations guide shows a text aggregator turning 10 separate emails into one, cutting a run from 11 operations to 3.
- Put filters early, so items you don't care about stop before they reach the expensive steps. Filters and routers don't use credits.
- Watch AI steps. Make's AI apps using Make's own provider charge 1 credit per operation plus credits based on token usage, so a long prompt on every item adds up.

### Estimate your own usage in five steps
1. Write the process down: what starts it, every step, and what happens when something is missing. Our [process map template](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/process-map-template-small-business/) helps.
2. Count the modules after the trigger. Leave out routers, filters and error handlers.
3. Estimate how many items go through each month (enquiries, invoices, uploads), and multiply by the module count.
4. Add the trigger: one credit per item for an instant trigger, or one per check for a scheduled one (checks a day x 30).
5. Add a margin for retries and growth, and compare the total with the plan's monthly credits.

### A worksheet to copy
Paste this into a note or a spreadsheet and fill it in for each workflow you're thinking of building.
Make credit estimate (one workflow):
```
Workflow name: [e.g. new enquiry reply]
What starts it: [form / email / new row / schedule]
Instant trigger available? [yes / no]
If scheduled, how often does it check? [every __ minutes]

A. Trigger credits a month:
   instant = items a month; scheduled = checks a day x 30 = ____
B. Modules after the trigger (not routers, filters or error handlers): ____
C. Items a month: ____
D. Action credits = B x C = ____
E. AI steps? [none / yes: add Make's token-based credits]
F. Margin for retries and growth (add 20-30%): ____

Total credits a month = A + D + E + F = ____
Plan's monthly credits: ____
Who fixes it when it fails: ____
```

### When Make is worth it
- Your workflows branch: "if the client is VAT registered, ask for these documents, otherwise ask for those". Make's visual canvas shows every path at once.
- You need to reshape data between apps: split a name, format a date, merge a list into one email.
- Volumes are moderate and the triggers are instant, so 10,000 credits a month goes a long way.
- Someone in the business, or someone you hire such as a [Make.com expert](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/make-com-consultant/), is comfortable reading a scenario's run history when a step fails.

### When to pick something else
- Two or three popular apps in a straight line, no branches: Zapier is often quicker to set up. See [Zapier vs Make vs n8n](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/zapier-vs-make-vs-n8n/).
- Long workflows that run thousands of times, or data that must stay on your own server: n8n, on its cloud or [self-hosted](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/n8n-cloud-vs-self-hosted-small-business/), if someone can maintain it.
- Everything lives in Microsoft 365: Power Automate may already be in your licence. See [Power Automate vs Zapier](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/power-automate-vs-zapier-small-business/).
- Your practice or booking software already sends the reminders you need: use the built-in feature first. See [practice software vs simple automation](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/practice-software-vs-simple-automation-small-practice/).
- Nobody will look after it once it's built: any tool will drift. Read [do automations need maintenance?](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/do-automations-need-maintenance/) before you build, and keep the scenarios in your own account so you're never locked in to whoever built them.

If another tool fits the process better, you'll be told why in the plan. To see which of your processes could be automated, try the [plan builder](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/plan/).

## Business automation mistakes small businesses make, and how to avoid them
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/small-business-automation-mistakes/ (2026-11-11)

The most common business automation mistakes are automating a process nobody has written down, automating too much at once, letting an automation fail without anyone noticing, and letting it send things to clients with no person checking first. Most are avoided by mapping the job before building, starting with one workflow, turning on error alerts, naming one owner, and keeping a human approval step for anything a client sees.

Business automation mistakes are rarely about the tool. They come from what happens before the build (what you chose to automate and how well you understood it) and after it (who watches it, who owns it, and what happens when something changes). The good news is that almost all of them are cheap to avoid if you know them in advance. If you're new to the subject, our [business automation guide for small firms](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/small-business-automation/) covers the basics first.
Below are ten mistakes that come up again and again in vendor help pages, forums and project briefs, what each one looks like in a small service business, and the fix. At the end there's a pre-launch checklist you can copy. We haven't included any "X% of automations fail" figures, because we couldn't find one with a checkable source.

### 1. Automating a process nobody has written down
If three people in your business do the same job three different ways, an automation will copy one of them, usually the one the builder happened to hear about. The other two people work around it, and within a month you have the automation plus the old manual steps.
The fix: write the job down first, step by step, with who does what and where the information lives. Our [process map template](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/process-map-template-small-business/) takes about an hour for one job. If you can't agree on the steps, you're not ready to automate, and that conversation alone is worth having.

### 2. Automating a broken process
Automation makes a process faster, not better. If your client onboarding asks for the same document twice, an automation will ask twice, faster. If your quote follow-up goes to people who already said no, it will reach them more reliably.
The fix: while you map the job, cross out every step that exists only because "we've always done it". Automate what's left.

### 3. Starting with the biggest, hardest job
It's tempting to start with the job that hurts most. Often that's also the job with the most exceptions, the most people involved and the most systems. Big first projects take longer, cost more and are harder to judge.
The fix: start with one job that repeats often, follows the same steps each time and has a clear finish line, such as chasing documents, confirming bookings or [replying to new enquiries](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/reply-to-new-enquiries-fast/). Our guide on [what to automate first](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/what-to-automate-first-small-business/) has a simple way to score your options.

### 4. No definition of "working"
"Make onboarding easier" can't be tested. Without a clear finish line, nobody can say whether the automation does its job, and arguments about it never end.
The fix: write one sentence before anything is built, for example: "Every new client gets the welcome email and document list within an hour of signing, and anyone who hasn't uploaded everything after five days gets a reminder." If the build meets that sentence, it works.

### 5. Letting it fail quietly
This is the most expensive mistake, because you find out late. Automations stop when a login expires, a form changes or a plan runs out of usage, and unless someone is told, the first sign is a client asking why they never heard back.
Platforms do switch off workflows that keep failing, but that is not the same as telling the right person. Zapier, for example, can turn a Zap off on its own when its recent runs keep ending in errors, and the person who needs to know may never see the alert. Google's developer documentation says an app connecting to Google that is still in "Testing" status gets logins that expire after 7 days, which catches out many self-built workflows.
The fix: send error alerts to a person who will act on them (not a shared inbox nobody reads), and do a short monthly check. Our post on whether [automations need maintenance](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/do-automations-need-maintenance/) has a monthly checklist.

### 6. Removing the human from things clients see
An automation that sends the wrong invoice, the wrong reminder or a message to someone who just complained does real damage. The risk is higher when AI writes the text, because it can sound confident and still be wrong. If you're unsure where automation ends and AI begins, see [AI vs automation](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/ai-vs-automation-difference/).
The fix: let the automation do the gathering, sorting and drafting, and keep a person approving anything that goes to a client or moves money, at least until you trust it. A one-click "approve and send" keeps most of the time saved.

### 7. Building it in one person's accounts
If the automation runs in a freelancer's account, or a staff member's personal Google login, it stops the day they leave or their password changes. You may not even be able to see how it was built.
The fix: everything runs in accounts your business owns, with logins you control. Our [automation handover checklist](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/automation-handover-checklist/) lists what to ask for before you sign off a build.

### 8. Sending more client data than the job needs
It's easy to pass a whole client record from one app to the next "just in case". Every extra field is one more copy of personal data in one more system. Under UK GDPR, personal data must be "adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary": the ICO calls this the data minimisation principle.
The fix: for each step, pass only the fields that step needs, and know which apps hold client data. Our [GDPR checklist for automating client data](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/gdpr-checklist-automating-client-data/) goes through it.

### 9. No documentation and no off switch
Six months later nobody remembers what the automation does, what triggers it, or how to stop it if it misbehaves. So people are afraid to change anything, including the form or spreadsheet it depends on.
The fix: one page per workflow. What starts it, what it does, which apps and logins it uses, who owns it, and how to switch it off. Keep it where the team can find it.

### 10. Choosing the tool before the job
"We should use Zapier" or "let's try AI" is the starting point for a lot of projects that go nowhere. The right tool depends on the job, the apps you already pay for, how often it runs and who will look after it.
The fix: pick the tool last. Often the cheapest answer is a feature in software you already have. If you do need a platform, our comparison of [Zapier, Make and n8n](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/zapier-vs-make-vs-n8n/) explains the trade-offs.

### The mistakes at a glance
| Mistake | What it looks like | How to avoid it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Process not written down | Staff work around the automation | Map the job step by step first |
| Broken process automated | The same pointless step, done faster | Cut unneeded steps before building |
| Biggest job first | A long, costly project that's hard to judge | Start with one simple, frequent job |
| No definition of "working" | Endless debate about whether it works | Write one finish-line sentence |
| Fails quietly | A client tells you nothing was sent | Error alerts to a named person, monthly check |
| No human on client messages | The wrong message reaches a client | Approval step for anything clients see |
| Built in one person's accounts | It stops when they leave | Business-owned accounts and logins |
| Too much client data passed on | Personal data copied everywhere | Only the fields each step needs |
| No documentation | Nobody dares change anything | One page per workflow, with the off switch |
| Tool chosen first | Paying for a platform you didn't need | Choose the tool after the job is clear |

### A pre-launch checklist to copy
Run through this before any automation goes live, whether you built it yourself or someone built it for you.
Automation pre-launch checklist:
```
Workflow name: [name]
Owner (the person who gets alerts and decides on changes): [name]

[ ] The job is written down step by step, and the team agrees that's how it works
[ ] Steps that weren't needed have been removed
[ ] One sentence says what "working" means: [sentence]
[ ] Tested with real examples, including an awkward one (missing info, duplicate, late reply)
[ ] Error alerts go to the owner, and the owner has seen a test alert
[ ] Anything sent to a client, or anything that moves money, needs a person's approval
[ ] Runs in accounts the business owns, with logins the business controls
[ ] Only the client data each step needs is passed on
[ ] One-page description saved: trigger, steps, apps, logins, owner, how to switch it off
[ ] Monthly check booked in the owner's calendar
[ ] Staff know what changed and who to ask
```

### How Mike Automations avoids these
Most of this list is about the work around the build, so that's where we start. On a [free 15-minute call](https://mikeautomations.github.io/call/) we talk through one job and how it's done today. Within 48 hours you get a written plan with a fixed price, built on the tools you already use. Anything a client sees goes through your approval, it runs in your accounts, and you get a one-page guide with the off switch.
It's live in 2-3 days and costs [$2,000 one-off](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/pricing/), paid only once it's running and you're happy with it, as set out in our [pay-when-happy agreement](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/agreement/). If you'd like to sketch the job first, the [plan builder](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/plan/) walks you through it.

### What is the most common business automation mistake?
Automating a process before it's written down and agreed. The automation copies one version of the job, the team keeps doing the others, and you end up with the automation plus the old manual work.

### Why do automations stop working?
Usually because something around them changes: a login expires, someone edits a form or spreadsheet, an app updates, or the plan runs out of usage. Error alerts sent to a named person mean you hear about it before a client does.

### Should an automation send emails to clients without anyone checking?
Not at first. Let the automation gather information and draft the message, and have a person approve anything a client sees or anything that moves money. Once it has run reliably for a while, you can decide which simple messages can go out on their own.

### How many processes should a small business automate at once?
One. Pick a job that repeats often and follows the same steps, get it working and trusted, then move to the next. It's cheaper, easier to judge and easier for staff to adjust to.

## ChatGPT for small business admin: what to use it for, and what never to paste in
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/chatgpt-for-small-business-admin/ (2026-11-11)

ChatGPT for small business admin works best as a drafting assistant: first drafts of emails, policies, checklists and replies to common questions, plus tidying rough notes. Write prompts with placeholders such as [customer name] instead of real customer details, never paste in passwords, card or bank details, ID numbers or health information, and read every draft before it goes out. On individual ChatGPT plans (Free, Plus, Pro), OpenAI says your content may be used to train its models unless you turn off "Improve the model for everyone" in Settings > Data controls.

ChatGPT for small business admin is useful for one thing above all: getting you past the blank page. The reply to a tricky customer, the late-payment email, the cancellation policy you keep meaning to write. It drafts those in seconds. It doesn't know your customers, your prices or the law that applies to you, and it can be confidently wrong, so you stay the editor.
This post covers the admin jobs it does well, the ones to keep away from it, six prompts you can copy, the data settings to check before you start, and the point where copying and pasting into a chat window stops being the right tool. If you run an accounting practice, there's a separate set of [ChatGPT prompts for accountants](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/chatgpt-prompts-for-accountants/).

### What ChatGPT is good at in small business admin
Think of it as a fast junior who writes well, has never met your customers and doesn't check facts. Give it jobs where a wrong word costs you a minute to fix, not money or trust.
| Admin job | Use ChatGPT? | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| First draft of a customer email or reply | Yes | You give it the facts, it gives you the wording. You check and send. |
| Rewriting a message to be firmer or friendlier | Yes | Tone is where it's strongest. Paste the text with names removed. |
| Turning rough notes into a checklist or procedure | Yes | Good at structure. You add the steps it can't know. |
| A first draft of a policy (cancellations, deposits, returns) | Yes, as a draft | Check it against your terms and, for anything legal, get it reviewed. |
| Answers about tax, employment or consumer law | Only as a starting point | It can be out of date or wrong. Check the official source (gov.uk, IRS, your tax office). |
| Working out prices, totals or VAT | No | Use your accounting software or a spreadsheet. Sums must be right every time. |
| Anything with a named customer's personal or payment details | No | Keep those out of a general chat tool entirely. |
| Sending messages or making changes on its own | No | A person should approve anything that reaches a customer or moves money. |

### What never to paste into ChatGPT
The simplest rule: if you wouldn't write it on a postcard, don't put it in a prompt. Copy this list and pin it next to whoever does the admin.
This matters beyond good manners. In the UK and EU, data protection law keeps your business responsible for customers' personal data whichever tool you put it into. Our [GDPR checklist before automating client data](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/gdpr-checklist-automating-client-data/) covers what that means in practice. Placeholders sidestep the question: if no personal data goes in, there's nothing to account for.
Checklist: never paste these into a general AI chat:
```
[ ] Passwords, login codes, API keys or recovery codes
[ ] Card numbers, bank account details or payment links tied to a person
[ ] National Insurance, Social Security, passport, driving licence or tax ID numbers
[ ] Customer names together with their address, phone number or email
[ ] Health, medical or other sensitive personal information
[ ] Staff records: pay, disciplinary notes, sickness, appraisals
[ ] Contracts or documents a customer or supplier has marked confidential
[ ] Anything a customer told you in confidence

Instead: replace names with [customer name], numbers with [amount] and dates with [date]. Fill them in yourself after you copy the draft out.
```

### Check your ChatGPT data settings first
OpenAI's help centre (checked 11 November 2026) explains how your content is used:
- Individual plans (Free, Plus, Pro): OpenAI says it may use your content to train its models. To opt out, turn off "Improve the model for everyone" under Settings > Data controls, or choose "Do not train on my content" in OpenAI's Privacy Portal. Either one is enough.
- Thumbs up and thumbs down count. On individual plans, OpenAI says that if you give feedback on a response, the whole conversation may be used to improve its models, even if you've opted out.
- Temporary chats stay out of your chat history and aren't used to train models while they stay temporary. OpenAI may still keep a copy for up to 30 days for safety purposes. If you save one, it becomes a normal chat with your normal settings.
- Business plans: OpenAI says that by default it doesn't use inputs or outputs from ChatGPT Business, ChatGPT Enterprise, ChatGPT Edu or its API to improve its models.

### Settings are a second layer, not permission
Turning off training reduces one risk. It doesn't make it fine to paste in customer data: the chat is still stored on someone else's servers, and you are still responsible for it. Treat the opt-out as a second layer behind the placeholder rule, never a replacement for it.
If more than one person uses ChatGPT for your business, agree in writing which account type you use, who checks the settings, and what never goes in. Two lines in your staff handbook are enough.

### Six prompts to copy
Each prompt uses placeholders in [brackets]. Swap in general details, never a real customer's. Then read the result, fix anything wrong, and add the real names yourself outside the chat.
Prompt 1: reply to a common customer question:
```
I run a small [type of business] in [country]. A customer asked: "[paste the question with any names and personal details removed]". Write a short, friendly reply in plain English, under 120 words. Our policy is: [one or two lines on your actual policy]. If the answer depends on details we don't have, say we'll check and come back to them. Don't promise anything that isn't in the policy above.
```

### Prompt 2: a polite late-payment reminder
Once you've settled on wording you like, the reminder itself is a good candidate for plain automation rather than AI. Our guide to [invoice payment reminders](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/invoice-payment-reminders/) shows how that works.
Prompt:
```
Write a polite but clear payment reminder from a small [type of business] for invoice [invoice number], amount [amount], due on [date]. It's now [number] days overdue. Mention how to pay: [payment method]. Offer a quick call if there's a problem. Under 100 words, no threats, no legal language.
```

### Prompt 3: turn your notes into a step-by-step procedure
A written procedure is also the first step towards automating a task. Our [process map template](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/process-map-template-small-business/) helps you see which steps are repetitive enough to hand to a workflow.
Prompt:
```
Turn these rough notes on how we [describe the task, e.g. book in a new customer] into a numbered step-by-step procedure that a new member of staff could follow. Add an owner for each step and flag any step where something could be missed. Notes: [paste notes with names replaced by roles, e.g. 'office manager']
```

### Prompt 4: a first draft of a policy
Prompt:
```
Draft a short, plain-English [cancellation / deposit / late arrival] policy for a small [type of business] in [country]. Our rules are: [list your actual rules: notice period, what's charged, exceptions]. Write it so a customer understands it in 30 seconds. Don't add rules I haven't listed. At the end, list anything I should check with an adviser before publishing it.
```

### Prompt 5: make a message firmer, or softer
Prompt:
```
Rewrite this message so it's [firmer / warmer / shorter] but still polite. Keep every fact exactly as it is, and don't add new promises or dates. Message: [paste the message with names and personal details removed]
```

### Prompt 6: summarise a long email thread
Remove the email signatures before you paste. They're full of phone numbers, addresses and job titles that the summary doesn't need.
Prompt:
```
Summarise this email thread in five bullet points: what was asked, what was agreed, what is still open, who needs to do what, and any dates mentioned. Thread: [paste the thread with names replaced by 'Customer', 'Supplier' and 'Me', and all contact details, account numbers and addresses removed]
```

### A safe routine for using ChatGPT at work
1. Decide which account you'll use for work, and check its data settings before the first prompt.
2. Share the "never paste" checklist with anyone who does admin for you.
3. Write the prompt with placeholders, never real names, numbers or contact details.
4. Give it your real rules: your policy, your prices, your notice periods. It doesn't know them, and it will guess if you don't say.
5. Read the draft as if a stranger wrote it. Check every fact, date, price and promise.
6. For anything about tax, employment or consumer law, check the official source before you rely on it.
7. Copy the draft out of the chat, add the real details yourself, and send it from your own email.
8. On an individual plan, skip the thumbs up and down buttons on work chats.

### When copying and pasting into ChatGPT stops being enough
ChatGPT in a browser tab works when the job is occasional and different each time. It works badly when you do the same job twenty times a week: copying text in, copying drafts out, removing names, adding them back. That's a sign the job needs a workflow, not a chat window: [AI automation set up inside your own tools](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/ai-automation-services-small-business/), with a person approving each draft.
Often the honest answer is that the job needs no AI at all. A payment reminder or a booking confirmation follows rules, and rules are cheaper and more reliable than a language model. Our post on [AI vs automation](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/ai-vs-automation-difference/) explains the difference. Where AI does help, for example reading incoming enquiries and drafting replies, it can be built into your tools so the drafts land where you already work and a person approves each one before it's sent. That's what an [AI agent for a small business](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/ai-agent-for-small-business/) means in practice. Reading invoices and forms into a spreadsheet is another use, set out in [automating data entry with a human check](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/automate-data-entry-from-emails-and-pdfs/).
If you're not sure which admin job to start with, the [plan builder](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/plan/) asks a few questions and suggests one, and the [demo](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/try/) shows what an approval step looks like.

If one admin job keeps eating your week, I'll map how it works today and build it into the tools you already use: your inbox, your spreadsheet or CRM, your accounting software. Rules handle the predictable steps, AI drafts only where it genuinely helps, and a person always approves anything the AI prepares.
