### Is it safe to use ChatGPT for small business admin?
It can be, for drafting work with no personal data in it. Use placeholders instead of customer details, check your account's data settings, and read every draft before sending. Never paste in passwords, payment details, ID numbers, health information or staff records.

### Does ChatGPT use what I type to train its models?
On individual plans (Free, Plus, Pro), OpenAI says it may, unless you turn off "Improve the model for everyone" in Settings > Data controls or opt out through its Privacy Portal. OpenAI says it doesn't train on ChatGPT Business, Enterprise, Edu or API content by default.

### Are Temporary Chats private?
They stay out of your chat history and aren't used to train OpenAI's models while they remain temporary, but OpenAI says it may keep a copy for up to 30 days for safety purposes. They're not a reason to paste in customer data.

### Can ChatGPT send emails or update my systems for me?
Not safely on its own. For repeated admin jobs, it's better to build a workflow where rules handle the predictable steps, AI drafts where it helps, and a person approves anything before it reaches a customer.

## Google Apps Script for small business: what it can do, its limits, and when to skip it
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/google-apps-script-for-small-business/ (2026-11-11)

Google Apps Script for small business is Google's built-in way to automate Sheets, Gmail, Calendar, Drive, Docs and Forms with short JavaScript programs that run on Google's servers, with nothing to install. It suits small, internal jobs such as drafting reminder emails from a spreadsheet or filing form responses, but Google's daily quotas apply: a gmail.com account can email 100 recipients a day from a script and a Google Workspace account 1,500, and one run stops after 6 minutes.

Google Apps Script for small business is the automation tool most owners already have and never open. If your business runs on Google Sheets, Gmail and Google Drive, it's sitting in the Extensions menu of every spreadsheet, and it costs nothing extra on top of your Google account.
This guide covers what it's good at, the limits Google publishes, a short script you can copy and adapt, and the cases where a different tool, or no automation at all, is the better choice. Every limit below comes from Google's own developer documentation, checked on 11 November 2026.

### What Google Apps Script is
Google describes Apps Script as a development platform for building business applications that work with Google Workspace. You write code in JavaScript, in an editor that runs in your browser. Google's overview page says there's nothing to install: scripts are saved to Drive and run on Google's servers.
A script can be bound to one file (open a Google Sheet, then Extensions, then Apps Script) or stand alone in Drive. It has built-in services for Gmail, Calendar, Drive, Docs, Sheets and Forms, so it can read a row in a spreadsheet, write an email, create a document from a template and file it in a folder, all in one run.

### What it can do for a small service business
The best Apps Script jobs are small, repetitive and live entirely inside Google's tools. A few that fit most service businesses:
- Draft payment reminder emails for overdue invoices listed in a sheet, for a person to check and send. This is the script further down. For the full workflow, see our guide to [invoice payment reminders](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/invoice-payment-reminders/).
- When someone submits a Google Form (a new enquiry, an intake form, a booking request), copy the answers to a tracker sheet, create a client folder in Drive and email you a summary.
- Turn a row in a sheet into a Google Doc from a template: a quote, a welcome letter, a job sheet.
- Create Calendar events from a list of booked jobs or appointments.
- Add a custom menu to a spreadsheet, such as "Send this week's reminders", so the person running the sheet clicks one button instead of copying and pasting.
- A Monday morning email to yourself listing every client whose documents are still missing, built from a tracker sheet.

### Google's quotas and limits (checked 11 November 2026)
Google's "Quotas for Google Services" page sets different limits for consumer accounts (such as gmail.com) and Google Workspace accounts. Quotas are per user and reset 24 hours after the first request. Google also says all quotas can be removed, reduced or changed at any time without notice, so treat these figures as a guide and check the page before you rely on one.
| Limit | Consumer account (gmail.com) | Google Workspace account |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Email recipients per day (for example, with MailApp) | 100 | 1,500 |
| Email read/write, excluding send | 20,000 a day | 50,000 a day |
| Calendar events created | 5,000 a day | 10,000 a day |
| Documents created | 250 a day | 1,500 a day |
| Spreadsheets created | 250 a day | 3,200 a day |
| URL Fetch calls (talking to other apps' APIs) | 20,000 a day | 100,000 a day |
| Total trigger runtime | 90 minutes a day | 6 hours a day |
| Script runtime | 6 minutes per run | 6 minutes per run |
| Triggers | 20 per user per script | 20 per user per script |
| Email recipients per message | 50 | 50 |

### How triggers work, and the catches
A trigger is what makes a script run without you pressing a button. Google's documentation describes two kinds, and the differences matter for a business.
- Simple triggers, such as onEdit when a cell changes or onOpen when a file opens, can't use services that need authorisation. Google's example: a simple trigger can't send an email. They also can't run for longer than 30 seconds.
- Installable triggers can send email and run on a clock, from every minute to once a month. The time is slightly randomised: if you set a daily 9 AM trigger, Google picks a time between 9 and 10 AM and keeps it consistent.
- Installable triggers always run as the person who created them. If an employee sets up the reminder script, the emails go out from their account, and the script stops working if that account is removed when they leave. Set triggers up from an account the business owns.
- A script that runs on a trigger can't show a permission screen. Google's troubleshooting page says that if a script needs new permissions, someone has to open the editor and run it once to authorise it again.
- When a triggered script fails, Google sends failure notification emails. You can change how often they arrive, but you can only stop them by turning the trigger off. Make sure they go to an inbox someone reads.

### A script to copy: draft overdue invoice reminders from a sheet
This script reads a sheet called Invoices with these columns, in this order: Client, Email, Invoice, Amount, Due date, Status, Reminder drafted. For every unpaid invoice past its due date that hasn't had a reminder yet, it creates a Gmail draft and writes today's date in the last column. It creates drafts, not sent emails, so a person reads each one before it goes. For illustration: adapt the wording, and test it on a copy of your sheet with your own email address first.
Apps Script: paste into Extensions > Apps Script in your invoice sheet:
```
function draftOverdueReminders() {
  const sheet = SpreadsheetApp.getActive().getSheetByName('Invoices');
  const rows = sheet.getDataRange().getValues();
  const today = new Date();

  for (let i = 1; i < rows.length; i++) {
    const [client, email, invoice, amount, due, status, drafted] = rows[i];
    if (status === 'Paid' || drafted || !(due instanceof Date) || due >= today) continue;

    const body = 'Hi ' + client + ',\n\n' +
      'A quick reminder that invoice ' + invoice + ' for ' + amount +
      ' was due on ' + due.toDateString() + '.\n\n' +
      'If you have already paid, thank you, and please ignore this email.\n\n' +
      'Best wishes,\n[your name]';

    GmailApp.createDraft(email, 'Reminder: invoice ' + invoice, body);
    sheet.getRange(i + 1, 7).setValue(new Date());
  }
}
```

### How to set it up in 7 steps
1. Make a copy of your invoice sheet and name the tab Invoices. Put the seven column headings in row 1, in the order above, and use real dates in the Due date column.
2. In the copy, open Extensions, then Apps Script. Delete the empty function and paste the script.
3. Click Save, choose draftOverdueReminders in the function list and click Run.
4. Google asks you to authorise the script to use Sheets and Gmail. Read the permissions, then allow them with the business account that should own the emails.
5. Open your Gmail drafts and read what was created. Check names, amounts and dates against the sheet.
6. When the drafts look right, add a trigger: the clock icon (Triggers), Add trigger, choose the function, time-driven, day timer, and a morning hour.
7. Write down where the script lives, which account owns the trigger and who reads the failure emails. Keep that note next to the sheet.

### When not to use Apps Script
Apps Script is a good tool with a narrow sweet spot. Pick something else when:
- Your business runs on Microsoft 365 or Outlook. Apps Script is for Google's tools; Power Automate is the native option there, and our [Power Automate vs Zapier](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/power-automate-vs-zapier-small-business/) comparison covers it.
- The job is mostly about apps outside Google, such as Xero, QuickBooks, a booking system or a CRM. Apps Script can call other apps' APIs, but a connector tool does that with less code. See [Zapier vs Make vs n8n](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/zapier-vs-make-vs-n8n/).
- You send bulk or marketing email. 100 recipients a day on a gmail.com account runs out fast, and bulk email belongs in an email marketing tool anyway.
- Nobody in the business can read JavaScript. A script nobody understands becomes a problem the day it breaks, and scripts do break when someone renames a column or a tab. Our post on [whether automations need maintenance](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/do-automations-need-maintenance/) explains why.
- The work needs long processing. One run stops after 6 minutes, so a big batch has to be split into smaller runs.
- The data is sensitive, for example ID documents or health information. You can keep it in Google's tools, but you'll want proper access controls and a clear record of who can see what, not a script copied from a forum.

### Apps Script or a no-code tool?
|  | Google Apps Script | No-code tool (Zapier, Make, n8n) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Extra cost | None beyond your Google account | Free tiers, then monthly plans |
| Best for | Jobs inside Sheets, Gmail, Drive, Calendar, Forms | Jobs that join many different apps |
| Skills needed | Some JavaScript | None to start |
| Who it runs as | The person who created the trigger | The accounts you connect |
| When it breaks | Failure emails, then someone reads the code | Error log in the tool's dashboard |

### How Mike Automations would set this up
If your work already lives in Google Sheets and Gmail, Apps Script is often the cheapest way to run it, and it's one of the options we look at alongside no-code tools. We pick whichever is easier for you to keep running, set triggers up on an account the business owns, and write down how it works. Anything that goes to a client starts as a draft or waits for your approval. Our page on [Google Workspace automation services](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/google-workspace-automation-services/) covers what else can run inside Gmail, Sheets, Forms and Drive.
We start with a [free 15-minute call](https://mikeautomations.github.io/call/) about the job you want off your plate. Within 48 hours you get a written plan with a fixed price. It's built on the tools you already use, it's live in 2-3 days, and it costs [$2,000 one-off](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/pricing/), paid once it's running and you're happy with it. If you'd like to map the job yourself first, try the [plan builder](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/plan/).

### Is Google Apps Script free?
There's no separate charge: it comes with a Google account, and Google's overview says scripts are saved to Drive and run on Google's servers. What changes with a paid Google Workspace account is the daily quotas, for example 1,500 email recipients a day instead of 100 on a gmail.com account.

### How many emails can Google Apps Script send a day?
Google's quotas page lists 100 recipients a day for consumer accounts such as gmail.com and 1,500 a day for Google Workspace accounts, with a maximum of 50 recipients per message. Google says these quotas can change without notice.

### Can Apps Script run automatically every day?
Yes, with an installable time-driven trigger. Google says these can run as often as every minute or as rarely as once a month, and a daily trigger runs at a slightly randomised time within the hour you choose.

### Do I need to know how to code to use Apps Script?
To change a script safely, some JavaScript helps. You can copy a short script like the one above, but someone should understand it well enough to fix it when a column or tab name changes.

## Client onboarding automation for a small service business: steps, checklist and what to keep human
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/client-onboarding-automation-service-business/ (2026-11-11)

Client onboarding automation is a workflow that starts the moment a client says yes and sends everything that follows in order: the agreement, the first invoice, a welcome email, an intake form, a document request and a booking link, with reminders for anything still missing. It suits any small service business, because the steps are the same each time. A person should still agree the scope and price, check anything sensitive the client sends, and make the first real contact.

Client onboarding automation takes the same eight or nine steps you do after every "yes" and runs them for you, in the right order, without anyone retyping a name or forgetting a form. It works for accountants, agencies, coaches, consultants, IT support firms and most other service businesses, because the shape of onboarding barely changes from one client to the next.
Below are the steps, a table of what to automate and what to keep for a person, a checklist you can copy, a welcome email template, and the mistakes that make onboarding feel robotic. If you run an accounting firm, our [accounting client onboarding checklist](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/accounting-client-onboarding-checklist/) covers the extra regulatory steps such as ID checks and agent authorisation.

### What client onboarding actually involves
Onboarding is everything between "yes, let's do it" and the first piece of real work. Done by hand, it usually means copying the client's details from an email into a contract, then into an invoice, then into a spreadsheet, then into a calendar. Each copy is a chance to get a name or an email address wrong, and each step waits until someone remembers to do it.
The work itself is rarely hard. The trouble is that it is spread over a week or two, across four or five tools, and the client has to act at several points. That is exactly the kind of process a workflow handles well: clear steps, a clear trigger, and a clear "done" for each one.

### The 8 steps of an automated onboarding workflow
This is the order most service businesses can use. The trigger is one clear event: a proposal accepted, a form submitted, or a deal moved to "Won" in your CRM or spreadsheet.
1. Trigger: the client accepts. The workflow creates one client record (name, email, service, price, start date) and every later step reads from it, so details are typed once.
2. Agreement: the contract or engagement letter goes out for e-signature, filled in from the client record. See [engagement letter automation](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/engagement-letter-automation/) for how this works with templates.
3. First invoice or deposit: once the agreement is signed, the invoice is created in your accounting tool (Xero, QuickBooks or similar) and sent. Our post on [asking for a deposit](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/how-to-ask-for-a-deposit-on-a-quote/) has wording for this.
4. Welcome email: sent when the agreement is signed (or the invoice paid, if you prefer). It says what happens next, who to contact and when they'll hear from you.
5. Intake form: one form for everything you need to know, sent with the welcome email. Ask only what you will actually use. Choosing the form tool is covered in [Microsoft Forms vs Google Forms for client intake](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/microsoft-forms-vs-google-forms-small-business/).
6. Documents and access: a secure upload link for files, and instructions for giving you access to accounts through each platform's own user settings, never by sending passwords.
7. Booking: a link to book the kickoff call or first session, offered once the form is in, so the call starts with the answers already read. Whether to use [Google Calendar appointment schedules or Calendly](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/google-calendar-appointment-schedules-vs-calendly/) for that link depends on your plan and how many people take bookings.
8. Internal setup and reminders: the workflow creates the client folder, adds the client to your task list, reminds the client about anything still missing after a few days, and tells you when everything is in.

### What to automate and what to keep human
The rule is simple: automate the sending, the filing and the reminding; keep the judgement and the relationship. A person always approves anything that commits you to a price, a scope or a promise.
| Step | Automate | Keep human |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Scope and price | Filling the proposal from a template | Agreeing what you'll do and for how much |
| Agreement | Sending for e-signature, reminders, filing the signed copy | Approving any non-standard terms |
| Invoice or deposit | Creating and sending it, payment reminders | Deciding on discounts or payment plans |
| Welcome email | Sending it at the right moment | Writing it once, in your own voice |
| Intake form | Sending it, chasing it, saving answers | Reading the answers before the first call |
| Documents and ID | Upload link, folder, reminders | Checking anything sensitive or official |
| Kickoff call | Booking link and calendar invite | The call itself |
| Missing items | Polite reminders on a schedule | A personal call if a client goes quiet |

### Collect less data, not more
Automation makes it easy to ask for everything, which is a mistake. Long forms get abandoned, and every extra field is data you now have to protect.
In the UK, the ICO's guidance on data minimisation says personal data should be "adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary", and that you should identify the minimum amount you need for your purpose. In the US, the FTC's guide "Protecting Personal Information: A Guide for Business" puts it more bluntly: "Keep only what you need for your business." Either way, the onboarding form is where that starts.
Two practical points. Don't ask for bank details, ID numbers or passwords in an ordinary email or a general form; use a secure upload or e-signature tool. And check how your form tool handles files: Google's help page for Google Forms says that to answer a file upload question, respondents need to sign in to a Google Account, and uploaded files go to a folder in the form owner's Google Drive. If many of your clients don't use Google, a different upload link may be easier for them. Our [GDPR checklist for automating client data](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/gdpr-checklist-automating-client-data/) goes further.

### A client onboarding checklist to copy
Use this as the outline for your own workflow, or as a manual checklist until it's automated. Each line should have an owner and a "done" condition you can see.
Client onboarding checklist:
```
CLIENT: [name]    SERVICE: [service]    START DATE: [date]

[ ] Client record created (name, email, phone, service, price, start date)
[ ] Agreement sent for e-signature
[ ] Agreement signed and saved to the client folder
[ ] First invoice or deposit sent
[ ] Payment received (or terms agreed)
[ ] Welcome email sent
[ ] Intake form sent
[ ] Intake form completed and read by [owner]
[ ] Documents requested: [list]
[ ] Documents received and checked by [owner]
[ ] Access given through the platform's own user settings (no passwords by email)
[ ] Kickoff call booked for [date]
[ ] Client folder and tasks set up
[ ] Reminder schedule set for anything missing (day 3, day 7, then a personal call)
[ ] Onboarding complete: first piece of work scheduled
```

### A welcome email template
Write this once, in your own words, and let the workflow send it. It should tell the client exactly what happens next and what you need from them, in that order.
Subject: Welcome, [first name]: what happens next:
```
Hi [first name],

Thanks for choosing [business name]. I'm looking forward to working with you on [service].

Here's what happens next:

1. Please fill in this short form so I have what I need: [form link]. It takes about [10] minutes.
2. Upload any documents here: [secure upload link]. Please don't send passwords or ID numbers by email.
3. Once the form is in, book our first call here: [booking link].

If anything is unclear, just reply to this email or call me on [phone].

[your name]
[business name]
```

### Mistakes that make onboarding feel robotic
- Sending everything at once. Five emails in five minutes look like spam. Send each step when the one before it is done.
- Reminders that ignore replies. If the client has answered, the reminders must stop. Nothing undermines trust faster than a chaser for something already sent.
- No human touch at all. A short personal message or call in the first week matters more than any template. Automate the admin so you have time for it.
- Asking twice. If the client gave their address in the proposal, don't ask for it again in the intake form. One client record, read by every step.
- No owner for exceptions. When a client asks a question or sends the wrong file, someone has to be told. The workflow should flag it, not carry on.
- Building it before the process is clear. Write the steps down first. Our post on [what to automate first](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/what-to-automate-first-small-business/) explains how to pick the right starting point.

### Examples by type of business
The eight steps stay the same; what changes is the intake form and the documents. For illustration: a marketing agency needs brand files and access to ad and analytics accounts (see [agency client onboarding](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/agency-client-onboarding-automation/)); a coach needs a questionnaire and a session booking link (see [coach and consultant onboarding](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/coach-consultant-client-onboarding/)); an IT support firm needs a list of devices and users (see [MSP client onboarding](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/msp-client-onboarding-and-renewals/)). You can sketch your own version in the [plan builder](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/plan/) or see a working example in the [demo](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/try/).

### How Mike Automations would set this up
I'd start from the moment a client says yes in your current tools, whether that's an email, a form, a CRM or a spreadsheet, and connect the steps above using the software you already pay for: your e-signature tool, your accounting software, your email and your calendar. You approve every template once, and anything that needs judgement still comes to you.
We start with a [free 15-minute call](https://mikeautomations.github.io/call/) about how onboarding works today. Within 48 hours you get a written plan with a fixed price. It's built on the tools you already use, it's live in 2-3 days, and it costs [$2,000 one-off](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/pricing/), paid only once it's running and you're happy with it, as set out in the [pay-when-happy agreement](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/agreement/).

### What is client onboarding automation?
It's a workflow that starts when a client says yes and sends the agreement, invoice, welcome email, intake form, document request and booking link in order, with reminders for anything missing. A person still agrees the scope and price and checks anything sensitive.

### What tools do I need to automate client onboarding?
Usually the ones you already have: an e-signature tool, your accounting software for invoices, a form tool, email and a calendar. A workflow tool such as Zapier, Make or n8n, or a small custom script, connects them so details are typed once.

### What parts of onboarding should stay human?
Agreeing the scope and price, approving any non-standard terms, checking ID or sensitive documents, reading the intake answers and the first real conversation with the client. Automation should give you more time for these, not replace them.

### How much information should an onboarding form ask for?
Only what you'll actually use. The ICO says personal data should be limited to what is necessary for your purpose, and the FTC's guide for US businesses says to keep only what you need. Shorter forms also get finished faster.

## Estimate follow-up email templates for contractors (that don't sound pushy)
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/estimate-follow-up-email-templates-contractors/ (2026-11-10)

An estimate follow-up email for contractors works best as a short sequence: check the estimate arrived after 2 days, send one useful detail (like your next opening) after about a week, and send a polite close-out after 2 to 3 weeks. Stop the moment the customer replies or books. The templates below cover each step, plus a text version and a reply to a price objection.

These estimate follow-up email templates are for [contractors who send estimates](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/contractors/) and then hear nothing. Many estimates don't get a "no". They get silence. The customer got busy, is comparing bids, or lost your email under a pile of others.
A short, well-timed follow-up is often the difference between a lost job and a booked one, and most contractors never send one because there's no time between jobs. Below: a day-by-day schedule, five emails, two texts and an answer to the most common objection. Change the wording so it sounds like you.

### The follow-up schedule
Stop the sequence as soon as the customer replies, books or says no. You can [watch a quote follow-up sequence play out](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/try/) in a one-minute demo. Nothing annoys a customer more than a "just checking in" after they've already said yes.
| When | Channel | Goal | Template |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Same day | Email | Send the estimate with a clear next step | Email 0 |
| Day 2 | Text or email | Check it arrived, invite questions | Email 1 or Text 1 |
| Day 7 | Email | One useful detail: your next opening or a lead time | Email 2 |
| Day 10 to 14 | Phone call | A short call for larger jobs only | Your own words |
| Day 14 to 21 | Email | Polite close-out, easy yes or no | Email 3 |
| Any time | Email | Answer "your price is too high" | Email 4 |

### Email 0: sending the estimate
Subject: Your estimate for [job] at [address]:
```
Hi [first name],

Thanks for having us out on [day]. Your estimate for [job] is attached. It covers [two or three main items] and is valid until [date].

If it looks good, just reply "yes" and we'll send over a start date. If you'd like to change anything, reply with your questions or call me at [phone].

Thanks,
[your name], [company]
```

### Email 1: did you get it?
Subject: Re: Your estimate for [job]:
```
Hi [first name],

Just checking the estimate for [job] reached you. Happy to walk you through it or adjust anything. Questions are welcome here or by text at [phone].

Thanks,
[your name], [company]
```

### Email 2: one helpful detail
Only give a lead time or an opening that's true. A real detail is helpful; a made-up deadline is pressure, and customers can tell. Caterers use the same idea after sending a menu quote; see [catering quote follow-up](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/catering-quotes-and-final-numbers/).
Subject: Re: Your estimate for [job]:
```
Hi [first name],

A quick update: our next opening is the week of [date], and [material] currently takes about [time] to arrive, so booking soon keeps that date. If you'd like to go ahead, just reply and we'll hold the spot.

[your name]
```

### Email 3: the polite close-out
Subject: Should I close this out?:
```
Hi [first name],

I haven't heard back about [job], so I'll assume the timing isn't right and close this out for now. If you'd still like to go ahead, just reply and we'll pick it up. The estimate is valid until [date].

Thanks for considering us,
[your name]
```

### Email 4: when they say the price is too high
Subject: Re: Your estimate for [job]:
```
Hi [first name],

Thanks for telling me, that helps. The estimate includes [what makes it cost what it does: materials, warranty, permit, cleanup]. If the budget is tight, we could [option: phase the work, use a different material, drop an item], which would bring it to about [amount].

Would you like me to send a revised estimate with that option?

[your name]
```

### Two text versions
In the US, business texts sent from a regular 10-digit number have to be registered for A2P 10DLC through your texting provider, and the major carriers block unregistered business texts. Customers should agree to receive texts from you, for example with a checkbox on your estimate request form. Email works from day one.
Text 1 (day 2) and Text 2 (day 7):
```
Text 1: Hi [first name], it's [your name] from [company]. Did the estimate for [job] come through OK? Happy to answer any questions.

Text 2: Hi [first name], [your name] here. We have an opening the week of [date] for your [job]. Want me to hold it? Reply STOP to opt out.
```

### Tips that make follow-ups work
- Reply in the same email thread, so the estimate is one tap away.
- Name the job and the address. Customers who requested three bids need to know which one you are. Roofers can also attach [the photos and findings from the roof inspection](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/roofing-inspection-reports-and-quote-follow-up/), so the customer sees what the estimate is for.
- Ask one question per message. "Would you like to go ahead?" gets more replies than a paragraph.
- Keep a list of every open estimate with its date and value, so the big ones get a phone call. When a customer says yes, [ask for the deposit in writing](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/how-to-ask-for-a-deposit-on-a-quote/).
- Selling to UK customers? Say "quote" instead of "estimate" and adjust the spelling. The schedule works the same way.

### Make it automatic
A workflow can send these on schedule for every estimate, stop the moment the customer replies or books, and give you a daily list of open estimates worth a call. It can pull estimates from your job management software, your accounting software or your email. You still decide what to quote and what to say on the phone; it just makes sure no estimate is forgotten. If a change order comes up once the job starts, the same idea applies: see our page on [change order approvals](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/change-order-approval-workflow/).

### How we would set it up for you
A [free 15-minute call](https://mikeautomations.github.io/call/) about how you send estimates today. Within 48 hours you get a written plan with a fixed price and a clear definition of "working". It's built on the tools you already use, so your crew doesn't learn a new system. Live in 2-3 days. [Workflow automation is $2,000 one-off](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/pricing/) ($1,500 for the first 3 clients), and you pay once it's running and you're happy with it.

### How many times should I follow up on an estimate?
Two or three times over two to three weeks is enough for most jobs: a check that it arrived, one useful detail, and a polite close-out. Add a phone call for larger jobs. Stop as soon as the customer replies.

### Is it pushy to follow up on an estimate?
Not if each message is short, useful and easy to answer. Customers often appreciate the reminder. A close-out email that makes "no" easy to say also gets replies that tell you why you lost the job.

### Should I follow up by email or text?
Both work. Texts are read faster; email keeps the estimate attached. In the US, register your number for A2P 10DLC and get the customer's agreement before texting.

## How to reduce no-shows for service appointments
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/reduce-appointment-no-shows/ (2026-11-10)

To reduce no-shows for service appointments, do four things: confirm every booking straight away, send a reminder the day before that asks the customer to reply to confirm, make rescheduling a single tap, and phone anyone who hasn't confirmed. Most no-shows are people who forgot or felt awkward cancelling, and all four steps can run automatically except the phone call.

How to reduce no-shows is a question [every business that books time slots](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/service-businesses/) asks sooner or later: plumbers, electricians, cleaners, clinics, salons, [tutors](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/tutoring-centre-enrolment-and-termly-invoices/). A no-show costs you the whole slot: the drive, the preparation, and the job that could have been booked instead.
Most no-shows aren't rude. People forget, or something comes up and cancelling feels awkward, so they say nothing. Both are fixable with a simple reminder routine. Below: the schedule, the messages to copy, how to word your policy, and the rules on texting customers in the UK and US. Studios selling first classes have an extra step, covered in our guide to [intro offer follow-up for fitness studios](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/fitness-studio-intro-offer-follow-up/).

### The four things that work
1. Confirm right after booking, with the date, time, address and anything the customer needs to prepare. For a cosmetic treatment, that includes the pre-treatment instructions covered in [aesthetics clinic consent and aftercare](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/med-spa-consent-forms-and-aftercare/).
2. Remind the day before, and ask for a quick confirmation ("Reply YES to confirm"), so you know who to chase. For a bike service, the customer then gets [a drop-off receipt with the bike's details](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/bike-shop-service-bookings-and-repair-updates/).
3. Make rescheduling one tap. A customer who can move the slot easily won't just disappear. The same goes for a missed parcel: [failed delivery messages](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/courier-proof-of-delivery-and-failed-delivery-messages/) with a rebooking link get it delivered next time.
4. Call the unconfirmed ones. A short list each morning or the evening before is enough.

### A reminder schedule you can copy
| When | Message | Channel |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Straight after booking | Confirmation with date, time, address, what to prepare, how to reschedule, your policy | Email (and a short text if you have consent) |
| 2 days before (for long jobs or long journeys) | A heads-up with anything the customer must do first, such as clearing access or parking | Email |
| The day before, early afternoon | Reminder asking them to reply YES, with a reschedule link | Text |
| The evening before | You get the list of anyone who hasn't confirmed | Your phone or email |
| 2 hours before (early or long appointments only) | "On our way soon" or "see you at 9" | Text |
| After a no-show | A kind message offering a new slot | Text or email |

### Confirmation message
Email or text, sent on booking:
```
Hi [first name], you're booked in with [company] for [job] on [day, date] at [time], at [address]. [What to prepare, e.g. please make sure we can get to the boiler.]

Need to change it? Use this link: [reschedule link]. We ask for [24 hours'] notice to change a booking, so we can offer the slot to someone else.

Thanks, [your name]
```

### Day-before reminder
Text, the day before:
```
Hi [first name], a reminder that [company] is booked for [job] tomorrow, [day] at [time]. Please reply YES to confirm, or move it here: [reschedule link]. Thanks!
```

### After a no-show
Keep it friendly. The aim is to rebook the job, not to win an argument. If you charge a fee for missed appointments, it should already have been stated clearly at booking. A music school can offer [a make-up lesson from its timetable](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/music-school-lesson-scheduling-and-term-fees/) instead of a charge.
Text or email, same day:
```
Hi [first name], we were booked for [job] today at [time] but couldn't reach you. No problem, things come up. Would you like a new time? You can pick one here: [booking link], or just reply to this message.
```

### How to word your policy
State your policy kindly and once, in the confirmation, not as a threat in every message. Say how much notice you need and why: "so we can offer the slot to someone else" is a reason most people accept. If you take deposits or charge for late cancellations, say so plainly before the customer books, and be consistent. Salons and clinics with deposit policies have their own considerations; we cover that on [our page about salon cancellation policies and deposits](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/salon-cancellation-policy-and-deposits/).

### Email or text? The rules in the UK and US
Texts are read faster, so they work well for the day-before reminder. Email is fine for the confirmation and longer instructions.
In the UK, the ICO treats a message that only confirms or reminds someone about an appointment as a service message, not direct marketing, so the marketing consent rules for texts and emails don't apply to it. That only holds while the message contains nothing promotional: add an offer or a "book your next service" push and it counts as marketing.
In the US, business texts sent from a regular 10-digit number have to be registered for A2P 10DLC through your texting provider, and the customer should agree to receive texts, for example with a checkbox on your booking form. Include a way to opt out, such as "Reply STOP to opt out".

### What to automate
Everything above except the phone call. The workflow sends the confirmation and reminders, reads the YES replies, handles reschedule links, updates your calendar and gives you a list of who hasn't confirmed. For patients who never book at all, see [dental recall follow-up](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/dental-recall-follow-up/), and for patients who leave without booking the treatment their dentist recommended, see [dental treatment plan follow-up](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/dental-treatment-plan-follow-up/). If you already use booking or field service software that sends reminders, it fills the gaps rather than replacing it: for example the unconfirmed list, or the rebooking message after a no-show. Restaurants face the same risk with large tables, which is why [private dining bookings](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/restaurant-group-booking-and-private-dining-enquiries/) usually ask for final numbers and a deposit before the day.

### For illustration
For illustration: a customer books a boiler service for Thursday at 9 AM. They get a confirmation at once with a reschedule link. On Wednesday at 2 PM a text asks them to reply YES. At 6 PM you see two unconfirmed appointments and call them: one confirms, one moves to next week, and you fill the Thursday slot from your waiting list.

### How we would set it up for you
A [free 15-minute call](https://mikeautomations.github.io/call/) about how you book appointments today. Within 48 hours you get a written plan with a fixed price and a clear definition of "working". It's built on the tools you already use (your calendar or booking software, email and texting, where they allow a connection), so your team doesn't learn a new system. Live in 2-3 days. [Workflow automation is $2,000 one-off](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/pricing/) ($1,500 for the first 3 clients), and you pay once it's running and you're happy with it.

### When should I send appointment reminders?
Send a confirmation straight after booking and a reminder the day before that asks for a YES. For early-morning or long-distance jobs, add a short text a couple of hours before.

### Do I need consent to send appointment reminder texts in the UK?
The ICO treats a purely administrative reminder as a service message, not marketing, so the marketing consent rules don't apply. If the message includes anything promotional, it counts as marketing and the consent rules do apply.

### Should I charge for no-shows?
That's a business decision. If you do, state the policy clearly before booking and in the confirmation, and apply it consistently. A kind rebooking message often recovers more value than a fee.

## How to ask every customer for a Google review (and stay within the rules)
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/ask-for-google-reviews-automatically/ (2026-11-10)

To ask for Google reviews, send every customer the same short request shortly after the job, with the direct review link from your Google Business Profile, and one reminder a few days later. Don't ask only the happy customers and don't offer anything in return: Google's policy forbids both, and so does consumer law in the UK (the DMCC Act 2024, enforced by the CMA) and the US (the FTC's review rule).

How to ask for Google reviews is mostly a question of habit. Reviews matter for local search, and most happy customers are glad to leave one. They just need to be asked at the right moment (for many trades, [when the customer signs off the job](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/job-sign-off-and-completion-photos/)), with a link that opens the review form in one tap. A [cleaning business](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/cleaning-business-automation/), for example, can send it after a client's first few cleans, a [photographer](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/photographer-booking-contracts-and-deposits/) when the gallery goes out, and a [dog groomer](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/dog-groomer-bookings-and-vaccination-records/) after a first groom. A holiday let host who takes direct bookings can send it after checkout, alongside the other [guest messages for short-term rentals](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/short-term-rental-guest-messages/).
The trick is to ask consistently, and to ask everyone. Below: the rules in plain English for the UK and US, where to find your review link, the timing, copy-ready requests and replies, and what you can safely automate with the same tools that send your appointment reminders.

### The rules: ask everyone, offer nothing
Google's contribution policy (the "Fake engagement" rules) says businesses must not discourage or prohibit negative reviews, or selectively ask happy customers for positive ones. It also bans offering incentives, such as payment, discounts or free goods or services, in exchange for a review or for changing or removing a negative one. Asking only satisfied customers is often called "review gating", and it can get reviews removed.
In the UK, the Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024 (Schedule 20) bans fake reviews and reviews that hide the fact they were incentivised. The CMA's fake reviews guidance (CMA208, April 2025) says cherry-picking positive reviews can happen "by encouraging just those who are satisfied to leave reviews", and that stopping and starting review invitations to avoid negative ones is a problem too. Since April 2025 the CMA can enforce consumer law directly and, according to its own announcement, fine businesses up to 10% of their global turnover.
In the US, the FTC's Consumer Reviews and Testimonials Rule has been in effect since 21 October 2024. It bans fake reviews, offering an incentive conditioned on a review saying something positive or negative, and suppressing negative reviews through threats or intimidation. Courts can impose civil penalties for knowing violations.
The safe approach in both countries is simple: send the same request to every customer, offer nothing for it, and never filter who gets the review link. You can still invite private feedback ("tell us how we did"), as long as the public review link goes to everyone the same way.

### Get your direct review link
Customers need a Google account to leave a review. The direct link saves them searching for your business and picking the wrong listing.
1. On a computer, sign in and open your Business Profile (Google says the QR code can't be generated on a phone).
2. Go to the reviews area and choose "Get more reviews".
3. Copy the link, or right-click the QR code and save the image for receipts, invoices or a card you leave after the job.

### When and how to ask
1. Ask shortly after the job is finished and paid, while it's fresh: the same day or the next morning. For a phone repair, that's [the day the customer collects the device](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/phone-repair-shop-job-updates/).
2. Use the direct review link, so the form opens in one tap.
3. Keep it short and personal: name the job, thank them, one line with the link.
4. Send one reminder a few days later if they haven't left a review, then stop.
5. Reply to every review, good or bad, politely and within a few days.

### Review request (email or text)
Sent when the job is marked complete:
```
Hi [first name], thanks for choosing [company] for [job]. If you have a minute, an honest Google review helps other people find us: [review link]

Thank you! [your name]
```

### One reminder
Sent 4 or 5 days later, only once:
```
Hi [first name], just a gentle reminder in case it got buried: if you'd like to share how the [job] went, here's the link: [review link]. No worries if not. Thanks again, [your name]
```

### Replying to reviews
Keep critical replies calm and short, and move the conversation offline. A helpful reply to a critical review often reassures future customers more than another five stars.
Two replies to adapt:
```
Positive: Thanks, [first name]. Glad the [job] went well, and thanks for taking the time to write this. [your name]

Critical: Thanks for the feedback, [first name], and I'm sorry the [issue] wasn't what you expected. I'd like to put it right. Please call me on [phone] or email [email]. [your name]
```

### What to automate (and what not to)
- Automate: sending the request when a job is marked complete or an invoice is paid, the single reminder, and a log of who was asked and when.
- Automate: an alert when a new review arrives, so you can reply quickly.
- Don't automate: any filter that decides who gets the link based on how happy they seem. That's review gating.
- Don't automate: replies posted without you. A draft can be prepared for you to approve, but you should read and send it.

### How we would set it up for you
A [free 15-minute call](https://mikeautomations.github.io/call/) about how jobs are closed and invoiced today. Within 48 hours you get a written plan with a fixed price and a clear definition of "working". It's built on the tools you already use (your job or accounting software, email and texting, where they allow a connection). Live in 2-3 days. [Workflow automation is $2,000 one-off](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/pricing/) ($1,500 for the first 3 clients), and you pay once it's running and you're happy with it.

### Can I offer a discount for a review?
No. Google's policy bans incentives for reviews. In the UK, reviews that hide an incentive are banned under the DMCC Act 2024, and in the US the FTC's rule bans incentives conditioned on a positive or negative review. Just ask.

### Can I send the review link only to happy customers?
No. Google forbids selectively asking for positive reviews, and the UK CMA's guidance names encouraging only satisfied customers as a form of cherry-picking. Send the same request to everyone.

### What if a customer was unhappy?
Ask them the same way as everyone else, and fix the problem directly. A calm, helpful reply to a critical review often reassures future customers.

## AI in a small accounting firm: what to automate, and what to keep
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/ai-in-accounting-firms-what-to-automate/ (2026-11-10)

In a small accounting firm, AI is worth using for reading, sorting and drafting: identifying uploaded documents, pulling key fields for a person to check, drafting routine client replies and spotting what's missing from a client's set. It should not give tax advice, decide a treatment or send anything to a client or tax authority without a qualified person approving it. The firm stays responsible for client data, so every AI tool needs checked data terms.

AI in a small accounting firm is useful when it does the dull reading, sorting and drafting, and risky when it's trusted with judgement. It's not a substitute for professional judgement, and in a regulated profession it shouldn't send anything to a client unchecked. Used that way, it removes a lot of dull work without changing who is responsible for the advice.
This post sorts common tasks into three groups (good for AI, [good for plain automation](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/ai-vs-automation-difference/), keep with a person), explains the data rules on both sides of the Atlantic, and gives you a one-page AI policy you can adapt.

### Where AI helps today
- Reading uploaded documents and suggesting what they are (a P60, a W-2, a bank statement, a receipt) and which client folder they belong in
- Pulling key fields from documents, such as dates, amounts and reference numbers, for a person to check
- Drafting replies to routine client questions, in your tone, for you to approve
- Summarising a long email thread before you call a client
- Spotting what's missing from a client's set of documents against their checklist

### AI, plain automation, or a person?
Many jobs firms want "AI" for don't need it. A reminder that goes out on the 5th of the month is a rule, not intelligence, and rules are cheaper, more predictable and easier to explain. Use AI only where a step involves reading or writing free text.
| Task | Best handled by | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sending document requests and reminders | Plain automation | Fixed dates and fixed lists: no judgement needed |
| Filing emailed attachments into client folders | Automation, with AI to identify unclear files | Most files can be matched by sender; AI helps with the rest |
| Identifying document types and reading key fields | AI, checked by a person | Free-form documents, but errors matter |
| Drafting replies to routine questions | AI drafts, a person approves | Saves typing, keeps your name on what's sent |
| Categorising bank lines | Your accounting software's rules first, AI suggestions second | Rules are predictable; suggestions need review |
| Tax advice, treatments, fee decisions | A qualified person | Professional judgement and liability |
| Anything sent to HMRC or the IRS | A qualified person | You sign it, so you check it |

### Where AI doesn't belong
- Giving tax advice or deciding a treatment
- Sending anything to a client or tax authority without a person reviewing it
- Anywhere you can't explain what it did and why
- Any step where client data would go to a tool whose data terms you haven't read

### Keep a person in the loop
The safe pattern is simple: AI prepares, a person approves. Drafts wait in a queue. Classifications show how sure they are, so unclear items get a closer look. Nothing leaves the firm without a click from someone qualified, and every approval is logged with who approved it and when.

### Data protection, UK and US
In the UK, UK GDPR makes the controller "responsible for, and be able to demonstrate compliance with" the data protection principles (Article 5(2)). If your firm decides to put client data through an AI service, your firm is accountable for that choice, so keep a record of which tools touch which data and check each provider's terms on data use and storage.
In the US, the IRS's section 7216 regulations govern how tax return preparers may use and disclose tax return information, including when they need the taxpayer's consent. If client return data would go to an outside AI tool, check those rules with your counsel first. Federal law also requires professional tax preparers to have a written information security plan, and the IRS's Publication 5708 is a template for one. Your AI tools belong in it.
Consumer AI chat products and business products are treated differently. OpenAI, for example, says it doesn't train on content from its business workspaces or the API by default, while individual ChatGPT accounts [need the training setting turned off](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/chatgpt-prompts-for-accountants/). Read the terms of whichever tool you use.

### A one-page AI policy you can adapt
AI use policy (small firm):
```
1. Approved tools: [tool names and plans]. No other AI tools for client work.
2. Client data: never paste client names, addresses, tax references, bank details or figures into a tool that isn't on the approved list.
3. Approval: every AI-drafted message to a client or tax authority is read and approved by [role] before it's sent.
4. Advice: AI is never used to decide a tax treatment or give advice. It may draft general explanations.
5. Records: we keep a list of which tools process which client data, and review it every [6] months.
6. Mistakes: if AI output was wrong and reached a client, tell [name] the same day.
7. US clients only: check section 7216 consent requirements before any return information goes to a third-party tool.

Owner: [name]   Last reviewed: [date]
```

### Start with the boring part
The biggest gains usually come before AI: requests, reminders and filing that run on a schedule. Add AI where it removes a manual sorting or drafting step, with approval built in. Our [free 12-page guide](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/guide/), "25 AI Automations for Accountants & Small Firms", lists ideas in that order, from document chasing to getting paid.

### For illustration
For illustration: clients upload documents through one link. Each file is read and labelled ("P60, 2025 to 2026, client: J. Smith") and saved in the client's folder. Anything the system isn't sure about goes into a short review list for a bookkeeper. Client questions that arrive by email get a drafted reply waiting for approval. Nothing is sent without a click.

### How Mike Automations would build this
We start with a [free 15-minute call](https://mikeautomations.github.io/call/) about which tasks eat your team's week. Within 48 hours you get a written plan with a fixed price, which parts use AI and which use plain rules, and where a person approves. It's built on the tools you already use (Xero or QuickBooks, Gmail or Outlook, your shared drive), with client data kept in your accounts. It goes live in 2-3 days. [Workflow automation is $2,000 one-off](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/pricing/) ($1,500 for the first 3 clients), and you pay once it's running and you're happy with it.

### Can AI replace a bookkeeper in a small firm?
No. It can take over reading, sorting and drafting, but someone qualified still checks the work, makes the judgement calls and signs off what goes to clients and tax authorities.

### Is it safe to use AI with client data?
Only in tools whose data terms you've checked and approved, with a record of which tools process which data. Under UK GDPR your firm stays accountable, and US tax preparers also have [section 7216 rules](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/section-7216-consent-before-automation-or-ai/) on using return information.

### What should a small firm automate first: AI or reminders?
Usually reminders. Scheduled requests and filing give the biggest time savings with the least risk. AI comes next, for reading documents and drafting replies, with a person approving.

## How much does business automation cost for a small business?
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/business-automation-cost/ (2026-11-10)

Business automation cost for a small business comes in three parts: a one-off build, a few software subscriptions, and optional support. With Mike Automations, automating one process end to end costs $2,000 one-off ($1,500 for the first 3 clients), [custom systems](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/custom-software-vs-off-the-shelf-small-business/) start at $5,000, and support is optional at $150 a month. The automation platform underneath usually adds somewhere between nothing and a few tens of dollars a month for a small firm.

### 1. The build: what drives the price
This is the work of mapping the process, connecting the tools, writing the messages and testing the cases that go wrong. Three things drive it: the number of steps and conditions, how many tools are involved and whether they allow a connection, and whether the data is clean. A single process, such as document collection with reminders or estimate follow-ups, is a very different job from a full internal system.
Ways providers charge for the build:
- Hourly or day rate: flexible, but you carry the risk if it takes longer than expected.
- Fixed price per workflow: you know the cost before anything starts. Ask exactly what is included and what counts as "done".
- Monthly retainer or subscription: the build is spread over months; check what you keep if you stop paying.

### 2. Software subscriptions
Most workflows run on tools you may already pay for, plus an automation platform to connect them. For a small firm, the platform is often the smallest line on the bill. How each one charges matters more than the headline price: Zapier counts tasks (each action that completes), Make counts credits (roughly one per step), and n8n's cloud plans count executions (one per run of the whole workflow). Our comparison of Zapier, Make and n8n has the full table. For Make's credit-based pricing in detail, see [Make.com for small businesses](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/is-make-com-worth-it-small-business/).
Make sure every subscription is in your name and paid from your account. Then the workflow belongs to you, and you're never locked in to whoever built it.

### 3. Keeping it running
Apps change, passwords expire and processes evolve. Either someone in your team learns to look after the workflow, or you pay for support. Ask any provider three questions: what happens when something breaks, how quickly they respond, and whether you can leave and keep everything.

### How to judge whether it's worth it
1. Write down the hours the process takes each month, including the reminders and the chasing.
2. Multiply by what an hour of that person's time is worth to you.
3. Add what it costs when the job is forgotten: a lost job, a late-filing penalty, a client who leaves.
4. Add the platform subscription for a year, and support if you want it.
5. If the yearly savings are larger than the build plus a year of running costs, it's usually worth doing. If not, start with a smaller process. Our [automation ROI worksheet](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/automation-roi-worksheet/) walks through the sum line by line.

## How to stop chasing clients for VAT records every quarter
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/vat-quarter-records-chasing/ (2026-11-10)

A UK VAT return and payment are usually due one calendar month and 7 days after the end of the VAT period, so a quarter ending 31 December is due by 7 February. To stop chasing clients for VAT records, set your own cut-off about two weeks after the quarter ends, send each client a personal list of what's missing the day after the quarter closes, ask only about items the bank feed doesn't explain, and remind on a fixed rhythm until the list is complete.

Chasing clients for VAT records comes round four times a year for quarterly filers, and each time the same clients send their [invoices and receipts](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/collect-receipts-from-bookkeeping-clients/) at the last minute. The work isn't the return. It's getting everything in early enough to check it.
Since 2023 there's also a clearer reason for clients to care: late VAT returns now earn penalty points, and late payments attract penalties that grow with time. Below: the deadline you work back from, the penalties in plain English, a quarterly routine, the messages to send and a timeline you can copy.

### The deadline you're working back from
GOV.UK says the deadline for submitting a VAT return online is usually one calendar month and 7 days after the end of the accounting period, and the payment must reach HMRC by the same date. A quarter ending 31 March is due by 7 May. The deadline doesn't move for weekends or bank holidays, and the payment needs time to clear. Each client's online VAT account shows their exact dates.
All VAT-registered businesses should now be signed up for Making Tax Digital for VAT, so returns go through compatible software unless HMRC has agreed an exemption. Clients on the annual accounting scheme work to different dates, so check each client's set-up.
Your real deadline is earlier: the date by which you need the records to prepare, query and file without a rush. For most practices that's about two weeks after the quarter ends.

### Why clients should care: the penalty rules
For VAT periods starting on or after 1 January 2023, the old default surcharge was replaced. Mentioning these rules, briefly and calmly, gives clients a concrete reason to send records on time.
- Late returns: each late return earns a penalty point. A quarterly filer who reaches 4 points gets a £200 penalty, and another £200 for each further late return while at the threshold. This includes nil and repayment returns.
- Late payment: nothing if paid within 15 days. From day 16, a first penalty of 3% of the VAT owed at day 15. From day 31, another 3% of what's still owed at day 30 is added, and a second penalty builds daily at 10% a year on the balance. Late payment interest runs from the first day.
- Agreeing a Time to Pay arrangement with HMRC can mean lower or no late payment penalties.

### A quarterly records workflow
1. Tag every VAT client with their quarter-end (stagger groups are common), so requests go out on the right dates.
2. About two weeks before each quarter ends, send a short heads-up: what you'll need, and where to send it.
3. The day after the quarter ends, send each client their own list of what's still missing, with one upload link.
4. Where bank feeds already come into the accounting software, ask only about what's unclear, such as uncategorised transactions or missing purchase invoices, instead of asking for everything again.
5. Remind on a fixed rhythm (every 5 to 7 days) until the list is complete, then stop.
6. Keep one daily view for the team: ready to prepare, waiting on client, or close to the deadline.
7. Ten days before the HMRC deadline, phone anyone who still hasn't responded. A person decides whether to file with what you have.

### A timeline for a quarter ending 31 December
For illustration only. Move the dates to suit your own stagger groups and workload.
| Date | What happens | Who |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 17 December | Heads-up: quarter closes soon, keep receipts together | Automatic |
| 1 January | Personal list of what's missing, with the upload link | Automatic |
| 7 to 14 January | Reminders listing only what's still missing | Automatic |
| 15 January | Your cut-off. Anything outstanding goes on the team's call list | Team |
| 16 to 28 January | Prepare, query and approve the return | Team |
| 7 February | HMRC deadline for the return and cleared payment | Team and client |

### The message that goes out the day after the quarter ends
Subject: Your VAT quarter to [31 December]: [N] items to send:
```
Hi [first name],

Your VAT quarter ended on [31 December]. To file on time we need a few things by [15 January]:

- [Purchase invoices for the 3 supplier payments listed below]
- [What the £[amount] payment to [payee] on [date] was for]
- [Your cash sales total for the quarter]

You can upload everything here, from your phone or computer: [upload link]

The return and payment are due to HMRC by [7 February]. Late returns now earn penalty points, so getting these to us early keeps you clear.

Thanks,
[your name]
```

### What makes clients send records on time
- A personal list, not a generic "please send your VAT records"
- One upload link that works on a phone, with no login
- Reminders that list only what's still missing, and stop when it's done
- Your internal deadline in every message, well before the HMRC one
- Questions about specific bank lines, which are quicker to answer than "send everything"

### For illustration
For illustration: a bookkeeper has 60 clients on quarterly VAT. On 1 April each one gets a list for the March quarter. Clients with uncategorised bank lines get those lines to explain instead of a full request. By 15 April the bookkeeper sees 12 clients still waiting, and calls the 3 who haven't opened anything.
The same routine works for [MTD for Income Tax quarterly updates](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/making-tax-digital-income-tax-practice-workflow/) and for [year-end records](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/limited-company-year-end-records/), so it's worth building once. If you use Xero, our post on [Xero automation ideas for practices](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/xero-practice-automation-ideas/) shows where the bank feed can do some of the asking for you.

It starts with a [free 15-minute call](https://mikeautomations.github.io/call/) about how your VAT chase works today. Within 48 hours you get a written plan with a fixed price. It's built on the tools you already use (Xero, QuickBooks or FreeAgent, your email and cloud storage, where they allow a connection) and is usually live in 2-3 days. [Workflow automation is $2,000 one-off](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/pricing/) ($1,500 for the first 3 clients), and you pay only once it's running and you're happy with it.

### When is a quarterly VAT return due?
Usually one calendar month and 7 days after the end of the VAT period, for both the return and the payment. A quarter ending 31 March is due by 7 May. Check the client's online VAT account for their exact dates.

### Does this replace our accounting software?
No. The returns are still prepared and filed in your MTD-compatible software. The workflow handles the requests, reminders and the list of who's ready.

## How to automate engagement letters in a small accounting firm
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/engagement-letter-automation/ (2026-11-10)

To automate engagement letters, keep one approved template per service, fill it from the client's intake form, put each draft in a queue for a person to check, then send it for e-signature and remind the client until it's signed. When it's signed, the PDF is filed and onboarding starts on its own. The template, the scope, the fee and the final check stay with you, and the same workflow can re-issue letters when the scope or fee changes.

To automate engagement letters, you only need to automate the parts that are the same every time: the client's details, the services, the fee and your standard terms. Yet in many small firms the letter is still copied from last year's, edited by hand and emailed as an attachment. That's slow, and it's where mistakes creep in.
This post covers how the letter is put together, what can run on its own, the emails that go with it, and how to handle renewals when a client's work changes.

### Start from a template you trust
Automation only copies what you give it, so the template comes first. In the UK, ICAEW's Technical Advisory Service publishes an engagement letters helpsheet (last updated 10 March 2026) with sample wording. It splits a complete letter into parts: the engagement letter itself, schedules for each service (accounts, tax returns, payroll and so on), optional paragraphs, standard terms of business, and a privacy notice.
ICAEW describes the helpsheet as best practice guidance, not a professional standard, and says the wording should be tailored to each engagement with professional judgement. It also says the use of AI to tailor letters should be considered with caution. Other professional bodies, and US firms, will have their own sources. Use whichever applies to you, and check your template with your insurer or professional body if in doubt.
That structure suits automation well: one fixed covering letter, a schedule picked for each service the client takes, and terms that rarely change.

### What can be automated
1. Collect the client's details and the agreed services once, through an intake form or from the notes of your first call.
2. Build the letter from your approved parts: the covering letter, the schedules for the services ticked, your terms and privacy notice.
3. Fill in names, addresses, services, fee, start date and any [records cut-off date](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/records-cut-off-clause-engagement-letter/).
4. Put the draft in a queue for a person to check. Nothing goes out unchecked.
5. Send it for e-signature with one click, with a short covering email.
6. [Remind the client politely](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/document-chasing-email-templates/) every few days until it's signed.
7. When it's signed, file the PDF in the client's folder, update the client record and start the next onboarding step. What those next steps can be is set out in [the onboarding workflow for service businesses](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/client-onboarding-automation-service-business/).

### Which details come from where
| Letter field | Comes from | Checked by a person? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Client name, address, entity type | Intake form | Yes, against ID documents |
| Services and schedules | Tick boxes on the intake form or call notes | Yes |
| Fee and billing terms | Your price list or the quote agreed on the call | Yes, always |
| Start date and first year covered | Intake form | Yes |
| Records cut-off date | Your standard dates for each service | Only if it differs from the standard |
| Terms of business and privacy notice | Your fixed template | When the template changes |

### What stays with you
- The template itself, and any professional body requirements for its content
- The scope and the fee
- Anything unusual, such as a client with complex affairs or a service you don't normally offer
- The final check before anything is sent

### The covering email and the reminder
Subject: Your engagement letter from [firm name]: please sign:
```
Hi [first name],

Thank you for choosing us. Your engagement letter is ready to sign here: [e-signature link]

It sets out what we'll do for you ([services]), our fee ([fee]) and what we need from you, including sending your records by [cut-off date] each year.

It takes about two minutes on your phone. If anything doesn't look right, just reply to this email before signing.

[your name]

---

Reminder (sent after 3 days if not signed):

Subject: Quick reminder: your engagement letter

Hi [first name], just a reminder that your engagement letter is waiting here: [e-signature link]. Once it's signed we can get started. Thanks, [your name]
```

### Renewals: when to send a new letter
A letter that was right three years ago often isn't now. Many firms review every client's letter once a year, and re-issue it when something has changed. A workflow can do the noticing for you. The letter at the other end of the relationship is covered in our [client disengagement checklist](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/client-disengagement-checklist-accountants/).
- The client adds or drops a service, such as VAT, payroll or MTD quarterly updates
- Your fee changes, or you move the client to a different billing arrangement
- The client's structure changes, for example from sole trader to limited company
- Your standard terms or privacy notice are updated
- Rules change in a way that alters what you do, such as a client joining MTD for Income Tax

### Why it's worth doing
A letter that goes out the same day the client says yes keeps momentum. A letter that takes a week often means the client starts sending documents before the terms are agreed. Automating the draft and the chase removes the delay without taking the decision away from you.

### For illustration
For illustration: a new client fills in the intake form on Tuesday morning. By lunchtime a draft letter is waiting in the partner's queue. The partner checks the fee, clicks approve, and the client gets it for e-signature. It's signed on Thursday, filed, and the AML document request goes out the same day. The full sequence is in our [client onboarding checklist](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/accounting-client-onboarding-checklist/).
