### When is the 2025-26 Self Assessment deadline?
The online return and the tax owed are due by 11:59pm on 31 January 2027. Paper returns were due by 31 October 2026. To pay through a tax code, the online return must be in by 30 December 2026.

### What are the MTD for Income Tax quarterly update deadlines?
7 August, 7 November, 7 February and 7 May (the following tax year). HMRC will not apply penalty points for late quarterly updates in the 2026 to 2027 tax year.

### When are company accounts and Corporation Tax due?
For a private limited company, accounts go to Companies House 9 months after the financial year ends. Corporation Tax is paid 9 months and 1 day after the accounting period ends (for taxable profits up to £1.5 million), and the Company Tax Return is due 12 months after it ends.

### Can a company file its confirmation statement if a director hasn't verified their identity?
No. Companies House says it will not accept a company's confirmation statement until all directors have verified their identity, and the statement must give each director's Companies House personal code.

## Do I need practice management software for a small accounting practice?
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/practice-software-vs-simple-automation-small-practice/ (2026-11-11)

Do I need practice management software? For a 1-3 person accounting practice, usually not yet: if one or two jobs eat your time, such as chasing client records or sending engagement letters, a targeted automation on the email, folders and spreadsheet you already use fixes that with less cost and less change. A full practice management platform starts to pay when several people share the same client work, deadlines are tracked in more than one place, and you'd use most of its features every week.

Do I need practice management software? It's a fair question for a sole practitioner or a firm of two or three, because the platforms are built to do everything: client records, jobs, deadlines, a portal, e-signatures, time and billing. That's useful if you'll use it. It's an expensive, slow move if your real problem is one recurring job.
This post gives you an honest way to decide: the signs a platform is worth it, the signs one or two automations are enough, a decision table you can run through in ten minutes, and what to do if you already pay for a portal nobody uses. No product names, just the kinds of tools, so you can apply it to whatever you're looking at.

### What a practice management platform actually does
Most platforms bundle the same set of jobs. Knowing the list helps, because the real question isn't "is this software good?" but "how many of these do I need, every week?"
- A client database with contacts, entity details and the services you provide.
- Jobs and workflows: a checklist per job, who's doing it and where it stands.
- A deadline calendar that creates recurring jobs (year-end, VAT or quarterly returns, payroll).
- A client portal for documents, messages and signatures.
- Engagement letters and proposals with e-signature.
- Automated reminders and document requests.
- Time tracking, billing and sometimes payments.
- Reports on capacity and work in progress.

### Signs a platform is worth it
- Two or more people work on the same clients and need to see who's doing what without asking.
- Deadlines live in a spreadsheet, a calendar and your head, and one has already been missed or nearly missed.
- You'd use at least four or five of the features above every week, not just once a year.
- You plan to hire in the next year and want one way of working a new person can learn.
- You bill by time and need time records tied to jobs.
- You have time to set it up. Importing clients, building job templates and moving clients onto a portal takes weeks of evenings, not an afternoon.

### Signs one or two automations are enough
- You're on your own or with one other person, and you both know where every job stands.
- The pain is one or two jobs: chasing records, onboarding new clients, engagement letters or reminders before a deadline.
- Your existing tools work: a shared drive, your email, your accounting software and a client spreadsheet.
- Your clients won't log in to a portal, and you don't want to fight them about it.
- You don't want another monthly subscription, or a migration in the middle of the busy season.

### The decision table
Find the row that sounds most like your practice. If you land between two rows, start with the smaller change. You can still move to a platform later, and the clean client list and folders you build now make that move easier.
| Your situation | Likely best fit | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sole practitioner, main pain is chasing records | One automation on email, folders and a spreadsheet | The problem is one recurring job; a platform adds setup and a subscription for features you won't use |
| 1-2 people, onboarding is slow (ID checks, letters, forms) | One onboarding automation | Onboarding is a fixed sequence that can run on the tools you already have |
| 1-3 people, a portal you pay for but clients don't use | Keep the portal, add chasing and a no-login upload route | The portal isn't the problem; getting clients to use it is |
| 2-3 people sharing clients, deadlines tracked in several places | Practice management platform | Shared jobs and one deadline calendar are what the platform is built for |
| Growing to 4 or more people within a year, billing by time | Practice management platform | Time, billing and capacity reports matter more as the team grows |
| Any size, about to start a busy season | Wait, and fix the single worst job first | Migrating during January or tax season adds risk at the worst time |

### What one targeted automation looks like
For illustration: a two-person practice keeps clients in a spreadsheet and files in a shared drive. Their worst job is chasing year-end records. An automation reads the spreadsheet, sends each client a personal request with their own list, files whatever comes back into the right folder, ticks it off, and reminds only the clients who still owe something. A person checks the list each week and phones anyone who needs a call.
There's nothing new for clients to learn, nothing to migrate, and the practice keeps working the way it already does. The same pattern fits [document collection](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/bookkeeper-document-collection/), new-client onboarding and engagement letters.

### If you already pay for a portal
Plenty of small firms pay for a portal and still receive half their documents by email. Switching platform rarely fixes that, because the next portal has the same login problem. What helps is chasing that stops when the document arrives, a simple upload route for clients who won't log in, and emailed attachments filed automatically into the same place.
We cover the rollout side in [getting clients to use your portal](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/get-clients-to-use-your-client-portal/), and what a reminder add-on adds in [Karbon and TaxDome reminders](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/portal-reminders-add-on-karbon-taxdome/).

### Questions to answer before you buy anything
1. Write down the three jobs that cost you the most hours each month. If the top one is far bigger than the others, start there.
2. List the platform features you'd use every week. Fewer than four is a warning sign.
3. Count how many clients would need to change how they send you things.
4. Ask how long setup takes and who does it: you, the vendor or a paid consultant.
5. Ask how you'd get your data out if you left: clients, documents and job history.
6. Check where client data is stored and that there's a data processing agreement. In the UK, the ICO's guidance on contracts says that whenever a controller uses a processor, there must be a written contract in place.
7. Pick a start date outside your busy season.

### Compare the full cost, not the monthly price
A platform costs its subscription for each user, plus the setup hours, the effort of moving clients onto its portal and the risk of a messy migration. A targeted automation costs a one-off build, sometimes small monthly fees for the tools it runs on, and some upkeep when one of those tools changes. Neither is free. The useful question is which one gives you back the hours you're actually losing.
Whichever you choose, the same data rules apply. Check where client information will be stored, and who can see it, before it goes into any new tool.

It starts with a [free 15-minute call](https://mikeautomations.github.io/call/) about the job that costs you the most time. Within 48 hours you get a written plan with a fixed price. It's built on the tools you already use, live in 2-3 days, [$2,000 one-off](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/pricing/), and you pay once it's running and you're happy with it. If a full platform is the better answer for your practice, you'll hear that on the call.

### Do sole practitioners need practice management software?
Often not at first. If you work alone and the main pain is one recurring job, such as chasing records or onboarding, a targeted automation on your existing tools usually fixes it faster and for less.

### When should a small accounting firm move to practice management software?
When several people share client work, deadlines are tracked in more than one place, and you'd use most of the platform's features every week. Plan the move outside your busy season.

### Can I add automated chasing to the portal I already have?
Usually yes. Reminders, a no-login upload route and automatic filing of emailed attachments can sit alongside a portal, so you keep it without forcing every client to log in.

### Is a spreadsheet good enough to run a small practice?
For a sole practitioner or a firm of two, a well-kept client spreadsheet and a deadline calendar are often enough, especially with automated reminders reading from them. It stops being enough when several people edit it and nobody trusts it.

## How to get clients to send content, assets and logins on time
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/get-clients-to-send-content/ (2026-11-11)

To get clients to send content on time, give them one specific list of what you need for their project, one place to put it, a due date tied to the launch date, and reminders on fixed days that stop as soon as each item arrives. Ask for access to accounts (analytics, social, hosting) through each platform's own user invitations rather than shared passwords, and agree in the contract that the launch moves if content is late.

Knowing how to get clients to send content on time is half the job for an agency or a web or marketing freelancer. The site is built, the campaign is ready, and you're waiting on photos, page copy, a logo file and the login to their domain. The project sits still, and you send the same "just checking in" email for the fourth time.
This guide gives you a content request checklist for the common project types, a deadline and reminder sequence, templates to copy, and a safe way to get access to accounts. It works with a shared folder, a form and your email. Once the project is live, [client reporting automation](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/agency-client-reporting-automation/) takes care of the monthly numbers. It fits alongside your [client approval workflow](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/agency-client-approvals/), because late content and late sign-off cause the same delays.

### Why clients don't send content
- The request is vague: "send over your content" means nothing to someone who isn't a marketer.
- It arrives as one long email, so they put it off until they have time to do everything.
- They don't know where to send it, so files come by email, chat and a link to their personal cloud drive.
- Some items need someone else at their company, like the IT contact who has the domain login.
- There's no deadline, or the deadline isn't tied to anything they care about, like the launch date.
- Nobody tells them what's still missing, so they believe they've sent everything.

### The content request checklist
Send each client only the rows that apply to their project. A shorter, specific list gets finished; a long generic one gets ignored. Mark each item as "must have before we start" or "can follow later".
| Project type | Content | Assets | Access |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Website build | Page copy for each page, or notes for your writer; team bios; service descriptions; legal pages | Logo files (vector if they have one), brand colours and fonts, photos with permission to use them | Domain registrar, current hosting, analytics, Search Console, any booking or payment tool |
| Social media management | Topics, offers and dates for the month; things to avoid; approval contact | Recent photos and videos, logo, brand guidelines | Each social account via the platform's partner or business access, never a shared password |
| Paid ads | Offers, landing pages, target areas, budget limits | Ad images or video, logo | Ad account access as a partner, analytics, conversion tracking |
| SEO or content | Topics they want covered, product details, who to check facts with | Photos, diagrams, author details | Search Console, analytics, website editor |
| Email marketing | Offers, dates, sender name and reply address | Logo, header images | Email platform user, list export if moving tools |

### Make it easy to send
1. Create one folder per client with sub-folders that match the checklist: Copy, Photos, Brand, Legal.
2. Send the checklist as a personal list, not a generic form. Each line says what it is, why you need it and an example.
3. Give one place to send everything. A shared folder link works for most clients. A form works for written answers. Print and sign work adds one more step: [checking each artwork file against the job specification](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/sign-and-print-shop-artwork-approvals/) when it arrives.
4. Offer a fall-back: if they'd rather talk, book a 20-minute call where you fill in the copy questions together.
5. Track every item in one sheet: client, item, status (missing, received, approved), date received.
6. Tell the client exactly what's still missing in every reminder, not "any update on the content?"

### Getting access without sharing passwords
Passwords sent by email or chat are a security risk for your client and a liability for you. Most of the platforms you'll need let the owner invite you as a user with your own login, and remove you when the work ends.
Google's own help pages describe this for its tools. In Search Console, a property owner goes to Settings, then Users and permissions, and adds your Google Account email with a permission level. In Google Analytics, someone with the Administrator role adds your email in Access Management. For a Google Business Profile, the owner opens People and access and invites you as a manager. Social and ad platforms have similar partner or business access features: ask the client to invite you, and send them the exact steps with your email address.
If a client insists on sending a password, ask them to use a password manager's sharing feature and to change the password after the project. Never keep client passwords in your email or project notes.

### A note on forms
Forms are good for written answers like page copy notes, team bios and offers. For files, check how your form tool handles uploads. Google's help centre says that for a file upload question in Google Forms, respondents need to sign in to a Google Account, which stops some clients at the first step. A shared folder link, or a form tool that accepts uploads without an account, is often easier.

### The deadline and reminder sequence
Tie the content due date to the launch date in writing, at the start: "We need everything on the must-have list by [date] to launch on [date]. If it arrives later, the launch moves by the same number of days." Then remind on fixed days. Each reminder lists only what's still missing and stops for items already received. The days below are an example; set your own.
| When | Who gets it | Message |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Day 0 (kick-off) | Client contact | The personal checklist, the folder link, the due date and what it unlocks. |
| Day 3 | Client contact | What's arrived so far and what's still missing. |
| Day 7 | Client contact | The missing list again, with a one-click option to book a call to do the copy together. |
| Due date | Client contact | Today's the date for the launch on [date]; here are the items still missing. |
| Due date + 2 working days | Client contact and decision-maker | The new launch date if the items arrive by [day]. |
| Due date + 5 working days | Account lead | A phone call. A person handles it from here and may pause the project. |

### Templates
Content request (kick-off email):
```
Subject: What we need from you for [project], by [date]

Hi [first name],

To launch [project] on [launch date], we need the items below by [due date]. Everything goes in one place: [folder link].

Must have before we start:
- [item]: [what it is, one line]
- [item]: [what it is, one line]

Can follow later:
- [item]

Access: please add [your email] as a user in [platform]. Steps are here: [link to your steps]. Please don't send passwords by email.

If writing the page copy feels like a chore, book a 20-minute call and we'll fill it in together: [booking link].

If the must-have items arrive after [due date], the launch moves by the same number of days.

Thanks,
[your name]
```

### The reminder message
Keep it short and specific. A list of what's missing gets a faster answer than a general nudge.
"Hi [first name], thanks for the logo and photos. Still missing for the [launch date] launch: [item], [item]. Can you add them here by [day]: [folder link]? If [item] is the hard one, reply and we'll find another way."

### Put it in the contract
Most content delays are easier to handle when the rules were agreed before work started. Your proposal or statement of work should say who on the client side provides content, the due date, that the launch moves if content is late, and what happens if a project is paused for a long time, such as a restart fee or rescheduling. Have your own lawyer check the wording. Agreeing this during client onboarding makes every reminder later feel like a reminder, not a complaint.

### Where automation helps
The tiring part is keeping track: what's arrived, what's missing, who to remind and when. A workflow can send the personal checklist when a project starts, notice when files land in the folder, tick them off in the tracker, send each reminder on its day with only the missing items, and alert the account lead when content is late. A person still talks to the client and decides when a launch date moves.

If your clients ask you for automations too, see [white-label automation for agencies](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/white-label-automation-for-agencies/). It starts with a [free 15-minute call](https://mikeautomations.github.io/call/). Within 48 hours you get a written plan with a fixed price. It's live in 2-3 days, [$2,000 one-off](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/pricing/), and you pay once it's running and you're happy with it.

### How do I get clients to send content on time?
Send a short, personal checklist of exactly what you need, one place to put it, and a due date tied to the launch date. Remind on fixed days with only the missing items, and agree in the contract that the launch moves if content is late.

### Should clients send me their passwords?
Avoid it. Most platforms, including Google Search Console, Google Analytics and Google Business Profile, let the owner add you as a user with your own login. If a password must be shared, use a password manager's sharing feature and have the client change it after the project.

### What if the client never writes the page copy?
Offer a short call where you ask the questions and write the copy from their answers, or quote for copywriting. Either way, the launch date moves until the copy is approved.

### Can I charge for delays caused by late client content?
Only if your contract says so and the client agreed before work started, for example a restart fee after a long pause. Check the wording with your own lawyer.

## Do automations need maintenance? An honest answer
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/do-automations-need-maintenance/ (2026-11-11)

Yes, automations need some maintenance, but usually only a little. A workflow that connects your apps keeps working until something around it changes: a login expires, someone edits a form or renames a spreadsheet column, an app updates, or the plan runs out of tasks. Error alerts plus a ten-minute check each month, and someone ready to fix things when an alert arrives, is enough for most small businesses.

Do automations need maintenance? Anyone selling you one should give you a straight answer, so here it is: yes, a little. An automation is not a machine that wears out. The steps it follows don't change on their own. What changes is everything around it: the apps it connects, the logins it uses, the forms and spreadsheets it reads, and the plan it runs on.
This post explains the common reasons automations break, what monitoring looks like in practice, a monthly checklist you can copy, and an honest view of when paying for support makes sense and when it doesn't. Vendor details were checked on each vendor's own help pages on 10 November 2026.

### Why automations break
Almost every breakage described in vendor help pages comes from one of six causes. None of them is the automation "going wrong" by itself.
- Expired or revoked logins. The automation signs in to your apps with a saved connection. Changing a password, removing a user, or an app revoking access after a period of inactivity can break it. Google's developer documentation lists reasons a saved Google login can stop working, including not being used for six months, a password change on an account that uses Gmail access, and a limit of 100 live logins per Google account for each connecting app. It also says that if the app connecting to Google is still in "Testing" status, its access expires after 7 days. That last one catches out a lot of self-built workflows. Home-made scripts have their own limits too; see the quotas in our [Apps Script guide](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/google-apps-script-for-small-business/).
- Changed forms and spreadsheets. Someone renames a column, adds a question to a form, or moves a file to a new folder. The automation still looks for the old name and either fails or, worse, quietly fills in the wrong field.
- App updates and [API](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/automation-glossary-small-business/) changes. The apps you use change how other tools connect to them. The automation platform handles most of these changes, but sometimes a step needs to be rebuilt.
- Plan limits. Automation platforms count usage. Zapier's help centre says it holds all actions for all workflows in your account if you reach your task limit for the billing cycle, until you upgrade or the cycle resets. Make's pricing page says scenarios won't continue to run until credits are added again, and Make's help pages add that scenarios pause if a payment fails.
- Automatic shutdowns after errors. Platforms switch off workflows that keep failing. Zapier says it turns a Zap off if it errors on 95% of runs and has run more than 20 times in the past 7 days (Team and Enterprise accounts get an email and a grace period first). Make has an "errors before deactivation" setting, and a scenario that starts with an instant trigger is deactivated after the first error.
- Your process changed. You added a service, changed your prices, hired someone, or now need a different document from clients. The automation still does exactly what it did before, which is no longer what you want.

### The real risk: failing quietly
A broken automation that shouts is a small problem. You see the error, fix the login, replay the stuck runs, and move on. The expensive kind fails quietly: reminders stop going out and nobody notices for three weeks, or a form change means half the new enquiries land in the wrong column.
So the most important part of maintenance is not fixing things. It is knowing quickly when something needs fixing. That is what monitoring is for.

### What monitoring and maintenance look like
For a small business, monitoring doesn't need a dashboard. It needs three things, set up when the automation is built:
1. Error alerts that reach a person. Zapier and Make can both email you when a run fails, and n8n lets you set an error workflow, starting with its Error Trigger node, that runs whenever another workflow fails, so you can send yourself an email or a message. If you run n8n yourself, the server needs watching too: see [n8n cloud vs self-hosted](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/n8n-cloud-vs-self-hosted-small-business/). Make sure the alerts go to an inbox someone actually reads, not to the builder's old address.
2. A simple heartbeat. For workflows that run on a schedule, add a short summary at the end, such as "12 reminders sent this morning". If the summary stops arriving, something is wrong even if no error was raised.
3. A monthly look. Ten minutes once a month to check the run history, the plan usage and the connections. The checklist below covers it.

### A monthly maintenance checklist
Copy this table into your own notes and work through it once a month. Most months, every line will be fine.
| Check | Where to look | What good looks like | If not |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Run history | The automation platform's history or logs | Runs every day it should, no unexplained gaps | Open the failed runs, read the error, fix and replay |
| Errors and alerts | Your inbox and the platform's error list | No errors, or each one already dealt with | Fix the cause, not just the single run |
| Connections | The platform's list of connected apps | Every connection shows as working | Reconnect it with an account the business owns |
| Plan usage | The platform's billing or usage page | Comfortably under the monthly limit | Trim wasteful steps or move up a plan before it runs out |
| Forms and sheets | The forms and spreadsheets the workflow reads | No renamed columns, moved files or new required fields since last month | Update the workflow to match, then test it |
| Messages | A sample of what went out to clients | Correct names, dates and links | Fix the template; check whether anyone got a wrong message |
| Process | A five-minute chat with whoever uses it | It still matches how you work | Note the change and decide whether it's worth making |
| Off switch | The one-page guide | Everyone who needs it knows where it is | Show them again |

### Who should do the maintenance?
There are three honest options. The right one depends on how many automations you have and how much you want to think about them.
- Someone in your team. Fine for one or two simple workflows on a platform like [Zapier, Make or n8n](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/zapier-vs-make-vs-n8n/). They need the one-page guide, access to the platform, and half an hour to learn where the run history is.
- Pay per fix. When something breaks, you ask the builder and get a quote before any work starts. Cheap in a quiet year, slower when you need it.
- A monthly support plan. Someone else watches the alerts, makes small changes and keeps the connections working. You pay whether or not anything breaks.

### When our $150 a month support makes sense
With Mike Automations, small fixes are included for 60 days after go-live. After that, support is optional at $150 a month: hosting, monitoring and small changes by the person who built it, and you can cancel with 30 days' notice. Without it, I quote any fix before doing it. The full terms are on the [pricing page](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/pricing/).
It tends to make sense when:
- The workflow touches money or deadlines, such as invoice reminders or document chasing before a filing date, so a week of silent failure would cost more than a month of support.
- You run several workflows that depend on each other.
- Nobody in your team wants to open the automation platform, ever.
- Your process changes often and you want small changes made without a new quote each time.

### When you probably don't need it
In those cases, keep the one-page guide handy, turn on error emails, do the monthly checklist, and ask for a quote if something breaks. That is a perfectly good way to run it, and I'll say so on the call.
- You have one simple workflow, it has run cleanly for the first 60 days, and someone in your team is happy to do the monthly check.
- The workflow is useful but not critical: if it stopped for a week, you'd be mildly annoyed, not out of pocket.
- Your apps and your process rarely change.

### How we build to need less maintenance
Most maintenance can be avoided at build time. Every workflow we build runs in your own accounts, on tools you already use, with connections made through accounts the business owns rather than one person's login. Each one has error alerts going to an inbox you choose, an off switch, and a one-page guide that says where everything is. If you ever take it on yourself or move to someone else, the [automation handover checklist](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/automation-handover-checklist/) lists what you should receive.

### Do automations need maintenance?
Yes, a little. The workflow itself doesn't change, but logins expire, forms and spreadsheets get edited, apps update and plans run out of tasks. Error alerts plus a ten-minute monthly check cover most small businesses.

### Why did my automation stop working?
The usual causes are an expired or revoked app connection, a renamed column or changed form, the platform's monthly limit being reached, or the platform switching off a workflow that kept failing. The run history and error emails normally show which one.

### Will Zapier turn off my Zap if it fails?
Zapier's help centre says it turns a Zap off if it errors on 95% of runs and has run more than 20 times in the past 7 days. Team and Enterprise accounts get an email and a grace period first.
