## Automation handover checklist: what your business should receive
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/automation-handover-checklist/ (2026-11-11)

An automation handover checklist lists everything a business should hold when someone hands over an automation they built: the platform accounts in the business's own name, every login and app connection, written documentation of what each workflow does, a clear off switch, a one-page guide for staff, and the data processing terms for each tool that touches personal data. If the builder disappeared tomorrow, the business should still be able to run, pause, fix and change the automation.

An automation handover checklist answers one question: if the person who built your automation stopped answering emails tomorrow, could you keep it running? Too often the honest answer is no. The workflows sit in the builder's account, connected with the builder's logins, and nobody else knows how they work.
This post sets out what a business should receive at handover, why each item matters, and a checklist you can copy into an email to your builder. Use it before you pay, or with something that's already running. It applies whether the work was done by a freelancer, a consultant, or someone in your own team who is about to leave. It's one of the [common business automation mistakes](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/small-business-automation-mistakes/), and one of the easiest to avoid.

### 1. Accounts and ownership
The automation platform account (Zapier, Make, n8n or similar, and the server too if [n8n is self-hosted](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/n8n-cloud-vs-self-hosted-small-business/)) should belong to the business: registered to a business email address, paid from the business's card, with the owner or a named person in the business as account owner. The builder gets a user seat or temporary access, not the other way round.
This matters more than anything else on the list. If the account is the builder's, you don't own the workflows, you rent them. When you stop paying the builder, or they close their account, the workflows go with it. Our guide to [what automation really costs](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/business-automation-cost/) calls this out as one of the main cost traps. Agencies that resell automations to their clients need the same clarity: see [white-label automation for agencies](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/white-label-automation-for-agencies/).
Zapier's help centre describes the tidy way to handle this in a team account: before removing a member, the account owner can review their workflows and connected apps, transfer ownership of their Zaps to another user, and export a CSV of their Zaps and app connections for your records. Ask your builder to do the equivalent on whichever platform you use.

### 2. Logins and app connections
Every automation signs in to your other apps (email, cloud storage, accounting or job software, forms) through saved connections. At handover, each connection should be made with an account the business controls, ideally a shared business login rather than one employee's personal account, so it doesn't break when that person leaves or changes their password.
Ask for a list of every connection: which app, which account it signs in as, and who can reconnect it. Passwords themselves should be stored in your own password manager, never sent in an email or a chat message.
One specific trap with Google: if the builder set up their own Google Cloud app to connect to Gmail, Drive or Sheets and left it in "Testing" status, Google's developer documentation says its access expires after 7 days. Ask whether any custom Google app is involved, and whose Google account owns it.

### 3. Documentation that a stranger could follow
Documentation doesn't need to be long. It needs to let someone who has never seen the automation understand it in ten minutes. For each workflow, ask for:
- What starts it (a new form entry, a date, an email arriving) and what it does, step by step, in plain words.
- Which apps, files, folders and spreadsheet columns it reads and writes. Renaming any of these is the most common way to break it.
- What happens when something fails: where the error alerts go, and how to replay a failed run.
- Any limits it relies on, such as the monthly task allowance on the platform plan.
- A copy or export of the workflow itself, where the platform allows it, so it can be rebuilt if needed.

### 4. The off switch
Every automation should have an obvious way to stop it, and the right people should know where it is. On most platforms that is a toggle per workflow. For anything that sends messages to clients, it's worth also having a single switch, such as a cell in a settings sheet, that pauses all outgoing messages at once.
Test it at handover: turn it off, check nothing goes out, turn it back on. It takes two minutes and saves a very bad afternoon if a wrong message ever starts going out.

### 5. A one-page guide for your staff
Documentation is for whoever fixes the automation. The one-page guide is for the people who work with it every day. It should say what the automation does for them, what they still need to do by hand, where to look when a client says they didn't get something, where the off switch is, and who to contact. If it doesn't fit on one page, it's too long for anyone to read.

### 6. Data processing terms
If the automation handles personal data about clients or staff, which most do, data protection rules apply to the tools in the chain. In the UK, Article 28 of the UK GDPR says processing by a processor must be governed by a contract that covers, among other things, the type of data, the purpose, and that the processor deletes or returns the data at the end of the service. Most large tools publish standard terms for this: Zapier, for example, publishes a data processing addendum.
At handover, ask for a list of every tool that touches personal data, a link to each one's data processing terms, and where the data is stored. If the builder had access to your data, confirm in writing that their access has been removed or will be on a set date. US businesses don't have the same single rule, but the same list is still worth having.

### The checklist at a glance
| Item | What you should hold | Why it matters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Platform account | In the business's name, paid by the business, owner is someone in the business | Otherwise you rent the workflows instead of owning them |
| App connections | A list of each connection and the business account it uses | Personal logins break when people leave or change passwords |
| Passwords | In your own password manager | Never in an email or chat |
| Documentation | Trigger, steps, apps, fields, error handling, limits, export | Anyone can understand and fix it |
| Off switch | Known, tested, written in the guide | You can stop a bad message within a minute |
| One-page guide | For the staff who use it | They know what's automatic and what isn't |
| Data terms | A list of tools with personal data, their data processing terms, storage location | UK GDPR Article 28 contracts; you can answer client questions |
| Builder access | Removed, or a date when it will be | Nobody keeps access they no longer need |

### A handover checklist to copy
Automation handover checklist (copy into an email to your builder):
```
Hi [name],

Before we sign off the automation, could you confirm each of these and send what's missing?

Accounts and ownership
[ ] The automation platform account is in the business's name and paid by the business
[ ] [Owner name] is the account owner; you have a user seat only
[ ] Every workflow is owned by a business user, not your personal account

Logins and connections
[ ] A list of every app connection: app, account it signs in as, who can reconnect it
[ ] Each connection uses a business account, not a personal one
[ ] Any custom Google or Microsoft app used for the connections, and whose account owns it
[ ] Passwords saved in our password manager (not sent by email)

Documentation
[ ] For each workflow: what starts it, what it does step by step, which apps, files and columns it uses
[ ] Where error alerts go, and how to replay a failed run
[ ] Plan limits it depends on
[ ] An export or copy of each workflow

Off switch and guide
[ ] Where the off switch is (we'll test it together)
[ ] A one-page guide for the team

Data
[ ] A list of every tool that handles personal data, with a link to its data processing terms and where data is stored
[ ] Confirmation of when your access will be removed

Thanks,
[your name]
```

### When to use this checklist
- Before you hire anyone: ask whether they will hand over everything on this list. It belongs alongside the other [questions to ask before hiring an automation expert](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/questions-to-ask-before-hiring-an-automation-expert/).
- At the end of a build, before you pay.
- When a team member who built your automations is leaving.
- Once a year, to check nothing has drifted back into one person's account.

### How Mike Automations hands over
Everything we build runs in your accounts, on the tools you already use, so there is nothing to move at the end. Every build comes with a walkthrough, a one-page guide and an off switch. You own it: if we stop working together, it keeps running and I hand over everything you need. Keeping it running afterwards is covered in [do automations need maintenance?](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/do-automations-need-maintenance/)
To automate a process, book a [free 15-minute call](https://mikeautomations.github.io/call/). You get a written plan with a fixed price within 48 hours, the workflow is live in 2-3 days, and it costs $2,000 one-off, paid only once it's running and you're happy with it.

### Who owns my automations?
Whoever owns the platform account they run in. If the Zapier, Make or n8n account is in your business's name and paid by your business, you own the workflows. If it's the builder's account, you are effectively renting them.

### What should an automation handover document include?
What starts each workflow and what it does step by step, the apps, files and columns it uses, where error alerts go and how to replay a failed run, plan limits it depends on, the off switch, and a list of tools that handle personal data with their data processing terms.

### Should my builder send me passwords by email?
No. Connections should use business accounts you already control, and any passwords should go straight into your own password manager.

## Power Automate vs Zapier for a small business
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/power-automate-vs-zapier-small-business/ (2026-11-11)

Power Automate vs Zapier for a small business mostly comes down to where your work lives. If the firm runs on Outlook, Excel and SharePoint, Power Automate is often enough: most Microsoft 365 business plans already let you build cloud flows with Microsoft's standard connectors at no extra cost. If your work lives in Google Workspace or in many outside apps, or a flow needs a premium connector, Zapier is usually simpler, since its paid plans include premium apps.

Power Automate vs Zapier is the question most small firms on Microsoft 365 ask before they automate anything. You already pay for Outlook, Excel and SharePoint, and Microsoft's own automation tool sits in the same account. So do you need Zapier at all?
This post compares the two for a small service business with no IT department: solicitors, letting agents, accountants (see [Outlook automation for accountants](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/outlook-automation-for-accountants/)), clinics. Licensing and prices below were checked on Microsoft's and Zapier's own pages on 10 November 2026. Both change often, so check again before you buy. If you're also weighing Make or n8n, read [Zapier vs Make vs n8n](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/zapier-vs-make-vs-n8n/) as well. If you're on Google Workspace instead, [Google Apps Script](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/google-apps-script-for-small-business/) is the built-in option worth a look.

### What your Microsoft 365 plan already includes
Microsoft calls these "seeded" licences. Its licensing documentation (Microsoft Learn, updated October 2026) says Microsoft 365 licences let users create and run cloud flows with standard connectors. Premium and custom connectors are not included, and there's a daily limit of 6,000 actions per user. That limit is plenty for most small-firm workflows.
Standard connectors cover the Microsoft apps a small office uses every day, such as Office 365 Outlook, SharePoint, Excel Online (Business) and Microsoft Forms. Microsoft's standard list also includes some outside apps, among them Gmail, Google Sheets, Google Calendar, Dropbox, Slack, Trello, Typeform and DocuSign.
Premium connectors are where small firms usually get caught out. Microsoft's premium list includes Salesforce, SQL Server, Stripe, MailChimp and Calendly. The Xero connector listed there is a third-party one, and it's premium too. Once a flow uses a premium connector, you need a paid Power Automate licence.

### The comparison table (checked 10 November 2026)
Sources: Microsoft's Power Automate pricing pages (US and UK), Microsoft Learn's "Types of Power Automate licenses" and "Deep dive on specific licenses", and zapier.com/pricing, all read on 10 November 2026. Microsoft notes its UK prices exclude VAT and that the final price is shown at checkout.
|  | Power Automate | Zapier |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Free option | Included with most Microsoft 365 business plans: cloud flows with standard connectors only. The Free licence can't share flows. | Free plan: 100 tasks a month, two-step Zaps only, no premium apps |
| Entry paid plan | Premium: $15 per user a month, paid yearly (£11.50 ex VAT on Microsoft's UK page) | Professional: $19.99 a month billed yearly ($29.99 monthly) for 750 tasks, one user |
| How usage is counted | Per user, with a daily action limit (40,000 actions a day on Premium) | Per task: each action that completes. Triggers and filters don't count |
| Shared team account | Flows can have co-owners inside your Microsoft 365 tenant | Team plan: $69 a month billed yearly ($103.50 monthly), 2,000 tasks, up to 25 users |
| Apps | A large connector library, split into standard and premium | Zapier's pricing page lists 9,000+ apps; premium apps are included on paid plans |
| Desktop automation | Yes: desktop flows can click through older Windows software (attended RPA on Premium) | No: cloud apps only |
| Best fit | Firms whose work lives in Outlook, Excel and SharePoint | Firms on Google Workspace, or mixing many outside apps |

### Decide by where your data lives
| Where your work lives | Usually the better fit | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Outlook, Excel and SharePoint, nothing else | Power Automate | Standard connectors, already in your Microsoft 365 plan |
| Microsoft 365 plus one premium app (for example Salesforce or Stripe) | Compare both | Power Automate Premium for the person who owns the flow, or a Zapier paid plan. Price them for your real volumes |
| Google Workspace (Gmail, Drive, Sheets) | Zapier | No Microsoft licence to build on, and Zapier is simpler to set up for Google apps |
| Many outside apps (CRM, booking tool, forms, accounts) | Zapier | Wider app library, premium apps included on paid plans |
| An old Windows program with no online connection | Power Automate | Desktop flows can work through the screen; Zapier can't reach it |
| Files and client data must stay inside your Microsoft tenant | Power Automate | Flows run inside the Microsoft account you already manage |

### Who keeps it running
This matters more than the price. In Power Automate, the person who builds a flow is its owner, and Microsoft says the owner's licence can affect the flow. If someone leaves, the flow has to be handed to someone else. Microsoft's documentation explains how to change the owner, and adds a warning: if the new owner has no premium licence and the flow uses premium features, the flow runs for 30 days, then Power Automate turns it off until a licence is bought.
The fix is simple and worth doing on day one. Add a second co-owner to every flow, keep flows in a shared solution rather than one person's "My flows", and write down which licence each flow needs.
Zapier has the same risk in a different shape. On the Professional plan, everything sits in one person's account. If that person leaves, someone needs the login, or the Zaps have to be moved. The Team plan gives a shared workspace for up to 25 users, which is the cleaner choice once more than one person depends on the automations. If you'd like someone to build and fix the Zaps for you, see [hiring a Zapier expert](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/zapier-expert-for-small-business/).
With either tool, make sure the workflows sit in an account the business owns, not a freelancer's account, and that someone gets an email when a run fails.

### Premium connector checklist before you build
1. List every app the workflow touches, from the trigger to the last step. A one-page process map makes this quick.
2. Look each one up on Microsoft's connector reference (learn.microsoft.com/connectors). Each connector page shows whether it is Standard or Premium in Power Automate.
3. If every connector is Standard and you're on a Microsoft 365 business plan, you can probably build it with what you already pay for.
4. If even one connector is Premium, the flow's owner needs Power Automate Premium (or the flow needs a Process licence). Price that against a Zapier plan for the same volume.
5. Using a personal @gmail.com account? Microsoft's Gmail connector page says consumer Gmail accounts can only connect to a limited set of services in Power Automate. Google Workspace accounts aren't affected.
6. Check who will own the flow, add a co-owner, and decide who gets the failure alerts.

### A worked example (for illustration)
For illustration only: a small firm of solicitors on Microsoft 365. New enquiries arrive through a Microsoft Forms form on their website. They want each one saved to an Excel sheet on SharePoint, a folder created for the matter, the person on duty told by email, and a polite acknowledgement emailed from the shared Outlook mailbox. If they're still deciding which form tool to use, see [Microsoft Forms vs Google Forms](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/microsoft-forms-vs-google-forms-small-business/).
Every app in that list is Microsoft, and Forms, Excel Online (Business), SharePoint and Office 365 Outlook are standard connectors. Power Automate, inside the Microsoft 365 plan they already pay for, covers it with no new subscription. If nobody in the firm has time to build it, that's the kind of job a [Power Automate consultant](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/power-automate-consultant-small-business/) takes on.
Now change one detail: the firm takes enquiries through a booking tool that is only a premium connector in Power Automate. The choice becomes a real comparison: a Power Automate Premium licence for the flow's owner, or a Zapier paid plan sized to the number of enquiries. Either can work. Price both with your real monthly numbers.

### When you don't need either
The tool's subscription is rarely the main cost for a small firm. The time to build it properly, and to [keep it working when an app changes](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/do-automations-need-maintenance/), usually is.
- The task happens a few times a month. A checklist and a calendar reminder may be all you need.
- Your existing software already does it. Many practice, booking and accounting tools have reminders and templates built in. Turn those on first. If none of them fits, see [custom software vs off-the-shelf](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/custom-software-vs-off-the-shelf-small-business/).
- Outlook rules or a shared mailbox would solve it. Sorting, flagging and forwarding email doesn't need a workflow tool.
- The process isn't settled yet. Automating a process that changes every month means rebuilding it every month. Agree the steps on paper first.

### How Mike Automations would build it
If you'd rather not work out licences and connectors yourself, book a [free 15-minute call](https://mikeautomations.github.io/call/). Within 48 hours you get a written plan with a fixed price that says which tool the workflow runs on and why, which licences it needs, and who owns it. It's built on the tools you already use, in your own accounts, goes live in 2-3 days, and costs [$2,000 one-off](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/pricing/) ($1,500 for the first 3 clients). You pay once it's running and you're happy with it.

### Is Power Automate free with Microsoft 365?
Partly. Microsoft's licensing documentation says Microsoft 365 licences let users create and run cloud flows with standard connectors, up to 6,000 actions a day per user. Premium and custom connectors need a paid Power Automate licence (checked 10 November 2026).

### Is Power Automate cheaper than Zapier?
If every app you need is a standard connector, Power Automate can cost nothing extra on top of Microsoft 365. Once you need premium connectors, Power Automate Premium is $15 per user a month paid yearly, against Zapier Professional from $19.99 a month billed yearly for 750 tasks. Compare them with your real volumes.

### Can Zapier connect to Outlook, Excel and SharePoint?
Yes. Zapier connects to Microsoft apps as well as Google and thousands of others. The question is whether you need to pay for it when Power Automate already covers Microsoft-only workflows in your plan.

### What happens to a Power Automate flow when the person who built it leaves?
The flow needs a new owner. Microsoft's documentation explains how to change it. If the new owner has no premium licence and the flow uses premium features, it runs for 30 days and then turns off until a licence is bought. Adding a co-owner from the start avoids the scramble.

## AI vs automation: what's the difference for a small business?
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/ai-vs-automation-difference/ (2026-11-11)

The difference between AI and automation: automation follows rules you write (when this happens, do that) and does exactly the same thing every time. AI, such as a large language model, reads and writes like a person and can handle messy text, but it can be wrong in ways a rule never is. For a small business, use automation for anything that must be right every time, and AI for reading, sorting and drafting, with a person approving its work.

The difference between AI and automation gets blurred in most sales pitches, because "AI" sells. For a small business owner deciding what to spend money on, the difference matters a lot: one is predictable and cheap to run, the other is flexible and needs checking.
This post explains both in plain words, shows the same task done three ways, and ends with a table you can use to decide which one a job needs. Often the honest answer is plain automation, with no AI at all. Our [guide to automating a small business](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/small-business-automation/) shows where plain automation usually starts.

### Automation: rules that run the same way every time
Rule-based automation is a set of instructions you write once. "When a client uploads a document, save it in their folder, tick it off the list and email them what's still missing." Tools such as Zapier, Make, n8n and Power Automate run those rules for you, all day, without getting tired or forgetting.
The key point: given the same input, a rule gives the same output every time. If it breaks, it breaks in a way you can see and fix, such as a missing field or an app that changed its login. It doesn't guess.
Its limit is just as clear. A rule can only handle what you thought of in advance. A client who writes "sorry, the bank statement is attached to my other email" doesn't fit a rule. Neither does an enquiry that rambles for three paragraphs before it gets to the point.

### AI: software that reads and writes like a person
When people say AI today, they usually mean a large language model (LLM; our [automation glossary](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/automation-glossary-small-business/) explains this and other terms), the technology behind ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini. It reads text, works out what it means and writes a reply. That makes it good at the messy jobs rules can't handle: understanding a rambling email, pulling the key facts out of a letter, drafting a reply in your tone. Our guide to [using ChatGPT safely for admin](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/chatgpt-for-small-business-admin/) has prompts you can copy.
An AI agent goes a step further. It uses an AI model to decide which step comes next and then uses your tools to prepare it: sorting an enquiry, filling in a record, drafting the email. There's more on what agents can and can't do in [AI agents for small businesses](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/ai-agent-for-small-business/).
The catch is that AI can be wrong, and sound sure of itself while it is. Anthropic, which makes Claude, says in its developer documentation that even the most advanced language models can sometimes produce text that is factually incorrect or inconsistent with the context they were given. It calls this "hallucination", and notes that the techniques to reduce it don't remove it entirely.

### The same task done three ways (for illustration)
For illustration only: a small accounting practice gets an email from a client with some documents attached. Here is the same job done by hand, by rules, and by AI with a person approving.
|  | Fully manual | Rule-based automation | AI drafts, a person approves |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| What happens | Someone reads the email, saves the files, updates the checklist and writes a reply | Attachments are saved to the client's folder, the checklist is updated by file name, and a set email lists what's missing | AI reads the email and attachments, works out which documents arrived, and drafts a reply. A person checks it and clicks send |
| Handles a vague or unusual email? | Yes | No: it only follows the rules it was given | Mostly: it understands plain-language notes, but can misread them |
| Same result every time? | Depends on who does it and how busy they are | Yes | No: it can vary and needs checking |
| Running cost | Staff time on every email | A workflow tool subscription | The workflow tool plus AI usage, which grows with volume |
| Main risk | Things get missed in a busy week | A file named oddly isn't recognised | A confident but wrong reading reaches a client if nobody checks |

### What each one is reliable for
- Rules are reliable for: sending reminders on a schedule, moving data between apps, creating folders and records, chasing missing items from a list, routing a form to the right person, anything involving money, dates or legal wording.
- AI is reliable enough for: reading and summarising emails and documents, sorting enquiries by type or urgency, pulling names, dates and amounts out of text, drafting replies and first versions, as long as a person checks before anything goes out.
- Neither should decide on its own: refunds and payments, advice to a client, anything you would have to explain to a regulator. A person makes those calls.

### Cost and risk, in plain words
Rule-based automation has a predictable cost. You pay for a workflow tool and someone's time to build it. Once it's built, a run costs the same today as next month.
AI adds a usage cost that grows with how much it reads and writes. Zapier's pricing page, for example, says many actions cost more than one task, depending on the step type, the AI model tier and the number of tool calls. So the more the AI reads and writes, the more it costs: a busy inbox costs more than a quiet one.
The bigger cost is checking. If a person has to read every AI draft, that time is part of the price. It is usually still far quicker than writing every reply from scratch, but it isn't zero. If the client data is personal, also think about where it goes: our [GDPR checklist for automating client data](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/gdpr-checklist-automating-client-data/) covers the questions to ask.

### Decision table: AI, automation or neither?
Most useful setups are the last row: rules do the bulk of the work, and AI is used for one step that needs reading or writing. If you're not sure where to start, [what to automate first](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/what-to-automate-first-small-business/) walks through picking the first job. If you're comparing providers, our page on [AI automation services for small business](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/ai-automation-services-small-business/) sets out what's real today and who to hire.
| If the job is... | Use | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The same steps every time, with clear inputs (a form, a date, a status) | Rule-based automation | Predictable, cheap to run, easy to check |
| Reading free text people write in their own way | AI, with a person approving | Rules can't understand messy language |
| Must be right every time (money, deadlines, legal wording) | Rules, or a person | AI can be confidently wrong |
| Drafting replies in your tone | AI drafts, a person sends | Saves writing time, keeps a check before the client sees it |
| Happens a few times a month | Neither, for now | A checklist or template is cheaper than building anything |
| Mixed: a form starts it, then a messy reply comes in | Both | Rules move the work along; AI handles only the messy step |

### Questions to ask anyone selling you "AI automation"
1. Which steps use fixed rules, and which use AI? Ask to see them marked on the plan.
2. Where does a person approve the AI's work before it reaches a client or moves money?
3. What happens when the AI isn't sure? It should hand the case to a person, not guess.
4. What does it cost to run each month at our volume, including AI usage?
5. Where does our client data go, and which AI provider sees it?

### How Mike Automations would approach it
Book a [free 15-minute call](https://mikeautomations.github.io/call/) about the task you want help with. Often plain automation is enough, and I'll say so. Within 48 hours you get a written plan with a fixed price that shows which steps use rules, which use AI, and where a person approves. It's built on the tools you already use, goes live in 2-3 days, costs [$2,000 one-off](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/pricing/), and you pay once it's running and you're happy with it. A person always approves anything the AI prepares.

### Is automation the same as AI?
No. Automation follows rules you write and does the same thing every time. AI, such as a large language model, interprets text and writes new text, so it can handle messy input but can also be wrong. Many useful systems combine the two.

### Do I need AI to automate my business?
Usually not for the first jobs. Reminders, chasing, moving data between apps and creating records are all plain rule-based automation. AI earns its place where people write in their own words and someone currently has to read every message.

### Is AI safe to use with client emails?
It can be, with limits: AI prepares, a person approves, and it has no permission to send, pay or delete on its own. Check where the data goes and which provider processes it before you start.

## Automation ROI worksheet: will an automation pay for itself?
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/automation-roi-worksheet/ (2026-11-11)

Automation ROI for a small business comes down to one sum: what the process costs you each month now, minus what the automation costs to run, set against what it costs to build. Divide the one-off build cost by the monthly saving and you have the payback period in months. If that number is under 12, the automation usually pays for itself within the first year.

This automation ROI worksheet helps you decide, with your own numbers, whether automating one process is worth paying for. It has five parts to fill in: time saved, what that time costs, the cost of errors and delays, the one-off and running costs, and the payback period. It uses no industry averages, because an average tells you nothing about your firm.
Pick one process before you start, such as chasing documents, following up quotes or sending payment reminders. If you're not sure which one, our guide on [what to automate first](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/what-to-automate-first-small-business/) helps you choose. Work it out for one process at a time: a vague "we'll save loads of time" is how money gets wasted.

### Before you start: what to have to hand
If you haven't written the process down yet, a [simple process map](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/process-map-template-small-business/) takes about half an hour and makes every line below easier to fill in.
- One named process, with a clear start and end (for example: "from sending the records request to having every document in").
- A rough count of how often it happens: per week, per month or per season.
- Who does it now, and roughly what an hour of their time costs.
- Any real cost you can name when it goes wrong: a penalty, a lost job, a write-off, a client who left.
- The price of the build and of any software it needs. Our [pricing page](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/pricing/) has ours.

### The worksheet
Fill in the right-hand column with your own figures. Use monthly numbers throughout, so the lines add up. If the work is seasonal (tax season, year end), work out a full year and divide by 12.
| Line | What to enter | How to work it out | Your number |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A. Hours spent now | Hours a month the process takes by hand | Count every touch: reminders, chasing, copying data, checking, filing |  |
| B. Hours still needed | Hours a month it will still take once automated | Approvals, replies to unusual cases, a weekly check. Rarely zero |  |
| C. Hours saved | A minus B | Be honest: this is the number that matters most |  |
| D. Cost of an hour | What an hour of that person's time costs you | See the next section |  |
| E. Time saving | C x D | Money a month |  |
| F. Errors and delays | Monthly cost of what goes wrong now | Only costs you can name. Leave it at 0 if unsure |  |
| G. Monthly benefit | E + F | Money a month |  |
| H. Running costs | Platform subscription + any support, per month | From the vendor's pricing page and your provider's quote |  |
| I. Monthly saving | G minus H | If this is 0 or less, stop here |  |
| J. One-off cost | The build price | A fixed price, written down before work starts |  |
| K. Payback period | J divided by I | In months |  |
| L. First-year result | (I x 12) minus J | Money left after year one |  |

### Line D: what an hour really costs you
For a member of staff, start with their yearly pay, then add what you pay on top: employer National Insurance and pension in the UK, or employer payroll taxes and benefits in the US. Divide by the hours they actually work in a year, after holidays. That gives you a fair hourly cost.
For your own time as the owner, use one of two figures: what you would bill a client for that hour, or what you would pay someone else to do the job. Use the lower one if you're unsure. The hours you get back are only worth something if you use them for paid work, sales or rest you would otherwise not get.

### Line F: errors and delays, counted carefully
This is where ROI sums get inflated, so keep it strict. Only count a cost you could point to on paper. Good examples: a late-filing penalty you paid because records arrived late, a quote that went cold because nobody followed it up, an invoice you wrote off after it was forgotten, a client who left and told you why.
Take what it cost you last year and divide by 12. If you can't name a real cost, leave line F at zero. The time saving on its own should justify the build. Errors avoided are then a bonus, not the reason.

### Lines H and J: one-off and running costs
The one-off cost is the build: mapping the process, connecting the tools and testing what goes wrong. With us, one process end to end is $2,000 one-off, or $1,500 for the first 3 firms, agreed as a fixed price before any work starts. Our guide to [business automation cost](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/business-automation-cost/) explains how other providers charge.
Running costs are the platform that runs the workflow, plus support if you want it. Check how your platform counts usage, because a busy workflow can move you up a plan. Zapier's help pages say a task is any successful action, so a five-step workflow uses several tasks each run. Make's help pages describe credits, roughly one for each module that runs. n8n's pricing page says its cloud plans count executions, where one execution is a single run of the whole workflow. The [Zapier, Make and n8n comparison](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/zapier-vs-make-vs-n8n/) goes into more detail. Support with us is optional at $150 a month.

### For illustration: a worked example
For illustration only. Every input below except our prices is made up: replace it with your own. A small firm spends 4 hours a week chasing clients for documents, about 16 hours a month. Once automated, someone still spends about 1 hour a week (4 a month) on replies and odd cases, so 12 hours a month are saved. An hour of that person's time costs the firm $35. Last year two late returns cost $300 in penalties, which is $25 a month. The platform plan is assumed at $20 a month; check your own vendor's page.
| Line | Without support | With $150 a month support |
| --- | --- | --- |
| C. Hours saved a month | 12 | 12 |
| E. Time saving (12 x $35) | $420 | $420 |
| F. Errors and delays | $25 | $25 |
| G. Monthly benefit | $445 | $445 |
| H. Running costs | $20 | $170 |
| I. Monthly saving | $425 | $275 |
| J. One-off cost (build) | $2,000 | $2,000 |
| K. Payback period | 4.7 months | 7.3 months |
| L. First-year result | $3,100 | $1,300 |

### For illustration: when it doesn't pay
For illustration only, with made-up inputs. The same firm looks at a process that takes 1 hour a week, of which half an hour would be saved: about 2 hours a month at $35, or $70. Take off the $20 platform plan and the monthly saving is $50. A $2,000 build would take 40 months to pay back. That is a no. The better move is to pick a bigger process first, or to fold this small job into a larger workflow that is being built anyway.

### How to read your result
| Payback period | What it usually means |
| --- | --- |
| Under 6 months | A strong case. Check line B is realistic, then go ahead. |
| 6 to 12 months | Usually worth doing, as long as the process will still exist next year. |
| 12 to 24 months | Borderline. Look for a bigger process, or include errors you can actually name. |
| Over 24 months, or no saving | Don't automate this one yet. Tidy the process by hand first. |

### Copy this worksheet
Automation ROI worksheet (one process, monthly figures):
```
Process: ____________________

A. Hours spent now (per month): ____
B. Hours still needed after automation: ____
C. Hours saved (A - B): ____
D. Cost of one hour: ____
E. Time saving (C x D): ____
F. Errors and delays you can name (per month): ____
G. Monthly benefit (E + F): ____
H. Running costs (platform + support, per month): ____
I. Monthly saving (G - H): ____
J. One-off build cost: ____
K. Payback period in months (J / I): ____
L. First-year result ((I x 12) - J): ____

Decision: go / not yet / pick a bigger process
```

### Common mistakes
- Assuming the process drops to zero hours. Someone still approves, answers odd replies and checks it works.
- Counting time saved that won't be used. If the hours just disappear into the day, the saving is real but smaller than it looks.
- Forgetting running costs. A platform plan and optional support are paid every month.
- Inflating errors. Only count what you have actually paid for, not what might happen.
- Comparing an hourly quote with a fixed one. Turn every quote into a total before you compare.

### If you'd like us to work it out with you
On a [free 15-minute call](https://mikeautomations.github.io/call/) we go through these lines with you for the process you have in mind. If the numbers don't work, we say so. If they do, you get a [written plan](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/how-it-works/) with a fixed price within 48 hours. We build on the tools you already use, and the workflow is live in 2-3 days. It's $2,000 one-off, and you pay only once it's running and you're happy with it. No deposit and no hourly billing.

### What is a good payback period for an automation?
For a small business, under 12 months is usually a good result, because the process will very likely still exist after a year. Under 6 months is a strong case. Over 24 months usually means the process is too small to automate on its own.

### Should I count errors and delays in the ROI?
Only the ones you can put a real figure on, such as a penalty you paid or a job you lost. If you can't name the cost, leave it at zero and let the time saving carry the decision.

### How do I value my own time as the owner?
Use what you would bill a client for that hour, or what you would pay someone else to do the job, whichever is lower. The saving only counts if you use the hours for something that earns or matters more.

### Does this worksheet work in pounds?
Yes. Use any currency, as long as every line uses the same one. Our prices are set in US dollars and invoiced in pounds or euros at the equivalent rate.

## Automation glossary: 35 terms a small business owner meets, explained simply
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/automation-glossary-small-business/ (2026-11-11)

This automation glossary explains, in plain words, the 35 terms a small business owner is most likely to hear when someone offers to automate their admin: from trigger, action and webhook to AI agent, human in the loop, A2P 10DLC and DPIA. Each definition stands on its own and links to a longer guide where one exists.

This automation glossary is for owners of small service firms who keep hearing words like "webhook", "integration" or "AI agent" and want a straight answer. The terms are grouped by letter. Each one starts with the term itself, so you can find it quickly with your browser's search. To see how the pieces fit together in a real business, read [what small business automation is and where to start](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/small-business-automation/).
A few terms are rules rather than technology, because rules decide what an automation is allowed to do. Some apply only in the UK (MTD, the UK GDPR) or only in the US (A2P 10DLC, Section 7216). Where a rule is involved, the definition says which country it belongs to and who publishes it.

### A to C
Action. An action is a step an automation carries out after it starts, such as sending an email, creating a record or saving a file. One workflow usually has a trigger followed by several actions. Zapier, for example, counts each successful action as one task for billing.
AI agent. An AI agent is software that uses an AI model to read something (an email, a form, a document), decide which step comes next and use your tools to prepare it, such as a draft reply or a sorted enquiry. In a small business it should prepare work for a person to approve, not act alone. More in [AI agents for small business](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/ai-agent-for-small-business/).
AML checks. AML (anti-money laundering) checks are the identity and risk checks a regulated firm must do on its clients. In the UK, accountants, bookkeepers, tax advisers, solicitors and estate agents fall under the Money Laundering Regulations 2017, which require customer due diligence before and during the relationship. See [AML client ID checks](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/aml-client-id-checks-workflow/).
A2P 10DLC. A2P 10DLC (application-to-person messaging over 10-digit long codes) is the US carriers' registration system for business texts sent from software to people using an ordinary 10-digit US number. Twilio's documentation says anyone sending such texts to US numbers must register a brand and a campaign first. More in [missed call text back](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/missed-call-text-back-contractors/).
API. An API (application programming interface) is the official way one piece of software lets another read or change its data, for example adding a contact or fetching an invoice. If an app has no API, or keeps it for higher plans, automating it is harder or impossible.
Automation platform. An automation platform is the service that runs your workflows in the background and connects your apps, such as Zapier, Make, n8n or Microsoft Power Automate. You pay it a subscription, and it should sit in your own account so the workflows belong to you. Compare three of them in [Zapier vs Make vs n8n](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/zapier-vs-make-vs-n8n/).
Branching. Branching (also called conditional logic or a filter) is a rule inside a workflow that sends each case down a different path, for example "if the client is VAT registered, ask for the VAT return records; if not, skip it". Most real business processes need some branching.
Client portal. A client portal is a secure website where clients log in to upload documents, sign forms and see what you still need from them. It replaces email attachments, which are hard to track and less secure. See [client portal vs email](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/client-portal-vs-email-document-collection/).
CRM. A CRM (customer relationship management system) is software that keeps one record per client or lead, with their contact details, history, deals and tasks. Many automations start or end in the CRM, for example creating a contact when a web form is filled in. A spreadsheet or a tool like Airtable can do the same job at first; see [when Airtable beats a Google Sheet](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/airtable-vs-google-sheets-small-business/).

### D to H
Data mapping. Data mapping (or field mapping) is telling an automation which piece of information goes where, for example "the Email field on the form goes into the Email field in the CRM". Most errors in a new workflow come from fields that are mapped wrongly or left empty.
Data processing agreement. A data processing agreement (DPA) is the contract between your business and a supplier that handles personal data for you, setting out what it may do with that data. Article 28 of the UK GDPR requires one with every processor. See the [GDPR checklist for automating client data](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/gdpr-checklist-automating-client-data/).
DPIA. A DPIA (data protection impact assessment) is a written check of the risks to people before you start using their data in a new way. Under the UK GDPR it is required when the processing is likely to result in a high risk to individuals, and the ICO publishes a list of examples. The [GDPR checklist](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/gdpr-checklist-automating-client-data/) explains when a small firm needs one.
E-signature. An e-signature (electronic signature) is a way to sign a document online instead of on paper, such as typing a name, drawing a signature or clicking to accept. In the US the ESIGN Act says a signature may not be denied legal effect just because it is electronic; in England and Wales the Law Commission confirmed in 2019 that an electronic signature can validly sign a document. See [engagement letter automation](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/engagement-letter-automation/) and [client onboarding for coaches and consultants](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/coach-consultant-client-onboarding/).
GDPR processor. A processor, under the UK GDPR and the EU GDPR, is a person or company that handles personal data on behalf of another business, which is called the controller. When you use an automation platform, a form tool or an email service for client data, each one is usually your processor. More in the [GDPR checklist](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/gdpr-checklist-automating-client-data/).
Hallucination. A hallucination is when an AI model writes something that sounds confident but is wrong or made up, such as a deadline or a figure that doesn't exist. It is the main reason a person should check anything AI prepares before it reaches a client.
Human in the loop. Human in the loop means a person reviews and approves an automated or AI-prepared step before it takes effect, for example checking a drafted reply before it is sent. It keeps you in control of anything that matters to a client. See [AI agents for small business](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/ai-agent-for-small-business/).

### I to N
Integration. An integration is a working connection between two apps so that data moves between them without retyping, for example new invoices in your accounting software appearing in a spreadsheet. Some integrations are built into the apps; others are built with an automation platform.
KYC. KYC (know your customer) is the general name for checking who a client is before you work for them, usually by verifying ID and address. In UK regulated firms it is part of the customer due diligence the AML rules require. See [AML client ID checks](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/aml-client-id-checks-workflow/).
LLM. An LLM (large language model) is the type of AI model behind tools like ChatGPT and Claude: it has been trained on large amounts of text and writes text in reply to an instruction. In business automation it is used to read, sort and draft, not to make final decisions. See [ChatGPT prompts for accountants](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/chatgpt-prompts-for-accountants/).
Make. Make is an automation platform with a visual canvas, where each workflow (called a scenario) is drawn as connected modules. Make's help pages say it bills in credits, roughly one for each module that runs. Compared in [Zapier vs Make vs n8n](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/zapier-vs-make-vs-n8n/).
MTD. MTD (Making Tax Digital) is HMRC's programme that requires UK businesses to keep digital records and send updates to HMRC from compatible software. GOV.UK says MTD for Income Tax applies from 6 April 2026 to sole traders and landlords with qualifying income over £50,000, from April 2027 over £30,000 and from April 2028 over £20,000. See [MTD for Income Tax: a practice workflow](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/making-tax-digital-income-tax-practice-workflow/).
n8n. n8n is an automation platform that you can use as a paid cloud service or self-host on your own server. n8n's pricing page says its cloud plans count executions, where one execution is a single run of the whole workflow however many steps it has. Compared in [Zapier vs Make vs n8n](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/zapier-vs-make-vs-n8n/).
No-code. No-code describes tools that let you build workflows or apps by clicking and filling in settings instead of writing software code. Zapier, Make and most form and portal tools are no-code. No-code does not mean no thought: the hard part is still deciding exactly what should happen.

### O to S
Polling. Polling is when an automation platform checks an app on a schedule (for example every few minutes) to see whether anything new has happened. It is the alternative to a webhook, and it is why some automations start a few minutes after the event rather than at once.
Power Automate. Microsoft Power Automate is Microsoft's automation platform, closely tied to Microsoft 365 apps such as Outlook, Excel, SharePoint and Teams. It suits firms that already run on Microsoft 365. See [Power Automate vs Zapier](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/power-automate-vs-zapier-small-business/) and [Outlook automation for accountants](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/outlook-automation-for-accountants/).
Process map. A process map is a simple written or drawn list of the steps in a piece of work, who does each one and what triggers the next. It is the first thing to make before automating anything. Use the [process map template](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/process-map-template-small-business/).
Prompt. A prompt is the instruction you give an AI model, such as "summarise this email in two sentences and list any dates". Clear prompts with an example and a set format give far more reliable results. See [ChatGPT prompts for accountants](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/chatgpt-prompts-for-accountants/).
RPA. RPA (robotic process automation) is software that copies what a person does on screen, clicking buttons and typing into fields, to work with systems that have no API. It is useful for old desktop software, but it breaks more easily than an API connection when a screen changes.
Section 7216 consent. Section 7216 of the US Internal Revenue Code limits what a tax return preparer may do with a client's tax return information without the client's written consent. It matters before sending client tax data to new tools, including AI tools. See [Section 7216 consent before automation or AI](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/section-7216-consent-before-automation-or-ai/).

### T to Z
Task. A task is Zapier's billing unit: Zapier's help pages say a task is any successful action that runs in a Zap, while triggers don't use tasks. Other platforms use different units (Make counts credits, n8n cloud counts executions), so the same workflow can cost very different amounts. Work out the full cost with the [automation ROI worksheet](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/automation-roi-worksheet/).
Template. A template is a pre-written message or document with gaps that an automation fills in, such as a client's name, the missing documents and a due date. Good templates make automated messages read like a person wrote them. See [document chasing email templates](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/document-chasing-email-templates/) and [tax extension emails to clients](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/tax-extension-client-email-templates/).
Trigger. A trigger is the event that starts an automation, such as a new form submission, a [new email](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/gmail-automation-for-accountants/), a date arriving (an [MOT due date](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/garage-mot-reminders/), say) or a status changing. Zapier's help pages say a Zap's first step is always a trigger. Every workflow has exactly one starting trigger.
Webhook. A webhook is a message one app sends to another the moment something happens, such as "a client just signed", so the next step starts straight away. It is faster than polling, but the sending app has to support it.
WISP. A WISP (written information security plan) is the document that says how a US tax practice protects client data: who is responsible, what the risks are and which safeguards are in place. Under the FTC Safeguards Rule every paid tax preparer needs one, and IRS Publication 5708 gives a free template. See [WISP for tax preparers](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/wisp-for-small-tax-practices/).
Workflow automation. Workflow automation is using software to carry out the repeated steps of a business process without someone doing each one by hand, for example sending reminders until every document is in. It handles the routine; a person still handles the exceptions and approvals. See [our workflow automation services](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/services/).
Zapier. Zapier is an automation platform that connects thousands of apps through workflows called Zaps, each made of one trigger and one or more actions. It is the easiest to start with, and it bills by tasks. Compared in [Zapier vs Make vs n8n](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/zapier-vs-make-vs-n8n/).

### Which terms matter first
If you're new to this, five terms cover most conversations: trigger, action, integration, automation platform and human in the loop. Rules come next, and only the ones for your country and trade: the UK GDPR and AML rules for UK firms, A2P 10DLC and Section 7216 for US firms that text clients or prepare tax returns.
The best way to make the words concrete is to write down one of your own processes and label each step. Our guide on [what to automate first](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/what-to-automate-first-small-business/) helps you pick the process.

### If you'd rather not learn all of this
You don't have to. Mike Automations maps how your process works and builds the automation on the tools you already use. After a [free 15-minute call](https://mikeautomations.github.io/call/) you get a [written plan](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/how-it-works/) with a fixed price within 48 hours, and the workflow is live in 2-3 days. It costs $2,000 one-off, and you pay only once it's running and you're happy with it. A person always approves anything AI prepares.

### What is the difference between a trigger and an action?
A trigger is the event that starts an automation, such as a new form submission. An action is a step the automation carries out after that, such as sending an email or creating a record. Each workflow has one starting trigger and usually several actions.

### What is the difference between a webhook and an API?
An API is the official way one app lets another read or change its data when asked. A webhook is a message an app sends by itself the moment something happens. Automations often use both: a webhook to start, and the API to fetch or update details.

### Is an AI agent the same as an automation?
No. A standard automation follows fixed rules you set. An AI agent uses an AI model to read and decide which step comes next, which makes it more flexible but less predictable, so a person should approve what it prepares.

## n8n Cloud vs self-hosted for a small business
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/n8n-cloud-vs-self-hosted-small-business/ (2026-11-11)

n8n Cloud vs self-hosted, for a small business: n8n Cloud costs from €20 a month billed yearly, and n8n runs, updates and backs it up for you. Self-hosted n8n has no licence fee for internal business use, but you pay for a server and someone has to install, patch, back up and secure it. Without a technical person who will do that every month, n8n Cloud is the safer choice.

n8n Cloud vs self-hosted is the first decision a small business makes after picking n8n. The software is the same. The difference is who runs it: n8n, on its servers, for a monthly fee, or you, on a server you rent, with no licence fee but all the upkeep.
This post is for owners of small service firms with no IT department. Prices, limits and licence terms below were checked on n8n.io and in n8n's documentation on 10 November 2026. n8n changes its plans often, so check again before you buy. If you haven't chosen a tool yet, start with [Zapier vs Make vs n8n](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/zapier-vs-make-vs-n8n/). If Make is on your shortlist, read [whether Make is worth paying for](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/is-make-com-worth-it-small-business/) too.

### The comparison table (checked 10 November 2026)
Sources: n8n.io/pricing and docs.n8n.io, read on 10 November 2026. Prices are in euros, as n8n shows them. An execution is one run of a whole workflow, however many steps it has. n8n says the Business plan is currently only available self-hosted, and dedicated support with agreed response times is only on Enterprise, priced through n8n's sales team.
|  | n8n Cloud Starter | n8n Cloud Pro | Self-hosted Community | Self-hosted Business |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Price | €24 a month, or €20 a month billed yearly | From €60 a month, or €50 a month billed yearly | No licence fee. You pay for the server | €800 a month, or €8,000 a year |
| Runs included | 2,500 executions a month | 10,000 executions a month (50,000 for €145 a month) | No allowance from n8n: your server sets the limit | 40,000 executions a month |
| Runs at the same time | 5 | 20 (50 on the 50,000 plan) | You decide | You decide |
| Updates and security fixes | n8n, at least every two weeks | n8n, at least every two weeks | You | You |
| Backups | Automatic workflow backups (not credentials) | Automatic workflow backups (not credentials) | You | You |
| Where the data sits | n8n's servers in Frankfurt, Germany | n8n's servers in Frankfurt, Germany | Wherever you host it | Wherever you host it |
| Sharing workflows with colleagues | 1 shared project | 3 shared projects, admin roles | Needs a paid licence | 6 shared projects, single sign-on |
| Support | Community forum | Community forum | Community forum | Community forum |

### The real cost of each
n8n Cloud's cost is the plan price. Most small firms with a handful of workflows fit inside Starter's 2,500 runs a month: a workflow that runs once a day uses about 30 runs a month, and one triggered by each new enquiry uses one run per enquiry. Watch the time limit on a single run: n8n's pricing page says 5 minutes on Starter and 40 minutes on Pro, and time spent waiting, for example in a Wait node, doesn't count.
Self-hosted Community has no licence fee, but it isn't free. You pay for a server every month, and for the hours someone spends looking after it. That time is the bigger cost for most small firms. For illustration: if you pay someone £50 an hour and they spend two hours a month on updates, backups and checks, that's £100 a month before anything breaks. Use your own rate and hours.
Self-hosted Business only makes sense for bigger teams that need single sign-on, separate test and live environments, or more shared projects. At €8,000 a year it costs far more than Cloud Pro for a small firm. n8n also offers a Startup plan with 50% off Business for companies under 20 employees, if you qualify under n8n's terms.

### Who patches it, and why that matters
On n8n Cloud, n8n updates your instance for you. Its documentation says it upgrades every Cloud instance at least every two weeks so that security fixes reach everyone. You can choose a maintenance window, so the one or two minutes of downtime happen when nobody is working.
Self-hosted, updating is your job. n8n's own advice is to update at least once a month, read the release notes for breaking changes first, and test the update on a copy if you can. That advice exists for a reason. As of 10 November 2026, n8n's GitHub repository lists 223 security advisories published in 2026, 19 of them rated critical. The usual fix is to update to a newer version. On Cloud, n8n applies those updates. On a self-hosted server, the fix only arrives when someone installs it.
A self-hosted n8n also holds the passwords and keys for every app it connects to: your email, your accounting software, your client files. An out-of-date server on the open internet is a risk to client data, not just to the workflows.

### Who backs it up
n8n Cloud makes backups automatically, and instance owners can download workflows from them in the Cloud console. n8n's documentation notes that those backups contain workflows only, never credentials, so keep a record of which accounts each workflow connects to.
Self-hosted, a full backup is more than exporting your workflows. n8n's backup guide says it must include the .n8n folder, which holds the encryption key, and the database. Without that key, saved credentials can't be decrypted after a restore. n8n also recommends a full backup before every update. And a backup nobody has ever tried restoring is a hope, not a backup.

### The licence: what the Sustainable Use License allows
Self-hosted n8n is covered by n8n's Sustainable Use License, a "fair-code" licence n8n created in 2022. It isn't an open-source licence. n8n's documentation says you may use or modify the software for your own internal business purposes, or for non-commercial or personal use.
n8n's License FAQ makes this practical. Allowed: running n8n to help run your business, building automations for your clients on your instance as long as they can't create or edit them, and charging for building, setting up and maintaining workflows. Not allowed: hosting n8n as a service where your clients build their own workflows, or white-labelling n8n as your own product.
For a small firm automating its own admin, self-hosting sits comfortably inside the licence. n8n Cloud is a paid subscription with its own terms, so the Sustainable Use License doesn't apply to it. If your plan sits near the edge, n8n asks you to email license@n8n.io before you build.

### Self-hosting checklist: who will do each job?
Before you choose self-hosted, write a name next to every line. If any line stays blank, n8n Cloud is the better choice for now.
| Job | How often | Who in your firm |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Rent and set up the server, domain and HTTPS certificate | Once, then renewals |  |
| Install n8n updates after reading the release notes | At least monthly (n8n's advice) |  |
| Watch n8n's security advisories and apply urgent fixes | Whenever one is published |  |
| Full backup: .n8n folder, encryption key, database | Daily or weekly, and before every update |  |
| Test a restore from backup | Every few months |  |
| Check the server for disk space and failed runs | Weekly |  |
| Get an alert when a workflow fails, and fix it | As it happens |  |
| Keep a list of every connected account and who owns it | Whenever anything changes |  |

### When self-hosting makes sense
For most small service firms with a few workflows and no IT person, none of these is true. n8n Cloud Starter or Pro costs less than the hours a self-hosted server takes, and the patching happens without anyone having to remember it. Whichever you choose, the workflows still need someone to watch them: our post on [whether automations need maintenance](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/do-automations-need-maintenance/) explains why they break.
- Someone in the business, or someone you pay (for example an [n8n expert for small business](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/n8n-consultant/)), already looks after servers and will own every job in the checklist above.
- Client data must stay on infrastructure you choose, for example in a particular country, and your data protection assessment says so. The [GDPR checklist before automating client data](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/gdpr-checklist-automating-client-data/) helps you work this out.
- Your workflows run tens of thousands of times a month, so Cloud's execution limits would push you onto a much bigger plan.
- You need a community node or a setting that n8n Cloud doesn't allow.

### Is self-hosted n8n really free?
The Community edition has no licence fee for your own internal business use under n8n's Sustainable Use License. You still pay for a server, and for the time someone spends updating, backing up and securing it every month.

### How much does n8n Cloud cost?

### Where does n8n Cloud store my data?
