Yes. n8n's License FAQ says charging customers for workflow creation, setup and maintenance is allowed. What isn't allowed is offering n8n as a service where clients build their own workflows.

## Custom software vs off-the-shelf for a small business
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/custom-software-vs-off-the-shelf-small-business/ (2026-11-11)

Custom software vs off-the-shelf, for a small business: off-the-shelf software usually wins when a product already fits most of how you work, because it's cheaper to start and the vendor maintains it. Custom software wins when your way of working is what sets you apart, when you're paying for several tools that still don't fit, or when per-user fees keep climbing. Many small firms are best served by a middle path: off-the-shelf tools joined up with a few automations.

Custom software vs off-the-shelf is a question most small firms reach once spreadsheets, shared inboxes and three different apps stop keeping up. Do you buy another subscription and bend your process to fit it, or have something built around the way you already work?
This post compares the two honestly for a small service business: total cost, fit, lock-in and who maintains it. It ends with a decision table and a checklist. The cost example is for illustration: put your own numbers in.

### What each one means
Off-the-shelf software is a product many businesses use as it comes: a CRM, a practice management tool, a booking system or a job management app. You pay a subscription, usually per user per month, and the vendor builds, hosts and updates it.
Custom software is built for one business. For a small firm that usually means a simple web app with a login per person: clients, jobs, documents and tasks in one place, shaped around your steps rather than someone else's. You pay to build it, then for hosting and any changes.
There's a third option most comparisons skip: keep the off-the-shelf tools you have and join them up with automations, so information moves between them without retyping. It's often the cheapest fix, and it's covered below. A middle option is a database-style tool; we compare [Airtable and Google Sheets for a small service business](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/airtable-vs-google-sheets-small-business/).

### Total cost: work it out over three years
Comparing a monthly subscription with a one-off build price is comparing two different things. Put both on the same footing: what you'll pay over three years, including the time your team spends on workarounds. Here is a worksheet with a worked example. The figures are for illustration only, not market prices.
| Cost line | Off-the-shelf (for illustration) | Custom (for illustration) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Licence or build | 6 users × $40 a month = $8,640 over 3 years | $5,000 one-off build |
| Setup, data import, training | $500 once | Included in the build |
| Add-ons or a higher tier for one missing feature | 6 users × $15 a month = $3,240 over 3 years | None: the feature is built in |
| Price rises | Unknown: check the contract's terms | None on the build |
| Hosting and support | Included in the subscription | $150 a month = $5,400 over 3 years (optional) |
| Workarounds: retyping, spreadsheets on the side | 3 hours a week × 150 weeks × your hourly cost | Should drop, if the system fits |
| Three-year total before workarounds | $12,380 | $5,000 to $10,400 |

### What the worked example shows
In this example the two come out closer than most people expect, and the workaround hours decide it. If the off-the-shelf product fits well and nobody keeps a spreadsheet on the side, it's the cheaper and simpler choice. If your team spends hours every week bending the product to fit, that time usually costs more than either price line. Our [automation ROI worksheet](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/automation-roi-worksheet/) shows how to put a fair figure on those hours.
Two more points change the sums. Per-user pricing grows with every person you hire, while a custom build doesn't. And a subscription keeps going for as long as you use the product, while a build is paid once.

### Fit: the question that decides most cases
The UK government's guidance on choosing between building and buying technology (GOV.UK, "Define your purchasing strategy", updated September 2026) is written for public bodies, but its logic suits a small firm too. It suggests buying when a commercial product meets most of your needs and you don't need much customisation. It suggests building when your need is unusual, or when available products can't be adapted or connected to cover your core needs.
It also warns about bending a bought product too far: "Even small modifications to OTS software can remove most of the benefits of using it." For a small firm the lesson is simple. Use off-the-shelf software as it was designed, through its own settings. If you'd need to fight the product every day to make it fit, that's the sign it's the wrong product, or that custom is worth pricing.

### Lock-in: it happens both ways
Our [automation handover checklist](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/automation-handover-checklist/) lists what you should receive when anything is built for you, so you can move to someone else if you ever need to.
- Off-the-shelf lock-in: your data sits in the vendor's system. Check before you sign that you can export everything (clients, jobs, documents, notes) in a format you can open, and what happens to your data if you cancel.
- Price lock-in: once your team relies on a product, moving away is painful, so a price rise is hard to refuse. Read the contract terms on price changes and notice periods.
- Custom lock-in: a system only one developer understands ties you to that developer. Make sure the code, the data and the hosting accounts are in your business's name, and that you get written documentation.
- The same GOV.UK guidance says contracts must be explicit about who owns the data and the intellectual property, including the software code. Ask for that in writing whichever way you go.

### Maintenance: who keeps it working
With off-the-shelf software the vendor fixes bugs, applies security updates and adds features. You don't choose which features, and a change you didn't ask for can still alter how your team works.
With custom software someone has to keep it running: hosting, security updates, backups and small changes as your business changes. Agree before the build who does that, what it costs, and how quickly problems get fixed. A custom system with no maintenance plan is a risk, however well it was built.

### The decision table
| Your situation | Usually wins | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A well-known product does 80% or more of what you need, as it comes | Off-the-shelf | Cheaper to start, maintained by the vendor |
| You need to start next week | Off-the-shelf | Sign up and import your data; a build takes weeks |
| Your tools are fine, but people retype the same data between them | Middle path: automation | Joining the tools up is cheaper than replacing them |
| You pay for three or more tools and still keep a spreadsheet on the side | Custom | One system shaped around your steps replaces the patchwork |
| Your way of working is what clients pay you for | Custom | Off-the-shelf would make you work like everyone else |
| You're hiring and per-user fees keep climbing | Price both | A custom build doesn't grow with headcount, but it needs maintenance |
| Nobody will own maintenance of a custom system | Off-the-shelf | A product the vendor keeps up to date is safer |

### Before you decide: five steps
1. Write down how the work flows today, from the first enquiry to the final invoice. A [one-page process map](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/process-map-template-small-business/) is enough.
2. Mark each step the current tools handle well, handle badly, or don't handle at all.
3. Trial the best off-the-shelf product on your hardest real case, not the demo data. If it handles that through its own settings, buy it.
4. If it doesn't, price a custom system and the middle path (automations between the tools you already have) for the same steps.
5. Compare the three-year totals, including workaround hours, and check who owns the data and code in each option.

### How Mike Automations would build it
Start with the free [plan builder](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/plan/) to see which of your workflows could simply be automated. If joining up your current tools is enough, workflow automation costs $2,000 one-off ($1,500 for the first 3 clients) and goes live in 2-3 days. When spreadsheets and email threads stop being enough, a [custom system, from $5,000](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/services/), is a web app with a login per person that works on your phone, your spreadsheets moved over, and the first version live in 3-4 weeks, plus 60 days of fixes. It's priced by scope, in writing, before any work starts, it runs in your accounts and you own it.
Either way, it starts with a [free 15-minute call](https://mikeautomations.github.io/call/), and within 48 hours you get a written plan with a fixed price. No deposit and no hourly billing: you pay once it's running and you're happy with it. Optional support is $150 a month.

### Is custom software worth it for a small business?
It can be, when your way of working doesn't fit any product, when you pay for several tools that still leave gaps, or when per-user fees keep rising. If a well-known product already fits most of what you do, off-the-shelf is usually cheaper and simpler.

### How much does custom software cost for a small business?
It depends on scope: how many people need logins, how many tools it connects to and how much data moves over. At Mike Automations a custom system is from $5,000, priced in writing before any work starts. Add hosting and maintenance over the years you'll use it.

### What are the risks of custom software?
Mainly being tied to one developer, and nobody maintaining it after launch. Make sure the code, data and hosting accounts are in your business's name, that you get documentation, and that maintenance is agreed before the build.

### Can I start with off-the-shelf software and move to custom later?
Yes, as long as you can export your data in a usable format. Check the export options before you sign up, so your history can move with you.

## Self Assessment payment reminders for clients: 31 January and 31 July
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/self-assessment-payment-reminders-for-clients/ (2026-11-11)

A Self Assessment payment reminder for clients tells each client how much they owe HMRC, what it's made up of, how to pay and by when. For the 2025 to 2026 tax year, the balancing payment and the first payment on account for 2026 to 2027 are due by 31 January 2027, and the second payment on account by 31 July 2027. Late payment brings interest from the due date and, on the balancing payment, penalties of 5% of the unpaid tax at 30 days, 6 months and 12 months.

Self Assessment payment reminders for clients are a different job from chasing records. Once the return is filed, the practice has done its part, but the client still has to pay, and many don't look at the figure again until the week of the deadline. Some never saw that the bill includes a payment on account. Some find out on 30 January that a first-time Direct Debit takes 5 working days.
This post gives you a reminder schedule for 31 January and 31 July, what each reminder should say, what paying late costs, what to tell clients who can't pay, and an email you can copy. The dates and rules are from GOV.UK, checked in November 2026, for the 2025 to 2026 tax year. If you're still collecting records, start with [when to start chasing Self Assessment clients](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/when-to-start-chasing-self-assessment-clients/). Payment reminders work best once the return itself has been [approved by the client and filed](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/tax-return-approval-chasing/).

### What clients owe and when
GOV.UK says payments on account are each usually half of last year's tax bill, due by midnight on 31 January and 31 July. A client doesn't have to make them if last year's tax was less than £1,000, or if more than 80% of their tax was paid outside Self Assessment, for example through their tax code. That's why two clients with the same bill can owe very different amounts on 31 January.
| Date | What is due | Who it affects |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 30 December 2026 | Online return filed by now if the client wants a bill under £3,000 collected through their tax code | Employees and pensioners who already pay through PAYE |
| 31 January 2027 | Balancing payment for 2025 to 2026, plus the first payment on account for 2026 to 2027 | Everyone with tax to pay |
| 31 July 2027 | Second payment on account for 2026 to 2027 | Clients who make payments on account |

### Watch the weekends in 2027
31 January 2027 is a Sunday and 31 July 2027 is a Saturday. GOV.UK says that if the deadline falls on a weekend or bank holiday, the payment must reach HMRC on the last working day before, unless the client pays by Faster Payments or by debit or corporate credit card. So a client paying by Bacs or Direct Debit needs to plan for Friday 29 January, and allow 3 working days for Bacs or a Direct Debit used before, or 5 working days for a first-time Direct Debit. Your last reminder should go out early enough for that.

### What paying late costs
HMRC charges interest on tax paid late. Since 6 April 2025 the late payment rate has been the Bank of England base rate plus 4%. HMRC's interest rate table shows 7.75% from 9 January 2026 and 8.00% from 24 November 2026.
On top of interest, GOV.UK lists late payment penalties of 5% of the tax unpaid at 30 days, 6 months and 12 months. HMRC's Self Assessment Manual (SAM61250) says these penalties apply to the balancing payment and not to payments on account, but any payment on account still unpaid at the balancing payment date is counted in the balancing payment. So a client who skips the July payment pays interest from 31 July, and if it is still unpaid the following January, it can attract penalties too.

### A reminder schedule you can copy
Send the first message as soon as the client approves the return, while the figure is fresh. After that, remind only the clients who haven't told you they've paid. A client who replies "paid" drops out of the rest.
| When | What to send | Who gets it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| When the return is approved | The amount, how it splits into balancing payment and payment on account, the payment reference and how to pay | Every client with tax to pay |
| Early December | A short reminder of the amount and the date, with a link to set up a payment or Direct Debit | Clients who haven't confirmed payment |
| First working week of January | The amount, the 2027 weekend rule, and how long each way of paying takes | Clients who haven't confirmed payment |
| Around 20 January | A firmer reminder, and a line on what to do if they can't pay in full | Clients who haven't confirmed payment |
| Tuesday 26 January | Last reminder: pay by Friday 29 January unless paying by Faster Payments or card | Clients who haven't confirmed payment |
| Early February | What happens next: interest, the 30-day penalty, and a payment plan if needed | Clients who still haven't confirmed |
| Early July | The second payment on account, the amount and the date | Clients with payments on account |
| Around 20 July | Last reminder: pay by Friday 30 July unless paying by Faster Payments or card | Clients who haven't confirmed payment |

### What every reminder should include
- The exact amount, and what it's made up of. "£2,700: £1,200 for 2025 to 2026 and £1,500 towards 2026 to 2027" stops the "why so much?" reply
- The 11-character payment reference: the client's 10-digit UTR followed by the letter K. GOV.UK warns that a wrong reference can delay a payment or put it against a different bill
- Where to pay: gov.uk/pay-self-assessment-tax-bill, the HMRC app or their online account
- How long each way of paying takes, and the last day for slower methods
- One question: have you paid? A one-word reply is enough to stop the reminders
- What to do if they can't pay in full, so they talk to you before the deadline, not after

### A payment reminder email you can copy
January reminder to a client who hasn't confirmed payment:
```
Subject: Your tax payment of £[amount] is due by 31 January

Hi [first name],

A reminder that your Self Assessment payment of £[amount] is due to HMRC by 31 January 2027. It's made up of:

- £[balancing payment] for the 2025 to 2026 tax year
- £[first payment on account] towards 2026 to 2027

Your payment reference is [UTR]K. Please use it exactly, so HMRC puts the money against the right bill.

You can pay at gov.uk/pay-self-assessment-tax-bill or in the HMRC app. 31 January is a Sunday this year: online banking (Faster Payments) and debit card payments are fine up to the day, but for Bacs or Direct Debit please pay by Friday 29 January, and allow 5 working days if you've never set up a Direct Debit with HMRC before.

Once you've paid, just reply "paid" and we'll stop reminding you.

If you can't pay all of it, reply and tell us before the deadline. HMRC can agree a payment plan, and it's easier to sort out early.

Thanks,
[your name]
[practice name]
```

### Clients who can't pay in full: Time to Pay
GOV.UK says a client who can't pay may be able to set up a payment plan, also called a Time to Pay arrangement, to pay in monthly instalments. Some can set it up online; others contact HMRC. HMRC checks the plan is affordable, and will usually ask for around half of what is left each month after rent, food, bills and fixed outgoings. Clients with savings or assets are expected to use them first. Interest still runs on what's unpaid, so paying faster costs less.
For next year, a client who is up to date can set up a Budget Payment Plan: weekly or monthly Direct Debits towards their next bill, which can be paused for up to 6 months. Clients who struggled in January are the ones to suggest it to in February.
The bigger change is further off. HMRC's Timely payments factsheet (updated October 2026) says that from April 2029, clients who make payments on account will make smaller, more regular payments during the tax year, with the schedule not yet decided. Nothing changes for 31 January 2027 or 31 July 2027.

### Why this is worth automating
Payment reminders are the easy part to forget. The return is filed, the job is closed, and nobody owns the follow-up. A schedule like the one above, for 150 clients, is several hundred emails a year, each with a different amount and reference. That's exactly the kind of repeated, date-driven work a workflow does well, the same way it handles [Self Assessment document chasing](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/self-assessment-document-chasing/) earlier in the season. If clients still owe you records, our [Self Assessment records checklist for clients](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/self-assessment-records-checklist-for-clients/) covers that side.

### How Mike Automations would build this
A workflow can take each client's figures from the approved return, send the first email with the right amount and reference, remind on your dates only those who haven't confirmed, stop when a client replies "paid", and give you a list each morning of who has and hasn't confirmed. Every message uses wording you approved, and you decide who gets a phone call instead.
It starts with a [free 15-minute call](https://mikeautomations.github.io/call/). Within 48 hours you get a written plan with a fixed price and a clear definition of "working". It's built on the tools you already use (your email, your practice software where it allows a connection, and your client list). Live in 2-3 days, [$2,000 one-off](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/pricing/), and you pay once it's running and you're happy with it. To see how this fits with your other seasonal work, try the [plan builder](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/plan/).

### When do clients have to pay their Self Assessment tax?
For the 2025 to 2026 tax year, the balancing payment and the first payment on account for 2026 to 2027 are due by 31 January 2027. The second payment on account is due by 31 July 2027.

### Is there a penalty for paying a payment on account late?
Interest is charged from the due date. HMRC's Self Assessment Manual says late payment penalties apply to the balancing payment, not payments on account, but any payment on account still unpaid at the next balancing payment date is counted in that balancing payment.

### What if 31 January falls on a weekend?
GOV.UK says the payment must reach HMRC on the last working day before, unless the client pays by Faster Payments or by debit or corporate credit card. In 2027, 31 January is a Sunday, so the last working day is Friday 29 January.

## Spreadsheet vs CRM for a small service business: when to switch
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/spreadsheet-vs-crm-small-service-business/ (2026-11-11)

In the spreadsheet vs CRM choice, a small service business should stay on a spreadsheet while one or two people use it and nothing falls through the gaps, and move to a CRM when follow-ups get missed, several people work the same customers, or nobody can say where a customer is up to in under a minute. The switch is about reminders, history and shared access, not size: a spreadsheet holds far more rows than a small business will ever fill.

The spreadsheet vs CRM question usually turns up on a bad day. A quote went unanswered for three weeks, two people phoned the same customer, or someone sorted one column and not the others. The sheet that ran the business for years suddenly feels risky.
This post is for small service businesses (trades, clinics, agencies, practices, cleaning and property firms) deciding whether to leave the spreadsheet. It covers the signs, what actually breaks, what a switch costs in time and money, a decision table, and the steps to move without losing anything.

### What a spreadsheet does well
A spreadsheet is free or nearly free, everyone already knows how to use it, and you can add a column in five seconds. For a business with one owner, a few dozen active customers and a simple path from enquiry to invoice, that flexibility is worth a lot.
Size is rarely the problem. Microsoft's published limit for an Excel worksheet is 1,048,576 rows. If you're thinking about a CRM, it isn't because the sheet is full. It's because the sheet can't do anything on its own. If you're weighing a smarter spreadsheet first, read [Airtable vs Google Sheets](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/airtable-vs-google-sheets-small-business/); if you'd want it set up for you, see [hiring an Airtable expert](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/airtable-consultant-small-business/).

### Seven signs you've outgrown the spreadsheet
One sign on its own is usually fixable inside the spreadsheet. Three or more, especially the first and the last, mean the sheet is now costing you work you never see.
- Follow-ups depend on memory. Nothing tells you that a quote sent 10 days ago hasn't had a reply.
- More than two people edit the list, and you've had a "who changed this?" moment.
- Customer history lives in three places: the sheet, someone's inbox and the job notes on a phone.
- You keep a second sheet (or a colour code) just to track what stage each customer is at.
- Enquiries arrive from a web form, email, phone and WhatsApp, and someone copies them in by hand. Real estate agents add property portal leads to that mix, covered in [lead follow-up for real estate agents](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/real-estate-agent-lead-follow-up/).
- You can't easily answer simple questions, such as how many quotes went out last month and how many were accepted.
- When someone is off sick or leaves, their customers go quiet because nobody knows where things stood.

### What actually breaks first
It's almost never the data. It's the follow-up. A spreadsheet stores what happened; it doesn't remind anyone what should happen next. Renewal dates are a common example: an [IT support firm's renewal calendar](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/msp-client-onboarding-and-renewals/) only works if something warns you in time. What a small service business loses to a spreadsheet is mostly quotes nobody chased and enquiries nobody answered on the day. If that sounds familiar, read [how to reply to new enquiries fast](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/reply-to-new-enquiries-fast/) before you buy anything.
The second thing to break is shared editing. Two people sorting, filtering and typing in the same sheet will eventually overwrite something. Version history helps you find it, but only after someone notices.
The third is history. A CRM keeps each customer's emails, calls and notes on one record. A spreadsheet keeps a "last contact" cell that someone has to remember to update.

### What a CRM changes, and what it doesn't
A [CRM](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/automation-glossary-small-business/) (customer relationship management system) is a shared customer list with stages, tasks and history built in. Common examples are HubSpot, Pipedrive, Zoho CRM and the customer modules inside job management or practice software. Check each vendor's own pricing and feature pages for what's included today, because plans change often. As one example, we looked at [what HubSpot's free CRM can and can't automate](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/hubspot-free-crm-automation-limits/), and at [when to hire help with HubSpot automation](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/hubspot-automation-consultant/). If none of them fits, read [custom software vs off-the-shelf](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/custom-software-vs-off-the-shelf-small-business/) before you build anything.
What a CRM gives you: one record per customer, a pipeline with stages, reminders tied to each customer, and a log of emails and calls. What it doesn't give you is discipline. If nobody moves the stages or logs the calls, a CRM becomes a more expensive spreadsheet. A common way for the move to fail is the team quietly carrying on with the old sheet "just for now".

### Decision table: stay, improve the sheet, or switch
| Your situation | Best next step | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| One person, a few dozen active customers, follow-ups rarely missed | Stay on the spreadsheet | A CRM adds cost and admin for little gain |
| One or two people, follow-ups sometimes missed | Keep the sheet, add automated reminders | Fixes the real problem in days, with no new system to learn |
| Enquiries from several channels copied in by hand | Keep the sheet, automate the capture | Each form, email or message adds a row on its own |
| Three or more people working the same customers | Move to a CRM | Shared records, assigned tasks and history matter more than flexibility |
| You need pipeline reports for a partner, lender or investor | Move to a CRM | Stage and conversion reports are built in |
| Your work doesn't fit any CRM's stages (inspections, renewals, compliance dates) | A small custom system | You stop bending your process to fit someone else's software |

### What switching really costs
The subscription is the cost people compare, but it's rarely the biggest one. Most CRMs charge per user per month, and some have a free tier with limits. Check the vendor's pricing page and work out the yearly figure for your whole team, not just for you.
The bigger costs are time. Cleaning the data before import (duplicates, half-empty rows, "see email" notes) usually takes longer than the import itself. Setting up stages, fields and email connections takes a few days of someone's attention. And expect a few weeks of slower work while the team learns where things are.
Put that next to the cost of staying: the quotes that go unchased each month. If you want to weigh it properly, the [automation cost guide](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/business-automation-cost/) shows a simple way to set hours saved against what you'd pay.

### How to move from a spreadsheet to a CRM in 7 steps
1. Write down your stages first, on paper: for example enquiry, quote sent, accepted, job booked, invoiced, paid. A process map helps if the steps differ by job type.
2. Decide which columns you really use. Anything nobody has filled in for six months doesn't need to move.
3. Clean the sheet: merge duplicate customers, split full names into first and last, put phone numbers in one format, and give every row a stage.
4. Export a copy and keep it, read-only, as your record of how things stood on switch day.
5. Import a test batch of 20 customers, check every field landed in the right place, then import the rest.
6. Connect the inputs (your web form, your inbox, your calendar) so new enquiries create records on their own.
7. Pick a switch day and archive the old sheet that day. Running both "for a while" is how these moves fail.

### The middle option most small businesses skip
Many businesses don't need a CRM yet. They need the spreadsheet to stop relying on memory. A simple workflow can add each new enquiry as a row, remind you when a quote has had no reply after a set number of days, and draft a polite follow-up email for you to approve. The sheet stays the sheet; it just stops forgetting.
If you're not sure which route fits, the free [plan builder](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/plan/) walks you through your workflows and suggests what to automate first.

### How Mike Automations would help
Whichever route fits, it starts with a free 15-minute call about how customers move through your business today. Within 48 hours you get a written plan with a fixed price. If the answer is "keep the sheet and automate the follow-up", it's built on the tools you already use (Google Sheets or Excel, Gmail or Outlook, your web form), live in 2-3 days, $2,000 one-off, and you pay once it's running and you're happy with it. If your work needs its own small system, custom systems start from $5,000. There's no deposit and no hourly billing.

### Is a spreadsheet good enough as a CRM for a small business?
Yes, while one or two people use it and follow-ups don't get missed. Once several people work the same customers, or chasing depends on someone remembering, a CRM or an automated spreadsheet is usually worth it.

### How long does it take to move from a spreadsheet to a CRM?
For a small service business, cleaning the data and setting up stages usually takes a few days of focused work, followed by a few weeks of the team getting used to it. Cleaning the data is normally the slowest part.

### Can I automate follow-ups without a CRM?
Yes. A workflow can watch your spreadsheet, remind you when a quote has had no reply, and draft a follow-up email for you to approve, without changing where your data lives.

## Tax extension email to clients: 4 templates for Form 4868 season
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/tax-extension-client-email-templates/ (2026-11-11)

A tax extension email to clients should say three things plainly: Form 4868 gives them until October 15 to file, it does not give them more time to pay, and any tax owed must be paid by the April due date to avoid the failure-to-pay penalty and interest. For 2026 returns that means paying by April 15, 2027 and filing by October 15, 2027, unless the IRS postpones the dates for their area.

Every tax extension email to clients is fighting the same misunderstanding: "I'm on extension, so I'll pay in October." The IRS is clear that an extension is only for filing. Clients who don't hear that from you in writing find out from a penalty notice.
This post covers what the extension does, how to help clients estimate and pay by April 15, and four email templates you can copy: payment due, extension filed, documents still missing, and a final reminder. It sits alongside our [tax season client email calendar](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/tax-season-client-email-calendar/), which covers the rest of the season.

### What Form 4868 does and doesn't do
The IRS says that requesting an extension by the April filing due date gives an individual until October 15 to file without penalties, and that any tax owed must still be paid by the April date. Its interest page says the same in other words: extensions to file do not extend the date for payment of the tax, and underpayment interest applies even if you file an extension.
For 2026 returns, the IRS early-release draft of Publication 509 (2027) puts the Form 1040 and Form 4868 deadline on Thursday, April 15, 2027, and the extended filing date on Friday, October 15, 2027. It's a draft, so check the final version. The IRS also postpones deadlines for taxpayers in federally declared disaster areas, so check each client's county before you send any date.
Clients who are U.S. citizens or residents and are "out of the country" on the due date get an automatic 2 extra months to file and pay, according to the Form 4868 instructions. Interest still runs from the April date.

### The three ways a client gets an extension
The IRS lists three routes to an automatic extension to October 15:
- Pay all or part of the estimated tax electronically and mark the payment as being for an extension. No separate Form 4868 is needed, and the client gets a confirmation number.
- E-file Form 4868, through tax software or through you as their preparer.
- Mail a paper Form 4868, with or without a payment.

### How to estimate and pay by April 15
Form 4868 asks for an estimate of the total tax liability for the year (line 4), total payments already made (line 5) and the balance due (line 6). The instructions warn that the estimate must be made as accurately as possible with the information available: if the IRS later finds it wasn't reasonable, the extension is void.
For electronic payments, the Form 4868 instructions list IRS Direct Pay, the IRS online account, EFTPS, debit and credit cards, and digital wallets. Direct Pay takes the payment straight from a bank account; for the other options, check the current terms on irs.gov/payments before you recommend one.
If the client can't pay the full balance, the instructions say they still get the extension but should pay as much as they can to limit interest. The IRS also points clients who can't pay in full toward a payment plan.
| What the client pays by April 15 | What happens (per the IRS) |
| --- | --- |
| The full estimated balance | No failure-to-pay penalty or interest, if the estimate holds |
| At least 90% of the total tax, with the rest paid with the return by October 15 | Treated as reasonable cause for the late payment penalty during the extension (Form 4868 instructions); interest still runs on the unpaid part |
| Less than 90%, or nothing | Failure-to-pay penalty of 0.5% of the unpaid tax for each month or part of a month, up to 25%, plus interest from the April date |
| Nothing, and no extension filed | The failure-to-file penalty can apply as well: usually 5% a month, up to 25% |

### Template 1: payment due (send in late March or early April)
Subject: Your [year] taxes: we're filing an extension, payment is still due April 15:
```
Hi [first name],

We don't have everything we need to finish your [year] return by April 15, so we'll file an extension for you. That gives us until October 15 to file.

One important point: the extension is only for filing, not for paying. The IRS expects any tax you owe to be paid by April 15. If it isn't, you may owe a late payment penalty and interest.

Based on what we have so far, our estimate of the balance due is $[amount]. [Or: Please send us [items] by [date] so we can estimate what you owe.]

You can pay online at irs.gov/payments with IRS Direct Pay or your IRS online account. Please send us the confirmation number when you've paid.

Any questions, reply to this email or call [phone].

[your name]
```

### Template 2: extension filed (send on the day you file)
Subject: Your extension is filed: your new deadline is October 15:
```
Hi [first name],

We've filed the extension for your [year] return. The IRS accepted it on [date]. Your return is now due by October 15, [year].

The extension doesn't change your payment date. [We have your payment confirmation for $[amount], thank you.] [Or: We don't have a record of a payment yet. If you owe tax, paying now will limit penalties and interest.]

What we still need to finish your return:

1. [missing item, in plain words]
2. [missing item]

Please upload them by [internal date] here: [upload link]

[your name]
```

### Template 3: documents still missing (send in early summer)
Send this only to clients who haven't sent everything, and list only what's missing for that client. A generic "please send your documents" gets ignored. For the full summer triage, see [extension clients who still haven't sent anything](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/extension-clients-still-havent-sent-anything/).
Subject: Still needed for your [year] return: [N] items:
```
Hi [first name],

Your [year] return is on extension until October 15. We've received [items received], thank you.

We still need:

1. [missing item]
2. [missing item]

If you're waiting on someone else (a K-1 or a corrected 1099, for example), reply and tell us who and roughly when. We'll prepare everything else meanwhile.

Upload link: [upload link]
Our date for your documents: [internal date]

[your name]
```

### Template 4: final reminder (send in early to mid September)
Keep the final reminder factual and make sure your engagement letter supports the date you give. Its job is to put the deadline and the consequence in writing.
Subject: Final reminder: your [year] return is due October 15:
```
Hi [first name],

This is our last reminder before the October 15 deadline. We still don't have:

- [missing item]

If we don't receive it by [final date], we won't be able to prepare and file your return by October 15. Filing late can bring a penalty of 5% of any unpaid tax for each month the return is late, up to 25%.

Please upload today: [upload link]. If something is holding you up, call us on [phone].

[your name]
```

### Send them on a schedule, not from memory
1. In March, list every client likely to need an extension, with the reason (waiting on a K-1, client late, your capacity).
2. Send Template 1 to that list in late March or early April, with your estimate where you have one.
3. File the extensions and send Template 2 the same day, with each client's own missing list.
4. Record each payment confirmation number next to the client's name.
5. Send Template 3 in early summer to anyone not complete, then Template 4 by mid September.
6. Stop each client's emails the day their documents are complete.

### How Mike Automations would build this
Extension season is a list and a calendar: who is on extension, who has paid, what each client still owes you, and which email goes out when. A workflow can keep that list as documents land in your upload folder, send each client their own missing items on your dates, stop the moment a file is complete, and give you a short daily list of who needs a call. You approve the wording once, and every estimate and payment figure stays with you. If you want to see where this fits among your other workflows, the [plan builder](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/plan/) maps it out.
It starts with a free 15-minute call. Within 48 hours you get a written plan with a fixed price. It's built on the tools you already use (Gmail or Outlook, Google Drive or Dropbox, your tax software's client list where it allows a connection), live in 2-3 days, $2,000 one-off, and you pay once it's running and you're happy with it.

### Does Form 4868 give my client more time to pay?
No. The IRS says the extension is only for filing. Tax owed is still due by the April due date (April 15, 2027 for 2026 returns), and interest and the failure-to-pay penalty run from then.

### Does my client need to file Form 4868 if they pay electronically?
Not if they mark the electronic payment as being for an extension. The IRS processes the extension automatically and gives a confirmation number. Paying part or all of the estimated tax this way is enough.

### What if my client can't pay the full amount by April 15?
They still get the extension. The Form 4868 instructions say to pay as much as they can to limit interest, and the IRS offers payment plans for the rest. If at least 90% of the total tax is paid by April 15 and the rest with the return, the late payment penalty is treated as having reasonable cause.

## Karbon and TaxDome reminders: what they do, and what an add-on can add
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/portal-reminders-add-on-karbon-taxdome/ (2026-11-11)

Karbon and TaxDome reminders already email clients on a schedule until they complete a request, so most firms don't need a second reminder tool. What an add-on can do is handle the work around the portal: tell a person when the automatic reminders have run out, send a personal follow-up, file documents that arrive by email, and give the partner one list of who is still missing what.

Karbon and TaxDome reminders are one of the main reasons firms buy a practice platform. You set a request, set a schedule, and the software chases the client for you. So why do so many firms on these platforms still spend January writing chasing emails by hand?
This post looks at what each platform's built-in reminders actually do, using each vendor's own help documentation (we checked it on 11 November 2026, and give the date each article was last updated). Then it covers where work tends to be left over, and what a small workflow can do around the portal without replacing it. If you're still deciding whether you need a platform at all, read [practice software vs simple automation](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/practice-software-vs-simple-automation-small-practice/) first.

### What Karbon's client request reminders do
In Karbon, the things you ask a client for are called Client Requests. Karbon's help article "Send client requests" (last updated 17 October 2024) says requests go to the client by email, and can be sent straight away or scheduled to send a set number of days before or after a work item's start date. They can only go to people saved as a contact.
The same article describes three reminder settings, and two rules about when reminders stop:
- Gentle: seven days before the due date, on the due date, then every day after it's overdue.
- Urgent: every day.
- Custom: you choose how often.
- Reminders stop after the fifth one for a single request. Karbon says this is to reduce the chance of repeated emails being flagged as spam. Resending the request restarts the count.
- Once all the requests in a section are complete, no more reminders go out.

### How clients open a Karbon request
Karbon's "Overview of client requests" (updated 10 May 2023) notes that a request needs a due date for reminders to work, and that files the client uploads land on the work item automatically. Clients open requests through a magic link in the email. Karbon's "Client request settings and security" article (updated 30 August 2023) says the link is tied to the device it was first opened on, a new device needs a new link sent to the client's email address, and a full portal login is available on the Business and Enterprise plans.
Karbon's own help centre also accepts that five reminders can run out. Its article "Can I be notified if a client isn't responding" (updated 1 August 2022) suggests spacing the five reminders across the time you have, then using an automator to change the work status to "Resend Client Requests" after the last one, so someone sees it on the board.

### What TaxDome's reminders do
TaxDome's help article "Reminders explained" (help.taxdome.com, no update date shown on the page when we read it on 11 November 2026) says reminders work on every client-facing item that needs an action: organizers, client requests, proposals, invoices, signature requests, approvals and chat messages.
- You can schedule automatic reminders, send a manual one at any time, and set defaults on a template so every item created from it gets the same schedule.
- If you set reminders inside a pipeline automation, every item that automation sends inherits the same schedule.
- Reminders go to clients only: the contacts on the account who have the Notify option switched on.
- The reminder email looks like the original notification, flagged as a reminder, and the to-do moves to the top of the client's list in the portal and mobile app.
- Reminders stop when the client completes the action, when the set number of reminders is reached, or when another stop condition applies. TaxDome's separate "Reminders reference" lists the defaults for each type of item, so check it before you rely on a number.

### Where the work is left over
Read the documentation closely and the gaps aren't bugs. They come from what reminders are designed to do: send the same email to the client until the client acts. The jobs that fall outside that are the ones firms still do by hand.
| Situation | What the platform does (per its docs) | What's left for your team |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Reminders run out | Karbon stops after five; TaxDome stops when the set count is reached | Noticing it, and deciding who calls the client |
| Client still hasn't acted | Repeats the same notification email | A personal message from the person the client knows |
| Client emails documents instead | Not covered by request reminders | Saving attachments to the right client and ticking the request off |
| Contact isn't set up (no contact record, or Notify switched off) | Nothing is sent to that person | Spotting that the client was never reminded at all |
| Partner wants one view across all clients | Status sits on each work item or job | Pulling a weekly list of who is still missing what |

### What a small add-on can do around the portal
An add-on here means a small workflow that runs next to your portal, not a second portal. Clients keep using the platform they already know. The workflow picks up the jobs in the right-hand column above.
1. Watch for requests where the last automatic reminder has gone out and nothing has come back.
2. Send one short follow-up from the client manager's own mailbox, naming the exact items, with the portal link. Clients tend to answer a person faster than a system email.
3. If there's still no reply a few days later, add the client to a call list for that person, with the phone number and what's missing.
4. Pick up documents that clients email instead, save them to the right client folder, and tell the team which request they belong to.
5. Every Monday, send the partner one list: client, what's still missing, how many reminders have gone, and who owns the follow-up.

### The follow-up email after the reminders run out
This is the one message worth sending from a real person. Keep it short and specific, and keep the portal link in it so the client doesn't start emailing files.
Personal follow-up after the last automatic reminder:
```
Subject: Quick one about your [year] [accounts / tax return]

Hi [first name],

I can see we're still waiting for a few things from you:

- [item 1]
- [item 2]

You can upload them here, it takes a couple of minutes: [portal link]

If something is holding this up, or you'd rather go through it on the phone, just reply with a good time and I'll call you.

We need these by [date] to [file on time / finish your accounts].

Thanks,
[name]
```

### What to check before you add anything
First, make sure you're using what you already pay for. It's easy to switch reminders on for some templates and not others, or to leave requests without a due date, which in Karbon means reminders never start. If clients aren't opening the portal in the first place, fix that before you automate the chasing: our guide on [getting clients to use your client portal](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/get-clients-to-use-your-client-portal/) covers the rollout.
- Do all your recurring templates have reminders on, and do all requests have due dates?
- Is every client contact set up to receive notifications?
- Does your plan include the features you're counting on? Karbon, for example, ties the full client login to its Business and Enterprise plans.
- Does your portal allow a connection (an API or an integration) so a workflow can read request status? If not, a simpler version can work from the notification emails instead.
- If you want to add text messages, have you got the client's consent and a clear rule on what never goes by text? See [texting clients for documents](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/text-or-whatsapp-clients-for-documents/).

### How Mike Automations would build this
The aim is to leave your portal exactly where it is and pick up only the jobs it doesn't do. The workflow runs in your own accounts, using your portal where it allows a connection, your Gmail or Outlook, and your shared drive. A person in your firm still decides who gets a call and what is said.

It's live in 2-3 days, costs [$2,000 one-off](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/pricing/), and you pay once it's running and you're happy with it. Want to see which other workflows might be worth it first? Try the [plan builder](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/plan/).

### Does Karbon send automatic reminders to clients?
Yes. Karbon's help centre describes gentle, urgent and custom reminder schedules for Client Requests. Reminders need a due date, and they stop after the fifth reminder for a single request unless you resend it.

### What can TaxDome send reminders for?
TaxDome's help centre lists organizers, client requests, proposals, invoices, signature requests, approvals and chat messages. Reminders can be set per item, on a template, or inside a pipeline automation.

### Do I need to replace Karbon or TaxDome to automate chasing?
No. The built-in reminders cover the routine emails. A small workflow can run alongside them to flag clients whose reminders have run out, send a personal follow-up, and file emailed documents.

### Why do clients ignore portal reminders?
Repeated system emails are easy to ignore, and Karbon itself caps reminders partly because identical emails can be flagged as spam. A short message from the person the client knows, naming the exact items, is harder to overlook.

## QuickBooks Online client reminders: what's built in, and when a workflow helps
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/quickbooks-client-reminders/ (2026-11-11)

QuickBooks Online client reminders cover two things natively: automatic invoice reminders (up to three per invoice, scheduled up to 90 days before or after the due date) and Requests, which ask a client for details or files about a specific transaction. Anything else a firm chases, such as W-2s, 1099 forms, organizers or year-end documents, needs a separate process, and that's where a small workflow adds value.

QuickBooks Online client reminders are often the first thing a bookkeeper or small CPA firm looks at when chasing starts eating the week. The software already emails your clients, so can't it chase them for everything?
Partly. This post sets out what QuickBooks Online does on its own, using Intuit's own help articles (checked November 11, 2026, with the date each was last updated), and then where a workflow built around it is worth paying for. It's written for US firms, but the invoice reminder settings are much the same in other countries' versions.

### Automatic invoice reminders
Intuit's article "Send invoice reminders automatically or manually in QuickBooks Online" (US, updated October 5, 2026) describes the built-in reminder for unpaid invoices. This is what you use to chase your own fees, or what your clients use to chase their customers.
1. Go to Settings, then Account and settings, then the Sales tab.
2. In the Reminders section, select Edit and turn on Automatic invoice reminders.
3. Turn on Reminder 1 and choose how many days before or after the due date it goes out.
4. Edit the subject line, greeting and message, then save. Add a second and third reminder if you want them.

### The rules worth knowing
The same article sets a few limits that catch people out:
- Reminders can be scheduled up to 90 days before or after the invoice due date.
- You get up to three automatic reminders per invoice.
- QuickBooks only reminds on unpaid invoices that match your settings, and only on invoices you've already emailed.
- You can also send a one-off reminder by hand: Sales & Get Paid, then Invoices, find the invoice, open the Receive payment dropdown and select Send reminder.

### Workflows in QuickBooks Online Advanced
If you or your client is on QuickBooks Online Advanced, Intuit's article on workflows (updated August 5, 2026) says workflows can automate reviewing invoices, collecting payments and approving transactions, sending a reminder to your team or your customers when conditions are met. Pay bill reminders and unsent invoice reminders are set up by default for new Advanced companies, and you can turn them off under My workflows. The invoice reminder article also points Advanced users to workflows for invoice reminders. These workflows are for Advanced (and Intuit Enterprise Suite) only.

### Requests: asking clients about transactions
The other built-in way to chase a client is Requests. Intuit's article "Request information about a transaction" (US, updated October 30, 2026) describes it like this:
- You ask for details and files about a specific transaction, for example the receipt behind a card payment.
- The person gets an email with a link. Clients with a QuickBooks sign-in go to the Client Portal or sign in to their Intuit Account. Other people need to create or sign in to a free Intuit Account the first time.
- The first request for a company needs a one-time consent from that company's QuickBooks admin.
- Clients get a weekly reminder unless you send them a notification through the Inbox.
- Requests are available on all QuickBooks Online plans except QuickBooks Solopreneur.

### What QuickBooks doesn't chase for you
Between invoice reminders and Requests, QuickBooks covers money owed and questions about transactions already in the books. Most of what a firm chases in tax season is neither. This table is a quick way to see which jobs need something else.
| What you're chasing | Built into QuickBooks Online? | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Your own unpaid fees | Yes: automatic invoice reminders | Up to three reminders, only on invoices already emailed |
| A receipt or detail for a bank transaction | Yes: Requests | Weekly reminder; the client may need an Intuit Account |
| W-2s, 1099s, 1098s and other tax forms | No | These aren't transactions in the client's books |
| W-9s from your client's contractors | No | Needed before the 1099 run, often from people who don't use QuickBooks |
| Tax organizers and signed engagement letters | No | Usually handled by email, e-signature or a portal |
| Month-end: "send all receipts and statements" | Partly | Requests are per transaction, not per month |

### When a workflow adds value
A workflow is worth it when the same chase happens every month or every season, for many clients, and QuickBooks only covers part of it. Our page on [QuickBooks Online automation services](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/quickbooks-online-automation-services/) covers what to hire help for. Some examples, for illustration:
- Monthly bookkeeping clients: on the 3rd, each client gets one email listing their uncategorized transactions that still need a receipt, instead of one request per transaction. A reminder goes on the 8th, and the bookkeeper sees who hasn't replied on the 10th.
- Tax season: each client gets a personal list of documents built from last year's return, with an upload link, then reminders until each item arrives. See our [1099 season checklist](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/1099-season-checklist-bookkeepers/) for what to ask for and when.
- Your own fees: QuickBooks sends the reminders, and the workflow adds the step it doesn't take, such as a heads-up to the partner when a client is 30 days late so someone calls. Our page on [invoice payment reminders](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/invoice-payment-reminders/) covers that pattern.
- Clients who don't use QuickBooks: requests go by email with an upload link, so nobody has to create an Intuit Account just to send you a PDF.

### A monthly receipts email you can copy
If you send one email per client instead of one request per transaction, keep it short and put the list in it. Clients reply faster when they can see exactly what's missing.
Monthly missing receipts email:
```
Subject: [Month] receipts we still need

Hi [first name],

We're closing your books for [month]. These transactions still need a receipt or a quick note:

- [date], [payee], $[amount]
- [date], [payee], $[amount]

You can upload receipts here: [upload link]. For anything without a receipt, just reply with one line on what it was for.

If we have everything by [date], your [month] reports will be ready by [date].

Thanks,
[name]
```

QuickBooks keeps sending its own invoice reminders. The workflow handles the chasing it doesn't cover, and a person on your team still approves anything that goes to a client in a new way.

### Can QuickBooks Online send automatic payment reminders?
Yes. Turn them on in Settings, Account and settings, Sales, Reminders. You can set up to three reminders per invoice, up to 90 days before or after the due date, and they only go out for unpaid invoices you've already emailed.

## Document requests without a client portal: four options that work
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/document-requests-without-a-portal/ (2026-11-11)

You can handle document requests without a client portal by combining a dedicated email-in address, upload links (such as a Dropbox or OneDrive file request) for sensitive files, and e-signature for anything that needs signing. Clients don't need a login for any of these, so more of them reply. The trade-off is that you have to add the tracking and reminders yourself, which a small workflow can do.

Document requests without a client portal are how most small firms still work, and plenty of them prefer it. A portal is one more login for a client who sends you documents twice a year. Many of them forget the password and email the files anyway.
This post compares four ways to collect client documents without a portal: email-in, upload links, shared folders and e-signature. It covers what each one needs from the client, the security basics in the UK and US, and how to add the tracking a portal would give you. Translation agencies face the same file intake problem: see [translation quotes and file intake](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/translation-agency-quotes-and-file-intake/).

### Option 1: email-in to one address
Clients send documents to one address, such as documents@yourfirm, instead of to whoever they last spoke to. Rules in your mailbox then sort what arrives. Gmail's help centre, for example, says filters can send mail to a label, archive, star or forward it automatically.
It's the easiest option for clients, because they already know how to email. The weak spots are security (an unprotected attachment sits in two mailboxes) and sorting (a scan called "IMG_4031.jpg" doesn't say which client or which year it's for). Use it for low-risk items and replies, not for passports or full bank statements.

### Option 2: upload links
An upload link opens a page where the client drops files straight into a folder you control. They can't see what else is in it. Check the details for the tool you already pay for:
- Dropbox file requests: Dropbox's help article (updated 15 May 2025) says anyone can send you a file, whether they have a Dropbox account or not, and the destination folder is private by default. Basic, Plus and Family plans accept files up to 2 GB; deadlines need a higher-tier plan.
- OneDrive and SharePoint file requests: Microsoft's admin guide (updated 7 May 2026) says people who upload can't view, edit, delete or download files in the folder, or see who else uploaded. It only works on OneDrive for work or school, and your admin must allow "Anyone" links. It isn't available on personal OneDrive.
- Google Forms file upload: Google's help says respondents must sign in to a Google Account to answer a file upload question, so it isn't login-free for clients who don't use Google.

### Option 3: a shared folder per client
A shared folder in Google Drive, OneDrive or Dropbox gives the client one place to add files and see what they've already sent. It suits clients who send documents every month, such as bookkeeping clients, and who already use that service.
The risks are the ones you'd expect: the client can usually see and sometimes delete what's in the folder, links get forwarded, and folders stay shared long after the engagement ends. Share with the client's email address rather than an open link, and review who has access at least once a year.

### Option 4: e-signature for anything that needs signing
Engagement letters, authorisations and anything else that needs a signature don't need a portal either. An e-signature tool emails the client a link, they sign on their phone, and you get the signed copy back.
In the US, the ESIGN Act (15 U.S.C. 7001(a)) says a signature or contract can't be denied legal effect solely because it's electronic. In England and Wales, the Law Commission confirmed in its 2019 report, published on gov.uk, that electronic signatures can be used to execute documents. Some documents have special rules, so check with your professional body if you're unsure.

### The four options compared
| Option | Client needs a login? | Best for | Watch out for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Email-in address | No | Low-risk documents, quick replies | Unprotected attachments; unclear file names |
| Upload link (file request) | No (Dropbox, OneDrive work or school) | ID, bank statements, payslips, tax forms | Admin settings on OneDrive; plan limits on Dropbox |
| Shared folder per client | Usually yes, with that service | Monthly bookkeeping clients | Access that never gets removed |
| E-signature | No | Engagement letters, authorisations | Documents with special signing rules |

### Security basics, UK and US
UK: ICAEW's helpsheet on communicating safely with clients under UK GDPR says sending personal data in an unprotected email or attachment would be ill-advised. It suggests encrypted, password-protected attachments may suit many firms, with the password sent another way (by phone or text), and describes a secure file-sharing portal as generally the most secure option.
US: the FTC's guide to the Safeguards Rule (December 2024) lists tax preparation firms among the businesses it covers. It says to encrypt customer information on your system and in transit, and to use multi-factor authentication for anyone accessing customer information.
- Ask for sensitive items (ID, bank statements, payslips, tax forms) by upload link, not as email attachments. Property managers screening tenants face the same issue, covered in [collecting rental application documents](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/rental-application-document-collection/).
- Switch on multi-factor authentication for the mailbox and the storage account.
- When a client emails something sensitive, don't just hit reply with the attachment still in the thread. ICAEW makes the same point: move it to secure storage and remind the client of the upload link.
- Name and file uploads by client and tax year as they arrive.
- Remove access to shared folders and expire upload links when the work is done.

### A document request email you can copy
Whatever mix you use, the request itself matters most. Name each item, give one link, and say what happens next.
Document request without a portal:
```
Subject: Documents we need for your [year] [tax return / accounts]

Hi [first name],

To get started on your [year] [tax return / accounts], we need:

- [item 1]
- [item 2]
- [item 3]

Please upload them here: [upload link]. You don't need an account or a password.

Please don't email bank statements or ID. If you can't use the link, reply and we'll find another way.

If we have everything by [date], we'll [file / have your draft ready] by [date].

Thanks,
[name]
```

### What a portal gives you that you'll need to add
The real gap without a portal isn't collecting files. It's knowing who has sent what. A portal tracks each request and reminds the client. Without one, someone has to tick items off a list and write chasing emails by hand. That's the part to automate.
1. Keep one list per client of what you asked for and what has arrived.
2. When a file lands in the upload folder or the email-in address, rename it, file it, and tick it off.
3. Send reminders that list only what's still missing, so a client who has sent nine of ten items isn't asked for all ten again.
4. Give the team one daily view of who has sent everything, who has sent part, and who has sent nothing.

### How Mike Automations would build this
The workflow runs on the tools you already have: your [Gmail](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/gmail-automation-for-accountants/) or [Outlook](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/outlook-automation-for-accountants/), Dropbox, OneDrive or Google Drive, and the e-signature tool you use now. Clients get a link, not a login. It follows the same steps as any document collection workflow, and a person in your firm still checks what comes in.
It starts with a [free 15-minute call](https://mikeautomations.github.io/call/). Within 48 hours you get a written plan with a fixed price. It's live in 2-3 days, costs [$2,000 one-off](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/pricing/), and you pay once it's running and you're happy with it. To see what else could be automated in your practice, try the [plan builder](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/plan/).

### What's the best alternative to a client portal for document requests?
For most small firms, an upload link for sensitive files (such as a Dropbox file request, or a OneDrive file request on a work or school account), email for low-risk items, and e-signature for anything that needs signing. Add a simple tracker and reminders so you know who has sent what.

### Can clients upload documents without creating an account?
Yes, with some tools. Dropbox says anyone can send a file to a file request whether they have a Dropbox account or not. OneDrive file requests work the same way on work or school accounts if your admin allows Anyone links. Google Forms file uploads need a Google sign-in.

### Is it safe for clients to email tax documents?
It's the weakest option. ICAEW calls unprotected email for personal data ill-advised, and in the US the FTC Safeguards Rule expects tax preparers to encrypt customer information in transit. Use an upload link for anything sensitive.

### Are e-signatures legally valid for engagement letters?
Generally yes. In the US the ESIGN Act gives electronic signatures legal effect, and in England and Wales the Law Commission confirmed in 2019 that electronic signatures can be used to execute documents. Check special cases with your professional body.

## Gmail automation for accountants: what Gmail does and where it stops
Source: https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/gmail-automation-for-accountants/ (2026-11-11)

Gmail automation for accountants starts with what Gmail already does: filters that label, archive, forward or auto-reply with a saved template, scheduled send, and an out-of-office responder, plus Gemini drafting and summaries on eligible Google Workspace plans. Gmail stops at anything that needs memory: it can't track which client has sent which document, or send a reminder because nobody replied. That's where a workflow connected to your spreadsheet or practice software adds value.

Gmail automation for accountants is worth doing in two layers. First, switch on what Gmail and Google Workspace already include. It costs nothing extra and takes an afternoon. Second, find the jobs Gmail can't do on its own, and decide whether those are worth a proper workflow. Some of those jobs can be scripted inside your Google account; see [what Google Apps Script can do for a small business](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/google-apps-script-for-small-business/).
This post is for small accounting and bookkeeping practices in the UK and the US that run on Gmail. Every feature below was checked on Google's own help pages on 11 November 2026. Google changes menus and plans often, so check again before you rely on a detail.

### What Gmail can do on its own
- Filters. Google's Gmail Help says a filter can send matching email to a label, or archive, delete, star or automatically forward it. You build one from the search options, then click Create filter. Forwarding only affects new messages.
- Labels. Gmail's version of folders, except one email can carry several. Labels such as Clients/Smith Ltd or Records received are what filters apply.
- Templates. Turn them on under Settings, See all settings, Advanced. You can then save a draft as a template and insert it into any email. Google says templates can only be turned on and used from Gmail on a computer.
- Auto-reply with a template. Gmail Help explains that a filter can tick Send template, so every email matching your criteria gets the same saved reply.
- Scheduled send. Write an email now and send it later. Gmail Help says you can have up to 100 scheduled emails at once.
- Vacation responder. The out-of-office reply. Google says that in most cases it's only sent to people the first time they message you.

### Gemini in Gmail: what it adds, and on which plans
Google's help page on Gemini features in Gmail (checked 11 November 2026) lists Help me write, Suggested Replies, AI Overview conversation summaries and Summarize and draft emails, among others. Help me write and the thread summaries work on eligible Google Workspace plans in English and several other languages, globally. Some features are US-only for now, such as AI Inbox and Help me schedule.
Google also offers Workspace Studio, which builds simple automated "flows" across Gmail, Drive, Sheets and Forms, with Gemini for the AI steps. Its help page says work accounts need an eligible edition (Business Starter, Standard and Plus are listed) and that your Google Workspace admin must enable Gemini on the account. It's new, so test it on a small job first.
For a practice, these are drafting and summarising aids. They help with the reply in front of you. They don't know which documents a client still owes you, and a person should read anything AI drafts before it goes to a client.

### Gmail on its own vs a workflow
| Practice task | Gmail on its own | Where a workflow adds value |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sort incoming client email | Filters label it by sender or subject | Matches the email to the client record and the job it belongs to |
| Acknowledge documents received | A filter with Send template sends the same reply to everyone | Replies with what's still missing for that client |
| Save attachments | Not done by Gmail: someone drags them to Drive by hand | Saves each file to the client's folder for the right tax year |
| Chase missing records | Scheduled send, one email at a time | Reminders on a schedule that stop the moment the item arrives |
| Know who hasn't replied | Search, for example label:records-requested older_than:7d | A daily list of clients with open items and how long they've been open |
| Draft replies | Templates, or Gemini on eligible plans | Drafts that pull in the client's name, deadline and missing items for a person to approve |
| Deadline reminders | Not built in | Reminders driven by each client's dates in your sheet or practice software |

### Five Gmail filters worth setting up today
These use Gmail's own search operators, which Google lists on its search operators help page. Paste each line into the search box, check the results, then click Create filter. Change the words to match how your clients actually write.
1. Client documents in: has:attachment (filename:pdf OR filename:jpg) -from:me. Apply the label Docs to file, so nothing with an attachment gets buried.
2. Year-end and payroll records: subject:(P60 OR P11D OR W-2 OR 1099 OR "bank statement"). Apply the label Records and star it.
3. Newsletters and software notices: list:(your software's mailing address). Skip the inbox and apply a Reading label.
4. Anything from a key client's domain: from:(@clientdomain.co.uk). Apply the client's label and mark it important.
5. New enquiries from your website form: from:(your form's sending address). Apply New enquiry, and tick Send template to send a short acknowledgement.

### A template acknowledgement you can copy
Keep it honest: it promises a personal reply, not an answer. A filter sends the same text to everyone, so it can't mention what a particular client has or hasn't sent. For chasing wording that does, see these [document chasing email templates](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/document-chasing-email-templates/).
Saved Gmail template, sent by the "New enquiry" filter:
```
Subject: Thanks, we've got your message

Hi,

Thanks for getting in touch with [practice name]. This is a quick note to say your message has arrived. One of the team will reply personally within [one working day].

If it's about a deadline in the next few days, please say so in a reply to this email and we'll look at it first.

Best wishes,
[name]
[practice name]
```

### Where Gmail stops for a practice
Those gaps are where a workflow earns its keep. It reads your client list, sends each client their own request, saves what arrives, ticks it off and reminds only the people with open items. Gmail stays the place you and your clients write to each other. If you have no portal, [document requests without a portal](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/document-requests-without-a-portal/) compares the other routes. Tools such as Zapier, Make and n8n connect Gmail to the rest; [Zapier vs Make vs n8n](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/blog/zapier-vs-make-vs-n8n/) compares them. If you'd like to see which steps would run on their own in your practice, the [plan builder](https://mikeautomations.github.io/en/plan/) sketches one in a couple of minutes.
- It has no memory of the job. Gmail knows the email arrived. It doesn't know that Mrs Patel has sent her P60 but not her rental figures.
- Filters only react to email coming in. Nothing in Gmail sends a reminder because a client hasn't replied in a week.
- Attachments stay in the inbox until someone files them.
- Templates are fixed text. Every client gets the same words, whatever they still owe you.
- It doesn't talk to your spreadsheet, Xero, QuickBooks or practice software on its own.
